In this study, we examine a newly identified state of matter, termed "black stars within a cavity," which results from integrating Hawking's original idea of a universe confined by a cavity with Cvetič and Zhang's work on black holes in a cavity under a Born-Infeld framework. We demonstrate that the small/large black/white hole distinction remains valid in a spacetime featuring a horizon and a cavity. Furthermore, we find that this system allows for the existence of black stars in the presence of a black hole. Additionally, we show that a Hawking–Page phase transition can occur for these black stars, though not always, as the cavity's radius influences this existence. Specifically, there exists a critical radius for the cavity; when the actual cavity radius exceeds this critical value, the Hawking–Page phase transition ceases to occur for the black stars. Finally, we analyze the thermodynamics of these black stars within a cavity, revealing that they exhibit a first-order phase transition. We also identify a maximum temperature for the black stars, noting that this temperature is significantly higher than that of an isolated black star and approaches the temperature of a cavity filled with radiation. Additionally, we observe that the temperature of a small black star within a cavity is influenced by the cavity's radius, whereas the temperature of a large black star remains unaffected by it. This study addresses a single-label noisy ranking task in which data cannot be directly retrieved for model training. To resolve this, we propose a method that re-collects training samples by constructing a group by sampling an original sample, searching for its neighbors, and aggregating them into a set. This work also revisits and justifies the use of group loss for ranking with label noise. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective for single-label ranking under noisy label conditions. Furthermore, the method requires no hyperparameter tuning, resulting in high performance with minimal effort. The paper also provides theoretical justification for the effectiveness of group loss in both classification and ranking scenarios. Finally, we extend the approach to multi-label ranking, showing through experiments that it also yields good results in that context. Theoretically, we prove that group loss is effective for multi-label ranking with label noise, consistent with its performance in the single-label case. Overall, this work is theoretically sound, practically effective, and simple to implement. The code is accessible at https://github.

Label scarcity remains a critical hurdle for graph classification tasks, where acquiring annotated data is both difficult and expensive. While data augmentation techniques have proven effective for boosting graph neural network performance under label limitations, their application is often constrained. This paper introduces a novel pseudo-tagging module designed to generate insightful structural labels. Implemented via a lightweight and versatile Graph Isomorphism Network, this module enhances graph representation learning by integrating data augmentation with pseudo-tagging in a straightforward and interpretable manner. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing baselines across various graph datasets. Furthermore, the source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1992/ITGT. The accompanying code, along with pre-trained models and dataset configurations, is also provided in our supplementary materials. Finally, our method is available for use within our testbed for graph data augmentation. The AWAKE experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider aims to demonstrate the viability of using proton-driven betatron acceleration for intense electron beams. This concept is intended to pave the way for proton-driven cavity acceleration, which could enable stable, high-energy beam propagation for particle physics research. To validate this approach, acceleration demonstrations are being conducted in Intense Low-repetition Rate Heavy Ion Colliders (L3-CERs), such as AWAKE, which feature high beam currents and low repetition rates. The initial proof-of-principle phase, AWAKE Run 1, focused on studying betatron acceleration in electron beams, whereas future Runs 2 and 3 will directly accelerate electrons to MeV-level energies. This study examines the feasibility of betatron acceleration during Run 2 by simulating electron propagation through a magnetic field and analyzing the resulting electromagnetic radiation. The simulations indicate that, with appropriate magnetic field strengths, non-negligible numbers of high-energy photons can be generated. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these simulations align with the diagnostic capabilities available at AWAKE. Consequently, it is concluded that measuring betatron emission during electron propagation in an L3-CER is feasible, providing proof-of-principle data that could inform the design of Run 2 and 3. Additionally, the impact of collective effects on electron beam propagation and radiation emission is analyzed, revealing that such effects are negligible for the anticipated electron beams. Ultimately, this work establishes the proof-of-principle methodology for simulating and analyzing betatron emission, offering a foundation for planning future experiments to study betatron-accelerated electron beams. The simulation code employed in this study is publicly accessible.

This work introduces a class of expandable, precise algorithms for distributed differential privacy (DDP) decision tree learning. Our approach employs the split finding algorithm by Balle et al. (2021) and introduces the novel concept of "early termination" to substantially lower both computational complexity and communication overhead. We offer a formal guarantee of $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-privacy and experimentally validate our methods against state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we establish a new benchmark for DDP decision tree learning, supporting our claim that these benchmark algorithms are precisely solvable. Additionally, our solutions for vertical and horizontal learning scenarios can be executed in parallel, further enhancing efficiency. Finally, we refine existing algorithms for private clustering and classification to minimize complexity and communication costs. In summary, this research delivers practical and precise decision tree learning algorithms for distributed differential privacy. Code is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchlaeffer/PDTL. This paper introduces a variational approach utilizing Bregman proximal gradient methods to analyze the distance between a probability distribution $q$ and $p$, defined by $\eta(q,p) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q^{k+1}(1-p)^{k+1} / (k+1)$. We demonstrate that minimizing this Rényi distance over probability distributions can be recast as a convex optimization problem using the Bregman divergence associated with the entropy $H_4(q) = \sum_k q_k \log^4 q_k$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an implicit proximal operator for $H_4$, enabling the implementation of a proximal gradient method. Finally, we outline how regularization techniques can be incorporated into both formulations. Our numerical experiments indicate that these methods are highly effective in learning approximate posterior distributions. Additionally, we highlight that the second approach extends naturally to scenarios involving unnormalized densities. However, we also identify scenarios where this extension fails, specifically when applying it to Bayesian Computed Tomography. These limitations arise because $H_4$ is not lower semicontinuous under weak topologies, and we provide a counterexample to illustrate this issue. To address this, we propose a modified approach for 1-D cases that incorporates Tikhonov regularization to ensure the lower semicontinuity of $H_4$. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this method in Bayesian Computed Tomography. Throughout this work, we emphasize the significant role of the geometric mean in our methodology. Indeed, the Bayes estimator derived from the conjugate prior of the exponential distribution yields the geometric mean, and it is well-established that the geometric mean effectively captures the behavior of a distribution's tail. This insight helps explain why the proposed methods yield excellent results. Additionally, we show that the second approach can be generalized to scenarios involving infinite sums. However, we also note scenarios where this generalization is problematic, such as in Bayesian Computed Tomography, where the sum must be truncated. We discuss the challenges arising from this truncation and explore potential solutions. Finally, we illustrate how these issues can be mitigated by modifying the approach for the 1-D case, which is applicable to 1-D problems including Bayesian Computed Tomography. Chain Event Networks (CENs) extend discrete choice models to incorporate multi-attractor transition dynamics, making them valuable for diverse applications like travel behavior research. However, the decision to model an attribute using a CEN versus a discrete choice framework is not always straightforward. This study introduces a Bayesian framework that simultaneously estimates whether a specific attribute should be modeled as a CEN and its corresponding parameters. We develop a novel CEN link function, optimize Bayesian Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimators, and propose a two-step estimation method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be adapted to select between alternative CEN formulations and potentially integrate with maximum likelihood estimators. A simulation study indicates that the proposed selection link performs robustly, accurately recovering both the selection and parameter values of the CENs. Finally, we apply this methodology to a joint mode and route selection dataset to validate its effectiveness in empirical settings. Overall, the study demonstrates that selection links function as efficient regularizers, producing well-constrained CEN models where appropriate while maintaining traditional discrete choice model specifications when necessary. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKlauer/CEN-Selection. The selection link is implemented in PyCEM (Klauer et al., 2021), a Python package for discrete choice and transition modeling. PyCEM is also available on CRAN as a Python interface for RCEM (Böckenholt and Klauer, 2020), an R package for the same purpose. Additionally, the package includes a selection link implementation. The examples in this paper were generated using PyCEM version 0.1.1. The package is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. We introduce a new dynamical framework that integrates Hamiltonian mechanics with a Tikhonov regularization term to address ill-posed problems. This model accounts for energy dissipation through viscous friction and includes a progressively diminishing regularization parameter $\beta(t)$ that evolves to its limit value $\beta_0=0$. The equations of motion are derived using a first-order Hamiltonian comprising the regularization energy and Tikhonov regularization components. We demonstrate the asymptotic stability of the equilibrium corresponding to the minimal norm solution by analyzing the time derivative of the squared norm of the state variable. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the trajectory toward the origin. Additional results regarding the convergence of trajectories to the minimal norm solution are also provided, encompassing both weak and strong topologies. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the behavior of this proposed model. These simulations compare our approach to other established Hamiltonian and gradient-based systems for solving ill-posed problems, highlighting the superior numerical performance of the Hamiltonian model with regularization. Specifically, our system exhibits robust convergence to the minimal norm solution even when the initial condition is not in the domain of the fractional power $\frac{1}{4}$ of the linear compact operator. In contrast, existing Hamiltonian and gradient-based methods fail to converge to the minimal norm solution under this specific initial condition scenario. Consequently, our framework is particularly advantageous for solving real-world inverse problems characterized by significant data noise and kernel ill-posedness. The paper concludes with remarks on potential future extensions of this study. Additional materials are available at https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Maria-Delfina-Gonzalez-Bautista. Research into robot movement along narrow, narrow-confined barriers remains a promising but technically demanding field within modern control theory and robotics. This study addresses the unpredictable dynamics of a point particle traversing a flexible monolayer confined to a unit circle, driven by a tangential input and subject to friction and damping forces from the monolayer. We analyze the system's equilibrium points, revealing that barrier parameters and control forces can trigger a bifurcation from a stable global adhesion state to a mixed scenario involving both adhesion and delamination. Numerical simulations confirm this theoretical prediction, highlighting a critical control threshold that separates stable adhesion from partial delamination. Consequently, this threshold establishes a necessary condition for achieving stable robot adhesion on circular barriers. Furthermore, we derive stability criteria for equilibrium points and investigate the existence and multiplicity of non-trivial solution sets, noting that circular domain constraints can lead to multiple such solutions. Finally, we present numerical examples illustrating both adhesion and delamination outcomes. Overall, this research provides a foundational framework for modeling robot dynamics on curved adhering barriers and addresses key control challenges related to stable attachment and detachment. These findings offer initial insights into motion control for barrier-adhering robots and facilitate a deeper understanding of the physical and control issues inherent to such systems. Additionally, the proposed model holds potential for applications in biological and medical fields, including blood flow dynamics and cell migration. Future work will extend this framework to more complex geometries, such as curved surfaces. Specifically, we aim to develop a similar model for dynamic circular domains, thereby addressing control challenges related to barrier robots operating on moving surfaces. This proposed extension represents a significant step toward solving fundamental control problems in the field of robot motion control. Furthermore, the current framework serves as a basis for addressing various other control challenges, such as the time required for robots to reach target points, the necessity of adhering to specific paths, and the need to avoid obstacles. These issues are integral to the broader field of path planning, which remains a primary focus in robot motion control. Ultimately, this work offers a preliminary solution to these problems by offering a framework to examine the physical and control aspects of motion control for barrier-adhering robots. Specifically, it enables the analysis of critical control issues, including the force and energy requirements necessary for adhesion. In this context, the proposed framework acts as a preliminary tool for solving these challenges and offers a basis for addressing the energy efficiency of barrier-adhering robots. We investigate how extended impurities influence microwaves as they propagate through a superconductor driven by kinetic energy. These impurities create a mosaic of domains with varying thicknesses and orientations relative to the impurity's scattering potential. Our findings indicate that the impact of these extended structures is largely contingent upon the superconductor's doping level. In underdoped materials, microwaves spend a significant portion of their path in regions with low superconducting energy gaps, where scattering is minimal; consequently, the impurities have a limited effect on microwave conductivity. Conversely, in optimally or overdoped samples, scattersheets can induce a substantial decrease in microwave conductivity, a phenomenon we elucidate using a perturbation expansion in the Mayer cluster formalism. We demonstrate that at leading order, the correction to microwave conductivity is positive, whereas the next-to-leading order term is negative. Furthermore, we show that for wide scattersheets, this negative correction scales with the third power of the sheet width. Finally, we analyze how microwave conductivity varies with the root mean square (rms) fluctuation amplitude of the impurity positions. Our results reveal a transition from a regime where microwave conductivity is insensitive to position fluctuations to one where it is highly sensitive, a shift that is more pronounced in overdoped samples. This behavior aligns with the microwave spectroscopy of YBCO thin films, which exhibit extended structures with a distribution of widths. Specifically, our predictions regarding the doping dependence of position fluctuations in microwave transmission are consistent with recent experimental data. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the case of point-like structures, revealing that microwave conductivity is insensitive to structures in regions with small gaps, a feature that can be exploited to design superconductors with enhanced microwave properties. Finally, we examine the effects of time-varying position fluctuations, showing that microwave transmission is more sensitive to these fluctuations in overdoped samples compared to optimally doped ones. This insight may prove valuable for developing high-temperature superconducting materials with improved microwave transmission characteristics. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our theoretical results and the microwave properties of YBCO, which possesses an orthorhombic crystal structure. Our calculations suggest that the microwave transmission of YBCO is more sensitive to structures oriented along the $b$-axis than to those along the $a$-axis, a prediction that is supported by experimental observations. Plants are vital to human survival, yet their natural growth patterns often make them difficult to work with in many settings. While plant biologists can influence morphology by manipulating environmental factors, the specific effects of individual conditions remain complex and not fully understood. To address this gap, we introduce GrowSpace, a virtual simulation built within the Unity game engine to investigate plant growth. Our work involves adapting an existing growth algorithm and sculpting tools from Maya to create a specialized version that accurately reflects biological reality. We validated the system by comparing simulation outputs against a real potted plant and then deployed it to evaluate how growth is affected by various parameters. Our findings reveal that an increased water supply accelerates growth speed, whereas a higher concentration of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) primarily alters the direction of growth. Additionally, we outline the current constraints of our model and propose a research agenda to address them. We believe GrowSpace will be a valuable resource for computer science researchers. The code is accessible online at https://github.com/andrewchen2000/GrowSpace. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/4222222222. Future enhancements include expanding the simulation to support a wider variety of plant species. We hope this tool will facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration between computer scientists and plant biologists. We establish a "gluing theorem" for Weyl quantum disks with arbitrary angles, extending the universal quantum disk gluing theorem originally formulated by Lawler, Vahala, and Werner in their comprehensive study of Brownian loop and excursion domains across the universal covering space of a simply connected domain. Specifically, we demonstrate that the universal Brownian excursion from the complement of a closed curve in the universal covering space adheres to the Law of Large Numbers, converging in distribution to the SLE$_{8/3}$ loop process as the number of excursions increases. This result is achieved by conformally mapping each quantum disk instance to a Weyl quantum disk of angle zero and invoking Angstrom's formula. Furthermore, this finding offers a novel perspective on the equivalence between the SLE$_{8/3}$ loop process and the uniform limit of conditioned Brownian excursions. Additionally, we elucidate the connection between the universal quantum disk and two recently introduced free boundary Liouville Quantum Gravity models: the whole plane Liouville Quantum Gravity and the Liouville Brownian motion on the universal covering space of a simply connected domain. This relationship provides an alternative explanation for the recent discovery of the conformal invariance of the uniform limit of conditioned SLE$_{8/3}$ excursions. Finally, we offer an independent proof of the equivalence between the SLE$_{8/3}$ loop process and the uniform limit of conditioned Brownian excursions. This equivalence was previously derived by the second author as a consequence of the universal quantum disk gluing theorem; our approach instead relies on the free boundary Liouville Quantum Gravity representation of the universal quantum disk. Notably, our proof extends to broader settings beyond simply connected domains, thereby generalizing the result originally obtained by Liu, Sun, and Wang as a direct corollary of Liouville gravity. Finally, we present a version of our gluing theorem tailored for Weyl Liouville Quantum Disk angles, which may hold independent interest. This formulation enables a counterpart to the Liouville gravity representation of the universal disk gluing theorem, potentially offering fresh insights into the structure of Liouville gravity and advancing the program of constructing a Liouville gravity representation of the universal Brownian excursion from a simply connected domain. This approach builds upon the work of the second author regarding the Liouville gravity representation of the universal Brownian excursion from the half-plane. These insights may contribute to elucidating the relationship between Liouville gravity and Liouville Brownian motion

The image indicator (II) serves as a critical metric for assessing reservoir quality, yet its practical application is hindered by substantial variability across different studies. This inconsistency stems from numerous factors, including the specific reservoirs examined, the type of well logs utilized, and, most significantly, differing normalization methods. To address this, the current study proposes standardizing reservoir-specific image indicators to facilitate cross-study comparisons. We introduce a new standardization initiative designed to harmonize the two prevalent training datasets: the 3D seismic simulation by Zhang et al. (2019) and the 3D synthetic geological model by Zhang et al. (2021). This initiative employs a three-step framework: (1) developing a novel image definition, (2) proposing a standardization protocol, and (3) implementing a two-stage training strategy. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to standardize image indicators, thereby providing a foundation for future research. We anticipate that this initiative will enable subsequent studies to build upon these established image indicators, potentially advancing their effectiveness. To demonstrate the proposed standardization, we present a series of experiments across different datasets. The results indicate that models trained using this initiative can achieve a test accuracy of 90% when applied to unseen datasets. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan1998/Reservoir-Image-Classifier. Additionally, the code includes pre-trained models for the standard synthetic datasets mentioned above, which can be directly applied without further training. We hope this will assist researchers in rapidly advancing reservoir characterization. The code also offers a training interface for users to train their own models on custom datasets. This interface supports various input types, including seismic data, well log data, and reservoir property data. We intend to expand the scope of this standardization initiative in future work to further enhance reservoir characterization. This research was conducted during a visit to Stanford University. We conducted a phenomenological analysis of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction reactions using a cloud-baryon model that incorporates $S$- and $P$-wave resonances. This model was tested against experimental data for $K\Lambda$ production off the nucleon. The results indicate that $S$-wave resonances dominate the photoproduction cross sections at low energies, whereas $P$-wave resonances are responsible for the observed peak near the $K\Lambda$ threshold. Furthermore, the mass of the $S$-wave resonance is found to be lower than that of the $N(1650)S_{11}$ state. We also examined $K\Lambda$ photoproduction from the $\Delta$ resonance, noting that the $P$-wave state from which it originates is likely the $N(1700)P_{39}$ level. Additionally, our findings suggest that the $P$-wave $K\Sigma$ peak arises from an $N$ state with a mass of approximately $1.6\ GeV$. These results provide a theoretical basis for understanding the nature of $N$ states, particularly $S$ and $P$ waves, and their relationship with the $N\Delta$ transition resonance. Consequently, photoproduction experiments offer a valuable tool for investigating the properties of $N$ states and the $N\Delta$ transition resonance. Finally, the developed model can be applied to analyze future photoproduction data. We have also presented several predictions regarding peak positions and resonance masses that can be compared with forthcoming experimental results. This work serves as a foundation for future $K$ photoproduction studies. Additionally, we have made predictions for $K$ photoproduction off the $\Delta$ resonance, which may aid in the search for $N$ states and $N\Delta$ transition resonances. This study proposes that one of the gravitational wave events, GW190521, originating from the merger of two black holes, may have involved the birth of a primordial black hole. By integrating cosmological parameters with the black hole's mass, we estimate that this event could have resulted in the formation of a seed black hole approximately 13.8 billion years ago. This seed would have experienced roughly 7.5 million years of direct star formation before settling into an elliptical galaxy environment. We suggest that the presence of such a black hole in GW190521 could provide evidence of a first-order phase transition within the early universe. Furthermore, we explore how the parameters of the curvaton field can influence primordial black hole density and examine the observational constraints on primordial black holes derived from GW190521. Additionally, the spin parameters of GW190521 are analyzed, revealing that the premerger black hole possessed an extremely low spin. Finally, the observational evidence for this ancient black hole is discussed. Overall, GW190521 represents the earliest direct observation of a black hole, offering a unique window into the universe's conditions shortly after the Big Bang. This finding not only expands the observational scope of black holes but also deepens our understanding of the early universe. Consequently, it may facilitate the detection of a first-order phase transition in the early universe and help explain the existence of supermassive black holes. This paper introduces a framework for educational pathway analysis by integrating structural equation modeling (SEM) and topic modeling. Within our structural equation model, latent variables represent educational pathways, while observed variables correspond to career choices. Leveraging the parallel relationship between SEM and probabilistic topic models, we employ the latter to uncover unobserved career trajectories based on individual attributes and to derive latent topics from transition data between them. This approach allows us to construct a structural equation model that examines pathway characteristics, identifies high-transition pathways, and evaluates how specific individual factors influence career decisions. We apply this methodology to analyze survey data regarding high school and college education pathways, as well as career selections, collected from a group of high school students in Japan. The results provide valuable insights for high school counselors to assist students in making informed decisions regarding future educational and occupational directions. Additionally, we outline our code and data for reproducibility, which can be accessed at https://github.com/taiki-ito/SEM-Topic-Model. Finally, we discuss how our proposed framework addresses limitations found in existing research on structural equation analysis and educational pathway analysis. Specifically, our method avoids the arbitrary classification of professions into categories and captures the latent structures of career pathways. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework offers a novel solution to a significant issue in educational and career guidance by simultaneously identifying latent structures and offering advice to individuals. Our proposed framework holds the potential to enhance decision-making processes by providing guidance that is more aligned with individual inclinations. Additionally, we illustrate how this framework can be extended to support decision-making for organizations. For instance, a company could utilize their own employee data to identify organizational cultures and the impact of specific employee traits on job roles, enabling them to recruit candidates who better fit their organizational culture. We also show how this framework can be adapted to assist organizations in understanding how employee characteristics affect productivity. By employing our framework, an organization could identify employee traits that influence career pathways, allowing them to assign employees to roles that more effectively leverage their strengths. Ultimately, our proposed framework represents a promising tool for advancing decision-making processes in both educational and organizational contexts. To demonstrate this, we have applied our framework to analyze how organizational cultures affect employee job assignments. Our findings indicate that organizations can achieve better outcomes by recruiting employees whose characteristics align with their organizational culture. We believe our proposed framework can significantly contribute to improving decision-making processes in various settings. Finally, we illustrate how our framework overcomes several limitations of current research on educational and career pathway analysis by combining clustering and structural equation modeling. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon control framework utilizing differential contests. The acceleration of the leading vehicle is modeled as a differential contest with power $\alpha$ against inter-control-time, establishing an open-loop command for the leader and eliminating inter-platoon interference. A power level of $\alpha=1$ ensures an exponentially decaying spacing error. Following the leader, each subsequent vehicle employs a differential contest power $\beta_i$ to manage spacing errors with a decay rate of $\beta_i-1$. When $\beta_i=1$, the spacing error decays exponentially. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an infinite chain of such platoons remains input-to-state stable (ISS) provided that $\beta_i>1$. We analyze the stability of more complex scenarios, including infinite chains where $\beta_i$ approaches 1 and the effects of external disturbances, before proposing a vehicle architecture that enables load-sharing through differential contests. Finally, the paper presents experimental results from load transport tests involving up to 15 vehicles. These results highlight the benefits of differential contests in achieving high control performance, such as rapid error decay, and effective load distribution. The proposed control scheme is versatile and can be adapted for use with both automated and driver-operated vehicles. Additionally, we offer a general methodology for assessing stability in vehicle chains, which is applicable to various cooperative control strategies. This work revisits the well-known limitation of logistic regression, specifically the curse of interactivity, and addresses a related issue: the persistence of interaction effects even after transformation. To tackle these problems, we introduce RRL and VIF, two novel regularized feature selection algorithms. Our approach is grounded in the concept of $k$-wise sparsity. We demonstrate that L1 and $k$-Lasso methods fail to enforce $k$-wise sparsity; instead, we propose that the minimum description length (MDL) principle serves as an effective mechanism for this purpose. We derive an efficient algorithm to solve the minimum $\ell_2^p$ problem for $p \geq 1$, which approximates the $\ell^0$ norm and enables the identification of the best subset of size $k$. Furthermore, we present RRL and VIF, which utilize MDL-based feature selection combined with regularization to either retrieve the globally optimal solution or offer a favorable trade-off between sparsity and computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/RRL. Headlines serve as concise summaries that enable readers to quickly grasp the core content of news articles. We introduce a novel mechanism for amorphous and polycrystalline antiferromagnets that enables the decoupling of spins from their anisotropy axes, resulting in a chiral spin fluid. In this state, an in-plane magnetic field induces a planar spiral with a finite Chern number. We investigate a two-spinon excitation spectrum that forms a gapless path in the dispersion relation, while a quantum Hall gap appears in the spin Hall effect. This amorphous system supports quantized edge modes that are quantized despite experiencing backscattering from grain boundaries in the polycrystalline structure. We propose that this system can be realized in quantum magnets composed of weakly coupled, randomly oriented Heisenberg antiferromagnets, which are accessible through both cold-atom and solid-state platforms. Furthermore, we outline the experimental signatures of this chiral spin fluid and its associated topological quantum Hall effect in amorphous and polycrystalline antiferromagnets. Our proposed quantum magnets exhibit a topological order distinct from that of amorphous ferromagnets, offering a new avenue for exploring topological orders in quantum magnets. Additionally, the quantum magnets we propose can be accessed without the need for external magnetic fields. Finally, our findings suggest that the quantum Hall effect in amorphous and polycrystalline quantum magnets can be observed at the single-particle level. This represents a fundamentally new approach to generating a quantum Hall effect in amorphous and polycrystalline magnets, moving beyond the conventional reliance on the spin-orbit interaction present in electronic band structures. We demonstrate that this mechanism operates at the mean-field level, indicating that it functions at the single-particle level. Moreover, our findings provide a promising route toward discovering a quantum anomalous Hall effect in amorphous and polycrystalline quantum magnets. This is achieved by coupling Heisenberg antiferromagnets with ferromagnetic exchange interactions, thereby opening a new pathway to explore quantum magnets with non-trivial topological orders. Our proposed amorphous and polycrystalline quantum magnets offer a unique opportunity to investigate topological orders in quantum magnets, with grain boundaries serving as a source of disorder. We anticipate that this topological order can be accessed without the need for external magnetic fields. This paper introduces and evaluates various calibration techniques for large-scale radio interferometers, designed for efficiency and scalability to handle datasets from future facilities like the Square Kilometre Array. A key challenge in these arrays is the substantial volume of data generated by baselines comprising numerous elements. We present an optimized calibration approach utilizing data structures that enable $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ complexity (where $N$ is the number of antenna elements in a baseline) for visibility corrections related to gain, position, and bandpass. This contrasts with current state-of-the-art methods, which typically require $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ operations per visibility. Additionally, we describe a parallelization strategy for calibration that is compatible with the Beamer data reduction software and the BEOSAM framework for array data processing. We provide a detailed implementation of the method using a regular grid as a proof-of-concept. Finally, we present performance benchmarks on a system with 128 nodes, each equipped with 32 cores, to demonstrate the scalability of our approach. These results indicate that our technique is highly effective for large arrays composed of regular subarrays. Specifically, a calibration task involving 1 billion visibilities per iteration, with $N = 384$ antenna elements, was completed in approximately 10 seconds on this test system. Our parallelization method is approximately 10 times more efficient than that of the existing BEAM software. Furthermore, our parallelization is roughly 10 times faster than BEAM and about 2 to 3 times faster than the existing AMBER task on the same system. Our approach is not limited to regular subarrays; it can be adapted for sparse configurations by partitioning baselines into groups where intra-group distances are significantly smaller than inter-group distances. This allows the algorithm to remain highly efficient for all baselines within each group. We outline a strategy for achieving this optimization and provide a proof-of-concept implementation for such configurations. Our method is broadly applicable to any calibration task, including self-calibration, and can be integrated into any existing calibration framework. We have developed a proof-of-concept implementation for self-calibration that is compatible with the AMBER task. Our approach is also well-suited for on-cube calibration, where calibration solutions are computed on-the-fly during data reduction. We have developed a proof-of-concept implementation for this as well. This study introduces a novel method for investment portfolio allocation and provides an experimental validation of its efficacy. The approach is grounded in an autoencoding generalized adversarial framework. In this setup, an encoder transforms input data into a vector containing allocation weights for each asset, while a generator utilizes these encoded vectors to reconstruct the original data. Concurrently, a discriminator is tasked with distinguishing between the original data and the generated output. We demonstrate the method's success by applying it to construct a real-world portfolio using historical stock price time series. The findings indicate that the proposed portfolio yields higher returns and reduced volatility compared to the benchmark "buy and hold" strategy. Furthermore, additional experiments were conducted to evaluate robustness across various hyperparameters, network architectures, and training configurations. Finally, to illustrate the method's versatility, a second example was provided using data from the Consumer Price Index. Overall, the results confirm that the proposed approach is both effective and robust. Additionally, the study offers a comprehensive codebase featuring multiple model configurations and is open-source. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations. Specifically, the portfolio's performance is contingent upon the inclusion of asset class representatives in the training data; for instance, if the training set comprises only stocks, the model may underestimate the benefits of diversifying into other asset classes. Consequently, the model is optimized for short-term returns, and investors should consider their own risk tolerance and time horizon before making decisions. Moreover, the training process is sensitive to initial weight initialization, which can significantly impact the number of epochs required for convergence. Finally, we acknowledge the possibility of overfitting, which could lead to the selection of a portfolio that performs well on historical data but fails to replicate those results in live trading environments. To mitigate this, we recommend implementing cross-validation during the training and testing phases. Additionally, while backtesting on historical data demonstrates the method's effectiveness, it does not guarantee future performance. Therefore, further research is necessary to explore the underlying mechanisms of the model and its long-term stability. Finally, we propose developing a more robust, user-friendly version of the model that incorporates cross-validation and out-of-sample testing to facilitate easier adoption by investors. Our results rely on the four-loop strong coupling constant $\beta_4$ and the three-loop polarized non-singlet anomalous dimension $\gamma_{NS;3}$ as input parameters. The analysis was conducted using the C++ program `PolarizedQCD`, which is available as a standalone tool. Furthermore, we provide a set of polarized non-singlet matrix elements required for the matching procedure in the polarized case. These elements can be obtained by subtracting the evolution of lower-order matrix elements from the three-flavor scheme to those in the four-flavor scheme. Additionally, we examine the behavior of $A_{gq}(N)$ in the limits of small and large $N$, deriving the leading term for small $N$ and the subleading term for large $N$. Our three-loop findings for $A_{gq}(N)$ show significantly reduced dependence on the renormalization scale $\mu$ compared to the previous two-loop result. This study introduces a novel Bayesian deep learning framework designed to classify quasars based on their gamma-ray spectra. Utilizing data from the 4Fermi-LAT catalog, we trained a Bayesian multi-layer perceptron to analyze the log-likelihood distributions of 1,000 quasars and 1,000 non-quasar point sources. Additionally, we examined the uncertainty associated with quasars misclassified as non-quasar point sources and identified two distinct groups based on spectral characteristics. This research represents a significant step toward the future Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope catalog. The developed framework is publicly accessible to facilitate further scientific inquiry. Specifically, inequalities regarding the largest eigenvalue have been derived, alongside the analysis of spectral conditions necessary for a spectrum to form an integral spectrum. The study also addresses the signlessness largest eigenvalue, providing inequalities and examining the spectral criteria required for it to become an integral signlessness largest eigenvalue. Furthermore, the necessary conditions for the tensor union to be spectral are established, and it is demonstrated that under certain conditions, the spectral radius serves as the largest eigenvalue. Additional exploration includes the analysis of eigenvalue interlacing inequalities and the necessary conditions for the existence of eigenvalues within a specific set. Finally, the graph theoretical characteristics of the tensor union are examined. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for constructing hypergraphs with integral spectra. Additionally, the results generalize existing literature on eigenvalues, eigenvalue interlacing, and the graph theoretical attributes of disjoint unions. Specifically, the concepts of tensor union, spectral conditions for integral spectra, eigenvalue interlacing, and the graph theoretical analysis of the tensor union presented herein represent novel contributions. This white paper outlines the case for an intermediate-class space-based observatory, tentatively named the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST), which would offer high-resolution spectroscopy and imaging across a wavelength range from 300 nm to 2.5 $\mu$m. Designed to support fundamental research in astrophysics and cosmology, this instrument would complement and significantly expand upon the capabilities of current and upcoming facilities. The proposed mission would operate in a sun-synchronous polar orbit at an altitude of approximately 600 km, utilizing a 0.8-meter aperture and a single focal plane covering a field of view of 1.5 arcminutes. This setup would deliver spectroscopic and photometric data at a rate of 100,000 pixels per second, achieving a spectral resolution of roughly 100,000 in spectroscopic mode and 10 million in imaging mode. Supporting these instruments would be a large, active, and fast-readout optical element, such as a deformable mirror, and a backend featuring a large-format charge-coupled device (CCD) or complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) sensor. Such a mission would be ideal for training the next generation of astrophysicists and cosmologists, fostering innovation, and establishing India as a leader in space astrophysics. We argue that this mission should be prioritized in India's upcoming space and astrophysics roadmaps. A detailed technical proposal is currently being prepared and will be submitted to the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) for detailed study. ISRO is encouraged to allocate a suitable time frame for this intermediate-class mission. We believe that launching this telescope within the next decade is essential to maximize its scientific return. Furthermore, we recommend that India develop a dedicated astrophysics agency to plan, propose, and execute such missions. This agency would be responsible for implementing a comprehensive astrophysics and cosmology program that addresses both fundamental and societal challenges. Finally, we propose that India establish a world-class astrophysics institute to advance the field. This institute would be funded by a dedicated budget line in the national budget, separate from the current modest allocations for astrophysics. We believe that a robust, sustainable funding mechanism is necessary to ensure the long-term success of India's astrophysics endeavors. This study introduces a new method for analyzing the pathways of rare events in stochastic systems, termed the PGEMC (p-Gaussian enhanced minimum action) approach. Utilizing a global enhancement of action technique, this method seeks to maximize the transition probability between two specific states. The PGEMC framework serves a dual function: it first identifies minimum action paths connecting any two states, and subsequently, enhances these paths to elucidate the transition mechanisms underlying rare events. By focusing on transition mechanisms rather than merely the transition rates, the PGEMC approach offers deeper insights into the processes driving rare events. The efficacy of this methodology is demonstrated through its application to both a double-well potential and the water dimer system. In the case of the water dimer, the derived transition mechanisms align with the outcomes of an ab initio study conducted by the same authors. Furthermore, the efficacy of the water dimer mechanism has been corroborated by the broader scientific community. These findings collectively affirm the effectiveness of the PGEMC approach. Additionally, the methodology is adaptable for studying various types of rare events beyond chemical reactions. The computational cost of this approach is comparable to other action-minimization techniques, such as the string method or nudged elastic method, and is significantly lower than the computational expense associated with achieving high transition probabilities. Consequently, the PGEMC method is particularly advantageous for systems where high transition probabilities are challenging to achieve, such as those modeled by quantum mechanics. Ultimately, the success of the PGEMC approach in the presented examples demonstrates its robust effectiveness. We provide characterizations of these subclasses of $n$-order regular functions through typed lambda-calculi utilizing $k$-ary lambda-abstractions. A key finding demonstrates that an Stratonovich integral with such a flow can be expressed as an Itô integral with a corresponding equivalent adapted flow. To achieve this, we develop a procedure for integrating differential forms over the space of absolutely continuous curves. This approach generalizes solutions to Monge-Ampère type equations, which define the differential of this form. We identify the specific class of conditional distribution flows dependent on the driving signal that generate Stratonovich integrals expressible as Itô integrals, and provide a method to determine the stochastic differential equation of the driving signal that ensures this equivalence. Finally, the applicability of these findings is illustrated through a simplified model of a nonlinear sensor under observation noise. In this context, we derive the Girsanov-type formula for two measures on a finite time interval: one representing observations generated by a nonlinear sensor with conditional distribution drifts interpreted in the Stratonovich sense, and the other representing observations with Itô interpretations. We analyze the relationship between the drifts of these two measures and establish a formula for the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the conditional distribution of a finite-dimensional Markov process, given a nonlinear function of its observations. Furthermore, we derive the relationship between the conditional expectations of a nonlinear function of the process's state, based on observations interpreted under either Itô or Stratonovich frameworks. We also examine the case of a nonlinear function of the state and an auxiliary process that is conditionally Markov given the state. This paper introduces a concept of quasi-character designed to establish a group-theoretic analogue to the Sierpinski spectrum of a topological space, which models the Sierpinski triangle representing all open subsets of a topological space. A topological space $X$ is defined as standard when its Sierpinski spectrum is homeomorphic to the unit interval; this paper demonstrates that every metric space possesses a covering with standard subspaces. Furthermore, it is proven that an arbitrary space admits a countable family of pairwise disjoint standard subspaces that collectively cover the space. The concept of quasi-character is introduced to develop a standard structure space for groups, tree spaces, and surfaces. For a group $G$, the standard structure space $X(G)$ is defined such that its points correspond to $G$-invariant metrics on $\mathbb{R}$, where the topology is generated by $G$-convergence on the real line. The paper establishes that for a group $G$ acting on a set $S$, the metric extension property holds if and only if $S$ can be expressed as the union of pairwise disjoint sub-$G$-orbits. This condition ensures that the map $\Phi: X(G) \to X(S)$, which sends each $G$-invariant metric on $\mathbb{R}$ to its extension on $\mathbb{R}^S$, is a homeomorphism. Additionally, it is shown that if $G$ is a free group or a free surface group, then $X(G)$ is a compact, totally disconnected space. For a free group $F_n$ with $n \geq 2$, the space $X(F_n)$ is homeomorphic to the Cantor set. For a free surface group $\Sigma_g$ where $g \geq 2$, $X(\Sigma_g)$ is homeomorphic to the Pseudo-circle. However, for the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$, $X(\mathbb{Z})$ is homeomorphic to the unit interval. Finally, for a finitely generated free group $F_n$ ($n \geq 2$), every metric on $\mathbb{R}$ that is invariant under the action of $F_n$ is equivalent to a norm. The authors anticipate that these findings will facilitate the investigation of the topological structure of groups and their spaces. Cross-domain text-to-SQL generation is a difficult natural language processing challenge that has garnered significant attention recently. However, current state-of-the-art models often struggle with syntax errors because they lack an explicit understanding of sentence syntax structures. To address this, we introduce a novel neural parsing-aware model enhanced by a meaning extraction module and a supportive task. The model utilizes two neural networks: one dedicated to extracting useful syntax features, and another focused on generating the SQL structure. Additionally, the supportive task predicts the earliest non-terminal node to guide the tree-structured generation template. By incorporating this predictive mechanism, the model effectively mitigates syntax errors. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Spider and SchemaSQL benchmarks. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that each component contributes positively to the model's performance. Finally, we provide an online demo for user convenience. This study addresses secure navigation within multi-robot systems by introducing a risk-aware, multi-agent framework designed to prevent collisions and overcrowding. The proposed approach utilizes data-driven, risk-averse planning to mitigate the effects of uncertainty in both robot dynamics and obstacle locations. Specifically, the vision component of our method leverages point clouds from depth sensors alongside a particle filter to generate probabilistic maps of robot positions. These updated probabilistic representations feed into a multi-agent Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, which minimizes a cost function that simultaneously accounts for individual navigation goals and the security of the multirobot system. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing risk-aware navigation approaches and maintains a secure distance from other robots even as the number of robots increases. Notably, the security of the multirobot system in our approach is comparable to that of conservative risk-neutral methods, yet it achieves superior navigation performance relative to risk-aware techniques. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robustness against uncertainties in both dynamics and observation models. Finally, this method is well-suited for parallelization, enabling the development of distributed algorithms for risk-aware navigation in multirobot systems. This represents a significant advancement toward the collaborative use of multirobot systems in complex environments. To demonstrate the versatility of the proposed approach, we applied it to a multirobot formation following scenario. The entire framework is implemented in C++ and is available as open-source code. Additionally, to facilitate the easy deployment of similar solutions, we have developed an extensible, high-level API for design and simulation. This work supports the broader multi-robot community by providing a versatile platform for creating, testing, and deploying collaborative robotic solutions. The entire framework is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/RiskAwareMPC. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a dwarf galaxy situated approximately 780 kiloparsecs from Earth. This object was identified through an analysis of the Andromeda galaxy's optical and near-infrared images captured by the VLT Survey Telescope. We have determined the positions of six member stars, which were subsequently used to calculate the object's mean parallax and derive its physical scale. By analyzing the positions and magnitudes of these six stars, we estimated the object's distance to be roughly 780 kiloparsecs, with an uncertainty of 10%. We also estimated the distance using the color of the brightest member star. Furthermore, we determined the object's transverse velocity relative to the Andromeda galaxy and calculated its total mass, finding it to be approximately $1.1 \times 10^8$ solar masses. Our mass estimation indicates that And XXV contains a low density of dark matter in its central region. We conclude that And XXV is a dwarf galaxy that will likely merge with the Andromeda galaxy in the future. Additionally, we discuss the characteristics of And XXV, including its distance, total mass, and dark matter density. We also examine the nature of the object and the potential future of dwarf galaxies within the Local Group. This study is the first in a series dedicated to investigating dwarf galaxies within the Local Group. The second paper in this series will focus on the study of Andromeda XXVI (And XXVI). Grant-free massive connectivity supports numerous devices transmitting with low data rates and limited resources without performing channel estimation. This grant-free non-orthogonal pattern design aims to maximize device count by ensuring sufficient channel distinguishability. We propose designing binary non-orthogonal patterns through a dual-stage genetic algorithm. The first stage generates a diverse population of patterns tailored for the specific channel estimation method, while the second stage selects the optimal pattern based on estimated rates and other relevant metrics. Our results demonstrate that binary patterns generated by this dual-stage algorithm achieve higher rates than random patterns and perform comparably to patterns created by more complex generative approaches. Furthermore, this pattern design method remains effective across both pilot-based and grant-free non-orthogonal designs. The computational complexity of our proposed approach is lower than that of constructive non-degenerate superimposed code generation and remains comparable to random pattern design. Consequently, this method offers a flexible and efficient solution for pattern design in grant-free massive connectivity scenarios. Our findings indicate that binary patterns can support up to 1000 devices while maintaining reliable detection and decoding rates. Additionally, we observe that rates can be further enhanced by adjusting the observation window length and implementing appropriate detection strategies. Simulation results confirm that grant-free non-orthogonal patterns enable reliable detection even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. This research is particularly relevant for massive machine-type communication applications in IoT, such as smart cities and industrial settings, where numerous devices transmit small packets over shared channels without requiring channel estimation. By leveraging grant-free transmission, non-orthogonal pattern design supports connectivity for up to 1000 devices and offers the potential to scale beyond that limit. Our study demonstrates that grant-free patterns can achieve support for 2–3 times more devices than orthogonal pilot-based patterns of equivalent length, all while maintaining the same error probability. This is achieved by accepting a slight reduction in rate, which can be mitigated by increasing the number of time slots or extending the observation window. This study evaluates various variants of the commonly used Kays and London approximation and the less common M\"{o}ller approximation, both designed for simulating the thermodynamic properties of humid air. The analysis identifies the specific thermodynamic variables required to define the mixture and determines the appropriate formulation for the thermal equation of state. The resulting approximations are assessed against the rigorous IAPWS formulation. The molar specific heat capacity is handled via the Wilke approximation, while the thermal thermal conductivity and viscous diffusivity utilize the specific formulations appropriate for dry air as defined by the IAPWS Standard. Finally, the accuracy of the proposed approximations is verified by comparing the resulting thermodynamic potentials and transport coefficients against the more exact humid air formulation from Turner et al. The study concludes that the superior approximation is the one derived from the M\"{o}ller formulation, which is based on temperature and molar humidity. This version is made available as an open-source implementation in the C++ library CoolProp, which is freely accessible. The authors encourage researchers to use this formulation in simulations of humid air flows. The implementation includes a flag to select between the IAPWS formulation and the approximated one, allowing for the comparison of results across different models. Additionally, the authors propose an alternative approximation based on the Kays and London formulation, though they note it is less accurate than the M\"{o}ller-based variant. This alternative is based on pressure and water vapor mass fraction, and its formulation is also provided as an option within the CoolProp library. Finally, the authors have prepared a header file for easy integration of the approximations into fluid dynamics solvers. This includes a thermodynamic equation of state, a function to calculate the relative humidity, and a subroutine to compute the speed of sound. The authors hope this will facilitate the development of more accurate and efficient models for humid air. This work was partially funded by the National Science Foundation under grant no. 1801000. Our approach leverages the parallel extensions technique introduced by S. R. S. Bhargava and B. S. Yadav. We present a novel method to generate these wCNs from hypophases across multiple ASR hypotheses. Our method for monitoring system dialogue states incorporates several new techniques, including entity normalization, multi-wCN fusion, and an efficient algorithm for proposing DS candidates. We conducted an extensive evaluation of our method within a web-based customer service application. Our results demonstrate that word-level monitoring of ASR uncertainty yields effective results and shows promising potential for enhancing DSM in various other scenarios. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of our methods and offer recommendations for future research. This study introduces a universal framework to investigate the intricacy of any problem, with the Hamiltonian cycle problem (HCP) serving as a representative example. Intricacy is quantified using the count of critical clauses within the problem's entry framework; these clauses are identified by negating them and assessing whether the revised framework remains entry-framework-like. The analysis reveals that the minimum intricacy for HCP on general graphs is 2, while it is 1 for planar graphs. Consequently, a planar instance of HCP possesses a less complex structure than its general graph counterpart. These findings suggest the existence of an intrinsic limit to the simplicity of the $NP$-completeness class. Furthermore, the framework enables the analysis of the uniqueness of entry frameworks, demonstrating, for instance, that the uniqueness class is $P$-complete. Finally, the paper concludes with an exploration of the relationship between entry frameworks and Markov logic networks. The proposed framework is considered a foundational step toward a more comprehensive theory of universal complexity. We introduce a general framework for inferring the entanglement of any quantum-optical system interacting with an unknown environment, relying exclusively on single-photon detection statistics. This approach demands no prior knowledge of the interacting party's state and requires no assumptions regarding the nature of interactions or entanglement within the target pair. Specifically, we optimize the measurement basis and the entanglement metric to maximize information gain using Fisher information analysis. This methodology is applied to identify and verify entanglement in three relevant ocular systems: (1) two metaparticles generated by two distinct optical vortices, (2) two optical vortices, and (3) an optical photon and an atomic vortex. Our results demonstrate that this framework effectively discriminates between both pure and mixed entangled states across all considered configurations. Furthermore, we illustrate how to adjust the entanglement measure to enable discrimination between specific pairs of states within a predefined set. These findings hold significant promise for advancing quantum communication and sensing protocols that utilize quantum optics. Additionally, they facilitate the calibration of entanglement measures and enhance the sensitivity of quantum-metric-based interferometers. Finally, we outline a viable experimental pathway to validate these conclusions. Notably, our proposed metric can be observed using current experimental techniques, such as those employed in recent studies of optical vortex entanglement. This study provides an in-depth analysis of intermittent palm-tree-like structures observed in JET tokamak plasma, utilizing data from a comprehensive set of diagnostics. These palms are linked to the plasma edge and manifest as filaments with a characteristic length scale of approximately 1 cm. They appear in both inner and outer divertor legs, though with distinct morphologies: they are thin and vertically elongated in the inner leg, whereas they are broad and horizontally elongated in the outer leg. Their occurrence is associated with fluctuations in the inner edge emission intensity, which exhibit a characteristic time scale of roughly 10 ms. The morphology observed in the outer leg is the projection of the inner-leg palms onto that specific viewing angle. The origin of these palms is attributed to an edge turbulence mode with a characteristic wavelength of 1 cm. This conclusion is supported by a comparison with results from turbulence simulations, which reproduce the palm morphology and exhibit a consistent time scale. Furthermore, the emergence of these palms coincides with a drop in the inner edge emission intensity, indicating a non-stationary edge state. This finding aligns with recent observations of a similar phenomenon in other devices, where a transition from a fluctuation-dominated state to a more stationary state is accompanied by a corresponding shift in the morphology of the palms. This suggests a complex interplay between the edge and the palms, potentially mediated by the plasma boundary. Finally, a comparison with other devices reveals that, given the tokamak's physical dimensions, the origin of these palms is likely universal across all tokamaks. Additionally, the time scale of palm formation correlates with the edge rotation frequency, further underscoring the significance of rotation in the palm formation process. This study provides a deeper understanding of the origin and nature of palm structures, which is crucial for interpreting their impact on the edge-plasma state and confinement. This is particularly relevant for future tokamaks, where the edge and its interaction with the plasma boundary are critical for achieving and maintaining fusion conditions. Consequently, this research contributes to the broader understanding of the edge and its interaction with the boundary, a topic of significant interest for the future of fusion energy. Specifically, the paper addresses the following questions: What is the origin of these palms? What is their nature? How do they influence the edge and the bulk plasma state? What is the relationship between the edge and the palms? How do palms impact the edge state and confinement? And how do palms affect the bulk plasma state? This paper provides answers to these questions, based on the analysis of JET

The adoption of pretrained models has become increasingly prevalent in image classification tasks due to their robust feature extraction capabilities. However, researchers often struggle to fully leverage these advantages when integrating new classes, as performance can degrade significantly during the learning of additional categories. This issue is often exacerbated by the over-optimization of classification layers. To address this challenge in incremental learning, we introduce a straightforward yet effective benchmark that exposes these problems. We demonstrate that regularized gradient descent offers a promising alternative, substantially enhancing performance in incremental learning scenarios. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the sequence of adding new classes exerts a more profound influence on the effectiveness of gradient descent than previously assumed. This study tackles the task of identifying hate speech across three social media platforms by simultaneously processing posts in their native textual language alongside accompanying images. We introduce a multi-modal model that enhances detection capabilities through the integration of visual content. To address the challenge of limited data in specific languages, we propose a novel understanding-based model that leverages multiple source languages to improve performance across all targeted platforms. This approach yields consistent and substantial improvements by utilizing visual data. Additionally, we develop a new dataset containing balanced, manually annotated labels for both hate speech and non-hate speech. Finally, we evaluate our findings across different languages and provide a detailed analysis and discussion of our results. This work represents the first effort in hate speech detection to combine the advantages of multi-modal data with understanding-based models. This study examines how axonal growth influences the dynamics of self-organized synchronization within a network of excitatory neurons. We utilize a generalized version of the Wilson-Cowan model that incorporates axonal extent as a variable, alongside a type-I Wilson-Cowan neuron formulation. Our analysis demonstrates that networks containing axons with variable lengths exhibit significantly higher synchronization potential than those with fixed-length connections. Furthermore, axons of intermediate lengths prove optimal for achieving global synchronization. These outcomes are reinforced by numerical simulations. These findings offer crucial insights into the role of axonal development in the emergence of collective behaviors within the brain. Additionally, the study explores broader implications for understanding self-organized phase transitions in other Wilson-Cowan neuron models. Finally, we outline key challenges and future research directions regarding the relationship between axonal formation and brain development. Specifically, we highlight a potential link between our theoretical model and the recently identified gene, *ROBO1*, which regulates axonal growth. This gene is strongly expressed in the human brain and is associated with various psychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorder. We provide evidence of this connection and suggest it as a promising avenue for future investigation. Ultimately, we aim to elucidate the interplay between axonal formation and brain development, as well as the links between network architecture and brain function. These aspects are crucial for advancing our understanding of brain disorders. Specifically, we discuss the relationship between our findings and recent studies on gene expression patterns in autism spectrum disorder. These findings reveal an imbalance in the expression of genes promoting axonal growth, which could explain the reduced synchronization potential observed in autism. This aligns with clinical evidence of altered brain activity in autism patients. Consequently, our findings provide a compelling argument for the hypothesis that the brain's wiring architecture is intrinsically linked to brain function. This supports the broader perspective that brain structure is not merely a passive outcome of functional requirements but also plays an active role in shaping behavior. We conclude by discussing the implications of this hypothesis for understanding brain evolution. Specifically, we address the relationship between increased neuronal connectivity in the human brain and the emergence of human-specific cognitive abilities. Our findings suggest that increased connectivity may have contributed to these enhancements by increasing synchronization potential. This leads to the provocative hypothesis that brain evolution may have been driven more by axonal growth than by neuronal proliferation. We discuss this hypothesis in the context of our findings and suggest that it warrants further investigation. To this end, we present preliminary evidence supporting this hypothesis by analyzing the relationship between neuronal density and axonal length in the primary visual cortex of various primates

Creating antagonistic tests for program fixes is a pivotal step in the automated program repair process, yet it remains a challenging task for both humans and tools. This study investigates the potential of neural networks to generate antagonistic tests for fixed programs. We introduce a novel neural architecture designed to create antagonistic patches by directly targeting bug fixes and by incorporating information regarding the original faults. Through a study utilizing a substantial dataset of fixed Java programs, we demonstrate that our proposed model can effectively produce antagonistic tests. Furthermore, empirical results indicate that integrating this model with existing program repair tools can enhance their capability to repair a higher volume of bugs. Consequently, our model serves as a valuable asset for automated program repair tools, offering a distinct advantage over current test generation techniques by explicitly targeting identified bug fixes. The capability region (CR) defines all potential outcomes achievable through coordinated actions within a given system. This study investigates the CR of GIFC channels, which integrate general input and confusers. We begin by examining the scalar confuser scenario, where the confuser is scalar, the common random variable is scalar, and the main channel output is vector. We derive the optimal rate-distortion function (RDF) for the confuser and characterize the CR as a function of the RDF. Subsequently, we extend the analysis to vector confuser cases, deriving the optimal RDF and similarly defining the CR. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary of the presented results. This work serves as a preliminary step toward a comprehensive understanding of the CR in GIFC channels. Although the specific configurations considered here are limited, the underlying methodology is expected to be applicable to more general GIFC scenarios in future research. Furthermore, the techniques developed for scalar confurers may offer a foundation for addressing lossy compression problems in other communication channels. The concepts introduced in this paper are also anticipated to find applications in other signal processing domains. This article serves as an introduction to the capability region. The fundamental nature of matter under extreme conditions is a central focus of nuclear and particle physics. The collision structure of ultra-relativistic nuclear matter interacts with the Equation-of-State (EOS) to define characteristics such as multi-particle correlations and event-by-event fluctuations in observable final-state observables. This study focuses on extracting the EOS from a specific observable: the normalized kurtosis of net-proton charge rapidity ($\mathcal{F}_{4}^Y$). Utilizing the recently updated AMPT model, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{F}_{4}^Y$ is sensitive to the compressibility of symmetric nuclear matter ($K_{sym}$). Furthermore, we introduce a novel analytical framework to investigate the collision structure and EOS. By comparing experimental data with various AMPT configurations, we determine that radial flow and the EOS are the most influential factors shaping observables. We show that the collision structure can be represented by the ratio of the second-order anisotropic flow coefficient ($v_2$) to the transverse energy per participant ($E_T/A$). Finally, we establish a new instrument to explore the EOS using final-state observables, with future research planned to incorporate final-state effects and develop new theoretical models. Our findings indicate that $\mathcal{F}_{4}^Y$ is indeed sensitive to the EOS, and we have successfully established a new tool to examine the EOS of nuclear matter. This research was conducted using the CMS experiment at the LHC. Future planned analyses will utilize data from the ALICE experiment at the RHIC. We anticipate that this new tool will be utilized by the broader physics community to further investigate the EOS. Specifically, we will apply this tool to various hydrodynamic and transport model calculations to further explore the EOS. Additionally, we will analyze RHIC data using the same approach to determine whether the observed correlation between $K_{sym}$ and the $v_2/ET/A$ ratio in final-state observables is universal. This universality would imply that the correlation between $K_{sym}$ and the $v_2/ET/A$ ratio in the initial conditions is universal. We will also examine whether this correlation exists in other theoretical frameworks, such as the Boltzmann transport model. Finally, we will explore the possibility of extending this tool to other observables, such as $v_2/p_T$ and $k_{T}/A$, to further investigate the EOS. Detecting COVID-19 in its early stages is critical for limiting transmission and ensuring patient safety. While deep learning offers a promising solution, concerns regarding data privacy persist. We introduce ADV-CE, a novel framework designed to enhance the privacy of robust classifiers used for early COVID-19 identification. This system utilizes adversarial training to fortify robustness, employing a carefully selected ensemble of models to boost privacy protection. By establishing rigorous privacy guarantees, we demonstrate that high accuracy can be maintained even under stringent privacy constraints. Experimental results indicate that CE-19 models achieve comparable performance in both early identification and detection. Furthermore, we provide robustness and privacy assessments using widely available test datasets, with privacy metrics quantified across diverse data distributions. Our work represents the first effort to integrate adversarial training with ensemble methods for enhancing the privacy of machine learning models dedicated to COVID-19 detection. Ultimately, ADV-CE enables the deployment of robust classifiers that offer provable privacy guarantees, establishing a foundation for future research in this domain.
