Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing graph data, yet the intricate inner workings of graph convolution remain poorly understood. While prior research has primarily concentrated on interpreting specific, manually designed GNN parameters, we argue that the intermediate representations within a GNN are equally vital for comprehension. To address this, we introduce the Parameterized Interpreter GNN (PI-GNN), which converts a standard GNN into a parameterized version through the addition of an interpretable parameterized sub-GNN. This approach facilitates the explanation of both parameters and intermediate representations, with experimental results demonstrating its efficacy in improving a classification task's accuracy. We present a deep, wide-field optical survey of the RXCJ0232.2-4422 cluster, revealing 12 substructures. Our analysis indicates that 10 of these substructures are likely members of the cluster, with projected separations ranging from 0.1 to 0.3 Mpc. The majority of these substructures contain galaxies with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11}M_{\odot}$, suggesting they are massive clusters. We calculated the virial mass of the main cluster to be $M_{vir} = (1.0 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{15}M_{\odot}$ and determined the dynamical state of the RXCJ0232.2-4422 cluster. By examining the galaxy population, we identified 11 cold gas galaxies and 11 hot gas galaxies, with the latter exhibiting a temperature of $T_X = 7.0 \pm 0.2$ keV. Our findings suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4422 is a forming cluster, currently in the process of assembly. Furthermore, we identified 11 galaxies within the cluster that are undergoing active star formation. These results provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the LMM within this distributed environment, showing that communication costs between GPUs are minimal relative to computational expenses. Additionally, we examine how different loss functions and data preprocessing techniques influence outcomes. Finally, we explore strategies for load balancing and address specific challenges encountered during deployment. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/memory-modules. The search for weakly-interacting sub-femtometer particles is conducted through both accelerator-based experiments and natural cosmic-ray air showers. Although these approaches differ significantly in their experimental setups, they share many common analytical and interpretive methodologies. This review examines current and upcoming efforts to detect these elusive particles and their potential exotic nuclear physics consequences. We conclude by identifying several promising directions for future research. A comprehensive list of relevant references is also provided. Keywords: Dark Matter, New Physics. We present a modeling approach to examine the formation of consistent labeling systems within a dynamic environment where participants migrate and interact with neighbors to co-evolve the labeling system. This method integrates a dynamic probabilistic decision-making framework, specifically the labeled game, with an spatial migration process. In this setup, agents occupy lattice sites and accumulate utility based on their individual strategies and the local majority opinion, which can be interpreted as a labeled probabilistic decision-making game. Agents may switch sites at a specific migration rate, while their labeling systems evolve through imitation of more successful neighbors at a given imitation rate. Our results indicate that agents converge to a consistent labeling system, where adjacent sites in the migration network adopt identical labels. This consistency is quantified by the label inconsistency density—the proportion of sites with labels differing from their left-hand neighbors—which the system asymptotically approaches zero. Both the labeling system and label inconsistency density evolve over time, driven by the migration rate, imitation rate, and the expected payoff derived from the labeled decision-making game. We demonstrate that the density of cut edges in the resulting labeled graph serves as a robust metric for assessing the quality of the generated labeling system. Furthermore, we illustrate the model's effectiveness using two examples: one based on the "like" relation and another on the "greater than" relation. For the "like" relation, the labeling system achieves local consistency, ensuring that agents like themselves and their liked neighbors. In contrast, for the "greater than" relation, the system attains global consistency, establishing a total ordering of agents. In both scenarios, the labeling system consistently outperforms random labeling. These labelings are evaluated using graph theory concepts, such as equivalence relations and total order relations. Our approach is general and can be extended to model the co-evolution of various other labeling systems. Finally, we empirically validate the model's effectiveness through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. For instance, in a Twitter follower network, the proposed method successfully identifies communities. The experimental findings align with theoretical expectations. Supplementary materials, including source code and detailed results, are available at https://github.com/taiki-ito/LabelingGame. The associated paper is titled: Evolution Toward Linguistic Consistency in Labeling Game with Migrating Participants. (http://doi.org/10.21307/sigkdd.2021.2850)

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely used to solve partial differential equations, yet they frequently exhibit spectral bias, preferring to learn lower-frequency components before addressing higher ones. This paper demonstrates that incorporating a momentum term into the adversative training loop of PINNs can significantly mitigate this spectral bias. Our findings show that adding momentum not only accelerates training but also enhances the PINN's ability to capture high-frequency features. We validate these results on both synthetic datasets and a real-world scenario: estimating wind speed from pressure readings. Ultimately, we present a momentum-based PINN variant that reduces the number of training iterations by one order of magnitude compared to standard PINNs. The implementation is available at https://github.com/andreasmeyer12/PINNs-with-momentum. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be extended to other physics-informed generalized neural network frameworks.

This study investigates a coupled Klein-Gordon-Kelvin-Godunova system featuring partial damping. We establish stability outcomes for the dissipative system and demonstrate local stability for the undamped case. To achieve these results, we apply vector-valued Fourier and Laplace transforms to reduce the coupled Klein-Gordon-Kelvin-Godunova system to a first-order evolution problem, subsequently analyzing its stability. Furthermore, we prove that the operator generating this evolution is maximal accretive and possess the analyticity property for the associated semigroup. Finally, by invoking the Lax-Milgram theorem and additional functional analysis tools, we derive energy decay rates for the coupled system. These rates are not optimal; however, they improve upon previous findings by demonstrating that the coupling between waves can be weaker. Additionally, we confirm well-posedness for the undamped system and show boundedness of its semigroup using the Lax-Milgram theorem. These preliminary findings facilitate the application of the energy method to prove boundedness for the undamped system without relying on extra assumptions. Notably, we also address the absence of energy conservation in the undamped system, a condition previously required in similar studies. To achieve this, we extend the undamped damping operator to a larger space and demonstrate that its spectrum consists solely of zero, implying that the operator is maximal accretive and generates a bounded semigroup. This approach also yields a weaker coupling requirement compared to other relevant literature. To support these findings, we provide counterexamples illustrating that the weak coupling condition cannot be further relaxed. Finally, we examine the coupling effect on stability by presenting a counterexample that shows instability in the damped system when the coupling is weak. These examples underscore the critical role of coupling in stability analysis and suggest that the proposed methodology is more robust than alternative approaches. In summary, this work presents a novel and robust framework for stability analysis that is more effective than existing methods. In safety-critical domains, the ability to explain a reinforcement learning agent's behavior is as vital as its performance. However, black-box models, particularly deep neural networks, hinder interpretability because their internal decision-making processes remain opaque. This paper leverages the inductive logic programming language CLIP to generate rationalizations for trained reinforcement learning policies. By utilizing a forward inference process, we can explain decisions based on policy outputs, while a backward inference process allows us to determine which facts are necessary to derive specific decisions. We demonstrate that our approach successfully extracts both locally relevant facts and globally consistent policies. Furthermore, we show that learned policies can be transferred to agents with different architectures and states by providing them with background knowledge. Finally, experimental results on two benchmark continuous control tasks validate our proposed methodology. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of explainable inductive logic programming to the field of reinforcement learning. Project code and additional results are available at https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer1992/XMH-RL-CLIP.

We introduce a method for achieving asymmetric behavior in an isolated single photon added to a two-mode compressed state. This quantum compression triggers a significant transition in the added photon within the bipartite system. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the ASYMmetry in the reduced density matrix for both position and momentum. Furthermore, we compare the contributions of the added noncyclic and cyclic photons to this quantum asymmetry. Finally, we examine the impact of quantum deformation on asymmetry behavior in the added noncyclic photon. These findings deepen our comprehension of the noncyclic and cyclic characteristics of a two-mode quantum system. Additionally, our results offer insights into applications involving noncyclic states, such as quantum sensing and quantum metrology. Finally, the introduced method holds potential for detecting dark states in quantum systems. **Keywords:** Asymmetry, Dark state, Hamiltonian, Metrology, Noncyclic state, Sensing. This study focuses on the minimax characterization of $\alpha$-means for nonnegative functions using translates. Specifically, we examine the $n$-dimensional case where these means are defined through the translation of a function $g \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ over a compact set $K$. We demonstrate that under specific conditions on $p$, $n$, and $d$, a Fenton-type minimax result holds. Furthermore, we provide a Brunn-Minkowski type inequality that is equivalent to this Fenton type issue. Finally, we establish an asymptotic minimax characterization for $\alpha$-means by analyzing functions defined on the half-space. Additionally, we present an isoperimetric inequality for the half-space within the theory of translation means, which is equivalent to a Brunn-Minkowski type inequality in $(n-1)$-dimensional space. Notably, the Brunn-Minkowski inequality we derive holds for arbitrary measures, thereby generalizing F. Schneider's 1973 translation inequality. We also provide a minimax characterization for translation convolutions that follows from our primary findings. Finally, we outline an alternative approach to deriving Fenton-type minimax characterizations for $\alpha$-means by utilizing Brunn-Minkowski inequalities for convex bodies alongside Brunn-Minkowski type inequalities for translation means. In this context, we address Fenchel-essays' 1973 inquiry regarding whether the equality case in the Brunn-Minkowski inequality for translation bodies can occur when the bodies are not translates. This answer depends on whether a function representing the Lebesgue measure of section volumes for translation bodies can be expressed as a translation of a nonnegative function defined on a half-space. We confirm this possibility for $n=2$ using 1972-type Brunn-Minkowski inequalities and for star bodies via the Spherical Brunn-Minkowski inequality. However, this remains an open question for higher dimensions. To address this, we introduce an asymptotic characterization of translation $\alpha$-means that does not rely on any assumptions from Fenchel-essays' 1973 paper. We also establish an isoperimetric inequality for the half-space within translation means theory, which follows from our Fenton-type findings. This work extends the 1972 Brunn-Minkowski inequality regarding translation bodies. To ensure self-containment, we review the necessary background in convex geometry and translate means. Finally

We introduce an enhanced version of the liquid lithium scintillator detector, designed to investigate spin-dependent nuclear interactions within the lithium-6 isotope. This upgrade targets a significant improvement in detector sensitivity, specifically for light mass regions and spin-dependent $^6$Li channels. Furthermore, we establish that the ratio of spin-dependent to spin-independent cross sections can be constrained with greater than 95% confidence using a single nucleon species. This approach allows for expanded exploration of model parameter spaces and facilitates the cross-validation of results across different target nuclei. Finally, we examine the optimal selection of target species to maximize the sensitivity potential of this detector technology. These findings are especially pertinent to the recently proposed SuperCEvITA experiment, which intends to utilize $^{12}$C and $^{16}$O targets to search for sterile neutrinos. In that specific context, we analyze the resulting spin-dependent limits on light active neutrino mixing. Additionally, we explore the implications of combining our results with those from XENON1T and ABAR, which have established the most stringent constraints on sub-GeV active neutrino interactions to date. Finally, we outline the projected sensitivity of a large-scale LiOSE detector and its capacity to probe spin-dependent axion-nucleon couplings. This analysis demonstrates that a large-scale LiOSE detector could surpass the sensitivity of the ADMX experiment in certain mass regions. Furthermore, we show that a 10-year exposure could constrain axion-nucleon couplings down to $10^{-29}$ GeV$^{-1}$, thereby closing the parameter space for a 50% mixing angle with a 125 MeV axion. Our results also indicate that a large-scale LiOSE detector could achieve sensitivity to a 100% mixed, 71.4 MeV axion, effectively ruling out the axion window identified by the DarkSide-2k experiment. Finally, we discuss the constraints on the axion-nucleon coupling constant derived from the overlap between LiOSE and DarkSide-2k parameter spaces. This work was conducted under the SuperCEvITA project, which aims to develop a large-scale scintillator detector for neutrinoless double beta decay searches and the direct detection of dark matter, axions, and neutrinos. The study also addresses the detection of sterile and active neutrinos emitted by supernovae. Blind image restoration (BUR) is a challenging task that seeks to recover high-quality images from low-quality inputs without knowledge of the specific degradation parameters. This paper introduces a novel approach to BUR by leveraging the underlying generative process of image data, which is modeled as a mixture of kernels. The degradation parameters are estimated by maximizing the likelihood of the observed images under this model. To enhance computational efficiency, a parameterization based on the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the degradation matrix is utilized, and an efficient optimization algorithm is proposed. Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches in restoring images from severe under-sampling. Furthermore, the method is applied to reconstruct dynamic scenes from sequences of highly blurred images, yielding promising outcomes. Additionally, the method is employed for super-resolution (non-blind restoration), achieving performance that compares favorably with existing techniques on standard benchmark datasets. Finally, the method is extended to 3D volume restoration for medical imaging, yielding encouraging results. To facilitate future research, the method has been implemented in C++ and made available on GitHub. The source code, along with benchmark datasets and results, can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/BlindImageRestoration. Sebastian's contact email is sebastian.schaefer@tum.de. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a broad category of nonassociative algebras introduced recently, characterized by the presence of multiple bilinear products derived from the antilinear map $x\mapsto \bar{x}$. This paper establishes the applicability of associative Yang-Baxter equations involving anti-linear involution within the context of nonuniform associative algebras. Furthermore, we present a constructive method for generating solutions to the associative Yang-Baxter equations based on nonuniform associative algebras. Specifically, for any two spaces $V$ and $W$ equipped with two compatible nonuniform associative products $\cdot$ and $\odot$, and provided $f:V\rightarrow W$ is a two-sided morphism between these structures, the map $id\oplus f:V\oplus W\rightarrow V\oplus W$ defined by $id\oplus f:(v,w)\mapsto (v,f(w))$ yields an associative Yang-Baxter solution. Additionally, we demonstrate that the associated $R$-matrix $(id\oplus f)\cdot p_{id\oplus f}$ is both nondegenerate and regular, where $p_{id\oplus f}$ denotes the permutation operator. This paper presents a formal framework for validating the logical implications derived from specifying program behavior in a natural language that aligns with Hoare logic. This approach addresses a significant challenge in formally verifying software, specifically the difficulty of efficiently and accurately translating informal requirements into formal specifications. By formal natural language descriptions alongside Hoare triples, we propose a method that allows for the formal validation of reasoning about programs without bypassing the need to formally specify their behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using Hoare logic rules to construct proof term representations of proofs for first-order logic theorems is both sound and complete. Consequently, our framework not only facilitates formal reasoning about program correctness but also enables its automation through existing proof automation techniques. Additionally, the design supports modular reasoning about software, allowing programs to be verified independently of one another. In summary, this work provides a foundation for formally reasoning about software and offers a pathway to formally validate software translations. These tools assist both practitioners and researchers in formally reasoning about software and in formally validating their reasoning processes. This approach addresses two critical issues: (i) ensuring that practitioners do not make incorrect assumptions about software behavior, and (ii) enabling researchers to formally validate their reasoning about software. Both objectives are essential for advancing software engineering practices and fostering a culture of formal reasoning within the field. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for sharded systems that process high-throughput, low-latency requests. It features a streamlined protocol that minimizes network communication, reduces disk operations, and mitigates lock contention. However, Canopus's original design assumes all replica failures are instantaneous, a limitation that can lead to system halts when non-instantaneous failures occur. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that maintains safety despite non-instantaneous replica failures and behaviors from some nodes that violate common BFT assumptions. Compared to other existing solutions, RCanopus offers superior request processing performance. We validate these claims through extensive simulations that model various failure scenarios. Additionally, we identify novel optimization opportunities that further boost RCanopus's resilience and efficiency. We also evaluate the impact of different failure models, such as network partitions, on Canopus's performance, revealing that accounting for failure overheads is essential for accurate evaluation. Our experimental results demonstrate that, in most cases, RCanopus outperforms other BFT RSM systems for sharded architectures. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to propose specific optimizations for Canopus. We have open-sourced RCanopus on GitHub. Given its superior resilience and performance, RCanopus is well-suited for production deployment. Furthermore, the proposed improvements can be applied to other systems derived from Canopus to enhance their fault tolerance and efficiency. Finally, the methodologies used to analyze Canopus's failure behaviors can be leveraged by the broader BFT community to better understand failure characteristics and their effects on system performance. Recent experiments have indicated that cholesterol's influence on the bending modulus of lipid membranes is more intricate and significant than previously assumed. This study investigates the relationship between the bending modulus and cholesterol concentration using a coarse-grained model. We observe a maximum in the bending modulus at low cholesterol levels, aligning with prior research. Our simulations reveal that cholesterol enhances membrane rigidity by reducing the average area per headgroup and increasing interfacial tension, with the modulus scaling linearly with interfacial tension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the previously proposed scaling law, which relates membrane rigidity to the fractional area occupied by cholesterol, is only valid for very low cholesterol concentrations. Additionally, we find that the bending modulus is highly sensitive to simulation parameters, such as the spring constant applied to the initial constraint between head and tail groups. Finally, we show that cholesterol can increase membrane rigidity through two distinct mechanisms, resulting in non-monotonic behavior. These findings suggest that the interplay between different mechanisms could explain the conflicting experimental reports found in existing literature. This work underscores the necessity of conducting precise, quantitative measurements of the bending modulus across a broad range of cholesterol concentrations to fully elucidate cholesterol's impact on lipid membrane properties. This can be achieved by employing techniques capable of isolating the effects of cholesterol on both lipid packing and interfacial tension. We conclude that our theoretical framework can facilitate the design of appropriate experiments to clarify the relationship between cholesterol and membrane bending rigidity. Finally, our results indicate that cholesterol-induced changes in rigidity are more pronounced in membranes with pre-existing disorder, implying that cholesterol has a greater impact on disordered membranes. This aligns with experimental evidence showing that cholesterol preferentially partitions into liquid-disordered domains. These findings may help explain the non-monotonic dependence of membrane protein binding on cholesterol concentration. Specifically, since membrane proteins typically favor interfaces between ordered and disordered regions, an increase in cholesterol could either raise or lower the bending modulus, thereby either promoting or inhibiting line tension-driven binding. This underscores the critical role of the lipid bending modulus in regulating membrane protein binding. To fully understand cholesterol's effects on membrane properties, it is essential to experimentally determine the concentration dependence of the bending modulus in both liquid-disordered and liquid-ordered phases. We propose that this can be accomplished by utilizing nanodiscs, which allow for the independent control of lipid composition and cholesterol concentration. We have also conducted preliminary simulations on nanodiscs to support this conclusion. This conclusion is consistent with our earlier findings regarding the effects of membrane curvature on lipid binding

Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications; however, their black-box nature prevents users from accurately gauging response reliability. This paper introduces BayesOD, the first adaptation of Bayesian inference to a state-of-the-art deep object detector. By employing a novel strategy, we successfully mitigate the excessive computational costs typically associated with Bayesian methods. Our experiments demonstrate that, despite requiring more training time, BayesOD achieves detection accuracy comparable to non-bayesian detectors while providing a robust uncertainty metric for evaluating detection quality. Furthermore, our results indicate that specific components within BayesOD maintain robustness even when trained on limited datasets. Finally, we observe that integrating BayesOD with a non-bayesian detector can enhance overall performance. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/andreypavlov/BayesOD. A video demonstration of BayesOD is available at https://youtu.be/4222222222. Our implementation scores 45.4 on the benchmark task of quantifying detection uncertainty. Additionally, we explore how to leverage this uncertainty to improve object classification performance. Our approach yields a 2.5% improvement over baseline methods on the ImageNet dataset. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/_EXAMPLE_VIDEO_1 and https://youtu.be/_EXAMPLE_VIDEO_2. Our implementation scores 74.2 on the benchmark task of image classification.

Forecasting traffic flow represents a significant challenge within data mining research. A novel deep learning approach, utilizing a stacking technique that integrates multiple neural networks, has shown greater robustness and accuracy in predicting traffic flow on complete days of the week compared to models relying on a single traffic flow time series (TFTS) input. To address scenarios involving limited historical data, this paper introduces a new deep learning framework that processes traffic flow snippets (TFSN) as short, consecutive time intervals. The SNFTFS model is developed by sequentially stacking two neural networks that respectively ingest the TFTS and TFSNS. Experimental results indicate that the proposed TFTS+TFSNS stacking model outperforms a TFTS-only deep learning model in terms of mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and root mean square error (RMSE) for short-term traffic prediction. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a deep learning model for short-term traffic flow forecasting can be effectively designed to accept two sequential TFTS inputs. The findings are supported by a comprehensive analysis of traffic flow characteristics, data preprocessing, and extensive empirical evaluations. The associated code and data are accessible at https://github.com/chenyongchen/SNFTFS. A core component of revision theory involves identifying the most preferred implementations among the options available to an agent. This paper extends the concept of implementations to categories equipped with coherence natural transformations. We demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, this framework can be applied to Elgot monads within any monadic structure that includes an adjunction. Furthermore, we generalize several fundamental results from revision theory, such as the recovery property and various idempotency conditions, within this categorical setting. The paper concludes by outlining potential future applications of this generalized approach.

This study addresses the challenge of segmenting the hippocampus in MRI scans for both healthy individuals and patients suffering from Alzheimer's disease or epilepsy. We introduce a baseline approach leveraging extensive sets of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained through transfer learning. We also explore the possibility of enhancing hippocampus segmentation accuracy by analyzing the relationship among the diverse CNN training strategies employed. The trained models are evaluated using both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Additionally, we examine the utility of CNNs in segmenting hip MRI scans, which holds significant value for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. Our findings indicate that Random Forest (RF) methods outperform CNNs in terms of Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) values when applied to epilepsy cases. Conversely, for Alzheimer's disease, RF yields lower DSC scores compared to the average CNN performance across all training configurations. Furthermore, when assessing performance using Dice and Hausdorff Distance metrics, the ensemble average of 11 different CNN architectures surpasses the performance of an average Random Forest model. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the training processes, results, and underlying reasons for both RF and CNN methods. We conclude that the variability in performance between RF and CNNs is influenced by factors such as the number of annotated images and the specific characteristics of the underlying diseases. This research contributes to the advancement of computer-aided diagnosis tools for Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. The most critical component of space weather that impacts the design and operation of space systems is the flux of energetic charged particles. This study examines the propagation of protons from the cosmic ray adiabatic normalization depth to low Earth orbits (LEOrbits) using a 3D Monte Carlo code. This code is employed to simulate the transport of high-energy charged particles through the space environment, specifically modeling the diffusion of high-energy protons within Earth's magnetic field. A novel feature of this research is its focus on LEOrbits, where protons are trapped for extended durations. Consequently, these protons are absorbed by satellites, causing various forms of damage. The code was used to calculate the flux of trapped protons at LEOrbits and compare these results with trapped electron fluxes in the same region. Furthermore, the study investigates how varying the adiabatic cutoff energy influences the dynamics of trapped particles at these orbits. Finally, the research addresses the relationship between the energy of particles trapped at LEOrbits and their flux. This analysis is essential for understanding the effects of space weather on space systems, as well as on Earth's atmosphere, space plasma, and surface materials. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between solar activity and the dynamics of these trapped particles. To achieve this, the authors examined the correlation between the trapped particle index and the sunspot number across different solar cycles. This relationship is significant for understanding the impact of solar activity on LEOrbits. The research findings are also relevant to space weather forecasting, as they provide valuable data for predicting the behavior of trapped particles in space. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between cosmic rays and Earth's environment, which is essential for mitigating the risks posed by space weather to space systems and infrastructure. By providing a detailed analysis of the propagation of high-energy protons to LEOrbits, this work supports the development of more accurate space weather models and improves our ability to predict and mitigate the effects of space weather on critical space-based systems. Ultimately, this research has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the Earth's space environment and its interaction with the surrounding cosmos. By advancing our knowledge of the dynamics of trapped particles, this study paves the way for future missions and discoveries that will further our understanding of the universe and our place within it. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently become a prominent domain within machine learning. However, current GNN architectures often suffer from a lack of universal design principles, making it difficult to derive generalizable insights that can guide the creation of future models. This paper introduces the Local Structure Link Rewiring (L-SLR) skeleton, which offers a generalized definition of graph neural networks. L-SLR provides a framework to uncover the fundamental mechanisms underlying both message passing and graph convolution, demonstrating that all existing GNN models can be interpreted as specific instances of this framework. Furthermore, we propose the Pyramid-like GNN (P-GNN), a Shaw-Sammons Tree (SST)-based implementation of L-SLR. P-GNN constructs a pyramid-like structure by iteratively merging adjacent nodes and connects multi-scale layers through local structure link rewiring. This design enables the network to capture fine-grained and coarse-grained structural information effectively. Additionally, P-GNN addresses the vanishing gradient problem inherent in SSTs, thereby facilitating deeper network architectures. Empirical evaluations across six benchmark datasets show that P-GNN consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art GNN models. This work offers a universal skeleton for GNN design and establishes a robust foundation for developing future graph neural networks. Recent years have seen growing interest in private low-rank matrix completion, a technique designed to mitigate inference risks when releasing tabular data by approximating large matrices with lower rank. This study presents the Huber framework, built upon Low and Smith's (2017) framework for low-rank matrix fulfillment and Duchi, Golrezaei, and Shalev-Shwartz's (2018) framework for robust low-rank matrix completion. We provide theoretical analysis of the framework's error and sample complexity, evaluate its differential privacy characteristics, and conduct empirical tests on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our findings demonstrate that the framework can release tabular data under differential privacy constraints while maintaining data utility. Furthermore, we illustrate that incorporating robustness into a differentially private solution enhances performance when dealing with noisy data. Finally, we show that integrating this robust, private method into a federated learning context improves learning accuracy with differential privacy guarantees. We conclude that the Huber framework serves as a valuable tool for various data release and machine learning applications that require differential privacy. Notably, it is the first such solution to address these challenges within a federated learning context. To facilitate future research, we have made our code available on GitHub.

Keywords: Low-rank matrix fulfillment, robust matrix completion, differential privacy, federated learning.

The Attenuation, Polarization, and Polarization from Astrodust (PAH) (PADP+PAH) framework serves as a unified model for describing how dust affects light and generates polarization in the diffuse interstellar medium. This description relies on a singular set of dust properties, which are derived from a constrained set of physical observations. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the PADP+PAH framework, detailing its underlying assumptions, its successes and shortcomings, and its implications for future research. It is a valuable resource for researchers who are interested in studying the properties of dust in the diffuse interstellar medium. We report the discovery of a gas giant planet orbiting the young, extremely low-mass (ELM) star CIDA 1. This system was identified through the 2018 and 2019 ALMA continuum observations of protoplanetary disks around ELMs within the Chamaeleon II star-forming region. By analyzing the evolution of ALMA data from 2018 to 2019, we observed a significant change in the disk's morphology, specifically a new gap appearing at approximately 100 au. This discovery is notable because it marks the first time a massive planet has been detected orbiting an ELM star. Additionally, we present new optical photometry of CIDA 1, confirming its ELM status with a mass of 0.08 solar masses and a luminosity of 0.001 solar luminosities. Our analysis of the ALMA data reveals a gap in the disk that aligns with the expected location of the planet, which is situated at a period of roughly 1000 days. The presence of this massive planet is inferred from a surface density of at least 0.001 g/cm² at 100 au, indicating that ELMs can host both planets and a substantial reservoir of gas. These findings support the hypothesis that both planets and gas can more easily survive within the lower-radiation environment of an ELM star. This study investigates the popular puzzle "Lights Out," originally created by Simon Tatham and now widely distributed as both a free software component and in physical form for mathematical competitions. We introduce a variation of this puzzle, focusing on the challenge of eliminating all lights using the fewest possible moves. We present an algorithm that decomposes the problem into independent subproblems, each solvable via dynamic programming. This approach is demonstrated to be optimal. A key finding of our work is that the difficulty of the decomposition varies significantly depending on the board's aspect ratio. For rectangular boards with fixed height, we derive an exact formula for the maximum number of clicks required, which grows exponentially with board size. This insight enables the generation of extremely difficult instances, such as a 10-wide by 100-high board necessitating 184,560 clicks. Leveraging these insights, we propose a general method to transform any instance into one with the maximum possible number of clicks, facilitating this on demand. Finally, we examine the application of this technique in "Maximum Clicks Challenge" variations, where the objective is to reduce the puzzle to its highest-click configuration in the minimum number of moves. We outline a strategy to address this challenge and report the solutions for several specific instances. These results were achieved through a combination of custom software, strategic techniques, and human computation. This paper introduces a new total variation (TV)-based image segmentation framework that integrates image recovery techniques. The proposed energy minimization model couples data fidelity terms, which leverage established image recovery methods, with boundary regularization terms to identify the optimal segmentation. This model is grounded in the principle that segmented regions typically exhibit smooth gradients and are composed of distinct textures. The study presents a level set evolution equation derived from this method and offers both a numerical approximation and an efficient direct algorithm to solve it. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world images demonstrate that the proposed approach yields highly accurate and satisfactory segmentation outcomes, effectively handling challenges like low contrast, piecewise smooth images, and nonconvex energy functionals with local minima. Furthermore, the algorithm is robust against noise, validating its practical utility. Finally, the direct algorithm exhibits stable numerical performance, with convergence to the minimizer of the proposed model confirmed by numerical experiments. Additionally, the final segmentation results are independent of the initial level set configuration. These attributes—insensitivity to initial conditions and the ability to segment images with low contrast or weak edges—distinguish the proposed method from other level set-based segmentation techniques. Abstract interpretation operates within the framework of Semicontinuous Positively Ordered Algebras (POAs). This category includes all complete lattices, such as power sets of any set and lattice domains representing computational states with infinite precision. A POA is defined as semicontinuous when its supremum-preserving endomorphisms constitute a complete lattice ordered by the pointwise order. The operational model of abstract interpretation consists of four components: an abstract domain (a POA $D$), a Galois connection linking $D$ to concrete domains, a Galois invariant $D'$ representing program semantics, and a theory $T$ defined on the domain. This theory comprises two operators: $F$, which represents the semantics of program constructs, and $G$, which performs abstractions of programs. The operator $F$ is typically sup-morphisms from $D'$ to itself, while $F$ and $G$ together form a continuous adjunction between the powers of $D$ and $G$ to $D'$. Within this framework, the "rising phase" involves computing the least fixed point of the function $G \circ F$ for a specific input, whereas the "falling phase" involves calculating $(G \circ F)^\omega$, the limit of the rising phase. This paper introduces a new approach to abstract interpretation by decomposing the rising and falling phases into independent mechanisms. We demonstrate that the falling phase can be viewed as the limit of a chain of post-fixed points of $G \circ F$, characterized by a specific algebraic property termed "compactness." Utilizing this property, we show that the falling phase corresponds to the unique fixed point of $G \circ F$ that is both supremum-preserving and continuous. Furthermore, we illustrate that this perspective enables the development of novel techniques for the falling phase, such as approximations and sound upper bounds. These advancements are validated through a case study on loop invariant generation. The proposed solution offers a generic framework for computing tight abstract fixed points, applicable to any abstract domain, input set, or program construct. Additionally, it supports various strategies for calculating these fixed points, including abstraction before or after iteration, sound over-approximation, and heuristic methods. This flexibility allows for the easy integration of new techniques into existing frameworks. Finally, experimental results confirm the practicality of our solution. All code is accessible at: https://github.com/raphael-poux/decoupling-rising-and-falling-phases-in-abstr-interpret

We demonstrate that the intense dipolar character of the phonon mode in perovskite oxides results in profound geometric modifications of the phonon cloud, thereby altering the material's equilibrium structure. By employing ab initio calculations, we map out the phase diagram of phonon deformities across the chemical series of La1-xYxMnO3, revealing a transition from a smoothly varying trend to one characterized by non-monotonic and highly susceptible behavior. Our analysis of the phonon dispersion and the associated double-well potential indicates that these geometric phonons in the studied materials exhibit strong coupling with geometrically localized electrons, which governs the phase transition from ferromagnetic to spin glass states. This study highlights the critical role of electron-phonon interactions in this system and offers novel insights into the physics of the ferromagnetic to spin glass transition in perovskites. Furthermore, it presents a new paradigm for the physics of the ferroelectric transition in perovskites, driven by the fundamental concept of electron-phonon coupling.

Identifying anomalies is critical across numerous real-world applications, yet existing approaches often lack precision when an anomalous point is closely surrounded by normal data. This limitation stems from the fact that many current methods depend on the distance between the anomaly and its nearest normal point, rendering them vulnerable to noise. To overcome this, this paper introduces a novel framework that links anomaly detection to anomaly class embedding within the feature space. The proposed Closeness Graph-based method (CoGr) constructs a distance-based graph to embed anomaly class points into the feature space, utilizing a carefully selected subset of points that maintain the highest closeness to anomaly class labels. By isolating these closest neighbors, the method effectively circumvents the influence of noisy data. Furthermore, the Nearest Subspace Classification (NSC) strategy is developed to enhance the discriminative capacity of subspace classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in identifying anomalies proximate to normal data. Additionally, the method exhibits superior noise tolerance, and its substantial computational efficiency makes it suitable for practical deployment. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongtao1992/CoGr. We demonstrate that when the atom is in its ground state, a virtual stimulated emission process occurs, with a corresponding counterpart involving molecular dipoles. Furthermore, we calculate the electromagnetic fields emitted by the coupled atom-mirror system and determine the fields induced by the stimulated emission of virtual photons. Finally, we provide estimates for these effects in the context of neutral helium atoms interacting with various mirror materials, including graphene, carbon nanotubes, and a graphene layer. In these scenarios, the analysis relies on solving Maxwell's equations within a geometry confined to a single spatial dimension. We also address instances where this simplification is inadequate and explore the associated complications. For the applicable cases, we find that the induced effects are typically significant only at extremely short distances—on the scale of a few nanometers—though they may be amplified in ultra-cold atoms. Conversely, for a mirror of finite length, the effects can become appreciable at larger distances, though they are then confined to heavier atoms and higher velocities. We introduce an equitable understanding of graph communities, offering a novel and interpretable metric that identifies distinct subpopulations within a graph. By decomposing a graph into P communities, we apply an optimized Perron-Frobenius matrix to isolate the primary influence matrix, thereby separating the graph's connectivity into two components: within-community and between-community. This approach facilitates the discovery of localized, non-overlapping communities and provides the most significant eigenvalue and eigenvector as performance indicators for community segmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that this model, utilizing eLM-W and eLM-B features, surpasses other baseline models in both transductive and inducive tasks. Furthermore, we provide open-source implementations of these models for R and Python. This study serves as an initial exploration of equity in graph analysis, with promising future research avenues including the development of more interpretable features and the application of advanced machine learning techniques, such as deep learning, to enhance graph understanding. We investigate kinetic models governing the time evolution of enzyme concentration, specifically focusing on reversible reactions involving both enzymes and inhibitors. These models are formulated as ordinary differential equations utilizing Michaelis-Menten constants, which encode various reaction rate parameters. This paper examines the identification of these parameters from time series data. Specifically, we demonstrate the ill-posed nature of this inverse problem and propose an iterative estimation algorithm designed to recover the unknown parameters. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the practical efficacy of this algorithm. Additionally, we examine an alternative inverse problem aimed at estimating the reaction time, proving its well-posedness and deriving an explicit formula for the minimum norm solution. Finally, numerical simulations are performed to support these theoretical findings. This work serves as a sequel to [1]. Keywords: enzyme kinetics, parameter estimation, kinetic equations, Michaelis-Menten equation, inhibitor, iterative algorithm. This study reports a search for split supersymmetry at the Large Hadron Collider, targeting states characterized by compressed kinematics, one-step chargino decays, and metastable long-lived neutral hadrons. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 13.6 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment. No excess above the predicted standard model background was observed. The results are interpreted using both high-energy effective field theory (EFT) and specific supersymmetric particle spectra. The exclusion contours in EFT parameter space were extended to higher scales, surpassing prior limits. Additionally, no exclusion in supersymmetric mass parameters could be ruled out for masses below approximately 1 TeV. This work represents the most sensitive search for supersymmetry featuring compressed spectra involving metastable long-lived neutral hadrons conducted to date. Furthermore, for the first time, constraints are established for long-lived neutral hadrons with electric charges of $\pm \frac{2}{3}e$ and $\pm \frac{1}{3}e$ under the hypothesis of their decay into hadronic final states. The derived lower bounds on the masses of the decaying particles range from 150 to 700 GeV, contingent upon the specific decay scenario. These findings are expected to be accessible at the High-Luminosity LHC. A comprehensive overview of the search results is available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07701. This study examines the stochastic dynamics of termination times for significant yet non-recurring financial swells, such as real estate bubbles, observing that their durations typically drift toward a mean of several years. We propose a new diagnostics framework employing stochastic processes with time-varying rates to capture termination times that exhibit varying tendencies toward either mean-reversion or divergence. Specifically, we develop a Feller diffusion model featuring a time-varying drift, where the divergence or mean-reverting nature of the termination time is determined by the critical drift parameter. Furthermore, we design an estimation method to calculate this parameter for a specific bubble, thereby determining whether its termination time exhibits mean-reverting or diverging characteristics. By analyzing a comprehensive dataset of financial bubbles, we find that this modeling approach is highly effective for such events. Additionally, we demonstrate that the divergence parameter can be derived from the time-series properties of the switching rate. Finally, we illustrate that this model offers superior performance in likelihood estimation compared to established alternatives, including those by Hamilton (1989), Keane (1994), and Beare and Keane (2006). These findings suggest that stochastic drying-out models, characterized by time-varying stochastic mean-reverting termination durations, provide a more accurate representation of the transition into and out of bubble states. Consequently, our research introduces a novel class of stochastic models designed to capture the cyclical behavior of financial bubbles. Finally, we outline promising future research avenues, including the extension of these models to various time scales and the development of new stochastic processes to jointly model both entry and exit times from bubbles. Item recommendation systems incorporate diverse signals to enhance performance. Recent approaches have highlighted the value of user feedback, prompting the development of models that leverage reviews to generate personalized items. However, existing models face two primary limitations: first, they often fail to capture the richness of textual information in reviews, restricting their ability to extract key features; second, they typically treat all user feedback equally, ignoring the fact that items vary in quality and that different items attract different shoppers. To address these challenges, we introduce a Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) designed for items with reviews. This model first employs a text-based network to extract features from reviews, subsequently utilizing a shared attention mechanism to identify the most informative reviews. Furthermore, it applies a factorization matrix to distinctively encode the quality of both items and user sentiments. Finally, it integrates these signals to support recommendation generation. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world, real-time data demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms baseline models. We demonstrate that any Roelcke precompact collection of homeomorphisms acting on a surface must fix a point at infinity. By adopting a non-principal ultrafilter, we establish that this condition is essentially tight. Furthermore, although every Roelcke precompact collection on a surface admits a convergent constant subnet, this does not hold for the broader class of Roelcke precompact collections; in such cases, the action on the boundary of the surface is highly constrained. Additionally, we present a novel proof of a theorem by Mařík and Šemrl regarding homeomorphism groups equipped with the compact-open topology, which characterizes the maximal compact-subset-open graph subgroups. Finally, we outline several open questions concerning the characterization of Roelcke precompact subsets within the homeomorphism group of a surface. These inquiries are motivated by the phenomenon where the Roelcke precompactness of a collection on a surface fails to imply Roelcke precompactness when viewed as a subset of the homeomorphism group under the compact-open topology. We address this specific issue by identifying surfaces (such as higher-dimensional spheres) that possess point-free, homeomorphism-point-free Roelcke precompact collections. We further generalize this concept to the setting of homeomorphism groups on any locally compact Hausdorff space. In this context, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the Roelcke precompactness of a collection of homeomorphisms and their point-free variants, considering the uniformity induced by the compact-open topology. Our analysis reveals that the Roelcke uniformity associated with the compact-open topology is strictly coarser than the uniformity derived from all continuous uniformities on a compact space. Leveraging this observation, we present a unified framework for investigating the Roelcke precompactness of homeomorphism groups on compact spaces. This approach yields novel results for investigating the Roelcke precompactness of collections of homeomorphisms on compact spaces. Specifically, we establish that the Roelcke precompactness of a collection of homeomorphisms on a compact space is equivalent to the compactness of the closure of the collection within the homeomorphism space under the compact-open topology. This finding resolves an inquiry posed by M. Dales, J. K. Isbell, and J. D. Morgan. Furthermore, this result enables the identification of point-free Roelcke precompact collections of homeomorphisms on certain compact spaces, including the Cantor set and the unit interval. We introduce a new family of continuous variable splines defined on hex meshes, termed "tet splines." In trivariate space, these splines are constructed by joining "tetrahedrons" along the faces of the original mesh. Our technique leverages the specific topology of hex meshes, enabling the creation of continuous functions on arbitrary grids that are significantly harder to compute than those achievable through tesselations. We outline the underlying theory, provide an algorithm to generate these "fake tets," and demonstrate an interactive hex mesh model featuring up to 58 tets per hexahedron. Our findings open new avenues for research into continuous functions on hex meshes. The source code and interactive results are accessible at https://github.com/brunag/tetsinhex. Furthermore, tet splines are integrated into OpenSubdiv, the industry-standard tessellation framework utilized by major graphics software like Maya and Blender. This inclusion allows for the rapid experimentation and deployment of our methodology. Our work holds significant potential for advancing research on continuous functions over hex meshes. Specifically, we address and resolve several longstanding challenges in this domain, including: (i) the design of continuous subdivision schemes for hex meshes; (ii) the development of continuous variable splines on this grid type; and (iii) the creation of subdivision-based remeshing techniques that maintain continuity. Our approach meets and exceeds multiple criteria established by existing solutions. Additionally, the computational cost of our method is comparable to, or lower than, that of comparable approaches. Our contributions are detailed below: (i) We define a novel class of continuous functions on tessellations that transcend the limitations of prior works. By utilizing "fake tets," we construct functions that offer higher continuity, greater flexibility, and more extensive support than previous methodologies. Relation extraction remains a highly effective method for summarizing unstructured text using knowledge regarding entity relationships. This study examines a scenario where relation labels are multiclass categories within a knowledge graph (KG), and the target sentence contains multiple true relationships among various entity pairs. In this context, we propose a new sentence-KG alignment strategy by integrating a relation connection prediction task. This approach employs a two-stage framework: first predicting which entity pairs are connected within the sentence, and subsequently applying an existing link prediction model to establish the specific relationship for each connected pair. We evaluate these systems on the WikiRelations dataset, which links sentences to a knowledge base of relation labels. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework enhances text-to-KG alignment, boosting F1 scores in both recall and precision. Furthermore, we find that the proposed model is particularly advantageous for a scenario where the target KG is significantly larger than the one typically used during training. Finally, we provide an analysis of our system's performance on a newly constructed dataset that more closely resembles the target knowledge base. The implementation of our system is available at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee/RPG. Our results indicate that our system outperforms state-of-the-art methods, thereby establishing a new baseline for relation extraction using a knowledge base. This work underscores the potential of integrating large-scale knowledge bases into NLP tasks. Additionally, we discuss the benefits of leveraging pre-trained language models for this specific task. This study introduces a novel analytical method for simulating power converter delays via switching and dead-time skews. Dead-time skew is defined as the deviation from nominal dead time, a parameter that significantly influences the dynamic behavior of power converters. The paper presents the first analytical solution for the complete state-space averaging model of a buck converter that incorporates converter skew. Furthermore, Matlab's Curve Adjustment Toolbox is utilized to analyze the impact of skew on converter dynamics and to simulate the system's transient response. Additionally, the effects of skew on the system's eigenvalues are examined. Results demonstrate that, without skew, the converter operates in an under-damped regime; however, specific skew values can shift the system into a critically damped state, thereby eliminating ringing during transients. Ultimately, the proposed methodology enables the prediction of allowable skew limits that maintain the converter in a critically damped mode. This approach offers a straightforward and efficient means of analyzing and synthesizing low-dynamic-performance converters, which are increasingly demanded by modern power electronics applications. Consequently, this methodology facilitates the design of converters that meet stringent transient requirements. Moreover, the analysis can be readily extended to other converter topologies, such as the boost converter. Notably, the methodology is easily adaptable to any switching converter topology that exhibits skew in its averaged model. Finally, the study confirms that the proposed analysis is highly accurate, as it closely matches the behavior of the complete nonlinear model. This work investigates a non-parametric, metric-based framework for reinforcement learning. Instead of assuming a specific parametric form for the value function, we represent it as a graph within a metric space, where the distance between nodes reflects the smoothness of the value function relative to a predefined node partition of the metric space. We present a practical algorithm designed to learn these graphs in a graph-dependent manner, ensuring that a finite number of visits to each node is sufficient to accurately estimate the value function with a controllable margin of error. This margin allows for the separate control of the rough and grained aspects of the learned smoothness. We demonstrate that our proposed rough-grained smoothness offers advantages over traditional approaches, such as uniform smoothness across the state space. Furthermore, we provide empirical results showing that, compared to model-based reinforcement learning methods that rely on a single smoothness parameter, our approach enables more efficient learning when applied to various environments that exhibit different types of rough and grained smoothness. Additionally, we present a counter-example that highlights the limitations of uniform smoothness in this context. Finally, we outline open research questions concerning this framework and its connection to other areas of machine learning. This paper serves as a companion to our previous study: arXiv:2101.01131. The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) contains canonical face-selective regions, such as the fusiform face area (FFA), yet their precise functional roles remain unclear. While the relative positions of animate objects like faces and animals are well-established across species, the arrangement between animate and inanimate categories in the human VTC is less defined. This study employed high-density fMRI to map the spatial organization of these categories. Results revealed distinct selectivity zones for animate and inanimate stimuli within the FFA and the adjacent object-selective region (OFA), with selective correlations observed in both areas. These findings suggest that the OFA and FFA may serve complementary roles: the OFA specializing in inanimate objects and the FFA in animate ones. Furthermore, the location of the animate-selective region relative to the FFA showed a correlation with individual face-selectivity strength, whereas the position of the inanimate-selective region did not correlate with object-selectivity strength. Overall, this research identifies two potential mechanisms by which previously identified regions could integrate prior knowledge: through their anatomical adjacency and via the interactions between them. These insights provide a more nuanced understanding of selectivity within the VTC, highlighting the need to examine additional properties of these regions. Finally, the study offers updated maps of selectivity for key VTC regions, which can inform future research. This study introduces a new structure-preserving filter designed for high-order finite element (FE) simulations. The development of this filter is grounded in a conceptual framework where the solution to an high-order FE problem is viewed as a perturbed version of a low-order FE solution. Based on this perspective, we formulate a filter within a minimization framework that incorporates an additional term to regularize the high-order solution toward a piecewise linear approximation. This approach ensures that applied filters always drive the solution to a lower-energy state, thereby guaranteeing enhanced robustness and stability. The filter's stability and accuracy are validated through simulations of nonlinear problems in both 2-D and 3-D nonlinear elasticity. Additionally, the proposed method is compared against two established structure-preserving filters: the minimum principal stress filter and the energy filter. Numerical results confirm that the filter derived from convex optimization outperforms these existing techniques. Finally, the filter is applied to a complex geomechanics scenario involving a deep excavation in soft clay, where it successfully maintains the stability of the numerical solution. This is particularly significant for high-order FE methods, which are known to be highly sensitive to numerical instabilities. Furthermore, the filter demonstrates its capability to mitigate spurious oscillations that often hinder the stability of high-order methods in both geomechanics and general structural analyses. Finally, the filter proves effective in preserving the monotonicity of the solution. To our knowledge, this represents the first successful application of a convex optimization-derived, structure-preserving filter in finite element analysis. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang2017/Piecewise-Linear-Filter. Keywords: Convex optimization, structure-preserving filter, finite element method, spurious oscillations, high-order finite element method, nonlinear elasticity.

Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients have historically been observed exclusively during the hard-intermediate state, a regime characterized by a radio-loud transition and the emergence of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (LFQPOs) in radio frequencies. This study investigates the evolution of LFQPOs in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, focusing on the transition from the hard-intermediate to the soft state. Data were collected using the Insight-HXMT observatory, which offers a broad energy range and high time resolution. We identified a type-C LFQPO with a frequency of 0.7 Hz, exhibiting a consistent fractional amplitude of approximately 10% across both hard and soft spectral states. As the system evolves toward the soft state, the spectral energy distribution shifts, and the power spectrum transitions from a single-peak to a double-peak configuration. These findings suggest that type-C QPOs are not confined to the hard-intermediate state and may serve as a critical indicator of the radio-loud transition in black hole X-ray binaries. Furthermore, our results support the frequency mapping model, which links the evolution of LFQQPOs to the movement of the accretion disc and inner jet base. Additionally, we propose that the inner accretion flow, likely a thin accretion disc, is the probable origin of the type-C LFQPO. Finally, we demonstrate that the type-C LFQPO frequency in MAXI J1535-571 aligns with the Keplerian frequency at approximately 100 gravitational radii, a distance that correlates with the radio-loud transition. These conclusions are consistent with those of a prior study by the same group, which employed NuSTAR and RXTE data. Collectively, our results indicate that type-C QPOs may act as a marker for the radio-loud transition in black hole X-ray binaries. Additionally, the detection of type-C QPOs in the soft state suggests that the soft X-ray state of MAXI J1535-571 may be a transient feature. These insights may aid in understanding the nature of the radio-loud transition and the origin of LFQPOs. However, further investigation is required to confirm the link between type-C QPOs and the radio-loud transition. This paper introduces a new social inherent motivation framework designed for the dependable, intelligent, and safe enablement of human-to-robot collaboration. Our approach posits that a robot's internal desire to enable its partner to achieve transfer learning can serve as a powerful external signal for the robot. Specifically, when a partner demonstrates behavior that the robot can leverage for its own transfer learning, it should express appreciation; this acknowledgment encourages the partner to continue such practices. Conversely, the robot should respond positively to common behaviors that it can also utilize for its own transfer learning. By recognizing the value of such actions, the robot can foster the development of behaviors in its partner that are transferable. This mechanism is particularly critical for robot teams operating in dynamic and unpredictable environments, where a robot's own data may be insufficient to handle every scenario. In these instances, the robot's motivation to facilitate the partner's transfer learning becomes essential for team cooperation. Our proposed externalization of this social motivation allows robots to effectively communicate with one another, thereby promoting the emergence of transferable behaviors. We provide a theoretical analysis of how this motivation functions and demonstrate its efficacy through both theoretical proofs and simulations. Our approach offers a promising avenue for understanding social motivation and significantly enhances the robustness of robot teams in handling unpredictable real-world scenarios. We demonstrate that this framework enables the transferable learning of object detection and segmentation tasks between two robots. Furthermore, we show that a robot equipped with social motivation learns an object detection task 1.5 times faster than one without such motivation when performing collaborative work. We believe that our understanding of social motivation will play a pivotal role in advancing robot collaboration. This study introduces a physics-informed education-based framework for single-shot substance identification, leveraging patterns in X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) data. The method integrates three key components: first, a deep neural network (DNN) that maps powder diffraction patterns to substance labels; second, a physics-based DNN mapping that visualizes the DDN output to help learners understand the substance identification process; and third, a contrastive education-based mapping that displays the input powder pattern to facilitate the learning of distinguishing features. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using synthetic XRD data from 100 substances within the 5–150 degree 2Theta range. The proposed method achieves 99% accuracy in identifying unknown substances, maintains 100% accuracy for substances similar to the training set, and significantly improves interpretability for humans. These contributions establish a new direction for single-shot substance identification and set a benchmark for contrastive education-based teaching in science. We provide an overview of Lie 2-groups, offering a straightforward and explicit characterization of them as stacky Lie groups. Additionally, we present the characterization theorem for the delooping of a compact Lie group into an invertible Lie group. Finally, we examine the relationship between 2-Lie algebras and Lie 2-groups. In this context, we define an equivariant Lie's third equivalence as the correspondence between invertible Lie groups and free Lie 2-groups. Furthermore, we construct an equivariant Lie's continuation for invertible Lie groups with compact components by defining double quotients. Through examples, we illustrate that every double cover of a compact Lie group is a free Lie 2-group with a connected component of the identity. By viewing compact Lie groups as geometric objects within the category of Lie 2-groups, we define a dimension function. We prove the existence of a compact Lie group with a dimension of 1/2, demonstrating that the dimension does not necessarily take integer values in the category of Lie 2-groups. Additionally, examples show that the fundamental group of a Lie 2-group is not invariably an abelian group. We introduce a novel image matching approach that eliminates the reliance on feature detectors. Instead, it generates corresponding keypoint interest points and computes dense feature descriptors. By utilizing a transformer-based transformer-to-transformer transformer network (TTT), the method establishes direct links between interest points across different images, enabling the efficient extraction of global, semantic, and local scene information for matching. After interest points are refined by a keypoint transformer for precise subpixel localization, cross-cost volumes are computed to extract robust feature descriptors for each point. These descriptors facilitate robust matching through graph matching, which handles occlusions and noise through robust loss functions. The resulting match graph is optimized via differentiable matching to generate matching cost volumes for place recognition. Our code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-eth/LoFTR. Furthermore, we have established a new benchmark for place recognition in complex environments, focusing on matching interest points and descriptors that capture both global scene context and local details. Our method achieves a 3.5x speedup over leading techniques while delivering a 10-fold improvement in place recognition performance. Additionally, it demonstrates a 2x performance gain over state-of-the-art global descriptors like SuperGlue and D2-Net in homography estimation, all-rotations rotation recovery, and achieves a 3.5x speedup over the leading real-world place recognition system, NetVLAD. Finally, our approach outperforms all existing methods in large-scale retrieval tasks, achieving a 10x improvement over the current state-of-the-art. Our method is lightweight, requiring only 100 MB of memory, making it ideal for deployment on edge devices for place recognition. We have also released a new dataset for place recognition, Cityscapes-Kitti, which includes over 100,000 images from 1,000 scenes. We anticipate that our method will serve as a strong foundation for future research in interest point and descriptor matching. Magnetograms, which capture the time-dependent vector magnetic field on the Sun's surface, are fundamental for solar physics research and space weather forecasting. However, the limited sensitivity of existing magnetometers often results in derived data that is incomplete or biased. This study examines the impact of these instrumental constraints on observational datasets by analyzing over 15 years of observations from the HINODE ground-based solar observatory. Our findings indicate that the observed magnetic field vector magnetic field exhibits a bias toward alignment with the local solar vertical, a distortion that intensifies as field strength decreases. Consequently, the resulting magnetic field geometry is often physically unrealistic. We further demonstrate that a straightforward correction method can effectively mitigate this bias, thereby enhancing the quality of observational datasets. These corrected data are particularly valuable for scientific investigations requiring a precise understanding of the true solar magnetic field structure. A Python-based automated pipeline is also introduced to facilitate this correction process. The solar magnetic field data with bias correction (SOLBC) are accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen/SOLBC. This study introduces a novel method for designing large-scale demand response mechanisms. We propose a new approach combining two key innovations: (i) the aggregative game method, which offers a straightforward analytical framework for designing incentive-compatible demand response markets, and (ii) immediate load invoicing, which enables consumers to observe the impact of their demand fluctuations on the grid in real-time. We demonstrate that this method ensures participants have a vested interest in managing their demand to achieve a socially optimal outcome. Furthermore, we establish existence and continuity properties for the aggregative game and outline a practical implementation strategy. Finally, we validate the approach through a numerical case study involving an industrial facility. The results indicate that the proposed method can significantly reduce overall energy costs by optimizing the timing of energy consumption. Additionally, we show that the method remains robust when accounting for significant uncertainties in electricity prices and the specific value of immediate load invoicing. This validation was achieved by solving a stochastic optimization problem that incorporates these uncertainties. We anticipate that this method will be applicable to a broad range of demand response programs across various sectors, such as industry, services, and utilities. Moreover, the framework is adaptable to other markets where consumers can access information regarding how their actions affect the system. These features suggest potential extensions to other markets, including water, natural gas, and even non-market domains like traffic networks. Finally, we discuss how the method can facilitate the design of new demand response markets for electric vehicles. In this context, electric vehicle drivers would utilize aggregative game-based strategies to optimize the timing of their charging and discharging, while also receiving instantaneous feedback on their contribution to system objectives through the immediate invoicing mechanism. This ensures that drivers are incentivized to optimize their own operations in a way that also benefits the system as a whole. In this scenario, electric vehicle aggregators would submit to the Demand Side Administrator (DSA) the amount of power they are willing to offer for charging and discharging, rather than specifying exact times. The DSA would then determine an optimal time profile for each aggregator based on the submitted data. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents a literature review; Section 3 details the DSA mechanism; Section 4 presents a case study utilizing the method; and Section 5 provides concluding remarks. The detailed proofs for the theorems presented in this paper can be found in [1].
