The Trellis Code Combining (TCC) scheme is a multi-antenna technique that offers a substantial performance gain over Maximum Ratio Combining (MRC) with minimal complexity. It is applicable to Gray-coded modulation formats, including BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, and others. A key component of TCC is the efficient calculation of logarithmic likelihood ratios (L-values) at the receiver. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based quantization method for these L-values, designed to significantly lower computational costs. By employing a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a tailored architecture, the proposed approach enables rapid computation. We demonstrate the method's efficacy for binary phase shift keying and quaternary phase shift keying, showing that the resulting TCC variants outperform MRC in terms of error performance while utilizing only the smallest number of non-zero elements per antenna. Furthermore, the proposed scheme exhibits robustness against noise and channel impairments. Finally, the approach is equally applicable to L-values generated by other methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation. Experimental validation was conducted using hardware-accelerated simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first instance where deep learning is utilized for the quantization of L-values. We anticipate that this method will contribute to the efficient implementation of TCC. The associated code will be made publicly available. Keywords: Deep Learning, Trellis Code Combining, Likelihood Value Quantization, Hardware Acceleration.

This study examines the problem of determining if an undirected planar graph can be embedded in 3D space such that every edge is realized as a monotone curve rising from bottom to top (upward planar embedding). We introduce an linear-time algorithm for chordal graphs and a breadth-sensitive algorithm for broader graph classes. These methods are parameterized by the treewidth $k$ and the count of vertices with treewidth-dependent degrees, resulting in a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm. Additionally, we present a vertex-addition rule that maintains upward planarity. For the broader category of outerplanar graphs, we develop a parameterized algorithm driven by the treewidth of the graph minus any subset of vertices with treewidth-dependent degrees. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirected outerplanar graphs admit a linear-time algorithm for deciding UP-embedding. Furthermore, we prove that for a specific family of treewidth-3 graphs, the upward planarity problem is NP-complete. Notably, this family encompasses planar UP-acyclic graphs, thereby establishing that the UP-acyclic condition is essential for achieving linear-time upward planarity algorithms. Our algorithms rely on a novel concept: UP-trees, which extend the concept of tangles found in bidirected graphs. We show that UP-trees offer significant advantages over tangles in the context of upward planarity. Additionally, we provide a parameterized algorithm for Maximum Acyclic UP-Subgraph, which is NP-hard for planar bidirected graphs, based on the feedback treewidth. This approach yields a parameterized 2-approximation algorithm for UP-subgraphs in bidirected series-parallel graphs. The research was conducted within the framework of the algorithmic framework for UP-embedding of bidirected series-parallel graphs. Notably, we introduce a new concept: UP-embedding of bidirected series-parallel graphs, which generalizes the UP-embedding of bidirected series graphs. We demonstrate that UP-embedding of bidirected series graphs is UP-acyclic and can be linearly time-embedded. Furthermore, we establish that UP-embedding of bidirected series-parallel graphs admits a parameterized algorithm based on treewidth and vertices with treewidth-dependent degrees, and provide a polynomial-time characterization of UP-embedding of bidirected series-parallel graphs. Finally, we show that UP-embedding of bidirected series-parallel graphs is NP-complete. However, the unpredictable nature of individual contributor expertise introduces significant challenges, including noise and bias within these datasets. To address this, we propose a novel classification framework designed to filter errors from crowdsourced data through a three-stage process: first, an expert model model the human probability distribution over class labels; second, a model aggregator aggregates the predictions from the models; and third, an expert model selector selects the most likely class label based on a model aggregator. This approach is applied to the classification of Wikipedia edit revertability. Our results demonstrate that the proposed ensemble method outperforms a baseline using only the most accurate model by 1.5% in both training and testing accuracy, while also offering insights into the uncertainty inherent in the predictions. This technique holds promise for various domains where crowdsourced data is prevalent, such as image labeling and medical diagnosis. In the context of edit revertability classification, our findings indicate that a substantial portion of the data remains uncertain, suggesting that additional human involvement may be necessary for optimal classification. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that while certain contributors have a higher likelihood of being experts, others may still possess a probability of expert knowledge exceeding 50%. These results highlight the value of ensemble methods in mitigating the impact of uncertainty in crowdsourced data. Finally, our entropic metrics provide a deeper understanding of the data's uncertainty profile. This insight can inform strategies for recruiting contributors to improve the quality of the classification process. By leveraging the diverse knowledge and expertise of a large number of contributors, we can achieve a high level of accuracy in classification tasks, while also gaining insights into the uncertainty of the predictions. This approach has the potential to revolutionize the way we utilize crowdsourced data for classification tasks, while also providing a deeper understanding of the uncertainty within the data. The vortex lattice in underdoped high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors displays unusual characteristics, including a singularities-free line-width at zero field, a linear dependence of line-width on magnetic field, and a square lattice structure confirmed by scanning tunneling microscopy. This study examines small-angle neutron scattering data from underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.5}$, focusing on vortex lattice line-widths. Our findings indicate that square-lattice vortices persist up to very high fields, with a line-width scaling linearly across the entire range, suggesting that the transition to a stripe lattice is prohibited by thermodynamics. Instead, the system undergoes a first-order square-to-stripe transition, a scenario that aligns with recent STM observations. This outcome underscores the critical role of strong electronic correlations in driving the stripe order found in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed features of the square lattice can be accounted for within a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau framework. In underdoped samples, fluctuations are significantly enhanced due to the presence of meta-stable electronic states characterized by competing tendencies toward stripe and square lattice orders. Consequently, the average vortex lattice behaves as if it possesses an effective coherence length that is nearly independent of temperature and doping, thereby generating the peculiar phenomena noted above. Additionally, we explore the potential for a novel percolation-like path that enables a second-order transition between competing vortex phases. This mechanism relies on the existence of locally favored, highly anisotropic elastic properties of the electronic fluid, which may be accessible near a quantum critical point. Ultimately, our results suggest that the vortex lattice in underdoped high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates exhibits a rich variety of exotic states, such as glassiness and emergent hydrodynamics, arising from the competition between lattice and electronic length scales. This underscores the necessity of a strongly correlated electronic fluid framework to understand the vortex lattice in these materials. Notably, the elliptic flow ($V_2$) and triangular flow ($V_3$) of thermal photons show minimal overlap, enabling the isolation of the $V_2$ signal. This study presents results from PHENIX data collected at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. Additionally, photon anisotropic flow serves as a complementary method to particle flow for extracting the quark-gluon plasma's shear viscosity. Our analysis, which integrates data from both central and peripheral collisions, yields a shear viscosity over entropy density ratio of $\eta/s = 0.10 \pm 0.04$. This value is consistent with the $2/3$ prediction for an ideal gas and aligns with the constraint derived from particle flow. Furthermore, we provide the first measurement of the $V_3$ signal, observing a maximum at low transverse momentum ($p_T$) that diminishes at higher $p_T$. The combined $V_2$ and $V_3$ signals exhibit a non-monotonic $p_T$ dependence, with both $V_2$ and $V_3$ contributions peaking at low $p_T$. These findings suggest that future analyses, incorporating measurements across a broader $p_T$ range and a more diverse event sample, could significantly enhance the precision of the $\eta/s$ extraction. We investigate magnetic configurations in three-dimensional lattices composed of corner-sharing triangles. By examining a fully interacting Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice, we identify a three-dimensional arrangement of nearly classical states rich in topological defects, characterized by a finite density of such defects in the quantum regime. This configuration emerges below a secondary temperature threshold in the classical model, which lies significantly below the primary ordering temperature. We propose that these two distinct transitions correspond to the formation of this structure and its subsequent long-range ordering. Additionally, we analyze this phenomenon in the Kagome lattice and propose a novel lattice with increased frustration. Across all cases, we observe a qualitative resemblance to fully frustrated metaphosphates, offering a potential explanation for the magnetic behavior found in these materials. Finally, we discuss the relationship between this mechanism and the spin-ice scenario observed in the body-centered cubic lattice. This study is grounded in a theoretical framework that integrates the advantages of both classical and quantum statistical mechanics. New drug development frequently relies on extensive experimental frameworks involving multiple treatments evaluated across numerous patients. These studies often incorporate a primary endpoint to establish the benchmark for determining whether a new drug should advance to costly and time-consuming phase III trials. While conventional approaches rely on primary analyses to declare treatment effects, these methods often overlook the potential of secondary endpoints. Although data-driven techniques have recently been suggested to identify statistically significant secondary outcomes, they typically fail to account for multiple hypothesis testing (MHT) control. This paper introduces an alternative framework that integrates secondary endpoints via an extensive analysis while adhering to a predefined false discovery rate (FDR) target through regulation. This strategy balances the need for multiple comparisons with strict control over the type I error rate. Subsequently, we propose an algorithm designed to estimate the FDR target FDR and select hypotheses to maximize statistical power. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this methodology using a real-world case study. The proposed method is applicable to any regression setting where an extensive dataset allows for multiple comparisons, offering a valuable tool for regulatory bodies to manage error rates in such scenarios. Its utility extends beyond pharmaceuticals to include other domains, such as agriculture, where it can help identify which crop varieties yield the most significant improvements. This paper introduces QuickAR, a framework designed to automatically reformat inquiries to facilitate answer retrieval. While the Incognito system previously addressed inquiry reformulation for e-commerce by employing a deep learning model to predict reformulation candidates, it does not support multiple reformulation options. To enable rapid and effective automatic inquiry reformulation for any given question, we propose leveraging crowdsourced data. QuickAR utilizes this reformulation knowledge base to identify the most suitable candidate that resolves an inquiry. We assess the system's performance in e-commerce by comparing it against the Incognito approach and a simple baseline, demonstrating that QuickAR successfully and efficiently supports reformulation for both English and non-English inboxes. Furthermore, we analyze the quality of the incorporated reformulation knowledge to ensure it accurately captures user reformulation intent. Our findings indicate that QuickAR enhances answer retrieval performance by 10% over the prior method and by 2.5% compared to the baseline. Additionally, we show that the proposed method for automatically generating reformulation candidates yields high precision and recall rates. This paper investigates strategies for enhancing the performance of unsupervised neural networks on standard discourse enrollment tasks. We assess multiple hyperparameter configurations and employ a neural network architecture built upon the combination of Convolutional Neural Networks and Deep Sigmoid Belief Networks. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields significant improvements in crucial neural network Entrainment Distance (ED) metrics, specifically reducing root mean square errors by 20% to 40%. Furthermore, we analyze the trained networks and connect their operational mechanisms to relevant theories in conversational enrollment. This study represents an initial step toward achieving unmonitored ED analysis. Additionally, we contribute a comprehensive suite of supervised and unsupervised neural network methods for ED analysis to the publicly accessible OpenOPI platform. This work underscores the potential of unsupervised neural networks to learn complex nonlinear enrollment behaviors from raw audio data without requiring pre-labeled datasets. Consequently, these methods offer a promising avenue for future research into non-intrusive, unmonitored discourse enrollment. Our findings provide the foundation for subsequent work on automatically detecting non-compliant users and identifying suspicious activity in UN monitored camps. This research also advances the goal of non-intrusive UN monitoring and aligns with the broader objective of developing automatic methods for analyzing human-human interactions. We conclude by proposing a new research direction for automatic analysis tools to investigate changes in human behavior resulting from social interactions. This framework builds upon existing research in behavioral change analysis and contributes to the broader understanding of human behavior. We introduce a collection of open-source, web-based tools designed for the visualization and analysis of imaging data alongside spectral information. Although currently deployed on the RCSED cloud, this platform is envisioned to serve as a foundational framework for future implementations across various other cloud services or as standalone software. All source code is publicly accessible via GitHub under permissive licensing. These tools were specifically developed to satisfy the extensive analytical requirements of Raman imaging experiments conducted on complex materials and biological specimens. However, their functionality extends far beyond Raman spectroscopy, making them highly adaptable for integration with other spectroscopic and imaging modalities. Furthermore, the code is readily available for inclusion in other software packages or for deployment by researchers utilizing high-performance computing resources. A demonstration video of the tools in action is available on YouTube. We anticipate that this new toolkit will facilitate advanced multi-modal and multi-scale analyses that are currently unattainable using existing commercial software. Additionally, the platform offers scalable and high-performance computational capabilities for both interactive visualization and deep learning applications. We believe this framework will make advanced analytical workflows more accessible to a broader audience and will enhance the reproducibility of multi-modal imaging and spectral data analysis. Our goal is to foster collaboration and innovation by providing a robust software foundation for multi-modal imaging spectral analysis. We look forward to supporting researchers in their multi-scale and multi-modal image analysis endeavors. We invite feedback, collaboration opportunities, and contributions from the community. Temporal action segmentation is a difficult computer vision challenge that involves pinpointing action boundaries and dividing videos into a sequence of actions. While most current methods are supervised, learning these annotations is often costly and time-consuming. To address this, we introduce an unsupervised approach for temporal action segmentation. Our proposed Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP) learns to segment videos by predicting the co-occurrence relationships among actions. The core of this method is a self-supervised pre-training phase where the model is trained to reconstruct actions based on their context. This is achieved through a Co-occurrence Activity Matrix (CAM) that captures pairwise action relationships. To ensure efficient segmentation, the model is subsequently fine-tuned for boundary prediction using ground truth annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that SSCAP attains competitive performance compared to supervised methods for temporal action segmentation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhang/SSCAP.

Software testing education remains a critical component within computer science curricula, yet it is frequently overlooked in research. This study examines two distinct instructional approaches for teaching testing to undergraduate computer science students majoring in Artificial Intelligence: the traditional method, which delivers detailed technical information alongside standard testing concepts, and an inquiry-based method, which offers conceptual feedback alongside an information-hiding technique known as Conceptual Remarks. To evaluate these methods, we conducted an experiment comparing their effectiveness in teaching testing to artificial intelligence majors. Our findings indicate that the inquiry-based approach yields outcomes comparable to the traditional one but results in students retaining less specific testing knowledge. Furthermore, the inquiry-based approach demonstrates the potential to significantly reduce the time required to deliver testing concepts. Finally, we discuss how these results inform future directions for software testing education. Domain adjustment techniques typically depend on access to both training and labeling resources for the source domain. However, practical scenarios often restrict labeling capabilities even when the source dataset is readily available. In this study, we introduce a source-only domain adjustment framework designed to eliminate the need for a target domain. Our approach utilizes deep theory transfer to build domain adjustment models without requiring a target domain. Furthermore, we incorporate a theory-regularized unsupervised clustering loss to enhance clustering performance even without access to the target domain's labeling resources. Additionally, we develop specific strategies to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in the context of source-free domain adjustment. Experimental results across three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches. The code is available at: https://github.

This study evaluates domain-informed neural architectures for domain knowledge integration, specifically targeting the localization of particle-primary (cp)-event interactions in experimental data from particle physics. To this end, the work introduces domain-informed neural network designs formulated for event data, conceptualized as a collection of worldlines representing the temporal evolution of secondary particles. These architectures facilitate the selection of interaction times and the reconstruction of corresponding spatial coordinates. The study involves training various neural network architectures on simulated data and assessing their performance on hold-out test data. Results indicate that domain-informed neural architectures enhance both the robustness and performance of neural networks designed for interaction localization in astroparticle experiments. Furthermore, domain-informed residual connections are shown to further improve these architectural outcomes. Finally, the paper outlines future research directions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/Domain-informed-NNs. Keywords: Astroparticle data analysis; Machine learning; Event reconstruction.

Atmospheric retrievals serve as a potent instrument for characterizing exoplanet atmospheres, yet they face significant hurdles in accurately determining molecular abundances and identifying potential biosignatures. These challenges stem from numerous factors, including a vast array of molecules and their diverse chemical states, the presence of hazes and condensates, and the complex interactions between molecules. Consequently, researchers require a comprehensive repository of line lists and cross sections that comprehensively accounts for molecules and phenomena pertinent to exoplanet atmospheres. We introduce EXOPLINES, a newly developed database designed to meet these needs. This resource is optimized for modeling brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets, featuring a collection of 40 line lists that span a wide spectrum of molecules and isotopologues. These spectra were selected from established brown dwarf and solar system databases, as well as newly compiled line lists. EXOPLINES offers a user-friendly interface for calculating line lists and includes a web-based calculator to facilitate the rapid computation of cross sections. The database is accessible online at https://exoplines.space. We anticipate that EXOPLINES will become a vital tool for the exoplanet community, aiding in the interpretation of observations and facilitating the planning of future missions. Furthermore, we plan to continue expanding the database with additional line lists and cross sections. This paper is part of the exoplanet retrieval series. Future installments will explore retrieval methods, while this specific series will address the exoplanet resource aspect. This work offers a comprehensive overview of the principles of grounding, alongside current challenges and future avenues. We examine multiple grounding techniques that rely on different abstract domains and demonstrate how they can be unified under a single principle rooted in abstract interpretation. Additionally, we propose a new algorithm based on the lazy evaluation of this abstraction. Our study incorporates several illustrative examples drawn from logic programming, knowledge representation, and computational biology. Ultimately, we argue that the ability to ground programs and knowledge bases on large data sets constitutes a critical challenge for answer set computation. Furthermore, grounding and the subsequent SMT encoding serve as a valuable application domain for advanced programming and optimization techniques. We emphasize that integrating program analysis with domain-specific optimizations is a significant future research direction. Finally, we illustrate how domain knowledge can be leveraged to optimize the grounding process and reduce the complexity of the resulting encodings. Through these contributions, we aim to highlight the broad applicability and potential of answer set computation. Finally, we identify an urgent need to develop software engineering tools that facilitate the efficient grounding of large programs and knowledge bases. This demand is driven by the necessity to manage increasingly vast datasets through effective grounding and SMT encodings. We conclude by emphasizing that automating the grounding process and enhancing software tooling represent essential future directions for the field. The paper is structured to include exercises and experimental results, with several findings derived from our own research and others. Resource theories provide a framework for quantifying and analyzing quantum resources within physical operations. This study establishes a universal principle for characterizing global quantum resources via local monotones in both finite- and infinite-dimensional systems through spectral analysis. We introduce the broadest possible conditions for state transformations and demonstrate that these criteria reduce to the standard finitely dimensional ones when dealing with finite resources. Furthermore, we apply these generalized transformation rules to solve both one-shot and asymptotic problems across various quantum resource theories. Specifically, we address conversion restrictions in qubit systems using arbitrary local monotones and investigate the distillation of entanglement from unsteerable states in a broad class of infinite-dimensional systems. Finally, we discuss how to derive the optimal distillation rate within the set of free operations. These findings are expected to extend to other generalized quantum resource theories in the future. Additionally, the optimal distillation rate is expressed in a compact form utilizing two newly defined quantities: entanglement fidelity and entanglement purity. These definitions hold universal significance for quantifying quantum resources. Notably, we exhibit that these two measures reduce to existing definitions when applied to specific quantum resource theories. We introduce a framework that decouples data collection from the analysis of statistical inferences. Inferring complex probability distributions is inherently difficult, yet many such distributions can be approximated using a relatively simple set of sufficient statistics, termed "moments." Our framework addresses two critical questions: first, can a target distribution's unknown moments be estimated from structured samples generated by known moment estimates of the approximation? Second, can the target distribution be recovered given knowledge of at least one valid inference algorithm? We provide algorithms that answer the first question affirmatively for a broad class of hierarchical distributions, including Bayesian networks and exponential families. For the second question, we establish both affirmative and negative results based on the specific Inference algorithm employed. These findings delineate the information-theoretic and algorithmic requirements for inferring high-dimensional, yet sparse, structured distributions. Notably, our results demonstrate that existing algorithms are not merely practical but are also optimal from an information-theoretic standpoint. For instance, we show that the standard belief propagation algorithm is optimal for inferring exponential families. Finally, we present empirical evidence suggesting our results extend to practical, message-passing-like algorithms that are not strictly algorithmically tractable. Collectively, these results offer a unified perspective on data collection, algorithm design, and the resulting inferences. Specifically, they indicate that structured data collection can yield substantial algorithmic benefits, even when those algorithms remain computationally intractable. Furthermore, our results provide a unified explanation for why belief propagation is optimal across a wide range of structured inference scenarios. Finally, we outline a roadmap for future extensions of this framework to other algorithmic and information-theoretic settings. This work investigates the inference of non-stationary time series that follow a robust tail distribution. Specifically, it examines models where the data $y_t$ follows a $G$-AR$(p)$ process defined by $\phi_0(L)y_t = \phi_1(L)y_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_{p}(L)y_{t-p} = e_t$, with the innovation term $e_t$ possessing marginal distributions drawn from a scale mixture of normals. In this framework, the density of $e_t$ is defined as $g_t = \int \phi(\mu, \sigma) dG(\sigma) d\mu$, where $\phi$ represents a normal density and $G$ is an unspecified mixing distribution for the scale parameter $\sigma$. The study provides initial evidence that the quasi-maximum likelihood estimator (QMLE) for the model parameters is both consistent and asymptotically normally distributed. Additionally, it proposes a conditional MLE-based approach to estimate the unknown mixing distribution $G$, demonstrating that this method preserves the desirable asymptotic properties of the QMLE. Finally, a finite-sample analysis is conducted on a finite-dimensional, non-stationary, multidimensional time series to illustrate these asymptotic properties. The analysis involves estimating the unknown mixing distribution alongside the parameters of the $G$-AR$(p)$ model, followed by a one-step forecast analysis. These findings are substantiated through a simulation study. Finally, the proposed methodology is applied to the S&P500 index, analyzing its returns over the period from January 1950 to December 2020. This application includes estimating the mixing distribution $G$ alongside the model parameters, yielding significant insights into the return series. Notably, the results indicate that the distribution of returns is highly leptokurtic and skewed. Furthermore, the one-step forecast error is found to be significantly smaller than the historical variance, suggesting that the underlying data generating mechanism is likely more complex than a standard AR model. Consequently, the study advocates for the use of finite-dimensional, non-stationary, and nonlinear models to achieve a more accurate description of the return series. Finally, the estimated mixing distribution $G$ is demonstrated to be consistent with established findings from other research. Specifically, $G$ is unimodal, exhibiting a mode at a scale parameter value that is substantially lower than that of a normal distribution. Post-loops short codes constitute the most promising path toward fully practical quantum LDPC (QLDPC) codes, yet their decoders typically operate in $O(n^2)$ time due to the need for $O(n)$ message updates per symbol. We introduce a novel architecture featuring linear-time duration decoders for post-loops QLDPC codes, comprising an $O(n)$-size, constant-depth circuit. This is accomplished by limiting message updates to position-dependent neighbors, thereby achieving $O(n)$ operation and depth. We subsequently analyze the reliability of these decoders and demonstrate that any code within this family can be refined to enhance decoder performance. Specifically, we present a family of codes where the logical error rate decreases with the loop length. Our findings indicate that combining our decoder design with position-dependent loop length inflation yields a system surpassing the performance of all known linear-time duration decoders. Furthermore, we outline an open problem that could potentially enable the decoding of all post-loops QLDPC codes in $O(n)$ time with constant depth. Finally, we extend this framework to generalized post-loops codes, which are constructed from multiple copies of a base graph, and demonstrate that our decoder remains applicable to this class. This results in a family of codes exhibiting constant double-exponential decay in performance relative to the rate and block length. Additionally, generalizing our decoder to constant overhead, we prove that any constant-rate code can be decoded in $O(n)$ time and constant depth. The proposed decoder is well-suited for implementation on both gate-based and analog quantum hardware. For analog devices, decoding can be completed in $O(n)$ time and $O(d)$ communication depth using only local interactions. Gate-based implementations can achieve $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ communication depth with a multiplicative constant of $O(d)$. We anticipate that these decoders will play a pivotal role in the development of large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures. This study examines distributed algorithms for constructing distance-$r$ dominating ensembles on sparse high-girth graphs using random bitcoin mining. Following an initial seed ensemble, each unselected vertex independently and stochastically expands its neighborhood to distance $r$ from existing vertices. The analysis demonstrates that with high probability, the resulting ensemble is distance-$r$ dominating, while the size of the ensemble remains close to the theoretical minimum. Furthermore, distance-$r$ packings are derived, and it is proven that any initial seed packing yields a final distance-$r$ dominating ensemble whose size is bounded by a polylogarithmic factor of the original seed size. These techniques are extended to address distance-$r$ packings and independent ensembles within high-dimensional lattices. Specifically, for high-dimensional lattices, we establish that any initial seed packing can be transformed into a distance-$r$ packed ensemble where the expansion in size is bounded by a small constant. Additionally, we derive a new upper bound for the independent ensemble of a high-dimensional lattice, improving upon the previous bound by a single dimension. Finally, we generalize these findings to establish analogous results for hyperbolic lattices. For hyperbolic lattices, we demonstrate that any seed ensemble can be converted into a distance-$r$ dominating ensemble with an increase in size bounded by a single constant, and for lattices with a sufficiently large girth, we show that any seed independent ensemble can be expanded into a full ensemble without increasing its size. However, for high-dimensional lattices with a small girth, this specific result does not hold. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that enables the construction of large ensembles from small seed ensembles on high-dimensional lattices. The remainder of this work explores the properties of these ensembles. Additionally, we provide an upper bound on the size of minimum distance-$r$ dominating ensembles. To achieve this, we derive an upper bound on the size of minimum distance-$r$ dominating ensembles and provide a constructive proof for any dimension $d \geq 1$. Recent research has established connections between bulk-bounday, kramers, and mass-edge phenomena that give rise to topological states. While these correspondences are well-understood in Hermitian and nearly Hermitian systems, extending them to strongly non-Hermitian frameworks remains a significant challenge. This study investigates a generalized correspondence within a two-dimensional disordered elevated non-Hermitian topological insulator. Our analysis demonstrates that the bulk-eigenvalue correspondence (BEC) must be refined to the bulk-renormalised-eigenvalue correspondence (RECor), and crucially, this refinement is essential for accurately describing the conditions under which bulk, mass-boundary, and Green's function singularity regimes interconnect. These findings offer a pathway for investigating topological phases in strongly non-Hermitian materials and enhance the understanding of unique features found in Green's functions and eigenvalue distributions for topological insulators. Additionally, we present the first theoretical and experimental evidence of a spectral gap opening at the edge of a topological phase in a strongly non-Hermitian system, achieved through dephasing noise in a photonic crystal. This gap emerges at a specific mass parameter, accompanied by a transition from the mass-boundary to the Green's function singularity regime. This behavior is attributed to a corresponding spectral gap opening in the bulk-renormalized spectrum, a phenomenon predicted by our theoretical results. Our work thus introduces a novel mechanism for noise-induced topological phase transitions. Finally, we show that this transition can be reversed by modifying the spatial distribution of the dephasing strength. These results hold significant implications for advancing the fields of topological physics and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. This contribution provides an overview of the search strategies employed by the CMS experiment in 2011 and 2012 to detect supersymmetry (SUSY) at a 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collider. The analysis examines various phenomenological models grounded in both generic and highly motivated SUSY frameworks, utilizing a dataset of 5 fb⁻¹ at 7 TeV and 20.3 fb⁻¹ at 8 TeV. Key scenarios discussed include gauginos within the mSUGRA/pSSG framework, heavy and light Higgs sectors, heavy neutral vector states, vector-like quarks, and heavy first-generation vector-like leptons. These searches are evaluated based on their current limits and the expected sensitivity of the experiment, offering insights into the future exploration of the SUSY parameter space. Furthermore, the discussion addresses the anticipated experimental reach at 13 and 25 TeV, incorporating considerations of future luminosity and luminosity spectra. Finally, this analysis was supported by the funding grant 1059/12-1.

We introduce a new neural rendering approach designed for new view synthesis from a single image, focusing on creating controlled, photorealistic scenes with non-uniform brightness. Unlike previous methods that rely on 3D scene reconstruction, our framework directly learns a brightness field from a single input image, enabling the creation of 3D scenes with arbitrary brightness distributions. This capability facilitates the generation of novel effects, such as backlit subjects with bright highlights against dark backgrounds, using only a minimal set of user inputs. Specifically, we train a conditional generative model conditioned on both a background image and a foreground subject to predict the foreground brightness distribution. Combined with a view encoder and a view decoder, this model facilitates neural rendering. While the base model is optimized on a multi-view dataset, we subsequently train the background and foreground conditioners on a separate single-image dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines in both rendering quality and training efficiency. Furthermore, we show that the proposed background and foreground conditions can produce diverse, photorealistic outputs, including smooth gradients and complex lighting patterns. We introduce a novel connection between integrable conformal field theories (CFTs) and higher-dimensional gauge theories (DW-theories) characterized by dipole deformations, known as hue geometries. This dual framework features a nontrivial background comprising a nonvanishing Kaluza-Klein 2-form field strength. For integrable CFTs, this background is encoded within the coset's Drinfeld-Sentker (SD) matrix. By explicitly constructing the bulk field strength from the SD matrix, we demonstrate that cosmic chiral algebras serve as the necessary conditions for hue-kinematics duality. This relationship mirrors the role of Jacobi identities in kinematic algebra and Yang-Mills theory, thereby extending integrability-based constructions of gauge theory backgrounds and their interconnections with CFTs. Furthermore, we elucidate how gauge and gravitation interact in hue gravity, revealing that the nontrivial Kaluza-Klein 2-form field strength is essential for establishing a consistent color-kinematics correspondence. Finally, we show that cosmic chiral algebras can be derived from the reduction of exceptional generalized geometry, which also governs DW-theory. Given the success of generalized geometry in establishing connections between CFTs and 11D supergravity, it is plausible that hue gravity will similarly bridge integrable CFTs and 11D supergravity. Additionally, we provide a concise review of hue gravity, dipole geometries, and their ties to noncommutative geometry. These findings suggest that integrability-based generalizations of the Kerr-Sen construction could yield a comprehensive understanding of hue gravity, dipole geometry, and their relationships with both 11D supergravity and noncommutative geometry. Ultimately, this work establishes links between hue gravity, noncommutative geometry, and integrable CFTs, offering a pathway to explore hue gravity through the lens of integrable CFTs. This approach may enable the construction of hue gravity solutions from known CFTs and vice versa, while also facilitating the derivation of holographic correspondences between 11D supergravity and CFTs in nontrivial hue backgrounds. Consequently, this research expands the realm of holography into a new dimension by incorporating hue gravity. Finally, we propose that hue gravity offers a viable framework for investigating quantum gravity in nontrivial backgrounds, such as those found in string theory. Specifically, we highlight the potential of hue gravity to address longstanding challenges in quantum gravity, including black hole entropy, the information paradox

Piston surges, triggered by the sudden deceleration of a jet, represent a recognized mechanism for generating piston-driven shocks and plasma waves. This study presents LOFAR observations of a shock wave within the low solar corona, identified as such through its progression along a jet-driven piston surge. Utilizing LOFAR's broad frequency range, we performed multi-wavelength imaging of the surge, revealing a minor radio flare coincident with the solar flare that produced the surge. Furthermore, we detected a radio brightening in the quiescent Sun at frequencies below 100 MHz, occurring approximately 10 minutes prior to the surge. These findings suggest that both the piston surge and the quiescent solar brightening result from the deceleration of a jet-driven shock. Additionally, the low-frequency brightening associated with the surge indicates a source temperature below 10^6 K, offering insight into the temperature of shock-heated plasma. This detection represents the first clear example of a jet-driven piston surge, demonstrating that such surges are a frequent phenomenon in the low corona. The multi-wavelength observations of this surge provide a valuable case study for investigating the physics of piston-driven shocks and shock-heated plasma in the low corona. Finally, the surge may contribute to the recently proposed theory that jets are a primary driver of low-frequency radio emission from the quiescent Sun. By driving shocks through their deceleration, jets may be responsible for a significant portion of this emission. Consequently, studying low-frequency observations of jet-driven piston surges can significantly advance our understanding of the low corona. This paper is part of a series examining the characteristics of a jet-driven piston surge and its associated shocks and waves; the full series is available at https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-4339/20203850. We investigate the general two Higgs doublet model, where both Higgs doublets contribute to the electron and muon anomalous magnetic moments, thereby accounting for various flavor anomalies. By employing likelihood functions derived from Belle and CLEO data regarding rare muon decays, we establish stringent constraints on this framework. Additionally, we explore the electron anomaly within this scenario, demonstrating that the same parameter space can simultaneously satisfy the Belle muon anomaly and the Fermilab $(g-2)$_e result. Our analysis indicates that the muon decays $h\to\mu^+\mu^-\to e^+e^-$ and $\mu^-\to e^-\gamma$ are the most significant probes of new physics, with the latter reaching a sensitivity of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})$. Furthermore, we show that certain regions capable of explaining the flavor anomalies also predict a large enhancement in the production cross-section of the lightest CP-even Higgs boson at the LHC, which subsequently decays into $Z$ bosons. This offers a promising avenue for discovering the preferred lightest Higgs mass at the CMS experiment via the $h\to ZZ^\ast\to 4l$ channel. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings on the electron and muon mass ratio. In this framework, the ratio of Yukawa couplings can be substantially larger than unity, leading to a deviation from the standard $2.93\times10^{-3}$ mass ratio. We also analyze the implications for the branching ratio $\text{BR}(h_i\to e^+e^-)$, which can be significantly larger than in the Standard Model, and the partial decay width $\Gamma(h_i\to e^+e^-)$, which may be enhanced by up to two orders of magnitude. These predictions are consistent with current LEP data, which set an upper limit on $\Gamma_{e^+e^-}$ of approximately $1.5\times10^{-4}$ for a Higgs mass of $125$ GeV. Finally, we discuss the implications for the production cross-section of the lightest Higgs boson at the LHC, which can be enhanced by up to an order of magnitude. This research examines the stochastic dynamics of random swirls, modeled via a functional random differential equation (FRDE) defined by $r^{\prime}(t)=-\kappa s \frac{r(t)}{t}+\sigma \dot{B}(t)$, where $r(t)$ represents the radial distance of a particle in a two-dimensional swirl at time $t$, $\kappa$ denotes the constant angular velocity, $s=\text{sign}(\kappa)$ indicates the rotation direction, and the right-hand side comprises a "twisting" component alongside a white noise term $\dot{B}(t)$ derived from a standard Brownian motion. The equation is subject to an initial condition $r(1)=r_{0}>0$, with the singular force on the left side representing a centripetal effect and $\sigma$ acting as a noise intensity parameter. The study analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the solution as $t\to\infty$, demonstrating that the process is transient and determining the distributional limit of $r(t)^2$ using the gamma distribution. Furthermore, it investigates the role of the noise parameter $\sigma$ in the asymptotic regime, showing that increasing $\sigma$ stabilizes the particle's position. Finally, explicit computations are performed for the first two moments of $r(t)$, and limit theorems are derived for the rescaled angular position $\theta(t)$ as $t\to\infty$. These theorems reveal that $\theta(t)$ does not converge in distribution but instead satisfies a functional central limit theorem. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the asymptotic behavior remains independent of the initial radius $r_0$. The paper concludes with numerical simulations that validate the asymptotic results and illustrate the noise's impact on the swirl. Finally, the FRDE is reformulated as an ordinary differential equation (ODE) on a half-open interval, and this alternative perspective is employed to derive the aforementioned results. This approach offers a novel framework for analyzing similar swirl dynamics, enabling the calculation of the density of $r(t)^2$ via the Laguerre polynomial family and determining the mean and variance as explicit functions of the model parameters. Additionally, the first exit time is analyzed, and its mean and variance are expressed in terms of the fractional exponential integral. Finally, the asymptotic behavior of particle trajectories is investigated, revealing that while the asymptotic angle distribution is not unique, it can be characterized through an approximation. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to expose the unique characteristics of bosonic systems. By directing $N$ indistinguishable photons through an interferometer with various coupling strengths, the resulting output probability distributions display significant interference effects. To investigate the entanglement inherent in this process, we examine the many-body quantum states of photons at the interferometer's output. We derive a method to represent these complete output states in Fock space and subsequently define a measure of many-particle entanglement based on the purity of the reduced substates. Our findings indicate that output purity rises as the number of interfering photons increases, peaking at intermediate coupling strengths, a trend that aligns with the evolution of entanglement. Furthermore, the maximum entanglement is determined by the number of available transverse modes. These results offer both a theoretical and experimental means to assess the entanglement generated during boson sampling. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the fundamental role of many-particle entanglement in producing the distinct phenomena observed in this quantum model. Finally, the proposed metrics for output purity and entanglement can be extended to broader bosonic many-body problems. Specifically, the approach to characterizing entanglement in boson sampling inputs and outputs is demonstrated within the context of entangled sources. This reveals that the entanglement arising from source preparation competes with that generated during interference, establishing an optimal range for the number of input modes. These insights provide a foundation for future experiments aimed at maximizing entanglement in boson sampling. The accompanying Python code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumEngineeringGroup/boson-sampling-purity-and-entanglement. Keywords: Boson sampling, entanglement, quantum information. Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently demonstrated the capability to master complex tasks within fully observable settings. However, real-world scenarios are often only partially observable, a challenge that tests the memory capacity and temporal reasoning of RL agents. This paper introduces a novel recurrent architecture designed for such environments, featuring two key innovations: a convolutional state memory bank and a conviction module. The memory bank retains the history of past observations, which the conviction module filters to identify the most reliable information. This stored history is then projected into a lower-dimensional state space, which, along with the action, is optimized by an RL agent. Experimental results on three Atari games and a non-trivial grid environment indicate that this architecture effectively handles partial observability, outperforming other methods that utilize similar approaches to partial observability like Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Double DQN. Additionally, the architecture is shown to improve the sample efficiency of DQN on a matrix game. Finally, we present a simplified version of the "Chase" game to illustrate the algorithm's interpretability. Through this example, we show that the architecture's internal state representation is intuitive and that the trained network's decisions can be explained based on its perception of the environment. This contrasts with the black-box nature of Deep Neural Networks, which do not exhibit these properties. The source code is available at: https://github.com/alexei-tsvetkov/Recurrent-QLearning. Our findings suggest that the proposed architecture can serve as a foundation for developing more interpretable and robust agents for interacting with partially observable environments. Furthermore, the architecture's favorable sample efficiency and clarity of decisions may facilitate the application of machine learning in various domains, including robotics and medicine. The primary challenge in human action detection is identifying contextually relevant video segments while filtering out irrelevant or distracting ones. While visual cues often guide human attention, they fail in cases where the object of interest is visually similar to other objects. Furthermore, existing methods typically rely on visual features to learn discriminative representations, neglecting the learning of task-specific importance criteria. To address this, we introduce a data-driven approach that utilizes contextually relevant examples to weakly guide action detection. Our method employs two components: a context graph that models the relationships between objects and scene regions, and a GCN-based classifier that leverages contextual examples for detection. Additionally, we developed a novel action detection dataset, UCSD-Act, comprising 100 hours of untrimmed video with annotations for object relevance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/zhongtaoact/UCSD-Act.

This paper details the methodology, results, and key findings from the second Image Resemblance Challenge (IRC2021), organized by the European Society for Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing, and Geoinformation Information Science. The primary objective was to develop and evaluate a metric for capturing the visual resemblance between two images. The dataset comprised four classes: two comprising semantically similar images with comparable compositions, and two with similar content but differing compositions. The competition was won by a multi-modal transformer-based approach that integrated image-text pairs with a Perceptual Loss component. Second-place results were achieved by a VITL-based model utilizing a multi-head attention mechanism to aggregate patches into a single image representation. Other leading methods leveraged contrastive learning techniques, including Siamese networks, masked autoencoders, and vector-quantized autoencoders. Notably, a simple baseline model that averaged feature representations from various vision transformers ranked fourth, demonstrating that current vision transformers are already effective at encoding image similarity. Overall, most winning strategies employed contrastive learning frameworks, which aligns with current research trends. However, a future direction involves exploring more robust training schemes that mitigate overfitting to specific dataset characteristics. Furthermore, while a straightforward baseline performed well, indicating that simple, lightweight models could be viable alternatives to complex state-of-the-art architectures, this remains an area for further investigation. Finally, developing a metric that extends beyond 2D image similarity to encompass 3D data, such as point clouds, would represent a significant advancement. Such a metric would be highly valuable for various geospatial applications, including change detection, 3D mapping, and the analysis of time-series data. Ultimately, a robust image similarity metric is essential for the automated processing of large-scale image datasets. Its applications range from image classification and object detection to change detection and object tracking. By mitigating class imbalance and alleviating the need for manual annotation, these methods can significantly enhance the performance of numerous machine learning models. This work demonstrates that contrastive learning can yield impressive results even without extensive training, offering a promising pathway for future research. Furthermore, the image similarity metric introduced here is valuable for a wide array of geomatics applications, including change detection, 3D mapping, and time-series analysis. Specifically, in change detection, the metric facilitates the automatic identification of similar patches across two datasets, thereby reducing the manual effort required for labeling. This capability is particularly advantageous when working with high-resolution satellite imagery, where the volume of data to be processed is immense.

This chapter explores diffusion processes and semigroups that degrade toward diffusionless mechanisms, highlighting the frequent and significant impact of perturbations—such as nonlinear reactions—on the resulting limiting theory. A recurring phenomenon driven by this interaction between degradation and perturbations is the criticality problem: determining the necessary characteristics of a perturbation to sustain nontrivial stationary solutions. We examine a model featuring a small, singularly rescaled parabolic equation driven by a specific class of nondegenerate potentials, the diffusion approximation, metastability within a broad class of degenerate problems, and the homogenization of such equations in periodic media. Although these topics are not directly interconnected, they are unified by a shared underlying mathematical structure. The first two sections focus on scenarios where the primary mechanism is the competition between a nonlinear reaction and a nondegenerate potential, exemplified by the theory of criticality in semigroups and the criticality problem for equations featuring a small, singularly rescaled parabolic term. The third section addresses equations characterized by a degenerate potential; here, the defining feature of the degenerate scenario is that the semigroup generated by the equation is typically not ultracontractive, a property essential for standard semigroup techniques. This section covers the spectral gap problem and metastability. Finally, the fourth section investigates the homogenization of degenerate equations within a periodic medium, demonstrating how effective operators emerge from the superposition of a fractional power of the Laplacian and a periodic potential. Collectively, these diverse areas illustrate how degeneration transforms the fundamental architecture of parabolic problem-solving. Specifically, the ultracontractivity of the semigroup is pivotal for establishing optimal extinction rates, a key aspect of criticality analysis, and metastability relies on spectral gap estimates. Furthermore, the spectral gap problem serves as a natural extension of criticality analysis, as the existence of a spectral gap is essential for deriving optimal convergence rates toward equilibrium states. Ultimately, this chapter aims to elucidate the distinct features of degenerate equations and to outline several open questions within this field. Readers with a background in parabolic equations will find that the core techniques and concepts presented here are accessible, provided they are willing to navigate a variety of specialized examples. The various definitions and notations employed herein may differ from those used in individual research papers, yet the fundamental techniques and concepts remain consistent. We have made every effort to ensure clarity regarding the origins of these differences. This work serves as an introduction to the fascinating and vibrant field of degenerate parabolic equations, offering an overview of current research

Federated Learning (FL) has become a promising approach for training machine learning models across multiple clients while safeguarding data privacy and enabling cross-client collaboration. However, FL faces significant hurdles, including privacy risks, low communication efficiency, and extended training durations. To address these issues, we introduce a novel privacy-preserving FL framework designed for educational data, termed "Confidential & Communication-Efficient Federated Education" (DP-REC). This framework integrates a lightweight, privacy-focused algorithm called "Differential Privacy Recommendation" (DP-REC) with a high-performance, privacy-aware communication strategy. DP-REC serves as a confidential filter that reduces the feature space for clients, thereby minimizing communication overhead. Concurrently, the high-performance, privacy-aware strategy dynamically adjusts the frequency of model updates based on the confidentiality levels of each client. Our evaluation results demonstrate that DP-REC significantly lowers communication costs while maintaining high training performance and ensuring robust data privacy. Furthermore, we assess the practicality of DP-REC using real-world education datasets, with source code available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2019/DP-REC. Source code for real-world applications can be found at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2019/FL-EDU-PIR. Both implementations support cross-platform federated learning for education, including Android and iOS mobile devices. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus, Perseus, Auriga, and Ophiuchus molecular clouds using the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) to study the FUV fields illuminating these sources of active star formation. By analyzing FUV images alongside existing radio and submillimeter data, we identified young stellar objects (YSOs) and their associated FUV-emitting regions. Our results indicate that FUV emission is primarily driven by newly formed stars, with the intensity of FUV fields varying significantly across different clouds. Specifically, Taurus, Auriga, and Ophiuchus exhibit FUV fields comparable to the local interstellar medium, while Perseus displays a field roughly ten times stronger. Furthermore, GALEX FUV observations reveal that YSOs in these regions are often embedded in bright FUV-emitting clouds, suggesting that FUV radiation from young stars may play a critical role in the evolution of molecular clouds and the subsequent formation of new stars. Finally, we present a catalog of FUV-emitting regions and their associated YSOs for these clouds, which will facilitate future multi-wavelength studies of FUV illumination in star-forming regions. This catalog is accessible at http://www.astro.pku.edu.cn/~zhangyq/fuv_catalog.html. Ultimately, this study represents the first survey of FUV illumination in young star-forming regions, with the catalog serving as a valuable resource for FUV investigations of young stellar objects. Modern document retrieval systems are essential for large-scale search environments. Recent advancements have introduced deep neural network-based ranking models utilizing graph neural networks to enhance retrieval accuracy. However, these models depend on carefully designed graph structures and high-quality feature representations, which are labor-intensive to construct and often fail to automatically adapt to the specific characteristics of retrieval tasks. This paper introduces a graph neural network retrieval model that effectively addresses these challenges by automatically learning representation embeddings for document tables. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a numerical study on the PDF Table Retrieval (PTR) task, showing that it generates high-quality embeddings that integrate both local and global table information. Additionally, we present the first graph neural network model applied to OCR text retrieval, which produces competitive results compared to established baselines. The code is accessible at https://github.com/yzhang124/GraphTable. This work underscores the potential of graph neural networks as a general-purpose representation encoder for document retrieval. Our findings indicate that such models can automatically learn task-specific representations, thereby reducing the need for manual engineering and expanding the applicability of graph neural networks to novel retrieval domains. The proposed model is expected to be valuable for PDF retrieval tasks, including chart retrieval, graph extraction, and document ranking. Furthermore, extending this approach to web pages could significantly improve the performance of web chart retrieval systems. Our approach is well-suited for retrieval tasks where only partial text is available, such as charts, formulas, and tables. We establish a general framework for analyzing games characterized by incomplete knowledge, interpreting them as a sequence of one-shot signaling interactions among players who evolve cognitive structures through Bayesian updating. Our primary finding demonstrates that a comprehensive equilibrium in these games can be significantly simplified by reducing the search scope to a set of signaling games where the signaling component adheres to David P. Wilkins' (2017) definition of "honesty." This result extends the fundamental theorem of signaling games, which links Bayesian Nash equilibria (Sobel, 1996) to honest signaling, to the context of multi-stage games. The proof relies on the concept of sequential stability, which ensures that no player can enhance their expected utility by deviating from the established cognitive structures. Furthermore, we illustrate the framework's applicability to scenarios involving the accumulation of signaling information over time, such as the gradual revelation of a player's type. The proposed framework holds significant implications for modeling long-term interactions, including reputational dynamics. Our findings rest on the assumption that players update their beliefs based on all prior signaling history. The framework's validity is supported by evidence from various theoretical and empirical studies in cognitive science regarding human belief revision. Specifically, we demonstrate the framework's consistency with several prominent models of human belief revision, notably the Bayesian framework. Additionally, we present experimental evidence indicating that the assumption of cumulative belief updating is consistent with actual human behavior. Consequently, we conclude that our framework offers a robust method for investigating signaling phenomena within games of incomplete knowledge. Ultimately, these outcomes will contribute to more effective resource allocation and poverty alleviation efforts. This study introduces the first fully false-positive-free collection, filtering, and membership inquiry structures. The proposed algorithm enables the creation of a compact collection of $n$ distinct items using only $O(n)$ bits of space. Any item not in the set is detected with certainty, while items that are present are located with a space complexity of $O(\log\log\log(1/\delta))$ bits, where $\delta$ represents the failure probability for non-members. This error-free collection approach is subsequently integrated with techniques from approximate filters to develop the first fully false-positive-free approximate member inquiry and filtering structures. In these frameworks, a random bit string of size $s = \omega(\log n)$ is generated; a non-member is identified with certainty, whereas a member is found with high probability, requiring $s = \omega(\log n) + O(\log\log\log(1/\delta))$ bits, with $\delta$ denoting the failure probability for non-members. Furthermore, an approximate membership inquiry structure achieves a query time of $O(1 + \log\log\log(1/\delta))$ and uses $O(\log\log\log(1/\delta)) + s$ bits, where $s$ denotes the time required to locate a random bit string containing exclusively 1s generated by a biased coin flip that returns 1 with probability $\epsilon = \omega(1/n)$. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the fully false-positive-free collection scheme is nearly optimal by proving a lower bound of $\Omega(n - \log\log\log(1/\delta) + (1/\delta)\log n)$ bits, which is just one $\log\log\log(1/\delta)$ bit away from the achievable upper bound. Consequently, the primary trade-off involves $\log\log\log(1/\delta)$ bits of space in exchange for guaranteed certainty. Notably, this research also investigates whether the fully false-positive-free collection strategy can be made sublinear in space; however, we establish that any such collection must occupy $\Omega(n)$ bits, indicating that the proposed scheme is optimal within the class of sublinear-space structures. Finally, the paper concludes by presenting an open problem: determining if any data structure exists that can store $n$ items in $o(n)$ bits while maintaining 100% certainty in both collection and locating non-members. This paper introduces a new framework designed to resolve the persistent challenges in Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH): noise reduction, area projection errors, and the accurate handling of free surface boundary conditions. The proposed approach is an extension of the Multi-Scale Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (MS-SPH) method originally developed for single-phase flows. It incorporates a novel variable kernel approximation to eliminate area projection errors and maintains a stable, well-resolved free surface through the synergistic use of two distinct artificial viscosity terms and a new artificial compressibility formulation. The method's validity is confirmed by a convergence test, and it is applied to complex two-phase fluid-structure interaction problems, demonstrating excellent agreement with existing literature and revealing new insights. The framework effectively mitigates the aforementioned issues, yielding stable and accurate results even in scenarios involving close-range interactions. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robust performance in handling fluid-structure boundary conditions, even when boundary particles are relatively coarse. These findings establish the method as a promising tool for future applications in fluid dynamics and fluid-structure interaction research. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andreafiorucci/ms-spah. Machine learning is expanding rapidly, yet the computational demands of training large models often make quantum-enhanced alternatives attractive. We introduce QML Variational Models (QVMs) that require fewer hyperparameter optimizations, exhibit greater model capacity, and can be learned unmonitored or monitored via batch gradient descent. Implemented end-to-end in PennyLane, these QVMs are accessible on any hardware capable of executing their constituent operations, such as the Qutria-1 (3-level) and Quantinemu-1000 simulators, as well as the IQM 43-qubit Sycamore processor. Our findings demonstrate a significant improvement in final test accuracy for classification tasks when utilizing QVMs, particularly in monitored scenarios under low noise conditions. Additionally, we explore hybrid quantum-classical architectures where classical layers are optimized alongside quantum layers, a configuration that further boosts performance in low-noise environments. We conclude by identifying potential future enhancements to QVMs, including the integration of quantum kernel methods, state preparation and measurement (SPAM) error mitigation, and other emerging quantum machine learning techniques. The provided code allows for customization regarding the selection and configuration of quantum kernels, space complexity, and specific task selection. This work establishes a promising foundation for future research into more powerful, efficient, and accessible quantum-enhanced machine learning models. Pitch-shifting is a fundamental operation in speech processing that typically involves two approaches: source-model based systems, which utilize a synthesizer to re-synthesize speech from an acoustic model, and time-frequency (TF) based methods, which directly shift the spectrum of speech. TF-based techniques are generally computationally efficient, yet they often compromise perceptual quality and degrade timbre. This paper introduces Pitch Augmentation, a novel TF-based approach that applies pitch augmentation to speech. This method enhances both timbre and pitch manageability without significantly increasing computational costs. We evaluate several Timbre-preserving pitch-shifting algorithms (TPPA) and incorporate them into the pitch-shifting layer of FastPitch, a neural network-based system. Experimental results demonstrate that these methods effectively improve timbre while successfully managing pitch. Additionally, we conducted an ablation study on the pitch-perception layer of FastPitch, showing that these pitch-shifting techniques also yield significant improvements in pitch-perception. This paper introduces Hopper, a novel Transformer-based framework designed for multi-hop inference in spatiotemporal applications. In these contexts, the outcome of one prediction step serves as input for the subsequent stage, a process referred to as multi-hop inference. This approach is essential in multi-agent systems where actions are interdependent and in dynamically evolving environments that must be predicted sequentially. We demonstrate that Hopper can integrate state-of-the-art Transformer-based inductive graph neural networks, such as Performer and Performerformer, enabling them to execute multi-hop reasoning. Furthermore, we establish empirical evidence showing that Hopper enhances both performance and sample efficiency compared to leading single-hop baselines. Finally, we validate the utility of Hopper within multi-agent reinforcement learning by applying it to two prominent game environments. Additionally, we illustrate its application in predicting short-term traffic congestion, highlighting its potential for real-world spatiotemporal decision-making. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/Hopper. All experimental results are available at https://github.com/DeepMind/Hopper/tree/master/hopper-experiments. A new method is introduced to isolate $WW$ events from the dominant $t\bar{b}$ signal and background. The resulting $W$ boson mass is determined to be $M_W = 80.28 \pm 0.65$ GeV, where the uncertainty of 0.65 GeV reflects a systematic limit achievable with the current dataset. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective solutions for remote scenario monitoring and support. While optimal control depends on understanding user needs and preferences, existing literature has failed to adequately examine human factors in TPR control. To address this gap, we developed a new interactive user experience (UX) evaluation method for TPR control that engages participants in an experiment to assess their own performance. This new approach revealed that users often struggle to control the robots, leading to significant performance losses. To gather comprehensive insights for future research, we conducted a user study with 15 participants. Our findings indicate that only 10% of users successfully reached their targets, whereas 90% failed to reach them. Additionally, we identified a critical phenomenon: when TPRs move at high speeds, they induce motion sickness in users. These insights are essential for developing more intuitive TPR control strategies. To validate our method, we performed a replication study with 16 participants, confirming that the performance outcomes of the initial study were reproducible. Finally, we summarized the motion sickness issue and its underlying causes to provide a basis for future research. This study offers a fresh perspective on the human factors associated with TPR control. By evaluating user performance, we uncovered a previously unknown motion sickness issue, underscoring the necessity for more intuitive control methods. Furthermore, the experimental results suggest that a motion model incorporating human sensory perception could enhance both tracking and path planning for TPRs. Ultimately, this research expands the scope of TPR technology by deepening our understanding of human factors, with potential applications in other mobile robot domains. The complete code and codebook for this study are available at: https://github.com/robertorodriguez/TPR-QoE-Evaluation. Our results demonstrate that the interactive QoE evaluation method is effective for assessing TPR user performance and successfully uncovered a novel motion sickness problem. Mafia, or Werewolf, is a widely enjoyed social game of deduction. In this scenario, two rival groups operate in the dark: civilians must identify which of the other players belongs to the opposing faction, while members of the rival groups remain concealed as they strive to expand their numbers. This work details a numerical simulation of the game that reveals optimal strategies for all three groups and establishes a mathematical model of Mafia as a two-player game with imperfect information. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between this game and other problems in game theory, specifically including the "Beauty Contest" game. Finally, the paper examines the anticipated outcomes when human participants play Mafia. This research constitutes a doctoral thesis. For an accessible introduction to the concepts discussed, we recommend viewing a video version of this work available in English on YouTube. Additionally, we have released a computer program that implements the Mafia game, which can be downloaded from our website. This program includes a user-friendly interface and an intelligent AI capable of playing as either a Mafia member or a civilian. We believe this tool will be valuable for individuals wishing to learn the game or to assist those aiming to refine their skills. Keywords: game theory, perfect information, imperfect information, mean field, beauty contest.

This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering technique designed for high-dimensional data, termed the entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (Enfwk-m). In many real-world datasets, specific data points within certain dimensions are more critical than others. To address this, we developed an Enfwk-m method capable of automatically assigning weights to each dimension based on their significance. To evaluate these weights, we employed the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the original data distribution and one where each dimension is treated as uniform. Additionally, to enhance computational efficiency, we implemented a stochastic clustering algorithm. A comprehensive set of experiments was conducted to assess the superior performance of this approach. Our findings indicate that the Enfwk-m method achieves high accuracy in clustering high-dimensional data, outperforming existing state-of-the-art fuzzy k-means approaches. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness across diverse scenarios, including cases with missing data and varying cluster shapes. Finally, the method's effectiveness is illustrated through its application to the analysis of gene expression data in breast cancer research. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChunyanLi1990/Enfwk-m. Keywords: fuzzy clustering, high-dimensional data, dimension weight, Kullback-Leibler divergence.
