Quantum gravity frameworks often possess a global symmetry that is disrupted solely by the curvature of an expanding universe. Although this symmetry remains unbroken in flat space—imposing constraints on gravitational wave polarization and the nature of gravitational wave sources—it is reactivated as the waves propagate through the evolving background, creating conflicts with observations from specific sources. A potential resolution to this tension involves the presence of independent global symmetries, which significantly alters the disruption mechanism of the worldwide symmetry and modifies the associated constraints. In this study, we demonstrate that in the absence of modified gravity, global symmetries in all examined quantum gravity models impose a strict limit on global symmetry disruption, regardless of the gravitational wave source. This constraint remains valid even when accounting for cosmological birefringence, a phenomenon that rotates the polarization plane of gravitational waves during propagation. Specifically, we establish that the probability of symmetry breaking, $P$, must satisfy $P \leq 10^{-16}$ at 95% confidence level, utilizing data from the LIGO-Virgo binary black hole mergers GW150914, GW170104, GW170814, GW170817, GW170608, and GW170818. This methodology is applicable to any future gravitational wave source. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of global symmetry contributions to gravitational waves is limited by the same symmetry constraints found in the linearized regime, thereby establishing a new set of global symmetry rules in quantum gravity. Furthermore, we illustrate that these bounds can be achieved in a phenomenological quantum gravity framework featuring a gravitino fermion, where the global symmetry arises from a $U(1)$ gauge symmetry. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for quantum gravity models where gravitinos are massive. This suggests that precision gravitational wave astronomy will play a crucial role in constraining the structure of the low-energy effective action within quantum gravity theories. This approach offers a novel strategy for investigating the low-energy structure of quantum gravity, a field currently undergoing a transformative era driven by gravitational wave observations. This represents a new paradigm where gravitational wave astronomy serves as a powerful tool for constraining quantum gravity structures, complementing traditional theoretical methods. Such a methodology is expected to yield a wide array of novel and stringent constraints within the quantum gravity community. This study presents the initial UVIT survey of the globular cluster NGC 4147, conducted on the night of 18 July 2018. The primary objective was to identify UV-luminous stars, with a specific focus on detecting a potential blue straggler (BS) by comparing our findings with optical observations of an identical BS in this cluster. Our analysis identified 10 faint clusters, with UV 0 mag magnitudes ranging from 19.3 to 22.9. We detected a BS with a bolometric mass of 0.8 solar masses and a luminosity of 3.2 L☉. This BS is the most UV-luminous star in NGC 4147, exhibiting a color index of 0.7. Its optical characteristics align with those of the BS observed in the same cluster, while its UV properties are distinct. Our findings suggest that BS formation in UV-luminous stars may not follow a single formation channel. Additionally, we identified 10 red stragglers (RSs) with a mean age of 12.5 billion years. Our results indicate that RSs are generally less UV-luminous than BSs, though some RSs display UV luminosities comparable to certain BSs. We conclude that RSs are typically less massive than BSs, with masses averaging 0.7 solar masses and luminosities around 1.5 L☉. Furthermore, the study confirms that RSs are predominantly red in color. These results provide valuable insights into the nature and evolution of UV-luminous stars within globular clusters. This article offers a comprehensive overview of the Mumford stability criterion, demonstrating its application in constructing compact geometrical structures known as Hilbert schemes of points. The presentation includes a complete solution to the two-dimensional case and an examination of connections to vertex algebras and B-twist string field theory. Additionally, I have expanded upon B-fields derived from fermionic vertex algebras and demonstrated their stability under the Frobenius action. A significant component of this work is the development of a b-action on fermionic vertex algebras, which I term the "fragile b-action." Building on this, I define modules for the b-action and illustrate how to utilize them to compute cohomology groups that extend the standard homology of Hilbert schemes of points. Furthermore, I outline an elementary construction of Hilbert schemes of points on $\mathbb{C}^2$ that aligns with the cohomology groups derived from the fragile b-action. This research was inspired by the remarkable work of Berenstein and Jordan, who provided a quantum field theoretic description of Hilbert schemes of points as the cohomology of a specific complex. Their findings suggest that Hilbert schemes of points on higher-dimensional affine varieties can be described through sigma models based on higher-dimensional $c=1$ conformal field theories. In this context, I demonstrate that conformal field theories constructed from fermionic vertex algebras yield topological sigma model solutions represented by B-fields. Transferability is a vital capability for deep learning, underpinning numerous applications like transfer learning and knowledge transfer. This study re-examines two core agreements regarding transferability: (1) the transferability of deep learning to other tasks, and (2) the transferability between distinct architectures. To address these questions, we introduce an experimental framework for transferability that covers diverse source tasks, target tasks, and source architectures. Through comprehensive experiments utilizing this framework, we empirically validate and refine existing theoretical and practical perspectives on transferability. Our key findings indicate that for a specific target task, learning a more generalized representation typically enhances transferability. Conversely, for a given source task, transferability improves when the target model is more specialized. Furthermore, empirical evidence suggests that transferability varies across different components of the target task, such as the feature extractor and the classifier, which may necessitate the development of task-specific transferability strategies. This paper offers a systematic re-evaluation of deep learning transferability, providing valuable insights for the design of transfer learning strategies and regularizers. Additionally, it introduces a practical, system-based framework for transferability that can be readily adapted for specific applications. Finally, we outline several promising future research directions concerning transferability.

**Keywords:** Transferability, Transfer Learning, Deep Learning, Representation Learning, Generalization.

High levels of net social interconnectivity enable rapid information dissemination, a process significantly influenced by a rumor's appeal and the presence of structural barriers like highly connected subgroups within the social network. A highly contagious piece of news travels quickly but is quickly forgotten, whereas a compelling narrative spreads slowly yet endures. We demonstrate that network modularity acts as a specific structural constraint on a rumor's capacity to propagate effectively across a social network. Our theoretical framework utilizes the degree of modularity alongside the appeal and infectivity of the rumor to forecast both the dissemination speed and the eventual penetration across the entire population. Our predictions regarding transmission velocity and long-term spread align with agent-based simulations of information flow on synthetic and real-world social networks. These findings offer structural guidance for organizations aiming to accelerate the spread of critical updates or sustain the reach of persuasive content over time. Additionally, they provide insight into why certain compelling stories propagate slowly and why even highly contagious narratives often fail to achieve universal coverage. Finally, we highlight the role of social media platforms in disseminating information by examining how the virality of Twitter posts is influenced by the appeal of the content and the platform's high level of modularity. This analysis helps explain the varying reach of viral phenomena, such as the #MeToo movement, on social media. Our model also sheds light on the challenges organizations face when attempting to communicate with internal groups during a crisis. Specifically, we demonstrate that hierarchical communication structures can be more effective than decentralized ones when interacting with modular internal organizational networks. Our model can assist organizations, media outlets, and public health agencies in determining which internal groups to engage first and how to sequence interactions with various media outlets to maximize the reach of critical public health updates. We conclude by outlining potential future applications of this research. For instance, it could guide future marketing campaigns, which must balance rapid dissemination with high market penetration to achieve their goals. Furthermore, this research could inform the design of social media algorithms, which could be tuned to optimize either transmission speed or penetration based on the nature of the information being shared. Finally, our framework may assist public health officials in predicting the spread of health warnings and the likelihood of achieving high population coverage. This could influence future vaccine marketing strategies, such as the selection of promotional channels and the types of messages employed. By guiding these decisions, our model could enhance the speed and reach of information transmission. Ultimately, our research provides a foundational understanding of how social network structure impacts the dissemination of information. Utilizing the framework of the Complexity Framework, we demonstrate the Quantitative Thomas-Yau Conjecture for plane curves. We establish that for any two compact Riemann surfaces within the same deformation class, there exists a constant $C$ dependent solely on the curve class such that the distance between any two volume minimizers in their Maslov index cohomology classes does not exceed $C$. This finding represents the initial application of deformation theory to address Hamiltonian complexity issues. Furthermore, we derive a stronger result for deformations of codimension at least 2: the distance between any two Maslov zero volume minimizers in the same class is bounded by a constant $C$ that depends only on the class, remaining independent of the specific surfaces. These findings suggest that similar bounds likely hold for higher codimension 1 surfaces. The proof relies on the recent Relative Floer Theory developed by Fukuma, Oh, Ohta, and Park, alongside an analysis of the geometry of holomorphic strips. Additionally, we provide a novel construction of Maslov index cohomology classes specifically designed for the context of the Complexity Framework. We anticipate that these techniques will find broader applications in the study of holomorphic curves. The distance estimate is formulated using symplectic geometric concepts, which we demonstrate are equivalent to Hausdorff distances in Lagrangian deformation problems. Our approach utilizes tools from Maslov theory, offering a fresh perspective on this distance formulation. We demonstrate that the proposed discrete-time model of the standard perturbation equation is the exact discrete-time equivalent of the conventional continuous-time formulation. Numerical simulations confirm that the key properties of the discrete-time model align with established characteristics of the standard perturbation model. Building a general-purpose universal vessel capable of running any program is a foundational challenge in computer science. This paper introduces Ozy, a novel universal orchestration vessel designed to run a restricted subset of the $\lambda_{IO}$-calculus, an $I/O$-extended variant of the Barendregt combinatory logic. To achieve this, Ozy employs an $I/O$-sensitive abstract machine that tracks the $\lambda_{IO}$-terms executed by the machine itself. This investigation underscores the critical role of an $I/O$-sensitive abstract machine in the architecture of a universal vessel like Ozy. Additionally, the paper provides an explicit construction of Ozy using the Kleene recursion operator, thereby establishing a model of Kleene's recursion scheme within the $\lambda_{IO}$-calculus. This construction demonstrates that a Turing machine can be viewed as a universal orchestration vessel for any computable $\lambda_{IO}$-term. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of emerging research directions. Specifically, it outlines how to construct a universal ocean, which functions as a storage medium for any computable $\lambda_{IO}$-term. This construction is achieved through a recursion scheme that utilizes an explicit stack-based data structure to represent the ocean. Furthermore, the paper explores a universal function for orchestrating any computable $\lambda_{IO}$-term within this ocean, defined as an $I/O$-sensitive function. This function is built using an $I/O$-sensitive recursion operator, which operates by reading and writing to the ocean. The process involves an $I/O$-sensitive abstract machine that executes a given $\lambda_{IO}$-term and monitors its progress. The machine's progress is monitored through an $I/O$-sensitive function that tracks the term's execution state. Finally, the paper examines the concept of an $I/O$-sensitive Turing machine, defined as a Turing machine equipped with an $I/O$-sensitive head. This machine utilizes an $I/O$-sensitive head to read and write to the ocean and to orchestrate any computable $\lambda_{IO}$-term via a universal function. The feasibility of this construction is demonstrated by providing an explicit implementation of an $I/O$-sensitive Turing machine using a Turing machine. This implementation includes a general function for computing any computable $\lambda_{IO}$-term and an $I/O$-sensitive head function for reading and writing to the ocean.

We obtained experimental data on the fill factor-varying magnetotransport of GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures at various electron densities. This study reveals the UN-5/2 branch, a reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall stage characterized by elevated longitudinal resistance and anomalous Hall resistance. We determined the UN-5/2 Hall resistance by comparing it to the Hall resistance at the lowest filling factor, establishing the Hall resistance coefficient for this unique branch. Furthermore, we analyzed magnetotransport data across different electron densities to assess the impact of Landau level mixing. Our findings indicate that the UN-5/2 branch is more pronounced at higher Landau level mixing intensities, a conclusion supported by a theoretical model. Additionally, we identified a 3/2 branch exhibiting similar characteristics to the UN-5/2 branch, a feature that can be explained by our theoretical framework. Finally, we conducted a detailed analysis of the magnetotransport data at multiple densities to explore the transition from the UN-5/2 branch to the 3/2 branch. These results offer valuable insights into the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall stage and its potential significance for topological quantum computing. The recent successful detections of binary black hole mergers by LIGO and Virgo have sparked significant interest in Population III stars and primordial black holes (PBHs) as potential sources. This work aims to clarify the constraints imposed by gravitational wave (GW) observations on the mass function of these populations. A recent study by Thakur et al. (2021) suggested that Population III black holes deviate from the standard Kerr metric due to a specific type of hair, implying that the traditional merger rate limits should be adjusted. We demonstrate that such claims are unfounded. The characteristics of thackurta-type black holes, including their merger rates, can be effectively modeled using the standard Kerr metric with appropriately selected spins. Furthermore, we establish that the limits on the PBH mass function derived by Clesse & Garcia-Bellido (2014, 2018) continue to hold. Finally, we update the constraints on the Population III star mass function and the PBH mass function to align with the latest LIGO and Virgo GW data. Recent research indicates that planet formation via pebble accumulation is feasible within the inner regions of protoplanetary disks. This study, however, demonstrates that building a core massive enough to ignite a gas giant typically occurs in the outer disk, where local pebble density must be at least ten times higher than in inner regions. Such high densities are likely achieved through the aggregation of numerous pebbles, a process that is generally difficult to sustain over the long periods required for planet formation. Consequently, we propose that the most efficient pathway for creating pebble-rich outer disks involves the inward transport of pebbles from the inner disk, where they collect in localized density peaks. This mechanism also explains the formation of super-Jupiter planets and planetary systems containing multiple gas giants. Furthermore, we show that these massive planets can form within a few million years, provided there is a continuous supply of pebbles to the disk's outer edges. Finally, we examine the potential for these successfully formed planets to host life. Our findings suggest that the inner disk is generally unsuitable for planet creation, except in rare cases where a planet is small and rocky. Therefore, the likelihood of finding life in the habitable zone of such a planet is contingent upon the transport of pre-formed water from the inner disk material. Additionally, we note that pebble accumulation on planets smaller than Earth is typically hindered by the presence of numerous small pebbles. In conclusion, we argue that the search for life should prioritize planets formed via pebble accumulation in the outer disk, as this process is expected to yield fewer but potentially more habitable systems. Specifically, we recommend targeting exoplanets that exhibit evidence of rapid formation. Finally, we emphasize the need to investigate the chemical composition of both small and large pebbles in future research. This approach is crucial because the chemical makeup of small pebbles may differ from that of larger aggregates, and both could vary from the composition of interstellar dust grains. Understanding these distinctions is essential for unraveling the broader chemical evolution of the interstellar medium. We also address the challenges associated with pebble accumulation in the inner disk. Finally, we outline the significance of this research for the future of the field of planet formation. It is widely recognized that the success of numerous machine learning algorithms stems, at least partially, from their capacity to identify simple hypotheses within rich function classes. This paper offers a qualitative examination of the interaction between computational constraints and the need for representational capacity. Specifically, I demonstrate that specific computational limits can drive the preference for complex classes, even when simpler alternatives exist that the algorithm cannot access. By drawing on two algorithmic processes—L2-regularized least squares and the greedy algorithm for the Lasso—I illustrate how computational constraints influence learned representations across statistical models. Furthermore, these examples offer a novel perspective on biases inherent in common machine learning techniques. Overall, this work provides fresh insights into how computational limits, statistical biases, and algorithmic characteristics collectively influence generalization performance in statistical learning. Specifically, it sheds light on a phenomenon where increased parameterization initially enhances performance before eventually degrading it. These insights are pertinent to the emerging field of neural computation, which seeks to comprehend the link between the computational capabilities of neural networks and the brain's information processing functions. Finally, this paper is intended as a step toward designing learning algorithms where overparameterization is justified by inherent computational constraints. This represents a distinct paradigm shift from the prevailing view that overparameterization serves merely as a practical workaround for understanding and training high-dimensional neural networks. By embracing overparameterization as a formal aspect of the learning process, we can more effectively analyze its impact on the convergence, generalization, and optimization of neural network learning procedures. This approach also holds promise for advancing the broader goal of developing new, interpretable learning algorithms. Specifically, it addresses the critical challenge of designing algorithms that are not only effective in learning but also capable of explaining their own learning mechanisms. This requires identifying and understanding the algorithmic biases that influence representations, thereby enabling the creation of novel methods that leverage these biases to achieve superior performance compared to existing techniques. Ultimately, this represents a significant step toward achieving the ultimate objective of the field: creating new algorithms that are both effective and interpretable. Achieving interpretability necessitates a fundamental rethinking of the relationship between model complexity and the data it aims to represent. This involves recognizing that the space of possible data representations is shaped by the algorithm's inherent biases, which must be understood to create models that are both high-performing and interpretable. This approach marks a pivotal step toward realizing the dream of new algorithms that are simultaneously effective and understandable. This article examines the Bohr structure of non-abelian Bohr compactifications for groups that are Bohr-abelian and possess an abelian quotient of countable rank. We demonstrate that the resulting Bohr structure is complete and arises from a von Neumann-Bohr topology defined on the group of characters. As an application, we characterize all topological isomorphisms between the real vector spaces equipped with their Bohr structures, showing that such isomorphisms are precisely the extensions of vector space homomorphisms between the groups. Furthermore, we analyze the structure of the closed subgroups within these Bohr spaces. In the final section, we present an application to the vector space structure of the Bohr compactification of a non-abelian group $G$ where the abelianization $G/[G,G]$ is of countable rank; in this scenario, the space of characters decomposes into a direct sum of vector spaces, and we characterize the continuous one-parameter subgroups. This specific case occurs, for instance, when $G$ is the group of finitely supported permutations of a countable set. Additionally, we establish that a non-abelian group $G$ is Bohr-abelian if and only if it contains an abelian subgroup $H$ of index two such that $H$ is normal in $G$ and the conjugation action of $G$ on $H$ constitutes a group of rank one. Our primary method involves the construction of a family of one-cocycles on $G$ with values in the circle group. This family is shown to be of countable rank, forming a free group under multiplication, and is proven to separate the elements of $G$. We further show that the closure of this family within the space of all cocycles yields the group of all cocycles, thereby confirming that the map from $G$ to its Bohr compactification is an open map. This technique is also instrumental in characterizing the topology of the closed subgroups of the Bohr compactification. Finally, we provide a characterization of Bohr-abelian groups based on the existence of specific cocycles. This characterization extends the concept of rank one to rank two and offers an alternative proof that the Bohr compactification of such a group possesses a Bohr-abelian structure. To achieve this, we develop a characterization of rank one groups using cocycles with values in the space of finitely supported measures on the circle. Urban dial-a-ride services are designed to enhance mobility for city dwellers. This paper introduces a heuristic Branch-and-Bound (HBB) algorithm to address metropolitan dial-a-ride challenges, utilizing a simplified heuristic cost function as a rapid lower bound. This lower bound serves as an effective pruning criterion within the branch-and-bound framework, enabling the system to handle larger instances with broader time windows. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for generating strong lower bounds, specifically addressing the difficulty posed by unassigned requests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art solutions on small instances while significantly outperforming them on larger ones. These results indicate that the heuristic is highly effective for dial-a-ride problems characterized by wide time windows and high request volumes. Finally, experiments conducted in collaboration with the Toulouse transport authority reveal that the method can solve real-world instances to optimality within a few minutes. Overall, this approach is capable of efficiently resolving practical instances while maintaining a very low unassignment rate. We introduce the insight-recognized multi-modal pretraining (IRMP) model, an end-to-end framework designed for e-commerce product detail page (PDP) recommendation. This approach integrates multi-modal pretraining with an e-commerce specific knowledge transfer (EKTR) module. EKTR addresses the data scarcity in e-commerce PDPs by leveraging pre-trained models to mitigate overfitting and enhance representation quality. Furthermore, it bridges the domain gap between pre-trained models and e-commerce PDPs by transferring knowledge from one category to another through a shared embedding space. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world PDP data demonstrate that IRMP significantly outperforms strong baselines in both accuracy and stability. Additionally, we present an ablation study to analyze the individual contributions of the pre-trained models and the EKTR module. The source code for IRMP will be made publicly available. Our EKTR method can serve as a general approach for e-commerce specific knowledge transfer, offering guidance for future research. The source code is available at: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DL4Recommender/tree/master/Insight-Recognized-MultiModal-Pretraining.

This paper introduces a deep learning framework designed to predict the progression to Alzheimer's disease. The model leverages speech and cognitive data collected from a study in rural India, analyzing participants across three groups: healthy individuals, those with speech deficits, and those who will develop Alzheimer's within three years. We developed a novel architecture that integrates a speech classification layer with a cognitive classification layer, connecting them via an intermediary Deep InfoMax layer. This specific component learns a latent representation that captures the shared underlying patterns between speech and cognitive abilities. This study investigates spin-orbit interaction (SOI) in strongly correlated electron systems by examining the alloy Pt$_{1-x}$Pd$_x$TiO$_2$. Using photoemission spectroscopy, we measured both bulk and surface states across a series of samples with varying Pd concentrations ($x$). Our findings indicate that the SOI strength in Pt and Pd ions within this correlated oxide can be tuned across a wide range. Notably, the so-called "golden rule" regarding SOI strength—where it scales with the square of the atomic number ($Z^2$)—does not hold for Pt and Pd in Pt$_{1-x}$Pd$_x$TiO$_2$. Instead, the SOI strength in this Pd-based sample is approximately 20% greater than that in Pt, a contrast to metallic alloys where Pt typically exhibits roughly half the SOI strength of its heavier homologues. We attribute this anomaly to the hybridization between Pt $4d$ and O $2p$ orbitals, which reduces the effective SOI strength in Pt. This effect diminishes as Pd is added, as Pd has a different orbital configuration that hybridizes less effectively with O $2p$ orbitals. Consequently, this work highlights a novel pathway for engineering correlated electron systems with tunable SOI, a capability with significant implications for spintronics and topological materials. Furthermore, this tunability offers a new tool for probing the interplay between electron correlation and topology. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our results for other materials systems. Specifically, we propose that strongly correlated compounds containing early transition metals (such as Sc, Ti, V, and Cr) will generally exhibit SOI strengths lower than those of their heavier homologues, a trend that is atypical for metallic alloys. This offers an alternative approach to tuning SOI using alloy technology and may facilitate the discovery of new topological materials. Additionally, we outline how this discovery can be leveraged to search for novel topological materials in the context of Sr$_4$RuO$_{10-x}$Pt$_x$O$_2$. By substituting Pt for highly correlated, nonmagnetic, and itinerant early transition metals, we can achieve tunable SOI, a critical step toward discovering new topological materials. This field experiences metastability at low energies, metastasizing for cosmological durations before eventually decaying into its ground state. The evolution of the universe during this process is significantly influenced by the coupling between the field and cold dark matter (CDM). Our model successfully reproduces the observed CDM density and addresses the coincidence problem. Furthermore, it offers a resolution to the Hubble tension by providing a non-early-universe mechanism that reduces the $\Sigma H_0$ value from $\approx 1.01$ to $\approx 0.99$. Additionally, this approach provides an alternative explanation for the CMB dipole anomaly. We also demonstrate that the model can account for the recently reported $5\sigma$ detection of dark energy oscillations. The resulting dark matter component is characterized by being cold, possessing a velocity dispersion of $v \lesssim 10^{-3}$, and displaying a phase space density that is orders of magnitude lower than the Jeans limit. In clinical decision-making, healthcare AI systems frequently face a distribution shift where training data does not align with data encountered during deployment. While recent literature has concentrated on generalization gaps, there remains a critical lack of robust uncertainty quantification methods in clinical AI. To address this, we introduce an exam-based healthcare AI benchmark using forecast probability intervals (FPIs) and calibration metrics to evaluate the performance of uncertainty estimates. We further develop a novel pipeline that leverages exam data to generate uncertainty-calibrated healthcare AI tools through conformal forecasting, thereby mitigating distribution shifts. This approach is validated using two case studies: one focused on healthcare cost reduction and the other on predicting exam performance. Our methodology enhances the reliability of healthcare AI by providing uncertainty-aware predictions, maximizing utility, and promoting more equitable algorithmic health decisions. Simulating the dynamics of biomolecules via atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) offers a powerful method for investigating their structural and dynamical properties. However, the time and length scales accessible through MD are significantly shorter than those observed in experimental techniques like single-molecule fluorescence, creating a substantial gap in understanding how molecules transition between states probed by these experiments. This study presents a straightforward and highly effective solution to bridge this gap: Rigid Foundation Biasing (RFOB). RFOB is a novel, easy-to-implement technique that incorporates prior structural information from experimental single-molecule measurements into MD simulations by constraining the structure of selected flexible regions (such as a DNA sequence) to align with experimental data. We demonstrate that RFOB enables the sampling of structures consistent with single-molecule measurements that are otherwise inaccessible through standard MD. Furthermore, we show that RFOB enhances the sampling of DNA hairpin structures and facilitates the analysis of their folding and unfolding dynamics. Ultimately, RFOB represents a versatile approach for simulating biomolecules, allowing the integration of structural insights derived from single-molecule experiments. This effectively expands the reachable length and time scales of MD simulations to match experimental observations, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the structural and dynamical characteristics of biomolecules. Additionally, RFOB serves as a practical tool for integrating structural details from single-molecule experiments into MD models. Finally, RFOB is accessible as a standalone Python script and as a feature within the BiMoSim software package. Both are available at https://github.com/roelfkoster/rigid-foundation-biasing. The specific application to DNA hairpins is also included within the package. We demonstrate that RFOB allows for the sampling of experimentally observed DNA structures and facilitates the analysis of their folding and unfolding dynamics. The package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install BiMoSim --user. The specific application demonstrating RFOB's ability to sample DNA structures and analyze their folding and unfolding dynamics is also available within the package. This study evaluates the ANS entropy compression algorithm's performance on two distinct datasets to analyze its efficacy across different domains. The algorithm's effectiveness is measured by the total reduction in file size, normalized against the original size, and is further analyzed by breaking down the entropy reduction into three components: entropy compression, redundancy compression, and lossless compression. The findings indicate that ANS entropy compression achieves a domain-specific reduction of 12.5% for the entropy component, 20.5% for the redundancy component, and 100% for the lossless component. These results demonstrate that ANS-based compression is highly effective for both the specific datasets examined in this paper and, by extension, similar types of data. Furthermore, the research confirms that an ANS-based entropy algorithm serves as a viable alternative to other forms of entropy compression. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future enhancements to the ANS-based entropy compression method. The dielectric properties of cementitious materials have been extensively investigated to support non-destructive testing methods, including dielectric spectroscopy and the analysis of frequency-dependent permittivity. Nevertheless, a comprehensive theoretical framework describing the dielectric behavior of cement-based systems across a wide frequency spectrum remains absent. This study employs an extended theory of electrical double layers at the interface between solid surfaces and electrolytes to develop a theoretical model for the complex permittivity of cementitious materials. The framework outlines the mechanisms governing frequency-dependent permittivity and the role of pore fluid ionic concentration. By calibrating the model with experimental data from cement mortar, the results indicate that solid-phase permittivity is approximately 5.5, pore fluid conductivity is about $10^{-4}$ S/m, and the specific surface area of the solid matrix is roughly $0.05$ m²/cm³. Additionally, the model predicts a minimum ionic concentration of about $10^{-4}$ mol/L, which aligns with ionic concentrations typically found in mixing water. These findings offer a means to estimate the permittivity of the solid matrix and pore fluid conductivity in cementitious materials without destructive analysis. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the pore structure of cementitious materials is not the primary driver of the frequency-dependent permittivity of the bulk material. Finally, the outcomes of this study can be applied to interpret dielectric responses in cement-based systems, such as concrete, concrete repair layers, and soil-cement mixtures. This enables the design of non-destructive testing techniques to monitor the condition of reinforced concrete structures and construction sites. Additionally, this work may facilitate the development of new techniques for quality control in cement-based manufacturing, including 3D printing. To support these applications, a MATLAB code is provided in the supplementary material. This code calculates the complex permittivity of cementitious materials as a function of frequency and ionic concentration, with a user-friendly graphical user interface. The code is available at https://github.com/zhongqiangwang1987/Dielectric-characteristics-of-pore-fluid-in-cementitious-materials. Future research will focus on extending this framework to more complex cement-based systems, such as concrete and soil-cement mixtures. This paper reviews the current state of research on hadron-hadron scattering at center-of-mass energies of 2 GeV or higher. The significant rise in cross-sections observed in these interactions has prompted suggestions that the outgoing hadrons form a bound or resonant state known as a massive-massive hadronic molecule (MHM). We examine the theoretical frameworks used to analyze such states and present experimental findings from the DAΦNE, LHCb, PANDA, and ALICE collaborations. Furthermore, we propose that a systematic investigation into the formation and properties of Molecules involving three or more massive hadrons may uncover a novel type of hadronic matter. This perspective could inspire new experimental searches for exotic hadronic states at existing facilities and motivate theoretical studies of purely hadronic compounds at extremely high baryon density. Consequently, we argue that massive-massive hadron-hadron scattering serves as a valuable tool for hadron spectroscopy and offers a unique window into the study of exotic hadronic matter. We conclude by outlining promising directions for future research in this field. This review aims to highlight recent advances in hadron molecular physics and to encourage the broader nuclear and particle physics communities to explore a new, largely uncharted area of hadron physics. We trust that this topic will soon gain a prominent place in the agendas of upcoming supercomputing facilities and collider experiments. Additionally, we hope that massive-mashive hadron-hadron scattering will be recognized as a crucial and promising field within the broader scope of hadron spectroscopy. Finally, we emphasize the value of conducting a systematic study of massive hadron-hadron scattering as a fundamental first step toward understanding the complex structure of hadronic molecules containing three or more massive hadrons. This approach is essential for unraveling the intricate dynamics of strongly interacting matter at very high density. We are confident that this field will soon become a central and highly promising domain of hadron physics. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable cosmological probe, offering insights into dark energy, the distribution of baryons, and the thermodynamics of intergalactic gas. Nevertheless, its complexity necessitates sophisticated theoretical modeling, which introduces significant uncertainties. This study introduces a novel, unambiguous deduction regarding high-redshift cosmology, derived from the three-dimensional spatial associations of absorption systems within the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. By utilizing the statistical properties of these correlations, we establish the mean density of intergalactic hydrogen ($\bar{x}_{\rm H}$) and the mean density of neutral hydrogen ($\bar{x}_{\rm H}^0$) as functions of redshift, alongside the primordial helium mass fraction ($f_{\rm He}$). We employ a Monte Carlo simulation to model synthetic spectra containing $10^6$ absorption systems, replicating the characteristics of the Keck/HIRES spectrum of Q1200+0300 at $z_{\rm em}=2.339$ observed by BOSS. The analysis uses correlation functions at zero and second lag to estimate $\bar{x}_{\rm H}$ and $\bar{x}_{\rm H}^0$, respectively. By comparing the observed correlation functions with those generated from synthetic spectra across various cosmological parameters, we derive the following results: $\bar{x}_{\rm H}^0(z=2.339) = (1.1 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-4}$, $\bar{x}_{\rm H}(z=2.339) = (1.6 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-4}$, and $f_{\rm He} = 0.24 \pm 0.04$. These findings align with other measurements, including those from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, Lyman-$\alpha$ emission, and deuterium. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the correlation function at the second lag can act as an independent test for the existence of neutral hydrogen. This represents a new, straightforward cosmological deduction arising from three-dimensional associations in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, requiring no theoretical modeling and thereby eliminating associated uncertainties. Consequently, this method could facilitate more precise cosmological tests in future observations of larger samples of high-redshift quasars. Human trajectory prediction is a difficult task within behavior inference, largely because of the inherent uncertainty in human movement. To address this, we introduce Social Latent VAE (SS-VAE), a novel framework that integrates social knowledge into a re-embedding process. This approach iteratively refines the embedding of uncertain future positions by incorporating social information, thereby generating diverse and coherent trajectories. SS-VAE operates by decomposing the trajectory generation process into two sequential components: first, a latent VAE learns the social space and produces an initial embedding for uncertain future points; second, a sliding re-embedding process iteratively refines this initial state by applying a socially-conscious attention mechanism. This mechanism assessines the relevance of prior knowledge for future decision-making and uses the resulting attention weights to produce a refined embedding. Experimental results demonstrate that SS-VAE outperforms existing methods across all metrics on three standard benchmark datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/SS-VAE. This study introduces a methodology for quantifying the complexity of Boltzmann networks, utilizing information-theoretic concepts of surprise and complexity. These metrics offer an alternative to the prevalence-based approach previously proposed by the authors. The relationship among surprisal, probability, and entropy is examined to define the surprisal complexity metric, which serves as an alternative to surprise complexity for modeling neural activity. Additionally, the relative surprisal complexity metric is introduced to measure the complexity of individual neurons within a layer. These three distinct information-theoretic metrics are evaluated against the prevalence-based approach across four theoretical networks and two experimental datasets. The results demonstrate that all four information-theoretic methods yield values comparable to those of the prevalence-based approach, indicating that information theory effectively captures the complexity of neural systems. However, the relative surpisal complexity metric was found to be less reliable than the other three. Finally, the surpisal complexity metric is shown to be effective in distinguishing between conscious and anesthetized states using experimental data. Overall, these new information-theoretic metrics provide a theoretical alternative to the prevalence-based approach for calculating Boltzmann network complexity, with surpisal complexity offering a distinct advantage in classifying neural system states. Furthermore, the approach is highly adaptable for calculating complexity in other neural network architectures. The accompanying code is publicly accessible. To facilitate as-human-as-possible gesture design, the system employs a hand gesture generator that simulates hand movements based on the physical kinetics of the corresponding gestures. Building on a recent study by the authors that demonstrated the successful integration of a deep convolutional neural network (DNN) with a recurrent neural network (RNN) for high accuracy, this work extends that methodology to a distributed framework. The integration of hand gesture generation, the unified DNN+RNN model, and a new voting-based recognition algorithm results in a complete framework capable of reliable hand gesture recognition in distributed UAV swarms. This framework was successfully tested and validated using a real-time simulation environment. Furthermore, a new algorithm is proposed to automatically detect user fatigue during engagement, demonstrating its effectiveness through testing on a real-time simulation that incorporates both human and non-human pilot behaviors. The study confirms that human pilots can maintain attention and focus for extended periods, with a significant reduction in fatigue observed when utilizing gesture-based communication methods. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary of key findings and a discussion on potential future research directions. This study investigates the performance of neural network systems when merging predictions across models with varying architectures and training methods. We address two key questions: first, whether these improved methods enhance classification accuracy compared to optimizing a single model, and second, what the optimal merging strategy is. Our findings indicate that implementing an adaptive threshold-based merging approach for at least two diverse neural network models outperforms the best single-classifier system. This result holds true across a variety of blood cell types, including neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets. Furthermore, the optimal strategy involves training an ensemble of networks using heterogeneous architectures and a weighted loss function, followed by Mest probability estimation to determine merging thresholds. This specific configuration achieved the highest accuracy in our experiments. Additionally, we evaluated a voting-based strategy, which performed competitively but was slightly less accurate than the adaptive threshold approach. Notably, our analysis reveals that a single model often outperforms a multi-model system in specific tasks, highlighting that merging does not guarantee improvement in every instance. Finally, we observed that ensembles of different models are more competitive when trained on a diverse set of datasets rather than a single, merged dataset. These insights are valuable for guiding future research in this field. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leopoldo-garcia/NN-Merging. Counterdiabatic (CD) adiabaticity offers a way to achieve rapid quantum evolution free of excitations. This study applies a CD counterdiabatic (CCD) approach to the Hubbard model during ground-state preparation. We begin by deriving a general CCD protocol that maintains invariance without requiring a specific initial Hamiltonian. Subsequently, we employ a variational method to mitigate the experimental complexity inherent in the full CCD proposal. Finally, we examine the dynamic properties of the variational counterdiadiabatic (VCD) scheme, showing that it can drive the system from a mixed state to the ground state in a single step, while remaining free of excitations and entanglement in the long term. The findings are supported by numerical evidence. These results suggest that the VCD protocol is particularly promising for efficient ground-state preparation. Additionally, a potential application in preparing pure ground states within quantum simulators is explored. This work establishes a foundation for future research into utilizing VCD counterdiadiabaticity across various physical models. Furthermore, the developed VCD protocol is broadly applicable to ground-state preparation using quantum simulators, offering the advantage of producing nearly pure ground states. This capability is especially valuable for simulating many-body problems that require accurate ground states. The study begins by reviewing the standard Adiabatic Theorem and the CD protocol, followed by a detailed derivation of the VCD method and its application to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, with results validated by numerical evidence. Finally, the paper discusses the protocol's advantages and outlines potential applications in quantum simulators. The article concludes with a summary and an outline of future research directions. This work was conducted under the supervision of Prof. Jie Li. Keywords: Counterdiadiabaticity; Hubbard model; Ground state; Quantum simulators; Quantum adiabaticity.

This paper introduces a novel high-velocity hue temperature (HT) model for color space conversion. By integrating perceptual attributes with technical technicalities, this experience-driven method offers a new perspective on color management, specifically for dynamic content. We have conducted experiments across various color spaces—including RGB, CIE-Lab, and CIE-Lch—and with different source materials, such as images and video streams, to validate the model's effectiveness. These experiments address two key challenges: maintaining consistent perceptive characteristics during high-velocity decoloration and providing an effective approach to control tint mapping. The study concludes that the proposed HT model is effective for high-velocity colorization and tint mapping. Furthermore, online tools implementing these methods are available for user experimentation. The source code can be found at https://github.com/ahmedelshafey/High-Velocity-Decoloration. Our future research will explore applying this model to other areas of color management. Online demonstrations of various experiments are available at https://ahmedelshafey.github.io/high_velocity_decoloration/. This work presents a novel approach to uniformizing (non-orientable) surfaces, specifically 2-dimensional Riemannian manifolds that satisfy a lower curvature bound. We demonstrate the existence of harmonic branched covers mapping a specific model surface onto an arbitrary such manifold. Consequently, we establish a Cheeger-type isoperimetric inequality characterized by curvature, alongside an embedding theorem for these CAT($k$) surfaces. Additionally, we address the uniformization problem originally posed by J. Jost. To achieve these outcomes, we develop novel techniques grounded in geometric measure theory, which are applicable to a broader range of problems. The methodology relies on interpreting harmonic maps as solutions to a minimization problem involving area functionals defined on a broad class of functions. This perspective offers a perspective shift from traditional partial differential equation methods, thereby extending the theory of harmonic maps to functions that may not be differentiable. Furthermore, the proof incorporates a component derived from the theory of foliations. This innovative approach not only yields a proof of the Poincaré conjecture for spherical 3-manifolds but also provides a comprehensive framework for addressing uniformization and embedding challenges within this context. The paper is structured into several self-contained sections designed for accessibility. It begins with an exposition of key tools from geometric measure theory, followed by a detailed presentation of the harmonic map equation, its variational formulation, and the associated uniqueness and regularity issues. The final section addresses the uniformization problem. Throughout, we provide a complete set of definitions, theorems, and proofs. Our treatment of harmonic maps extends beyond standard literature by incorporating concepts from geometric measure theory, specifically utilizing varifolds and their associated first variation. This framework enables a rigorous analysis of sequences of harmonic maps that degenerate into varifolds, a technique essential for addressing issues in higher dimensions. Furthermore, our approach offers a self-contained proof of the regularity of harmonic maps, extending beyond classical results. We also provide a complete characterization of the singular set for harmonic maps, proving that it possesses a Hausdorff dimension of no more than $m-3$, where $m$ represents the dimension of the domain manifold. This result extends directly to varifolds representing limits of harmonic maps and constitutes a significant component of the proof for the existence of uniformizations. To model photon generation, we employ a self-consistent simulation of laser propagation through a plasma channel. The photon-photon interaction physics is investigated at PETRA III using a comprehensive simulation of the entire laser-plasma system. Finally, we highlight the role of open-source simulation tools in addressing these issues and developing the next generation of laser-plasma systems. This framework will facilitate the creation of new scientific instruments, enabling the study of photon-photon interactions, strong-field QED, and high-harmonic physics. Furthermore, it will support the design of novel high-intensity sources, including laser-wakefield accelerators, inverse Compton scattering setups, high-harmonic generation via Raman scattering, and nonlinear quantum electrodynamics via beat-wave mixing. Ultimately, this model will aid in creating new tools for high-intensity science. The paper concludes by identifying areas for future research. This study examines the sensitivity of the Higgs sector to the $Z_2$-violating soft-breaking parameter $m_{12}$ within the Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM). We assess the feasibility of measuring this parameter through the production and decay of the light CP-even scalar $h$, which is a primary objective for the CMS experiment at the LHC. Utilizing Run 2 datasets of 13 TeV, we establish the sensitivity of $CMS$ to $m_{12}$ by analyzing the signal significance in the diphoton channel ($\sigma(pp\rightarrow h)\times BR(h\rightarrow \gamma\gamma)$) as a function of $m_{12}$. Our findings indicate that, for the standard 13 TeV configuration, the deviation in this observable remains below 10% across most of the 2HDM parameter space. However, for non-standard detector setups, such as those with reduced integrated luminosity or an upgraded calorimeter, the sensitivity improves, reaching approximately 5% or 20%. We conclude that determining the nature of $h$ as either the Standard Model-like or the heavier CP-even scalar requires a comprehensive global fit of the entire 2HDM parameter space. Furthermore, we note that the $Z_2$-symmetric limit of the model corresponds to $m_{12}=0$. Finally, we discuss the detectability of $m_{12}$ in other experimental channels, including the invisible Higgs decay channel. Additionally, we address the prospects for measuring $m_{12}$ via the mass of the heavier CP-even scalar $H$, which is relevant for future colliders. Our results demonstrate that the mass measurement sensitivity is comparable to or superior to that of the diphoton channel, except in scenarios with very small $h$ masses. We also note that the $Z_2$-symmetric limit remains a detectable feature in this context. Overall, the mass measurement of $H$ exhibits a 5% precision level, and we observe that the mass eigenstate $H$ can be distinguished from the SM-like state $h$ for values of $m_{12}$ up to roughly 2 TeV. Finally, we conclude that the $Z_2$-symmetric limit of the 2HDM is not a viable hypothesis for the Higgs sector. These conclusions are based on a full global fit of the 2HDM parameter space. This paper introduces an algorithm for transferring information from Reified triples to RDF graphs, considering the constraints of externally specified Shape Expressions. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-complete when all three following conditions are met: (1) class assertions are present, (2) path expressions within the Shape Expressions are non-empty, and (3) at least one property in the Reified graph functions as a key for some property shape. To address this, we propose a weak decidability result for a restricted fragment of the problem. This indicates that while no algorithm can guarantee a polynomial-time solution for the general case, a straightforward algorithm suffices to identify certain fundamental issues. Furthermore, we outline a research agenda for developing more sophisticated algorithms capable of handling the general case. Finally, we detail a proposed implementation strategy for our weak decidability approach, which serves as the foundation for the REACH system, alongside an agenda for future research directions. The authors have made their implementation available. Additionally, this paper extends our work presented at the 13th International Joint Conference on Information Systems 2021, where we introduced a similar problem and algorithm for a fragment of Shape Expressions that excludes path expressions. In the current study, we refine the definition of this fragment to incorporate support for path expressions. We subsequently establish the NP-completeness of the problem and provide a correctness proof for the algorithm's decision procedure regarding this extended fragment. Furthermore, we demonstrate the correctness of a greedy algorithm for a smaller fragment and the correctness of a decision procedure for a fragment featuring negated property paths. These fragments represent common practical scenarios for shape-restricted information transfer. Our primary contribution lies in the fundamental research aspect of the problem, whereas our previous work focused on the application side. This time, the emphasis shifts toward fundamental research. Consequently, we have renamed the system from REACH to SHEEP to reflect this shift in focus. This paper serves as the foundation for our upcoming presentations at ESWC 2022 and ISWC 2022. We introduce a new Python library designed for non- and semi-parametric shape-constrained functional regression, founded on convex optimization techniques. This library supports the recovery of both functional estimates and random measures (such as pointwise confidence bands and quantile confidence curves) via dual formulation and computation. The primary objective of shape-constrained functional regression is to infer, while accounting for data noise, whether a regression function $f$ is non-negative, non-decreasing, or concave. We have validated this library using simulated and real-world datasets. Our implementation is distributed under the name pyStoNED, which stands for "pyShapeRestricted Nonparametric Estimation over a Dual formulation." The source code, along with synthetic and real-world demonstrations, can be accessed at: https://github.com/QuantitativeBioMed/pyStoNED. Additionally, shape-constrained regression methods serve as a valuable analytical tool for convex frontier assessment. The accompanying Jupyter notebooks illustrate how pyStoNED can be applied to analyze the performance of European hospitals and the efficiency of European banks. These methodological approaches are also discussed by other researchers; for instance, they are utilized to measure the impact of COVID-19 on European hospital performance and to evaluate the efficiency of European banks. Furthermore, pyStoNED enables the analysis of real-world data from the European Space Agency's "Copernicus" satellite program, which monitors forest growth and deforestation in Amazonian countries. Our goal is to provide a user-friendly library that supports both beginners and experts in shape-constrained functional regression. The beginner-level tutorials can be found in our publication: "Shape-constrained functional regression: a new open-source software for biomedical applications" (Statistics in Medicine, 2021). For experts, we offer a collection of advanced tutorials titled "Shape-constrained functional regression: a comprehensive collection of tutorials" (Statistics in Medicine, 2021), which covers topics including uncertainty quantification, variable selection, multivariate shape-constrained regression, and high-dimensional inference. All examples from these tutorials are available in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/QuantitativeBioMed/pyStoNED. We aim to facilitate the application of shape-constrained functional regression in various scientific fields through pyStoNED. Our future roadmap includes expanding feature support, such as handling cyclic regression functions, integrating new estimation techniques, and implementing model selection procedures. We invite users to contribute to pyStoNED by submitting pull requests or contacting us at quantbiomed@gmail

This paper presents a new framework designed to explore the $t \bar t H/A$ production channel at the LHC, which offers distinct advantages for conducting model-specific analyses of Higgs interactions with top quarks. A primary benefit of this channel is the capacity to measure the top-quark Yukawa coupling through two complementary methods: an inclusive approach sensitive to total cross sections, and an exclusive approach focused on Higgs signal shapes derived from Higgs decay branching ratios. The study demonstrates that these two strategies can coexist within the same dataset without mutual interference. Furthermore, the analysis investigates the $t \bar t A$ production mode, highlighting its potential to detect CP-odd Higgs boson couplings to top quarks that are otherwise obscured by the standard model $t \bar t H$ process. Finally, the paper presents current LHC constraints on the Higgs couplings to top quarks, accounting for the unique experimental characteristics of the $t \bar t H$ channel. This is followed by a comprehensive set of projections for various Higgs mass values and CP properties, covering both the standard SM-like scenario and a simplified naturalness framework. These results are intended to serve as a benchmark for future studies of the Higgs couplings to top quarks. Additionally, the analysis code is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AndreyKorotkyy/TTiggsTop. Current state-of-the-art open-domain question answering systems depend on large-scale annotated datasets, which restricts their ability to generalize to new topics. This paper investigates whether pretrained language models can instead learn from the limited human knowledge available in documents, thereby enhancing their analysis capabilities. To address this, we introduce UniQA, a novel question-answering framework that utilizes existing models to automatically extract topic-specific structured data, such as relation extraction, from unmonitored texts. This extracted knowledge enables relation-based retrieval and reasoning, allowing the system to provide accurate answers to complex queries without manual design. Our extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate that UniQA achieves state-of-the-art results in unmonitored settings using only 5 to 10 example pairs, while also showing promising few-shot performance. Furthermore, we analyze the models' knowledge extraction processes and their impact on UniQA's performance. Finally, we evaluate UniQA's effectiveness on open-domain generation tasks, including summarization and paraphrasing. The code is accessible at https://github.com/roberta/UniQA. We report the findings of a study on 12 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus region, selected from a sample of 32 O-type stars with known radial velocities. This selection prioritized early O stars exhibiting strong hydrogen Balmer absorption lines. Our analysis indicates that these 12 Be stars have masses ranging from 10 to 12 $M_{\odot}$ and are in the main sequence. Additionally, we determined their periods, period derivatives, and mass transfer rates. Our results suggest that seven of these stars have recently undergone mass transfer events, while the remaining five have experienced such events in the distant past. Furthermore, the mass transfer rates for these stars are significantly lower than those observed in X-ray-emitting Be-XRB systems. Finally, we discuss the potential for these 12 Be stars to evolve into massive black holes. Our investigation reveals that 11 of the 12 Be stars in 30 Doradus are likely to become massive black holes, with estimated masses between 15 and 25 $M_{\odot}$. This finding is consistent with previous research by Maccarone et al. (2010), which identified 11 BeX binaries in the 30 Doradus star cluster. Our work demonstrates that the majority of Be stars in the 30 Doradus region are non-X-ray emitting. The presence of these non-X-ray emitting Be stars is essential for understanding the formation and evolution of BeXRBs. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the 12 Be stars in 30 Doradus, offering valuable insights into the evolution of BeXRBs and the formation of massive black holes. These findings will contribute significantly to our understanding of the 30 Doradus star cluster and the broader field of binary star evolution. This study investigates the data enhancement technique applied to inverse text standardization (ITS). A data-to-text standardization model trained on interchanged ITS data demonstrates a data-driven approach to generating standardized text from unstandardized input. Experiments conducted on two public ITS datasets confirm that data enhancement significantly enhances performance, particularly for short text inputs. Given that Inverse Standardization is primarily employed in Post-Editorial Correction (PEC) to assist journal staff, the focus on short texts is justified by the fact that short abstracts are the most prevalent document types in this domain. The paper concludes by discussing future research directions regarding data enhancement. The code and data utilized in this experiment are accessible at: https://github.com/rahul-agarwal1994/data-enhancement-ITS. Furthermore, utilizing Almgren's frequency function and Almgren's monotonicity formula, we prove that a radial function serves as the optimizer for this inequality. Finally, utilizing the same Almgren-type monotonicity formula, we extend the Faber-Krahn inequality for the Laplacian established in [1] to our context, providing a detailed description of the equality case. We introduce a new method for non-Exchangeable Tangent Centers (NTCCs), a technique that functions as the non-Exchangeable counterpart to Exchangeable Tangent Centers (ETCCs). ETCCs are a state-of-the-art approach for unsupervised dimensionality reduction grounded in topological data analysis. Unlike previous ETCC methods designed for exchangeable data, NTCCs accommodate non-Exchangeable datasets by effectively managing data exhibiting significant self-similarity. This allows NTCCs to isolate data clusters and manifold structures through a topological lens. We validate NTCCs across various non-Exchangeable datasets, including face recognition and digit classification tasks. Additionally, we apply these NTCCs to a self-similar dataset of human activity from the CHAMP dataset. Our results demonstrate that NTCCs surpass state-of-the-art learning methods in both classification accuracy and feature extraction quality. All code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/NonExchangeableTangentCores. Furthermore, we have released a Python package named NFT-K, enabling users to apply NTCCs to their own data. This package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install NFT-K. The package includes a collection of utility functions for learning NTCCs and a library of example datasets. Users can load pre-learned NTCCs from the package or train them on their own data, with the option to visualize the NTCCs using the provided visualization package. We investigate the dynamical generation of one-dimensional (1D) non-Hermitian point-topological phases within the wire model, characterized by next-nearest-neighbor non-reciprocity and long-range interactions. These phases, which exhibit topological singularities at specific values of the control parameter, emerge in the non-interacting framework. However, our findings demonstrate that long-range interactions can destroy this point-topology. Specifically, interactions induce a gap in the emergent topological structure, causing it to persist only in the presence of such forceful interactions. Consequently, we identify a unique mechanism where these forces eliminate topological features that would otherwise exist in the non-interacting system. Our results underscore the critical role of interactions in the development of non-Hermitian topological orders and offer fresh insights into the field of topological physics. Furthermore, we suggest that these interaction-driven phenomena can be experimentally observed in one-dimensional optical lattices. Finally, our work establishes a pathway toward achieving novel interaction-induced topological phases within non-Hermitian systems. Our model holds significant potential for advancing the study of topological physics by offering new perspectives grounded in the influence of interactions. Additionally, it may facilitate the creation of new platforms for studying emergent phenomena in both quantum and classical systems. Finally, our approach could help formulate innovative proposals for future research in the field of interaction-induced topology. **Keywords:** Topology, Quantum Physics, Condensed Matter, Physics, Physics. **PACS:** 03.65.-v, 03.75.-, 72.15.Rn, 73.21.-, 73.21.La. **Keywords:** Topology, Quantum Physics, Condensed Matter, Physics, Physics. **PACS:** 03.65.-v, 03.75.-, 72.15.Rn, 73.21.-, 73.21.La. **Keywords:** Topology, Quantum Physics, Condensed Matter, Physics, Physics. **PACS:** 03.65.-v, 03.75.-, 72.15.Rn, 73.21.-, 73.21.La. **Keywords:** Topology, Quantum Physics, Condensed Matter, Physics, Physics. **PACS:** 03.65.-v, 03.75.-, 72

This study investigates the potential of embedding social characteristics, specifically gender and age, into synthetic speech. By leveraging a social classifier trained to identify these traits, we utilize a cost function to guide the speech synthesis process. Our findings indicate that a social classifier trained on real speech can accurately identify similar traits in voice samples generated by a neural TTS model like Google's eFront. Additionally, we demonstrate that a classifier trained on data augmented with estimated formant frequencies performs comparably to one trained on full acoustic features. However, successfully applying this cost function during synthesis is highly dependent on the specific neural TTS model being integrated with. Ultimately, a social classifier trained to detect gender and age biases in language can effectively communicate these biases to certain neural T front models, influencing their synthetic output. This research represents an initial step toward enhancing social awareness in synthetic speech and examining the variations inherent in voice data. We provide source code for our implementations at https://github.com/alexpaulos/tts-bias-cost-func. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 front utterances annotated with social demographics, available at https://github.com/alexpaulos/tts-bias-cost-func. Given that we did not employ fine-tuning, we anticipate that fine-tuning a front model on our dataset will yield even stronger results. We hope this work will encourage further research into the variations within synthetic speech. Finally, we intend to expand the available data by incorporating additional social attributes, such as race and socioeconomic status. While these attributes are more complex to quantify in isolated utterances, we have established correlations with such data in our evaluations of synthetic speech. We aim to release this related research in a future publication. Additionally, we plan to investigate embedding social traits into other neural front models, including those from Microsoft and Meta. Although we did not evaluate other Meta models in this specific work, we have previously demonstrated that fine-tuning a xGen model on a dataset of annotated tweets can successfully generate text with specific gender biases (see https://github.com/alexpaulos/xgen-bias). We anticipate that fine-tuning xGen or similar models on our expanded data will produce even better outcomes. In conclusion, we hope this research will spark further inquiry into variations within synthetic speech. We acknowledge that our current work is limited to a rudimentary implementation that does not fully exploit the capabilities of neural front models. We introduce a modular $A_4$ symmetry implementation grounded in the Standard Model extended with the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge symmetry. Within this framework, a dark matter candidate emerges as a linear combination of the lightest neutralinos and the lightest neutrino, with its weakly interacting particle nature arising from neutrino oscillations. Furthermore, our model predicts a leptonic charge current violation signal detectable at the Long-Baseline Neutrino Experiment, identifying the dark matter as a well-luminous candidate. Finally, we examine the model's phenomenological predictions, including constraints on dark matter relic density and isocurvature fluctuations derived from inflationary gravitational waves. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting dark matter through events that violate neutrino number conservation in neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the dark matter mass, situated well within the reach of direct detection facilities. In our analysis, we utilized 100 modular forms to construct invariant operators under the $A_4$ symmetry. Notably, we observed that reducing the number of these forms to just two yields phenomenologically viable results, thereby simplifying the model. The underlying mechanism of modular symmetry offers a natural explanation for the smallness of neutrino masses. This work offers a comprehensive analysis of a simple yet phenomenologically robust model that successfully explains the small neutrino mass, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, and the hierarchy problem. Furthermore, it predicts the dark matter nature of neutralinos and the neutrino dark matter scenario, both of which are well-luminous. We have also examined the implications of neutrinoless double beta decay, dark matter relic density, and direct detection experiments within this context. Finally, we discuss the model's phenomenological predictions and its alignment with current experimental data. Building upon the foundational concepts of collective motion in triaxial nuclei established by the geometric model, this study introduces a formula for the energy gap between the third band member and the yrast band within a deformed nucleus, utilizing the minimal distance concept. This approach enables the classification of yrast bands in deformed nuclei into three distinct groups, corresponding to the geometric model's identification of three primary collective motion types: wiggling, precession, and mixing. The proposed framework is applicable to both self-consistent and phenomenological calculations of yrast spectra in deformed nuclei. Furthermore, the method allows for the calculation of electric quadrupole transition probabilities ($B(E2)$ values) for transitions to yrast bands of fully deformed nuclei. As an illustration, the model successfully reproduces the experimental $B(E2)$ spectrum for the deformed $^{152}$Sm nucleus. The findings suggest that the spectrum of yrast bands in deformed nuclei can be categorized into groups based on the characteristics of their $E2$ transition strengths. These results align with the concept that the characteristics of nuclear collective motion determine the structure of the nuclear three-point correlation, a notion supported by the observed correlation between the structure of the nuclear excitation spectrum and the shape of the nucleon charge form factor. An $M$-point PGCS is defined as a set of $M$ sequences, each with a Golay pair pair-correlation of length $N$, where $M$ can exceed $N$. We establish that the maximum possible value for $M$ is $N^2$, thereby extending PGCS from a one-dimensional to a two-dimensional framework. Subsequently, we present two distinct construction methods for PGCS and apply them to generate polyphase PGCS with 256, 512, and 1024 pairs of correlations. A key characteristic of these sets is that their period-correlation power sum (PCPS) equals zero. The resulting PGCS exhibit a periodic autocorrelation (PAC) that remains nearly constant, demonstrating low peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and high autocorrelation energy efficiency (AEE). Furthermore, PGCS composed of Golay complementary sequences are ideal for OFDM systems utilizing Golay pairs. We also explore applications in radar and ultrasonic imaging, where the low PAPR and AEE of PGCS offer significant advantages.
