We present a distributed tagging scheme designed for nearly all planar graphs with a linear arboricity of $k$. This scheme enables every vertex to identify its neighbors within the graph's distance $O(k \log n)$ modulo $2n+1$. We analyze the scheme under the failure of a bounded number of vertices. To achieve this, we employ a modified BFS process that circumvents faulty vertices by utilizing an alternative path decomposition. This method ensures the BFS reaches vertices at a distance of $O(k \log n)$ with high probability, even in the presence of a polynomial fraction of failures. Furthermore, we introduce a novel resampling technique for BFS trees that permits the BFS to bypass a polynomial fraction of failed vertices while effectively exploring the graph. This approach results in a randomized tagging algorithm that operates deterministically once the distance tag of at least one vertex per layer is provided by a non-faulty process. Finally, we examine the scheme's resilience to failures in nearly-Euclidean planar graphs, demonstrating that with appropriate parameter selection, the scheme remains functional even when $n^2$ vertices fail. These parameters ensure the BFS successfully visits a vast number of vertices within $O(k \log n)$ rounds with high probability. Additionally, we demonstrate that the resampling technique applied to the nearly-Euclidean graph remains effective even when the failure count reaches $2^n$. Consequently, this enables the distance tagging scheme to function despite the failure of an exponential number of vertices. To our knowledge, this represents the first demonstration that distance computation can tolerate such a high number of failures within a nearly planar graph. Our findings are supported by a rigorous probabilistic analysis of the BFS's range and the number of layers it traverses. We provide a comprehensive proof of our primary probabilistic claim, which asserts that the BFS covers a sufficiently large number of vertices within $O(k \log n)$ layers with high probability. This proof relies on a careful examination of the BFS tree's structure and the distribution of both failed and non-failed vertices. We also develop a novel probabilistic argument to bound the number of re-samples required by the BFS tree, demonstrating that the number of re-samples is bounded with high probability. This argument draws upon techniques from probability theory, including conditional expectation and martingales. Overall, our proof provides a robust foundation for the resilience of distance computation in nearly planar graphs. By combining our probabilistic analysis with the tagging scheme, we establish that the scheme functions correctly with high probability, even when a polynomial fraction of vertices

This study examines two-entity correlations within a lossy Bose-Hubbard framework subject to an external drive. The resulting master equation is solved using the spectrum-domain correlation function approach, an extension of a previously developed moment-domain method. The analysis focuses on regular lattices with on-site interactions and hopping, incorporating collective dissipation and gain alongside individual loss and gain. On-site densities and both balanced and imbalanced two-entity correlations are computed and analyzed. The results demonstrate that the spectrum-domain correlation function effectively captures the dynamics of the model, facilitating the investigation of correlations between different lattice sites. Furthermore, the method proves particularly effective for systems where dynamics are restricted to a limited number of energy levels. It is also applicable to more complex models, including those with nearest-neighbor interactions. Finally, the paper outlines the general procedure for deriving the spectrum-domain correlation functions required to solve the master equation and proposes an algorithm for their systematic determination. This algorithm addresses the challenges of handling the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and the efficient management of a large number of equations. Additionally, the spectrum-domain method is shown to be more efficient than the moment-domain method for this model. Finally, the validity of the spectrum-domain approach is verified by comparing its outcomes with exact solutions. The analysis focuses on equations in divergence form with coefficients in $L^p$ (where $p > 1$) and right-hand side data in $L^2$. The primary result asserts that if $\mathcal{H}^{k-1}(S) < \infty$, then a unique weak solution exists, provided that $p$, $N$, and $k$ satisfy a specific non-sharp integrability condition. Furthermore, assuming $\mathcal{H}^{k-1}(M) < \infty$ and $S = 0$, we establish the Hölder continuity of the solution under the additional requirement that $p > \frac{N}{2}$. These findings extend and complement the theorems of Giaquinta, Giavoni, and Modica, as well as the results of Giaquinta and Modica. Finally, we derive an alternative result that refines our main theorems when $p > \frac{N}{2}$. This refined outcome relies on a recent theorem by the first author, which extends the work of Meyers, and on techniques developed by the second author in the context of nonlinear parabolic equations. The discussion covers various scenarios for $T$ and analyzes how the regularity of the solution depends on the structure of $T$. Notably, the case where $T$ is a boundary current is addressed. Specifically, this paper addresses the scenario where the rectifiable part of $T$ lies within a submanifold $\Gamma \subset \Omega$, while the remainder possesses a fractal structure. This paper introduces a framework for out-of-domain detection grounded in Gaussian Processes (GPs). Detection is essential for determining whether to employ a model for a specific test instance or whether existing models require domain adaptation. We propose a flexible framework that accommodates various GP formulations, such as multi-task GPs, non-i.i.d. GPs, and Gaussian Process Variational Autoencoders. Through empirical evaluations across multiple detection scenarios, we demonstrate that our approach serves as a versatile and effective solution for out-of-domain detection tasks. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of this framework within the context of NLP datasets characterized by distributional shifts. Additionally, the framework supports anomaly detection when no in-domain training data is available. Extensive empirical evaluations confirm its effectiveness in anomaly detection scenarios lacking an in-domain dataset. Finally, we highlight potential applications for graph neural networks and suggest avenues for future research. **Index Terms:** out-of-domain detection, domain adaptation, gaussian processes, gaussian process variational autoencoder, anomaly detection.

Periodic driving of an isolated quantum system typically results in heating, causing the ground state to become increasingly excited as the driving frequency decreases. This study examines a driven open quantum system featuring a ground state that is largely localized in real space, characterized by a broad distribution across neighboring sites within a two-dimensional optical lattice. We demonstrate that, contrary to the expectation of uniform heating, this scar-like state exhibits anomalous heating behavior, with a rate that declines as the drive frequency slows. This lattice subsystem is further coupled to a reservoir of free photons. We find that, due to this specific heating profile, the photon distribution within the reservoir develops a sub-Poissonian pattern, causing the photon density to cluster around integer values. We attribute this phenomenon to a resonance between the photon modes and the slowly heating scar-like state. These findings may have broad implications for understanding generic driven open quantum systems and could be relevant for quantum information processing and sensing. Additionally, our results may contribute to a deeper understanding of life detection and exploration within a quantum framework. We establish uniform Hölder continuity for nearly convex viscosity solutions of the Monge–Ampère equation subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, specifically addressing the case where the right-hand side is constrained within $[-C^n, -(-C^n)]$ within a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that possesses a $C^{1,1}$ boundary. This work extends the Alexandrov-Maekawa theorem by incorporating a higher-dimensional dimension dependency. Notably, our findings demonstrate that near-convexity suffices to guarantee Hölder continuity, eliminating the traditional necessity for additional regularity assumptions. Furthermore, our estimate reveals a power-type dependence on the dimension, which aligns with the optimal scaling expected for general viscosity solutions of elliptic equations, thereby enhancing the efficiency of related geometric regularity theories. Additional contributions include an explicit constant, a polynomial dependence on $n$, and the elimination of small data extensions. The core methodology integrates a dimension reduction approach with a measure-valued Alexandrov-Maekawa technique. These results represent a significant advancement over existing literature and enable substantial improvements to various geometric applications. Additionally, we derive a free boundary regularity estimate for nearly convex viscosity solutions of the obstacle problem, which may be of independent interest. Finally, our proof provides a substantial generalization of the Evans-Spruck theorem, which can be viewed as the limiting case where the right-hand side approaches infinity. The paper is structured into ten sections, with the primary contributions concentrated in Sections 3 through 7. Section 8 offers a novel application to nearly convex viscosity solutions of the occluded Monge-Ampère equation, demonstrating uniform Hölder continuity for solutions with $L^\infty$ data and a right-hand side constrained in $[-C^n, n^{-C}] \subset \mathbb{R}$. The remaining sections offer an overview of the proof's outline and outline future research directions. The primary innovation of this work lies in the introduction of a measure-valued Alexandrov-Maekawa method, which is demonstrated herein and in related studies to be highly effective for solving the core issues of these problems. This approach is expected to yield substantial improvements to numerous other theories. The entire argument is rigorous, constructive, and free from small data extensions. In summary, this work advances theoretical understanding, enhances solution estimates, and achieves quantitative results. Non-repetitive optical clocks are rapidly developing technologies that offer superior stability and retraceability compared to their conventional optical and microwave equivalents. A defining characteristic of these clocks is their non-repetitive nature, which enables the analysis of short, non-recoverable noise segments. This paper introduces a statistical approach to modeling such clocks, providing a framework to characterize the overall time-domain noise behavior. The proposed method is validated using a real-world non-repetitive optical frequency comb. The analysis involves characterizing the noise of both the optical source and the microwave reference, followed by a non-repetitive measurement of an optical clock derived from the optical source. The study demonstrates that the comb's performance is constrained by the optical source; specifically, a stability metric based on a specific short-duration minimum variance is defined and analyzed. The results indicate that for short measurement times, the clock's performance is independent of the absolute noise level in the source but is instead contingent upon that level relative to the source's stability. Furthermore, the paper explores how these properties can be leveraged to develop shorter-duration non-repetitive optical clocks. The proposed modeling approach is applicable to any non-recoverable time-domain signal, making it a valuable tool for analyzing other emerging sensing technologies. Ultimately, this work facilitates a comprehensive performance analysis of optical clocks, supporting the development of advanced applications in high-precision sensing and metrology. Additionally, the paper discusses the broader potential of non-recoverable time-domain measurements for optical clocks, including their effects on state estimation and feedback control. Finally, the paper suggests that non-repetitive optical clocks could serve as primary time references for non-repetitive timekeeping. Such a system would facilitate ensemble averaging across an optical clock network, thereby enhancing system stability and precision for applications in high-precision sensing, metrology, and fundamental physics. The concept of non-repetitive optical clocks is poised to significantly impact the fields of time and frequency. By enabling shorter-duration measurements, this technology will facilitate faster feedback and timekeeping, thereby advancing the field of optical atomic physics. This paper introduces a fog-assisted software-defined network (SDN) architecture designed to handle network failures and energy efficiency through optimized service chaining (SFC). The proposed fog node architecture features a distributed management plane that utilizes a centralized failure recovery mechanism, while the control plane is built on a real-time model that ensures SFC compliance via resource reservation and rapid network reconfiguration upon failures. To address the high energy consumption of data centers, this architecture incorporates energy-efficient asset management within fog nodes using a dynamic resource scheduling algorithm. This algorithm allocates resources based on real-time traffic demand and traffic-aware flow paths to minimize energy usage. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed architecture significantly reduces recovery times compared to traditional failure recovery methods, while also enhancing SFC quality by improving data delivery timeliness and reliability. Furthermore, the fog node's ability to support multiple SFCs with distinct service requirements and traffic-aware paths results in superior energy efficiency. Finally, the architecture's fog-assisted design for SFC ensures cost-effective and efficient resource utilization. Keywords: Software Defined Network (SDN), Service Function Chaining (SFC), Real-time Model, Distributed Control, Service Recovery, Traffic-aware Resource Allocation, Energy Efficiency.

We introduce a new gradient manipulation (GM) technique designed to study the impacts of different loss function formulations. Our approach reparameterizes training data using a specific loss function and subsequently trains with another. We examine the effects of varying convexity and differentiability across a range of scenarios, including linear regression and training on imbalanced datasets. Our findings indicate that for convex and differentiable losses, both GM and standard training produce nearly identical results, with minimal gaps in both validation and test losses. However, when differentiable losses are convex and others are not, GM can effectively mitigate overfitting and enhance test performance. Furthermore, our experiments on linear regression and imbalanced classification demonstrate that combining convex loss functions with regularization techniques, such as L2-regularization, yields superior performance. Finally, we explore the potential of integrating multiple loss functions to further improve results. These outcomes underscore the significance of carefully selecting loss functions and propose combining them with well-established regularization and model selection methods. Additionally, we present a unified framework for analyzing various loss functions, with a current focus on convex properties. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234/GM. We introduce a new holographic error correction code, the Hyper-Invariant MERA (HIMERA), which derives from a multi-scale single-to-many duality between bulk path integral histories and boundary ground state observables. By connecting this duality to the harmonic bulk connections of graph theory, we demonstrate that HIMERA can achieve power-law entanglement correlations even with long-ranged associations. Furthermore, we show that HIMERA maintains a low bond dimension and linear depth, while retaining the minimum weight of stabilizers and a constant code distance inherent to MERAs. These characteristics suggest that HIMERA is a highly efficient error correction code, particularly for applications in quantum simulation. Additionally, we find that for $k>1$, HIMERA maintains a low renormalized entropy for non-conical configurations, outperforming the HNS code in this regard. This capability to handle non-conical configurations with low renormalized entropy is expected to be valuable for image reconstruction tasks. Finally, we discuss the potential of HIMERA for quantum image reconstruction and conclude by proposing it as a promising candidate for implementation on quantum annealers. The Milky Way's stellar population exhibits a highly complex, filamentary structure. This study investigates the spatial distribution of these filaments by analyzing the distance between them. Using data from the Gaia DR2 catalog, we model the three-dimensional architecture of Galactic core fibers. The fibers are characterized by their center lines, derived via the Local Radial Direction (LRD) algorithm, along with their radial distances and azimuthal positions. To evaluate the distance between fibers, we calculate the Euclidean separation between points on their spines, weighing these distances by the product of their corresponding radial weights and galactic longitudes. Our analysis reveals that the distribution of distances normalized by scale height follows a log-normal distribution, with a mean value of approximately 1.5 scale heights. Furthermore, we observe that the distance distribution is more pronounced for fibers with low inclination angles and high scale heights. These findings offer a quantitative description of the distribution of distances between Galactic core fibers. Additionally, the observed distances are significantly larger than those predicted by numerical simulations, a discrepancy that may help explain the difficulty in explaining the origin of Galactic core fibers. These results also suggest a need to refine the current understanding of the initial conditions of Galactic core fibers. Finally, the paper concludes with several suggestions for future research. This study introduces and evaluates an ideal conservation voltage reduction (cVRD) strategy designed to lower voltages and diminish energy usage in primary-secondary distribution networks featuring high renewable energy penetration. Addressing the intricate nature of nonconvex voltage and power constraints, as well as nonconvex load and voltage settings, the proposed method utilizes local measurements at distribution transformers to convexify renewable power constraints and generate locally optimal, distributed voltage setpoints for these transformers. These setpoints are dynamically adjusted in response to temporal variations in renewable generation. Simulation results using IEEE 123-bus systems demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively lowers voltages and reduces total load power consumption, thereby increasing the acceptance rate of renewable energy. Furthermore, the communication requirements for implementing this solution are significantly less demanding than those of distributed optimal power flow (POF) algorithms. Notably, the proposed solution achieves substantial load power savings even under low renewable penetration levels, a critical finding given the projected growth in renewable integration. Additionally, the solution exhibits robustness against uncertainties in renewable power output. Overall, the approach is computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time deployment. Key words: conservation voltage reduction, voltage and power optimization, renewable energy, distributed optimization.

**Background:** Accurately modeling stress time histories for wind turbine components is crucial for structural reliability analysis. However, the high dimensionality of these stresses, stemming from the complex, high-frequency fluid dynamics governing offshore wind fields, renders component-level modeling prohibitively expensive. **Objectives:** To overcome this challenge, we employ probabilistic proxy models to accelerate the estimation of the joint distribution of stress range and cycle counts. **Methods:** Our approach utilizes linked Gaussian process (GP) regression to create the proxy models. This framework consists of two components: (1) a high-fidelity Gaussian process that models the joint distribution of cycle counts, and (2) a set of GPs that map stress time histories to these counts. **Results:** We present the outcomes of applying this framework to model root bending moment cycles for offshore wind turbines. **Conclusions:** The linked GP framework effectively reduces the dimensionality of the target distribution, thereby enabling reliable and computationally efficient probabilistic modeling of offshore wind-turbine stresses. Furthermore, the framework is flexible and can be extended to accommodate other data-driven or physics-based models. **Implications:** By facilitating more efficient stress modeling, this framework supports the development of highly accurate stochastic models for offshore wind-turbine components. Such models are essential for analyzing the impact of uncertainties in wind-turbine design and operational conditions on the reliability of offshore wind farms. Additionally, the framework can be adapted to represent the uncertainty surrounding stress time histories. **Keywords:** linked Gaussian process, probabilistic proxy model, offshore wind turbine, non-intrusive uncertainty quantification, non-intrusive uncertainty quantification. **Abbreviations:** GP, Gaussian process. GPR, Gaussian process regression.

We investigate the $R_\infty$ property within specific nilpotent quotients of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups, demonstrating that these quotients arise as images of mapping toruses associated with nilpotent groups under $H$-automorphisms. The first author previously established that mapping toruses are $R_\infty$-periodic with a minimal period of at most the order of the nilpotent group; we significantly refine this finding by proving that the minimal period does not exceed the order of the group's center. Leveraging this result, we identify instances where these mapping toruses genuinely exhibit $R_\infty$-periodicity. Furthermore, we determine the exact number of twisted conjugacy classes in certain nilpotent groups that result from nontrivial $H$-actions. Finally, we present a family of nilpotent groups where the mapping torus is $R_\infty$-periodic with a minimal period equal to the product of the orders of its constituent nilpotent groups. In the process, we also present examples of non-nilpotent groups possessing this characteristic. The arguments employed integrate techniques from number theory, graph theory, and group theory, with substantial reliance on computational data generated by the group theory software GAP. Additionally, we provide gap-filled proofs demonstrating that the mapping torus of the Baumslag group is $R_\infty$-periodic with a minimal period of at most 12, and that the mapping torus of the Nil-Anderson group is $R_\infty$-periodic with a minimal period of at most 6. These findings are supported by extensive tables of experimental results, many of which were derived using GAP. We also examine maps between finitely presented groups regarding their $R_\infty$ properties, revealing that while isomorphisms are generally $R_\infty$-periodic with a period of at most the group's rank, epimorphisms do not necessarily share this characteristic. Our analysis of epimorphisms between Heisenberg groups yields new findings on their image properties and establishes a novel criterion for identifying when an epimorphism is $R_\infty$-periodic. We conclude by formulating a conjecture concerning the $R_\infty$ property of mapping toruses derived from finitely presented nilpotent groups. Finally, we outline several open questions and areas for future research within the context of mapping toruses and their $R_\infty$ characteristics. Throughout

This paper presents a channel estimation framework designed to address nonlinear hardware distortions and a significantly reduced number of pilot symbols. The approach comprises two main components: first, a novel channel estimation method utilizing a hybrid Elman-Lee model channel estimator (HELM-C) that improves estimation accuracy under imperfect conditions by minimizing the root mean square error (RMSE); second, an optimization technique based on a multi-objective grey wolf optimizer (MO-GWO) to enhance HELM-C performance in short-pilot scenarios by optimizing the regularization parameter ($\lambda$) and dictionary matrix ($D$). Furthermore, the study examines the joint optimization of these parameters in OFDM systems featuring channel estimation flaws, nonlinear distortions, and partial synchronization errors. Results indicate that the proposed methods substantially enhance estimation precision, demonstrating that MO-GWO-based optimization is highly effective for channel estimation under imperfect operating conditions. Additionally, numerical simulations confirm that combining MO-GWO with HELM-C reduces estimation RMSE by 40% to 50% compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, the research explores reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted communication systems, proposing a new intelligent method for joint reflection coefficient (RC) estimation and selection (JRCS) within an RIS-enhanced OFDM (OFDM-RIS) system. This new approach, JRCS-ELM-C, leverages the proposed framework to deliver superior performance, achieving up to a 50% reduction in RMSE compared to existing methods. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that RIS deployment can lower RMSE by 30% to 50% relative to conventional OFDM systems. The study concludes that integrating RIS with OFDM-RIS offers a promising solution for next-generation communication systems. Keywords: Channel estimation, Elman-Lee model channel estimator, Gray wolf optimizer, Reconfigurable intelligent surface, Joint reflection coefficient estimation and selection.

The Individual Energy Assessment (IIA) theorem and a non-invasive fluctuation theorem (nIFT) were developed to address energy dissipation in single-particle systems. The IIA theorem links the average energy dissipated per fluctuation to local nonequilibrium properties, while the nIFT allows for the measurement of a new dissipation rate without perturbing the system. This study applies both theorems to an overdamped Brownian particle subject to time-dependent potentials. Exact solutions for various initial conditions reveal that the average dissipated energy is primarily determined by the initial condition, even when the potential is time-periodic and the system is quasi-periodic. Furthermore, when an analytical steady-state probability distribution is available, a new relationship emerges between the nIFT and conventional fluctuation theorem tests. We present specific test cases to validate the IIA theorem, demonstrate how to test the nIFT using a known steady-state distribution, and explore applications for potential energy surfaces. These findings suggest that these theorems can be utilized to test for non-invasive perturbations in experiments and to measure the total dissipated energy, including stochastic heating. Additionally, an algorithm for reconstructing conservative force fields is introduced. Furthermore, we establish that no infinitesimal deformations exist for any $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons under nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures. Additionally, we analyze the non-existence of deformations for Cayley instantons and present a novel class of manifolds where only the Cayley instanton exists alongside no others. The authors extend Ramanujan's findings on zeta values by incorporating Hurwitz zeta functions. For $n \geq 1$, $\y$, and $0 < s < 2$, the following identity holds:
\begin{align*}
\zeta(s,n,y)=&\,\frac{\Gamma(-s)}{(2\pi)^{-s}}\left[
\zeta\left(\begin{matrix} s& n\\ 0& 1 \end{matrix}\right)
F\left(\begin{matrix} 1& n-1 \end{matrix};s\right)
+\zeta\left(\begin{matrix} s& n-1\\ 0& 1 \end{matrix}\right)
F\left(\begin{matrix} 0& 1 \end{matrix};s\right)
\right]\\
=&\,\frac{\Gamma(-s)}{(2\pi)^{-s}}\left[
\zeta\left(\begin{matrix} s& n\\ 0& 1 \end{matrix}\right)
F\left(\begin{matrix} 1& n-1 \end{matrix};s\right)
-(-1)^{n-1}\zeta\left(\begin{matrix} s& n-1\\ 0& 1 \end{matrix}\right)
F\left(\begin{matrix} 0& 1 \end{matrix};s\right)
\right].

We conducted an exploratory study involving 20 participants to examine how typical Signal users perceive and understand the security app's PIN protection mechanism. This investigation targeted regular, engaged users to assess their awareness of the feature. Our findings reveal that a significant minority (45%) of these users are either unaware that the app even provides PIN protection or lack a clear understanding of what the PIN secures. Furthermore, this group holds numerous misconceptions, including the belief that the phone number alone is sufficient for account access, confusion regarding the difference between a PIN and a password, and the perception that enabling PIN protection merely activates end-to-end encryption. Additionally, many users hold incorrect views about the functionality of messages received prior to enabling PIN protection, with some fearing they will be lost. Finally, our analysis of user comments suggests that many see the feature as overly complex, indicating a potential lack of enthusiasm among typical Signal users toward PIN protection. These results highlight a significant gap between the intended design of Signal's PIN protection and users' actual perceptions, raising concerns about the feature's widespread adoption and effective use. To address these issues, we offer several recommendations for improving user comprehension and engagement with PIN protection. (This paper is a companion to [1].)

This study introduces an algorithm capable of accurately integrating any function defined over the unit sphere, provided its solar visibility from the sphere's center can be determined. The method's precision is governed by the number of evaluation points an underlying solar Gaussian quadrature scheme generates for that specific quadrature. Applications are demonstrated by integrating solar irradiance across the surfaces of spherical bodies, such as planets and satellites. The solar visibility function is treated as an input, although an algorithm to compute it is also provided. This tool is particularly valuable for the simulation and planning of surface solar energy systems on spherical objects within space. The paper includes examples and tests involving a satellite in low Earth orbit and another in a highly elliptical orbit around the Sun. The formulation and associated code are general and applicable to any sphere. The approach is also extensible to other spherical bodies where surface features, like mountains, do not obstruct the solar view from the center. The solar visibility function can be represented either as a fixed array or as a callable function.

This study examines the low-rank characteristics of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix and its outer-product-based variant (OGN) within the context of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Through comprehensive numerical experiments, we reveal the block-diagonal structure of OGN and the low-rank nature of GGN, uncovering the intrinsic curvature of loss landscapes in MLPs. Leveraging these findings, we introduce a rank-truncated OGN-based second-order optimization method named ViViT, which demonstrates superior performance in both training and inference compared to first-order techniques. Furthermore, ViViT enhances model robustness against poisoning attacks. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of ViViT in security applications, specifically addressing the challenge of defending against model poisoning attacks in machine learning. Our results indicate that ViViT significantly outperforms existing curvature methods, offering a promising solution for ensuring the reliability of machine learning systems. Zero-shot object localization is essential for ensuring long-term autonomy in dynamic environments where new obstacles can appear without prior training. This paper introduces ZSOP, a novel multi-shot method for estimating the global position and scale of class-specific obstacles. Unlike existing class-level estimation techniques that depend on object instances, ZSOP functions effectively with just one image per class. It utilizes a few-shot, class-specific Siamese network to estimate object locations relative to a class prototype, followed by a new upscaling module that maps these relative coordinates to a class-level global estimate. Because the upscaling module is designed to be domain invariant, it can be deployed in real-world scenarios without additional training. We evaluated the method on a self-collected dataset and benchmarked it against other object localization approaches on the nuScence dataset. The results demonstrate an average improvement of 10.5% in AUC over other methods. Furthermore, the ZSOP approach successfully identified all class-level obstacles in a real-world drive recorded from an autonomous vehicle, whereas previous methods failed in at least 50% of those scenarios. Graph data represents relationships among entities using nodes and edges, which can originate from various sources such as social networks, biological networks, or causal structures. However, existing statistical and machine learning techniques for graph data primarily focus on predictive modeling, often failing to offer robust inference regarding the causal impact of interventions. This limitation is particularly significant when analyzing counterfactual queries. This paper introduces a novel method for graph data analysis that builds upon VAINET (Kusner et al., 2017), an autoencoder designed to generate synthetic representations of interventional and counterfactual scenarios. VAINET relies on the assumption of an acyclic structural causal model (DAG) and a set of observed variables. We propose a new interventional and counterfactual network autoencoder (ICNNet) that offers greater flexibility by accommodating cyclic causal structures. This approach is derived from a variational autoencoder and is specifically designed to address interventional and counterfactual questions. Additionally, we present simulation results comparing VAINET and ICNNet, demonstrating that the proposed method achieves superior performance in scenarios involving unobserved confounders and provides more accurate estimates in certain counterfactual scenarios. Finally, we apply our method to a real-world causal inference problem concerning the relationship between air pollution and asthma. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChengyuanLi1992/VACANet. Keywords: Graph data, Causal inference, Intervention, Counterfactual, Autoencoder.

LOFAR's Irish station has recently been upgraded with a real-time transient-capture backend, enabling the recording of real-time transients from the LOFAR array. This system functions by triggering on significant deviations from the baseline total flux density and directing targeted recordings to either a dedicated tape drive or a file server. This paper details the first results from REALTA, which were obtained by analyzing a dataset comprising approximately 100 triggered events. The observations span a frequency range of 20–80 MHz and a time window from 2018 to 2019, covering a sky area of roughly 10,000 square degrees. Analysis of these data reveals that real-time transients are predominantly of solar origin, with a strong correlation between their intensity and the solar activity index. Additionally, the study identifies a few non-solar events, including a fast radio burst (FRB) and a potential repeating FRB. Furthermore, the paper establishes a new upper limit on the daily rate of extragalactic transients detectable by REALTA, which is lower than the rate observed by the Parkes MWA. This new limit is consistent with an upper limit on the annual FRB rate of $10^4$ MHz$^{-1}$Mpc$^{-3}$. Finally, the paper proposes several improvements to REALTA's data analysis pipeline to enhance future transient detection capabilities. Overall, this work demonstrates the potential of real-time transient capture for observing a diverse range of phenomena and underscores the value of such systems for future radio interferometers. Additionally, the paper includes a summary of various scientific applications for REALTA. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of how pre-released media features influence the box office revenue of films released through traditional distribution channels. We introduce a new, extensive dataset spanning 2000 to 2019, comprising 1,975 films and 10,826 reviews, which significantly surpasses previous collections in both sample size and depth. Utilizing this augmented dataset, we conducted rigorous experiments employing various machine learning and statistical methods to quantify the impact of specific pre-released features on revenue. Our findings indicate that the effects of these features are highly correlated with each other and the film category, suggesting that models trained on this data can effectively quantify these interrelationships. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these results are robust across different experimental configurations. By integrating this research with insights from film industry professionals, we offer recommendations for both producers and audiences. We conclude that our results are generalizable to other domains, such as video games and television series. The comprehensive dataset and associated code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/FeaturesAndMoney. This work expands upon the authors' prior research, which focused exclusively on IMDb ratings and examined only a limited dataset of films from a single decade. Specifically, the earlier version lacked the broader temporal and spatial coverage provided by the current dataset, which includes films from four distinct decades, and did not offer the granular details on pre-released features analyzed in this paper. Additionally, the earlier study did not incorporate the qualitative perspectives of industry experts included here. This research was conducted as part of the authors' internship at Netflix. We anticipate these conclusions will be valuable to professionals within the film industry. The authors are currently students at Carnegie Mellon University. Their interest in this topic stems from their own experiences working on feature films and their subsequent desire to understand the factors driving film success. This work offers a more quantitative exploration than their earlier research. Furthermore, by applying the concepts of singular and near-singular matrices, the research explores how low-frequency modes influence the stable convergence of operating points and validates these findings with real data. Additionally, when the network is sufficiently connected, we demonstrate that frequency regulation can mitigate unstable voltage convergence caused by parameter variations in non-electrical components, a phenomenon that contrasts with findings in electrical-only regulation models. This insight holds significant practical value, particularly for power networks characterized by non-homogeneity and inelastic loads. Finally, the potential applications of these findings in the power industry are discussed. The study's main contributions are as follows: (1) Deriving an auxiliary frequency regulation model based on physical principles and analyzing its mathematical properties; (2) Proving that frequency regulation with suitable parameters ensures stable behavior for both frequency and voltage in weakly-coupled power networks; (3) Utilizing singular and near-singular matrix theories to explain how low-frequency modes impact the stable convergence of operating points, with empirical validation using actual data; and (4) Illustrating the practical significance of frequency regulation in stabilizing power network operation through a specific case study. (5) Expanding the application scope of frequency regulation beyond the electrical domain into auxiliary scenarios. Specifically, the auxiliary frequency regulation model serves as a valuable tool for stabilizing power network operations in non-homogeneous networks, such as those involving gas networks. In the coming decades, numerous engineered cyberphysical systems (CPSs) will integrate cognition to enhance their functionality. A typical CPS consists of physical entities interconnected by communication and computation networks, where physical processes are monitored and managed by computational systems. These networks facilitate the collection of physical and environmental data, enabling systems to sense, learn, and make informed decisions. Currently, cognition is primarily located within individual computational units, such as servers or control centers. However, advancing cyberphysical systems will require the ability to deploy cognition across various domains, including the physical, communication, and computational layers. This capability will empower systems to dynamically adapt to environmental changes, learn from interactions, and optimize performance. By integrating cognition into non-computing physical elements within the system, we can enhance sensing, decision-making, and control mechanisms. This work investigates various approaches to creating a cyberphysical network of systems with cognition. We examine two primary methods for networked cognition: (i) distributed cognition, where physical entities possess cognitive capabilities, and (ii) emulated cognition, which mimics cognitive processes through the modification of physical entity behavior. We analyze these methods regarding their impact on system sensing, control, and communication networks. Furthermore, we address enabling technologies and methodologies, such as distributed learning, model learning, and hardware implementation, which facilitate the networking of cognition. Finally, we outline several open research challenges in this emerging field. We anticipate that integrating networked cognition into cyberphysical systems will significantly advance numerous emerging technologies. The origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra remains unresolved. This study investigates whether synchrotron self Compton (SSC) or external Compton (EC) scattering could be responsible, specifically examining scenarios where these processes occur within the broad line region (BLR) of active galactic nuclei (AGN). We employ the MAPPIES model, which utilizes Monte-Carlo methods to simulate the production of this excess via scattering of EC photons with finite energy and polarization. We apply this model to three AGN with measured magnetic field strengths in their BLRs: 3C 273, 3C 279, and 3C 276. Our results indicate that a magnetic field of approximately 100 Gauss is required to reproduce the observed UV/soft X-ray excess in these spectra. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that scattering EC photons with energies around 100 eV yields the best fit for the data. Finally, we estimate that the AGN population is likely to exhibit a degree of x-polarization in this energy range of roughly 10%. These findings offer a potential explanation for the long-standing mystery of the UV/soft X-ray excess. Additionally, if future observations confirm these predictions, they would provide the first evidence of magnetic fields within the BLR. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the viability of SSC or EC scattering as a mechanism driving the UV/soft X-ray surplus in AGN. To further test these hypotheses, we recommend that the future Euclid mission observe a sample of AGN with known magnetic field strengths in their BLRs. This would enable us to estimate the level of x-polarization in the UV/soft X-ray excess, thereby testing the predictions of this study. If these predictions are confirmed, it would constitute the first direct evidence of magnetic fields in the BLR. We conclude that this approach may prove to be the most effective method for detecting AGN magnetic fields in the BLR. Our findings may also hold significant implications for the proposed mission Polarized Extragalactic Survey of the Universe (PESQUAD). This mission aims to observe a sample of AGN with known BLR magnetic field strengths to search for the polarization of the accretion disc, thereby providing the first evidence of magnetic fields in the accretion disc. Specifically, the position and momentum correspond to the real and imaginary components of the complex variable, while the energy component represents the variation in the analytic extension's depth. This work addresses the challenge of distilling secret correlations from public ones using only local operations and virtual communication. We introduce a method for binary symmetric states—comprising secret and public bits that share the same pointwise XOR key—leveraging the observation that this distillation problem is equivalent to learning a nontrivial linear function of the secret bits using solely public bits. By applying this technique, we enhance the secret communication capacity of various vulnerable channels. For example, a general two-bit channel with 2^k outputs, where the secret component exhibits symmetry across all outputs, can transmit n bits while generating r random public bits such that the probability of success reaches 1/2 + 1/2^((r+1)/k). Furthermore, we propose a general construction for multi-bit channels that achieves the maximum possible value of r, given by r = m(2^K - 1), where m represents the count of 1s in the secret bit and K is a constant specific to the channel. Additionally, we examine a general scenario involving multiple symmetric pure-bit channels and their collective secret communication capability. Specifically, we analyze a system with two-bit channels producing three possible outcomes, demonstrating that the maximum r equals 3 times the length of the secret bit. These methodologies are also applicable to channels with higher bit depth, such as those with five possible outcomes. Finally, we explore an alternative approach to learning nontrivial functions of secret bits by examining the distributions of output bits. This leads to the virtual detection of symmetric pure states: two such states are considered detectable if their respective output distributions allow for the successful determination of the secret bit with a probability strictly greater than 1/2. We also examine nondeterministic channels, showing that certain symmetric pure states can be detected through an appropriate selection of input bit distributions. Consequently, we establish that two symmetric pure states are detectable if and only if they are learnable using public bits via an optimal linear function. Finally, we consider the case of two symmetric mixed states, proposing an optimization-based method to assess their detectability. As an application, we demonstrate that the secret bit in a symmetric mixed-state two-bit channel can be recovered with a probability of success equal to 1/2 plus the absolute value of the correlation between the secret and public bits. We also consider scenarios involving more than two symmetric mixed states. Finally, we illustrate the detection of symmetric pure and mixed states using examples derived from quantum mechanical systems with specific density matrices. This process, occurring within a non-Abelian QCD environment, involves a quark-antiquark pair emerging from a vacuum fluctuation at the string's terminus. The antiquark spirals inward along the string while the quark rotates outward, with the antiquark's angular momentum driving the creation of quark-antiquark pairs that facilitate further splittings. Ultimately, a meson containing the original quark detaches from the string's tip. Solar oscillations serve as a powerful tool for investigating the Sun's interior and its surface magnetic fields. By analyzing solar-mode frequencies, researchers can detect the influence of magnetic fields on solar plasma. This study examines how magnetic fields generate perturbations in solar-mode frequencies, specifically focusing on the resulting shifts in helioseismic travel durations. Using the data from the Dunn Solar Telescope, we identified filaments and currents near active regions and modeled the associated magnetic fields. We integrated these magnetic field models into the frequency modeling framework to calculate spectral perturbations, which we converted into travel-duration changes. Our results indicate that magnetic fields within active regions produce travel-duration signals exceeding 10 minutes, a finding consistent with helioseismic observations of travel-duration variations between the northern and southern hemispheres. Consequently, this work suggests a direct link between the strength of magnetic fields in active regions and the observed hemispheric differences in travel durations. This relationship may offer a new perspective on the global heliospheric magnetic field asymmetry. Additionally, we present a method for quantifying the contribution of magnetic fields to travel-duration measurements, a capability that could be applied to solar observations to study the origin of hemispheric magnetic asymmetry. Our methodology is also applicable to exoplanet host stars, enabling the investigation of the global magnetic field asymmetry in those systems. This could help explain the exoplanetary problem of hemispheric magnetic asymmetry. To achieve this, we propose that a high-resolution spatial resolution of approximately 0.5 arcsec is necessary. We conclude that the Dunn Solar Telescope, with its 0.1 arcsec resolution, is well-suited for this purpose. Finally, we discuss the potential of this approach to be utilized in future observations. Our analysis reveals that the magnetic field strength in active regions is at least 1000 G, and the field strength in filaments is approximately 100 G. These values align with previous findings regarding the strength of magnetic fields in the Sun's northern and southern hemispheres. Furthermore, we observed that the magnetic field strength in filaments is roughly 1% of that found in active regions. These results are also consistent with prior studies on the strength of the Sun's global magnetic field. Overall, this work demonstrates that magnetic fields in active regions and filaments are directly linked to the observed hemispheric asymmetry in travel durations. Magnetars, characterized by extreme magnetic fields, are hypothesized to generate gravitational waves through nonlinear self-interactions of these fields. This study investigates the cumulative gravitational wave signal produced by a stochastic ensemble of magnetic dipoles oriented randomly and rotating randomly within the pulsar timing spectrum band (10 Hz to 200 Hz). We estimate the signal amplitude using the $\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{GW}$ metric and compare it to the sensitivity of the LIGO and Virgo detectors in pulsar timing array band (PTA), pulsation band (PB), and null stream band (NSB) to assess signal detectability. Additionally, we provide an overview of the signal's characteristics across these frequency bands and discuss potential strategies for gravitational wave detection. Our findings indicate that the pulsar timing spectrum band is most promising for detecting magnetic waveform signals, provided that the average pulsar population exhibits a sufficiently high rate of magnetic field decay. Specifically, if the magnetic field decay rate of the pulsar population is approximately $10^{-11}$ per year, the magnetic waveform signal may be detectable in the PTA band. We further note that the expected strain in the PB and NSB is several orders of magnitude lower than that in the PTA band, suggesting that future research should prioritize the PTA band for detection efforts. Additionally, we propose that the null stream band could be utilized to isolate magnetic waveform signals from the background red noise generated by gravitational wave background and pulsar timing errors. Finally, we recommend that the LIGO and Virgo Collaboratory establish a dedicated working group to investigate the detectability of magnetic waveform signals in the PTA band. This group should conduct a comprehensive analysis of the signal's characteristics and develop strategies for detection. We also suggest that the group collaborate with pulsar timing array initiatives to explore potential detection methods. Furthermore, we propose that the LIGO and Virgo Collaboratory collaborate with pulsar timing array scientists to investigate methods for detecting magnetic waveform signals in the PTA band. Finally, we recommend that the LIGO and Virgo Collaboratory collaborate with the International Pulsar Timing Array Consortium to investigate methods for detecting magnetic waveform signals in the PTA band. In conclusion, we have demonstrated that the cumulative gravitational wave signal from ancient magnetic fields in the pulsar timing spectrum band is a significant source of gravitational waves that should be considered in the search for gravitational waves. This study addresses the emerging need for efficient, high-quality lpfimc by integrating a deep neural network (DNN) into a traditional compression framework. The proposed approach comprises three key components: 1) a new DNN architecture that bypasses the need for extensive superpixel training data by directly predicting a refined disparity map from raw lpfimc, thereby enhancing detail preservation; 2) an approach that leverages the DNN's superior detail recovery to boost compression performance; and 3) an optimization technique that minimizes compression artifacts by eliminating redundant data through a 2D DNN. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a 2.2 dB PSNR improvement at equivalent bitrates. Furthermore, the method is computationally efficient, requiring only 1.2 ms per image on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU. Finally, the DNN enables learning-driven generalization, allowing the system to handle image content never seen during training. Overall, the proposed method represents a significant advancement in lpfimc. The source code is available at https://github.com/SeungWooLee1234/LightFieldImageCompression. This study investigates the integration of noninteractive and interactive approaches within a vector-based cross-language information retrieval (CLIR) framework that employs neural machine translation (NMT) for query translation. We introduce a novel interactive framework that combines two existing methods, leveraging their respective strengths to enhance performance. We also explore the utilization of generated human translations as a supplementary training dataset alongside automatic NMT outputs. The research is based on an English-French machine translation task utilizing the TREC WL-106 collection, with evaluations conducted at TREC 2019 and 2020. Experimental results indicate that the proposed interactive framework surpasses both the individual interactive and noninteractive approaches, while the application of human translations yields a further significant performance gain. Furthermore, we assess various interactive questioning strategies and assess the robustness of our method against errors in human provided translations. Finally, we analyze the specific contributions of vector representations and NMT translations to CLIR performance. The source code and datasets are publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/lmdb-clir. Our findings suggest that high-quality human translations serve as a valuable resource for CLIR, and our code demonstrates a 20% improvement in retrieval performance when trained on vector representations derived from human translations. Additionally, our analysis reveals that while vector representations are essential for establishing a shared semantic space, they introduce greater uncertainty compared to translations, which exhibit higher confidence. Overall, our work advances the field of CLIR, and we welcome collaboration to further develop these methods. Contact: https://www.davide-salviotti.org. Collaborators: https://www.alexander-kroher.de. Corresponding author: Davide Salviotti.

This study introduces two approaches to small-geography estimation (SGE) within a low- and middle-income country (LMIC) setting, specifically focusing on the 2011 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) conducted in Lesotho. The design-oriented method leverages the survey's sampling design, whereas the model-focused approach utilizes external data from the World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDI). Validation was conducted by comparing estimates against those from the 2016 Lesotho Integrated Household Survey (LIHS). Results indicate that while both methods yield reasonable approximations for most metrics, the model-focused approach demonstrates superior performance in estimating means, while the sampling design approach excels at calculating proportions. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that SGE is highly sensitive to the number of observations; however, it demonstrates robustness when the number of estimations is large, even if individual estimates lack precision. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of handling outliers in SGE using both methods. Overall, the findings suggest that while estimates in this LMIC context are generally reliable, practitioners must remain cautious regarding precision, particularly regarding proportions. Additionally, repeated validation is advisable to ensure that estimates remain current. Future research should explore alternative models for SGE and assess their efficacy in producing accurate estimates. These conclusions are supported by an R package designed to facilitate practical implementation of the sampling design-based SGE approach. By providing both theoretical and practical resources, this package enables researchers to apply these methods to their own surveys. Given the availability of public data from sources like the World Bank, the package is particularly valuable for LMICs that have not yet invested in developing their own national statistical infrastructure. Wagering strategies often depend on adjusting stakes based on cumulative wins and losses. A well-known approach, the Kelly method, aims to maximize long-term growth by analyzing odds and potential outcomes. This study extends the Kelly system into a framework incorporating quantum mechanics. Drawing inspiration from the de Broglie-Bohm interpretation, the analysis introduces a key variable representing the probability of winning a specific bet. The authors derive a formula for the optimal fraction to wager, expressed as a function of this probabilistic variable. Finally, the research demonstrates that the average return following a sequence of bets follows a harmonic distribution. The remaining challenge involves developing an algorithm to compute the expected value of this harmonic distribution using the associated wave function. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions regarding the quantum extension of the Kelly criterion. This work is intended to serve as an introduction to the intriguing intersection between quantum mechanics and gambling theory. Additionally, the authors acknowledge the lighthearted possibility of testing these strategies in both quantum and classical casinos. For instance, in a quantum casino, a gambler might accept a bet with a non-zero probability of winning, whereas in a classical setting, they would reject a bet with a zero probability, even if the potential payout is infinite. Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest for their unique electronic and optical characteristics, including band gaps in the visible spectrum and band structure variations driven by metal types and chiral stacking. Recently, transition metal diatomides (MDs) have emerged as a new class of two-dimensional materials with comparable features, attracting substantial research attention. In this study, we utilize a high-precision hybrid density functional theory (DFT) framework to investigate the electronic and optical properties of MDs within MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge, S; and Z = N, P, As) in both monolayer and bilayer configurations. Our analysis examines three critical aspects: electronic band structure, optical absorption spectra, and exciton characteristics. Our findings indicate that the electronic and optical properties of MDs are governed by the specific metal atom and the interplay between SI and PI bands. Notably, MDs exhibit a stacking-independent exciton resonance, a feature that distinguishes them from TMDs and offers potential for applications in optical devices. Additionally, we provide a systematic examination of how the energy alignment between quasiparticle excitations in MA$_2$Z$_4$ and TiS$_2$ changes with respect to the constituent elements. This analysis is particularly relevant for designing heterostructures with MDs and SI monolayers. Finally, we offer a comprehensive overview of the electronic and optical properties of MDs to guide future experimental investigations. This work expands the known palette of two-dimensional materials for optoelectronic applications. Specifically, MDs offer tunable optical responses, tunable band gaps, and tunable quasiparticle energy alignments, making them promising candidates for next-generation optoelectronic devices. Furthermore, the distinct stacking-dependent exciton resonances in SI and PI phases of MDs could enable the development of unique optoelectronic devices with novel functionalities. This research was conducted using the Tianhe-2 supercomputer. This study reports on the ultra-rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, which was previously observed experimentally for the first time by the LHCb collaboration in 2017 but lacked theoretical validation. We demonstrate that this decay is feasible within both the Standard Model and various beyond-Standard-Model frameworks. Utilizing 2.8 ab$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 7$ and 8 TeV, we measure the branching ratio for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ to be ${\mathcal{B}}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (1.02 \pm 0.12 \pm 0.11) \times 10^{-8}$. The first uncertainty reflects statistical variation, while the second accounts for systematic effects. Furthermore, we conduct a model-independent analysis of the decay's differential rate and angular distribution, deriving constraints on the Wilson coefficients governing flavor-changing neutral currents at the two-loop level. Additionally, we investigate the sensitivity of future experiments, including the high-luminosity LHCb and the proposed Belle II facility. These analyses confirm that next-generation experiments can achieve precision measurements of this ultra-rare process with sensitivities surpassing the LHCb results. Such measurements would enable stringent constraints on new physics contributions, potentially reaching the level required to detect signals from two-loop flavor-changing neutral current processes. Additionally, we highlight the sensitivity of these future experiments to hadronic contributions arising from virtual photons and lepton universality violations. Finally, we explore the potential of these measurements to probe baryonic sectors of physics beyond the Standard Model. This work establishes a foundation for investigating similar ultra-rare hyperon decays, such as $\Lambda^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, which were previously inaccessible. These investigations could reveal new physics effects that are otherwise difficult to detect. The formation of stars and their associated protoplanetary disks is a critical phase in the evolution of stellar systems. We propose that the collapse of a prestellar core fragment, triggered by a nearby supernova shock wave, can directly generate a protoplanetary disk. This scenario is supported by hydrodynamical simulations that model the disk's formation through the fragmentation and rupture of a prestellar nucleus. The characteristics of the resulting disk—specifically its mass, radius, and temperature—align well with observational data for Class 0 YSOs. Our findings indicate that the disk originates from the direct collapse of the cloud material surrounding the central protostar, rather than being formed solely by the accretion of material onto a central mass. The initial conditions of the cloud, particularly the supernova-induced line density shock, significantly influence the final disk properties. Consequently, this research offers a novel perspective on the origins of protoplanetary disks and underscores the necessity of investigating the initial cloud conditions to comprehensively understand their impact on disk formation. A detailed analysis of this process will be the focus of our future work. Atmospheric scattering significantly influences the appearance of celestial bodies, yet current atmospheric general circulation models fail to accurately represent this process. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of various Rayleigh scattering models to identify the most suitable one for weather forecasting. We conducted on-sky observations of the twilight sky and the Moon during the day to measure key parameters, including the vertical optical depth, the Rayleigh scattering phase function, and Rayleigh polarization. These measurements were compared against four existing Rayleigh models: the RASPRO, RASSIM, RICHARDSON, and MACC models. Our findings indicate that the RASPRO model aligns most closely with the observed data, while the MACC model shows the greatest discrepancy. Furthermore, the RASPRO model was employed to simulate the polarization of linearly polarized light reflected by the lunar surface as seen from Earth. Finally, we propose a new Rayleigh scattering model that is more accurate than the currently available options. This proposed model is available at \url{https://github.com/sergey-panov/PyRayleigh}. Additionally, we outline a methodology for conducting on-sky observations to characterize Rayleigh scattering and provide PyRayleigh, a Python library for these observations, at \url{https://github.com/sergey-panov/PyRayleigh}. This library can be utilized to calculate Rayleigh scattering contributions to direct solar irradiance, radiative transfer, and atmospheric polarization. The PyRayleigh package is distributed under the GNU General Public License v3.0. Its functionality includes: (i) a lunar albedo function for simulating on-sky observations of Rayleigh-scattered light from the Moon; (ii) a function to compute the ratio of Rayleigh scattering to atmospheric scattering; (iii) a function to determine the degree of Rayleigh polarization; and (iv) a function to calculate the azimuthal angle of Rayleigh polarization. All four functionalities are implemented as command-line tools within the package. The PyRayleigh package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install PyRayleigh. The package details are available at: https://pypi.org/project/PyRayleigh/. The PyRayleigh package license is GNU GPLv3. The package homepage is: https://pyrayleigh.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. We introduce a multi-term temporal sequence modeling approach that employs Bayesian inference to derive a sparse, data-driven sequence model. Drawing inspiration from the Vedic tradition of chanting mantras across various time scales, this method enables the application of a suitable term from the sequence model based on available data and computational resources. By utilizing Bayesian inference, we can quantify the uncertainty associated with each term. Furthermore, we extend this framework to handle multi-dimensional data through tensorization. Numerical experiments on both 1D and multi-dimensional data demonstrate the method's efficacy in sequence modeling and prediction. Additionally, we show that our approach can detect anomalies in data streams. The widespread adoption of federated learning (FL) has made it a standard framework for safeguarding user privacy. Nevertheless, we have identified two critical challenges that hinder its practical deployment. First, we introduce Justice, a new fairness metric for federated systems that is significantly easier to calculate than traditional metrics. Second, we discovered Differential Confidentiality, a vulnerability where certain users face privacy risks because their data contributes disproportionately to model updates. We developed two novel privacy-preserving techniques to address these issues, with experimental results demonstrating that they effectively ensure both justice and differential confidentiality within federated environments. To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first comprehensive examination of these problems and their solutions in federated learning. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/FL-Justice. Additionally, FL-JUSTICE is the inaugural open-source FL library specifically engineered to guarantee justice and differential privacy. The source code for these methods will be released on PyTorch. This study examines a supersymmetric minimal framework for embedding the Standard Model within a new $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, utilizing the $368$-dimensional representation of $SO(10)$. Right-handed Majorana neutrinos are assigned to the dark energy sector, acquiring negligible masses through the decay of a dedicated dark energy superfield. We analyze the model's implications for the Higgs boson mass, the new gauge boson mass, and mixing angles, while investigating constraints imposed by electroweak precision tests and Higgs boson decay data. Furthermore, we consider the model's dark matter candidate and its compatibility with cosmological observations. Finally, we establish the parameter space for the Higgs boson and the $Z'$ gauge boson masses, noting that both lie beyond the reach of current experimental detectors. Consequently, this space will be accessible only through future upgrades at the LHC or, more likely, at the High-Luminosity LHC or a potential future 100 TeV proton-proton collider. Additionally, we determine that the lifetime of the dark energy superfield must be less than $10^{10}$ years to ensure it decays before the onset of cosmic acceleration. This requirement is met if the mass of the fermionic superpartner of this scalar field is approximately $10^{10}$ GeV. Finally, we discuss the model's testability at these future facilities. Finally, we note that the $SO(10)$ representation associated with this framework has been previously analyzed in Ref. [arXiv:hep-ph/0109200]. However, in that work, right-handed neutrinos were assumed to acquire masses at the same scale as other fermions. In contrast, our approach treats these neutrinos as dark energy, granting them vanishingly small masses and explaining their absence in experimental observations. This approach also resolves the issue of obtaining a vanishing cosmological constant. Our findings demonstrate that this framework offers a robust explanation for the smallness of right-handed neutrino masses and their non-detection. Furthermore, it provides a natural resolution to the fine-tuning problem associated with the cosmological constant. Thus, our analysis offers a comprehensive and consistent description of the particle physics sector. We conclude that this framework represents a promising path toward a unified theory beyond the Standard Model. This paper introduces a new unsupervised learning framework designed to identify the most promising radio resources for reassignment to interrupted services in an IRS-assisted wireless network. These sources are optimized to enhance throughput during service disruptions, considering radio resource constraints and the need to maintain quality of service for uninterrupted services. Additionally, the study addresses the optimization of IRS phase shifts to maximize throughput under disruption, subject to the same quality of service constraints for non-interrupted services. A dual-decomposition algorithm is developed to solve this problem by decomposing it into subproblems utilizing the phase shift property for signal reflection. Results demonstrate that the proposed radio resource optimization strategy significantly improves throughput during disruptions, while the IRS phase shift configuration achieves substantial gains for non-interrupted services. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the dual-decomposition algorithm is shown to be low. Finally, practical considerations regarding IRS deployment are examined. Numerical results confirm that the suggested resource optimization approach yields significant throughput improvements for interrupted services, whereas optimal IRS phase shifts deliver significant benefits for non-interrupted services. Finally, an IRS deployment strategy is proposed to maximize the throughput of interrupted services. In this context, interrupted services are assumed to be pre-assigned specific resource blocks, which are then optimized to further enhance their performance. Simulations indicate that the proposed optimization scheme for interrupted services, combined with the practical IRS deployment strategy, yields a significant improvement in throughput. Simulation results also confirm that the IRS phase shift configuration yields a significant performance gain for non-interrupted services. Finally, it is observed that the impact of IRS phase shift optimization on interrupted services is lower compared to its effect on non-interrupted services. The paper concludes that the proposed solution offers a practical and effective strategy for managing disruptions in wireless networks. Specifically, the solution involves two key components: first, optimizing IRS phase shifts to achieve significant performance gains for non-interrupted services; and second, reassigning radio resources to interrupted services to significantly boost their throughput. Additionally, an IRS deployment strategy is proposed to further improve the throughput of interrupted services. Overall, the results indicate that the proposed solution is highly effective for radio resource optimization in interrupted services and achieves significant performance gains for non-interrupted services. Furthermore, the practical IRS deployment strategy contributes to additional throughput improvements for interrupted services. Finally, it is noted that while IRS phase shift optimization has a lower impact on interrupted services compared to non-interrupted ones, it still provides performance benefits for both groups. The $\beta^-$-decay of $^{186}$Hg was investigated for the first time, with decay energies, half-life, branching ratios, and $\gamma$-ray energies all measured for the first time. Additionally, conversion coefficients for ten X-ray and $\gamma$-ray transitions were determined using HPGe detectors and National Bureau of Standards coefficients. The experimental results align well with theoretical predictions based on shell model calculations utilizing the KB3L effective interaction. This study establishes $^{186}$Hg as a valuable tool for investigating nuclear structure in the N=104–108 region. Additionally, the decay properties of $^{186}$Hg are examined in the context of its parent production via the $^{185}$Re(d,$\beta^-$) reaction using a 15 MeV deuterium beam. The analysis suggests that a double magic nucleus exists at N=108, with a shell gap of approximately 1.5 MeV. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of this reaction for producing high-purity, high-activity $^{186}$Hg sources suitable for medical applications. We introduce a unified framework that interconnects the dark sector, specifically dark matter and neutrino mass generation, within the supergravity extension of the type-II seesaw model. In this context, the neutral component of the singlet superfield, which constitutes the dark matter candidate, is stabilized by a cubic interaction term involving two scalar lepton Higgs fields. We investigate the impact of a heavy right-handed neutrino mass spectrum on these dynamics, demonstrating that a degenerate mass spectrum significantly enhances the dark matter abundance. Furthermore, we establish a specific relationship between the dark matter density and the reheat temperature necessary for successful thermal leptogenesis. Finally, we examine the experimental constraints and viable parameter space of our model. This framework is also discussed in a companion paper, which incorporates the $\mu$-term of the supergravity Type-II seesaw superpotential. Data-Informed Control (DIC) aims to leverage extensive datasets alongside supplementary information, such as physical laws, to enhance control performance. This study presents a novel framework that uses large-scale data to learn a controller capable of mastering multiple distinct locomotion tasks—specifically walking, flying, and swimming—simultaneously. The research addresses two critical challenges: (1) a severe limitation in available data, and (2) a lack of prior knowledge regarding the specific task objectives. To overcome these issues, the proposed approach integrates physical principles with data-driven techniques to create a unified controller. Validation was performed using large-scale simulations of animal behaviors, demonstrating the method's effectiveness across diverse biological and robotic scenarios. The video illustrating these simulation results can be found at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1242422222. This work underscores the versatility and promise of data-informed methodologies in achieving multi-task capabilities. The associated code and models are available at: https://github.com/ChenYuan2000/Multi-Task-Physical-DIC.
