This work investigates the Ward relations within three-dimensional Toda conformal quantum field theory, which involves a chiral algebra isomorphic to the rational $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ affine Virasoro algebra. The study establishes a system of second-order differential equations governing $n$-point correlation functions and explicitly calculates several cases for arbitrary $n$. Furthermore, multiple relation identities are conjectured. These findings are anticipated to be extendable to the general $\mathfrak{sl}_l$ scenario. Additionally, the established Ward relations are expected to aid in determining non-diagonal matrix elements between Fock space states for the chiral vertex operators of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ affine Virasoro algebra. Finally, various identities regarding the Jack symmetric functions $\phi^{(\alpha,\beta)}_n$ are derived; these functions correspond to the Schur functions evaluated at specific parameters $\alpha=3$ and $\beta=0$. The analysis encompasses not only standard Schur functions but also their generalizations involving multiple variables. The resulting relations encompass both Cauchy identities and dual Cauchy identities. Finally, the connection between Jack symmetric functions and the Kontsevich-Zorich tau-function is examined. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the Kontsevich-Zorich tau-function can be expressed as a vacuum expectation value involving a product of Schur functions. This formulation is expected to extend to the broader context of $\mathfrak{sl}_l$ Toda conformal quantum theory, where the relevant functions would be the Jack symmetric functions of type $l$. The derived identities for Jack symmetric functions are expected to generalize to these type $l$ functions as well. Furthermore, the second author has established a comprehensive theory of Jack symmetric functions of type $l$ capable of generating the Kontsevich-Zorink tau-function; this framework is also expected to extend to a broader class of functions. This research falls under the classification: 17B81. This paper introduces a novel class of Relation GANs (RGANs) designed to learn relation graphs by integrating unsupervised and supervised learning approaches. Connectionist autoencoders, or network layers, are employed as the representation network to model dependencies between inputs and class labels. By utilizing a triplet loss function, the system distinguishes between similar and dissimilar samples. Conversely, a generative adversarial network (GAN) acts as the discriminator to synthesize data from latent vectors that preserve the sample's original class label. We establish theoretical guarantees for these RGANs, demonstrating convergence under specific conditions. The proposed RGAN framework is applied to two scenarios: graph learning from image data and molecular property prediction. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of RGANs, with the first achieving state-of-the-art performance and the second showing promising outcomes. Additionally, we provide both empirical and theoretical evidence supporting the stability of these RGANs. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ashokkumar12345/RGAN. A twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKD) protocol is introduced that operates without requiring phase synchronization between twin fields, thereby eliminating the primary performance bottleneck of TF-QKD. In this framework, phase randomization is applied exclusively to one twin field, while the other remains unphased. The quantum key rate achieves the same scaling as standard TF-QKD protocols but reaches closer to the Shannon capacity. This method offers a practical upgrade to existing QKD systems by leveraging just one twin-field laser, simplifying optical components, and enhancing key rates. Additionally, the paper examines various technical performance metrics, including key rate-distance curves, gain functions, and error rates. The proposed approach is applicable to all TF-QKD protocols, benefiting both experimental and theoretical research in the field. Furthermore, this technique can be readily adapted for twin-field entanglement distribution. Finally, the work explores a connection between TF-QKD protocols and classical communication, specifically classical interference channel coding. This relationship establishes a bridge between quantum key distribution and quantum entanglement distribution, potentially offering a pathway to theoretically prove the optimal key rate and entanglement rate for TF-QKD. The findings are expected to advance the development of quantum communication theory. The codebook strategy for twin fields is derived from the finite blocklength analysis of classical channel coding, which is also discussed. The proposed solution is readily applicable to existing TF-QKD systems. The results demonstrate that the optimal key rate for TF-QKD is 3 dB higher than that of the BB84 protocol, with similar improvements observed in other scenarios. This represents the first time the optimal key rate for TF-QKD has been theoretically calculated. Notably, the optimal key rate in TF-QKD exhibits an infinite-distance behavior distinct from other QKD protocols, scaling as $\mathcal{O}(D^{-2})$ compared to the $\mathcal{O}(D^{-1})$ scaling of other protocols. This improved long-distance performance is attributed to the interference effect between signals from different users, a feature that is theoretically proven. The significance of TF-QKD is expected to grow as its development progresses. The proposed solution is easily implementable in existing TF-QKD systems. This article investigates various Toeplitz algebras defined on Fock spaces and introduces multiple Toeplitz operators relevant to Fock spaces, Bergman-type domains, and weighted Bergman spaces. We demonstrate that the Toeplitz algebra generated by a specific class of operators possesses a C*-subalgebra isomorphic to the Toeplitz algebra arising from a broad class of positive operators on Fock spaces. Additionally, we establish that the Toeplitz algebra on a Fock space contains a C*-subalgebra isomorphic to the Toeplitz algebra on a corresponding weighted Bergman space. Furthermore, by utilizing a specific deformation map, we show that the Toeplitz algebra on a Fock space admits a C*-subalgebra isomorphic to the Toeplitz algebra on a Bergman domain. Finally, we provide several results that clarify the structure and representation theory of Toeplitz operators on Fock spaces. In forthcoming research, these findings will be extended to weighted Bergman spaces. This work serves as a foundation for that subsequent study. Our approach offers a distinct alternative to the methods employed by Tohru Matsumoto. Matsumoto's technique involves deforming the Fock space into a weighted Bergman space over a bounded domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$ via holomorphic restriction, followed by a deformation back to the Fock space. In contrast, this paper employs a deformation map grounded in the Segal-Bargmann transform. This method utilizes a restriction to a Bergman domain $D$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ followed by a specific extension. The extension step is achieved through a continuous extension of holomorphic functions on $D$ to $\mathbb{C}^n$, a result established by Luef. This approach provides a natural framework for investigating Toeplitz operators on Fock spaces. Our results pave the way for future exploration of various Toeplitz algebras on Fock spaces. This paper acts as a precursor to that future investigation. Specifically, we examine Toeplitz operators on Fock spaces with symbols drawn from step functions, piecewise polynomials on D, and step functions on D. Our findings include a characterization of the essential norm of Toeplitz operators using the oscillation of their symbols and the essential norm of their deformed counterparts on Bergman spaces. We also present a sufficient condition for the commutativity of two Fock Toeplitz operators and establish a sufficient condition for the essential commutativity of their symbols. Moreover

Identizing objects with a open lexicon is a difficult task that has garnered significant attention in recent years. While most current approaches depend on predefined category labels, bounding box examples, and fine-tune object detectors to learn visual attributes, identifying a new category often demands substantial time and resources. To address this, we introduce pseudo bounding box supervision, a method that circumvents the need for bounding box examples while requiring only pseudo bounding box annotations. This strategy utilizes the detection capability of a pre-trained detector to generate the pseudo bounding box annotations required for unsupervised fine-tuning. Experimental results on the visual question answering dataset (VQA-CP) demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we validate the method's generalizability by achieving promising performance on the Cross-VOC dataset. The code will be made publicly available. All experimental results are accessible at https://github.com/Chongchou/Lexicon-Identification. The dataset is available at https://github.com/Chongchou/VOC-Checkpoint. The Pictet-Spessert (PS) cloud is a notable feature within the Rho Ophiuchus (Rho Oph) dark nebula, characterized by a prominent ionization front (IF) that curves around the infrared source S1. This study aims to determine the three-dimensional structure of the IF and analyze the gas distribution behind it. By analyzing H-alpha and [N II] 6548,6583 Å images alongside [S II] 6717,6731 Å and [N II] 5005,5007 Å data, we mapped the spatial distribution of ionized gas, atomic gas, and photodissociation regions (PDRs) surrounding the IF. Our findings indicate that the IF exhibits a concave shape toward the south-west, with a minimum angular separation from S1 of approximately 10 arcseconds. The thickness of the ionized gas near the IF is estimated at 100-200 parsecs, while the PDR gas forms a thin layer roughly 10 parsecs thick. The N II 5005,5007 Å emission reveals a PDR gas distribution that aligns with the IF, displaying a similar morphology. This PDR gas is situated between the ionized gas and the molecular cloud, exhibiting a column density of 10^20 cm^-2. These results suggest that the IF is not a thin plane but a thick, three-dimensional structure. Additionally, the detection of PDR gas between the ionized gas and the molecular material may help explain the observed reddening of S1. These observations support the hypothesis that the IF is a stratified structure influenced by the pressure of the ionized gas. Furthermore, the PDR gas detected between the IF and the molecular cloud may contribute to the clumpy morphology of the IF. Finally, the newly identified PDR gas could be a critical factor in shaping the IF's morphology. These conclusions are consistent with the model previously proposed by Nakano et al. (2010). The three-dimensional structure of the IF offers valuable insights for understanding the formation mechanisms of such structures. INTRODUCTION Transformers have rapidly become a cornerstone of machine learning, particularly in computer vision. Initially gaining prominence in natural language processing, they have successfully extended to image recognition, object detection, segmentation, and beyond. This document provides a thorough review of transformer applications in computer vision, covering various tasks such as image and video recognition, segmentation, and generation. By synthesizing insights from recent studies, this survey highlights the evolving role of transformers in vision and HPC. It serves as a valuable guide for researchers and practitioners navigating this dynamic area of artificial intelligence. This paper reviews the application of transformers in computer vision. This paper introduces a new class of factor models featuring time-varying factor loadings to forecast mortality rates. While loadings are unobserved, their time-varying nature is driven by a low-dimensional dynamic process, a framework we term the "factor state space model." We provide both a theoretical foundation and an empirical application of this approach, which we show outperforms competing methods in out-of-sample mortality prediction. This improvement stems from two key advantages: first, the model captures the non-linear mortality risk associated with climate change; and second, it addresses the limitations of traditional factor models that rely on linear relationships between mortality risk and climate change. Additionally, we derive the local factor loading process to develop an online Bayesian forecasting method that recursively updates forecasts as new data arrives. This method is computationally efficient and avoids the need to re-estimate the model with expanding datasets. Finally, we outline an approach to forecast mortality rates under climate change by analyzing the relationship between the dynamic climate process and factor loadings. This enables the prediction of mortality rates at specific locations and times, given a projected climate trajectory. These capabilities are particularly valuable for long-term mortality rate planning. Furthermore, we extend the model to a hierarchical structure to predict mortality rates for regions lacking historical data. This extension demonstrates that the proposed approach can effectively address data sparsity issues. Our methodology is applied to life annuity pricing to price longevity risk, proving that the model is adaptable for other purposes. For instance, it can serve as a foundation for mortality reduction research. Additionally, the hierarchical extension facilitates the comparison of mortality rates across different regions. Our methodology employs an efficient data augmentation technique to address non-Gaussian issues in factor loading processes. This results in a highly effective model with low computational costs, making it suitable for large datasets. We have implemented this approach in an R package to facilitate its application. Finally, we demonstrate how to conduct Bayesian forecasting of mortality rates using climate change scenarios. This allows for the prediction of future mortality rates under various climate change trajectories. This capability is essential for assessing the impact of climate change on mortality rates. These applications illustrate the model's adaptability for various uses. A primary obstacle in Neural Architecture Exploration (NEA) is the inherent disruption caused by the highly non-stationary nature of architecture performance, which hampers the convergence of sequential exploration strategies. This study examines the root causes of this disruption and proposes an algorithmic framework to mitigate it. Our analysis reveals that the non-stationarity stems from two distinct sources: (1) the non-stability of the mapping between architecture parameters and performance, and (2) the noisy estimation of absolute architecture performance. To address the first source, we develop an algorithm that mitigates non-stationarity by filtering out unstable mappings. To tackle the second source, we design an algorithm that alleviates the impact of performance noise by enabling the exploration process to dynamically adjust the estimated value noise of architectures. We have integrated these two approaches into a unified framework and evaluated it against several baselines across multiple tasks. The results demonstrate that our framework outperforms the baselines, thereby validating the effectiveness of this non-stationarity-aware exploration approach in NEA. Attribute-Based Time Series (ABTS) offers a flexible framework for modeling various types of time series data by integrating traditional time series methods with techniques from categorical data analysis. This approach involves analyzing the distribution of extra variables, known as attributes or covariates, over specific time intervals, typically defined by the series' periodicity. The primary motivation behind ABTS is to incorporate the impact of these external variables into time series models. This article introduces the theft R package, which provides utilities for handling, visualizing, and analyzing ABTS data. We demonstrate how to create rich multivariate time series models that include covariates by leveraging abts-specific functions within theft. Furthermore, we extend the theft framework to address partial ABTS scenarios, where the complete set of attributes is not consistently observed. Additionally, we provide open-source examples using the multi-source air quality dataset from Rome, Italy, to illustrate the package's capabilities. The source code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/QuantitativeMethods/abts-time-series-example. Keywords: Attribute-Based Time Series, Covariates, R, theft package.

This resolves a question posed by Gromov in [Gromov2006] within the context of non-positively curved manifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of a uniform curvature bound for complete geodesically convex subsets of a fixed complete CAT(0) manifold $M$ is equivalent to the strong amenability of the discrete isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}(M)$. Additional outcomes in this area stem from the framework of uniform curvature, which is detailed in the paper. This paper introduces a novel approach to assess translator dependability. We employ a classification-based technique, utilizing classification metrics and a confusion matrix to measure performance and derive multiple new dependability metrics. Additionally, we introduce a new suite of combination methods designed to enhance performance through the integration of multiple translations. Extensive experiments were conducted across three English-French translation pairs. Our findings indicate that combining models from different trained datasets yields the best results, with the best-case improvement reaching +10.21 points on the BLEU score. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the evaluation results generated by this new method are more interpretable than those produced by conventional machine-assisted evaluation. The source code and dependencies required to replicate our approach and metrics are publicly available at https://github.com/Amelie-Beaubatie/MT-translator-evaluation. We also provide a Python library that facilitates evaluation through a user-friendly interface, offering several pre-defined methods for easy adoption. This library is accessible at https://github.com/Amelie-Beaubatie/MT-translator-evaluation. We encourage researchers to utilize this library for their own translator evaluations. This work serves as a demonstration of the evaluation support for the new method, with a more comprehensive set of experiments and an in-depth discussion of evaluation support planned for future publication. Our goal is to foster a community of practice that can further develop this work and explore its application in various scenarios. This represents our first step toward making the method more interpretable and user-friendly. We welcome the research community to contribute to this evaluation support and explore its various applications. This work illustrates how to develop evaluation support for new methods and how to build a community of practice to further evolve such contributions. We look forward to your input and collaboration. In an open quantum or classical system subjected to a time-periodic field, energy absorption occurs through inelastic scattering processes. This study derives sum rules for energy absorption within a scattering framework, utilizing a scattering phase rule analogous to the Gamov sum rule for bound-state energy levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate within the same formalism that the derived sum rules remain valid in the limit where the external time-dependent field vanishes. Finally, connections to the recently proposed dynamical Kohn sum rule are established. These findings are supported by applications to two-dimensional and three-dimensional jellium models. Specifically, for 2D jellium, we compare our derived sum rules against those obtained from time-dependent density functional theory and exact solutions. Additionally, we investigate the sum rules for energy absorption in 3D jellium using the random phase approximation. We conclude by linking these derived sum rules to the Einstein sum rules governing the dynamic structure factor. The analysis begins by defining the fundamental problem of energy absorption in an open system under a time-periodic potential, followed by the derivation of scattering phase and energy sum rules for one-dimensional systems, and lastly, the formulation of dynamical Kohn sum rules within a scattering framework. Subsequently, we derive expressions for scattering eigenchannels and their associated sum rules. Finally, we apply these derived sum rules to the previously mentioned jellium model systems. Introduction. We begin by examining energy absorption in an open quantum or classical system, such as a jellium model, subjected to a time-periodic potential. This scenario is relevant to investigations of electron energy absorption in jellium under a time-dependent field, a topic explored in various studies [1-10]. These works explore the phenomenon through diverse theoretical frameworks, including the random phase approximation, the jellium-atom approximation, and time-dependent density functional theory. We investigate a free lottery system designed to encourage participation. In this scenario, a single winner is selected from all purchased tickets. To induce more buyers, the ticket price is dynamically reduced based on the count of current purchasers. Specifically, the anticipated value of the prize is defined by a non-increasing concave function of the total demand. Our objective is to determine the optimal pricing strategy that maximizes the lottery's anticipated value. We analyze the system under two distinct assumptions regarding prize allocation: a proportional scheme, where the winning prize is distributed proportionally to the number of tickets purchased, and a uniform scheme, where the prize amount remains constant regardless of purchase volume. For both scenarios, we establish the optimal pricing policy and provide numerical estimates of the system's performance. Furthermore, we introduce an online algorithm that achieves near-optimal performance with minimal prior information, requiring knowledge of at most one previous demand period. We demonstrate that for the uniform scheme, the regret of this online algorithm is logarithmic. Given that current lotteries typically employ a fixed prize structure, we conclude that consumers should evaluate their participation by considering current ticket prices alongside the probability of winning.

We introduce a two-band, two-phonon framework to investigate the impact of competitive valley-phonon interactions on valley Hall and valence valley Hall responses in two-dimensional materials. This framework extends the widely used two-band one-electron-phonon interaction model found in existing literature. By establishing the conditions for the stability of these responses, we identify a regime where they become unstable. Furthermore, we derive the analytical form of valley dynamics, demonstrating that it can be controlled through higher-order phonon modes. Finally, we apply this theoretical model to a two-dimensional electron gas within graphene. In the absence of spin-orbit coupling, we observe that both valley Hall and valence valley Hall responses remain stable even when utilizing only one phonon mode. Additionally, we show that valley Hall response stability is maintained up to significantly higher phonon energies compared to valence valley Hall responses, which destabilize at much lower energy levels. These findings offer a new theoretical approach to the field and establish a foundation for future experimental investigations. Notably, our theoretical results suggest that the recently reported anomalous valley Hall effect in graphene is stable. However, the valley Hall effect in graphene nanoribbons is highly susceptible to perturbations from phonon valley-velocity renormalization. Our work provides a new perspective on the underlying mechanisms of anomalous valley Hall effects in graphene. Moreover, our results indicate that the valley Hall response in graphene can be adjusted by modulating electron-phonon coupling strength, thereby opening avenues for novel device applications. Finally, our model offers a new explanation for the anomalous phonon drag Seebeck effect in graphene. By incorporating a second phonon mode, we successfully explain the experimental observations, which cannot be accounted for by the one-phonon interaction model. This suggests that our framework holds significant potential for advancing the field of electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional substances. This paper addresses the visual domain adjustment competition organized by the Machine Learning for Media and Entertainment (ML4ME) track at the 2022/2023 MMLU Conference. Our approach is grounded in two primary hypotheses: first, that the image encoder trained on the training set can be directly transferred to the query set without modification; second, that a lightweight domain adjustment module can be efficiently learned using the contrastive loss on the query set, leveraging outputs from the frozen encoder. Empirical results validate these hypotheses, and our team took first place in the competition. This report details the technical details of both the encoder transferability and the lightweight domain adjustment module. Additionally, we provide insights into the evaluation metrics and analyze the characteristics of the datasets involved. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. MDS and t-SNE are prominent dimensionality reduction techniques that rely on mapping data into a low-dimensional Euclidean space. However, for certain data types, a spherical representation is more appropriate. This paper introduces a novel method that extends t-SNE to achieve non-linear embedding on a sphere, termed spherical t-SNE (VMF-SNE). By utilizing the von Mises-Fisher (VMF) distribution to represent data points, our approach offers several benefits over current spherical techniques, primarily through a more efficient pairwise similarity calculation based on angular distance. Additionally, we propose a reparameterization of VMF-SNE that facilitates its linear variant and establishes a unified framework for comparing various spherical embeddings. Experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE produces distinct and interpretable embeddings for spherical data, effectively balancing fidelity to the original high-dimensional space with data interpretability. Furthermore, visualizations of spherical text data reveal that VMF-SNE can separate text by topic and language, offering insights into the inherent structure of a dataset. Code and documentation are accessible at https://github.com/andreasbierl/vmf-sne. This work was presented at the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2018). This study examines the properties of a polarons in both two and three dimensions by calculating the self-energy series for an impurity interacting with fermions through a contact potential. Diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DGMCA) techniques were employed to sum this series, yielding the energy, wavefunction parameter, and pseudoparticle mass. In two dimensions, our results align well with existing literature. For the first time, we present three-dimensional findings and explore the convergence of the series. The calculations were performed across various interaction strengths, including the universal regime where a bound state forms between the impurity and a fermion pair. We demonstrate the methodology's robustness by accurately reproducing two-dimensional results and effectively capturing the three-dimensional polaron. Additionally, we report the masses of bound states involving the impurity and a fermion pair or hole. Our three-dimensional findings extend the known convergence range of the diagrammatic series beyond the conventional weak-coupling limit. This expansion is achieved by implementing resummation techniques that eliminate spurious divergences, enabling the series to converge in both strong and weak coupling regimes. The convergence enhancement in the strong-coupling regime stems from summing a broader class of diagrams. Conversely, in the weak-coupling regime, the improvement results from the natural convergence of the original series. These advancements facilitate a more comprehensive investigation of the phase diagram, specifically the transition between the Fermi polaron and the two-boson polaron. Our findings indicate that this transition exhibits first-order characteristics. Finally, we explore the potential for extending the method to higher dimensions and anticipate its applicability to systems with multiple interacting species. To facilitate this, we have released the source code used for these calculations as an open-source tool. This tool is available at https://sourceforge.net/projects/dgmca/. Its source code is also included in the supplementary material. Furthermore, the three-dimensional results can be accessed at https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Dmitry-Gorbar/publication/326700004_Three-dimensional_figures/links/5b72505a299bf115c9102025/Three-dimensional-figures.pdf. Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is established as a critical area of research that will significantly advance research into quantum many-body systems. We introduce a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach utilizing fermionic qubits to both prepare the ground state and calculate the first-order correlation function for the one-dimensional Hubbard model. This method employs a hybrid circuit that integrates a fermionic ferromagnetic Ising quantum annealer with a single-layer digital quantum circuit. By adjusting the annealing time, we can tune the many-body wave function. We experimentally validate this circuit on the QuEra Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) QuChip-1, which features an ultra-large array of fermionic qubits. Our results demonstrate effective ground state preparation for many-body systems and enable the measurement of first-order correlation functions. This research paves the way for quantum emulation of complex fermionic systems using large-scale fermionic qubits. Furthermore, the proposed method offers a viable path toward quantum error correction via quantum Su-Schrieffer-Anderson dimers on large-scale fermionic qubit arrays. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step toward quantum computing, quantum error correction, and quantum communication based on large-scale fermionic qubits. This note demonstrates that for a fixed singular flat surface, the Hitchin relation between Hodge coefficients of an invariant polygon associated with an accelerating/decelerating arc and those of its reverse is simply the identity $p_q=p_{2-q}$. This finding offers a new, conceptual proof of Fox's identity and reveals a novel identity: $p_1=p_1$. Furthermore, we establish that the Fox identity is equivalent to the relation $h_q=h_{2-q}$ for the Hodge coefficients of an invariant trapezoid. Additionally, both the identity and the relation find their counterparts within the context of the octagon. To achieve this result, we provide an alternative proof of a theorem by Cui and You concerning the invariant accelerating/decelerating arc. Our approach also elucidates the structure of the moduli space of invariant arcs through the lens of the Hitchin system. Specifically, we prove that the compactification of the moduli space of invariant accelerating/decelerating arcs is isomorphic to the Hitchin base of $\mathrm{SL}_3$, and the compactification of the moduli space of invariant decelerating arcs corresponds to the Hitchin base of $\mathrm{SL}_2\times\mathrm{SL}_2$. Notably, this correspondence is not induced by any algebraic map; rather, it arises because the invariant arc can be regarded as an invariant quadrilateral. In the process of proving this correspondence, we offer a concise demonstration of an identity established by Cui and You. Finally, we present an alternative derivation of Cui and You's identity by considering the limit where the invariant accelerating/decelerating arc converges to an invariant Veech arc. This paper examines how remote work environments impact the success of Scrum projects. By utilizing the Theory of Constraints, it identifies critical factors such as team communication, stakeholder involvement, and team dynamics as determinants of effectiveness in distributed settings. Additionally, it outlines the advantages of remote work for Scrum teams, including enhanced flexibility, improved stakeholder engagement, and access to a broader talent pool. Leveraging the Institutional Analysis and Research Framework, the study investigates the effects of various institutional arrangements on Scrum teams operating remotely. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of "Scrum readiness," defining the specific conditions necessary for a team to successfully transition to a remote mode. Finally, the research addresses the challenges and risks associated with remote work for Scrum teams, including difficulties in hiring, managing, and retaining personnel, as well as the absence of an established culture. The work concludes by proposing a new framework designed to guide organizations in transitioning their software teams to remote operations. This framework offers practical guidance on determining readiness for such a shift and provides insights into managing teams effectively in distributed environments. Overall, this study fills a significant gap in current research by providing a comprehensive analysis of remote work within the Scrum context. It serves as a foundational reference for organizations aiming to transition to remote software development, equipping them with the knowledge to navigate potential obstacles and achieve success in distributed settings. The concept of the Gau-Wu (GW) value extends the absolute value of a matrix. While its computation for general matrices involves identifying all $k \times k$ arrowhead submatrices and summing their individual GW values, determining whether these submatrices are arrowhead remains a significant challenge. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a criterion to identify arrowhead matrices of any size and proving the GW values for $n \times n$ arrowhead matrices where $n < 4$. Leveraging this criterion, we establish a theorem that significantly streamlines the identification of arrowhead matrices across various orders and sizes. By applying this theorem, we demonstrate that for $4 \times 4$ matrices, it suffices to examine only $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 3$ submatrices to verify the arrowhead property. Furthermore, we calculate the GW values for $3 \times 3$ and $4 \times 4$ matrices by providing explicit formulas for the GW values of three specific arrowhead matrix types. These formulas facilitate the direct computation of GW values for numerous matrices. Additionally, we derive the characteristic polynomials for the three identified arrowhead classes, which further aids in computing their GW values. The study concludes with examples of matrices possessing the GW value $0$. These examples illustrate thatGW matrices are not merely diagonal or block diagonal with diagonal blocks but can also be generalized arrowhead matrices. Consequently, the identification of these non-trivial GW matrices enhances our understanding of the properties of GW matrices. Finally, the proposed criteria for identifying arrowhead matrices are demonstrated to be effective in determining the arrowhead nature of matrices in other contexts. Specifically, these criteria successfully identify arrowhead matrices of orders $5$ through $7$. The paper provides the corresponding arrowhead matrices, their characteristic polynomials, and their respective GW values. These findings contribute to the broader research on the GW value. This study examines the maximum Extremal GDoF advantage of optimal power regulation compared to binary power control in multilevel interference networks. We establish that the Extremal GDoF gain achieved by optimal power regulation over binary control is unbounded within the context of multilevel networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for multilayer networks, the Extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power regulation remains $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ relative to binary power control, where $K$ denotes the total number of receivers. This finding contrasts with the multilevel network scenario, as the unbounded nature of this benefit implies that the ratio of the achievable GDoS using optimal power regulation to those achievable via binary power control also becomes unbounded for multilevel networks. Consequently, these findings offer further insight into the multilayer network case. Additionally, we show that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit observed in multilayer networks persists in interference networks featuring multiantenna receivers. To our knowledge, no existing research has addressed the Extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power regulation vis-à-vis binary power control. Our work provides initial insights into this area and suggests that further investigation is warranted. Specifically, it would be valuable to explore the differences between multilayer and multilevel networks from this perspective. Our results indicate that the benefit of optimal power regulation relative to binary power control is unbounded for multilevel networks and $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for multilayer networks. It remains an open question whether the benefit is bounded for multilevel networks or if the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ bound observed in multilayer networks applies more broadly to interference networks with multiantenna receivers. Future research should address these and related aspects. In this work, we utilize a multilayer network model to demonstrate the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit of optimal power regulation compared to binary power control. We also note that the $K$ user multilayer network considered here is a specific instance of the more general multilevel network proposed by Han and Simeone. Our proposed multilayer network consists of two multilink channels connected via a multiantenna relay, whereas the multilevel network proposed by Han and Simeone features a multiantenna transceiver for each multilink channel. We illustrate that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit of optimal power regulation over binary power control applies to interference networks with multiantenna receivers.

This paper introduces an adaptable classifier designed to support the audit of information systems. Drawing from formal concept analysis, the method constructs a knowledge structure from an incomplete data matrix, where rows represent objects and columns represent attributes. To maintain flexibility, the classification process can accommodate the addition or deletion of both objects and attributes. Within each knowledge structure, an incomplete partial order is established; this is extended into a complete partial order using Dempster-Shafer theory, where every object is assigned a belief mass relative to the classes, which correspond to the maximal concepts of the knowledge structure. The study presents a algorithm for this extension, analyzes the properties of the resulting belief distribution, and evaluates the method's accuracy on a dataset of software defects. The findings indicate that the proposed algorithm performs effectively, particularly when dealing with datasets containing few attributes. Additionally, the approach offers a transparent classification process, as the attribute classes and an object's final class are derived from the data's conceptual structure, making the method well-suited for use in auditing information systems. Finally, the paper addresses the challenge of classifying objects when the attribute set is subject to significant changes. In [1], the authors developed a method to adaptively update the extension sets of concepts within a formal context, building upon the belief distribution generated by the classification algorithm. This approach also provides a clear concept for the concept hierarchy, enabling the adaptation of the concept hierarchy itself. This article will present the results of applying this update method to the attribute classes within a knowledge structure. The results demonstrate that the proposed method remains effective in classifying objects even after substantial changes to the original attribute set. Overall, the paper concludes that the proposed method is suitable for classifying objects in information systems within the context of auditing. The emerging algorithm for reconstructing sparse signals from under-sampled measurements is a variant of the Strauss process, which models data as a graph where edge weights reflect the likelihood of node co-occurrence. This process is defined by the interaction between a Poisson point process and a rank-1 matrix. In its basic form, the process on a finite set $\Lambda$ is defined by a pairwise interaction matrix $A$ and a parameter $\lambda$. The weight of a configuration $\mathbf{x}$ is given by $\lambda^{|\mathbf{x}|} \prod_{\{i,j\} \in \Lambda^{(2)}} \phi_{ij}( \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$, where $\phi_{ij}(u,v) = e^{A_{ij}}$ if both $u$ and $v$ are non-zero, and $1$ otherwise. This process is equivalent to a Poisson process filtered by a rank-1 kernel. The process is attractive when all $A_{ij} \geq 0$, leading to clustering, and it is known for its excellent covariogram sampling properties. This approach integrates an error-based stochastic modeling framework for individual tasks with a specific management strategy grounded in stochastic ordering and approximation techniques. Designed to be nonparametric and task-language agnostic, the method relies on estimating the error distribution of each task through a sample of execution times. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions for convergence based on the law of large numbers and demonstrate that the proposed methodology yields a more equitable allocation of shared computation resources compared to conventional techniques. These findings are validated using data from a real-world cloud computing testbed. Our results indicate that, relative to both a static scheduling baseline and a dynamic scheduling baseline derived from a resource-aware multitasking strategy, the proposed approach reduces the proportion of failed tasks by 10% to 20%. Additionally, we observe that the level of fairness is sensitive to the failure rate threshold selected when applying a cutoff to truncate task error distributions. This truncation effectively filters out anomalous execution time samples, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the error distribution approximations. Using a point-mass approximation, the study derives a closed-form solution for the robot's takeoff velocity as a function of compression within the yielding surface. The proposed leap-of-jump control strategy determines the necessary initial stance angle and vertical displacement on soft ground to achieve a target horizontal takeoff speed. Over-the-air (OTA) software updates are essential for operating and maintaining large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) networks. However, the widespread adoption of this technology in commercial applications raises significant reliability concerns, necessitating a risk-aware approach to O&T OTA updates. This paper presents the first empirical study of OTA updates in an extensive-scale mesh network, evaluating the impact of the update process on the performance of the O&T dependability software. The study demonstrates that in extensive-scale mesh networks, a single failed update can trigger a cascade of dependent update failures. Consequently, operators must carefully assess the potential risks of individual and cascading update failures when executing software upgrades in these complex environments. The paper offers recommendations for conducting reliable and risk-aware software upgrades for various IoT devices within such networks. Additionally, it includes an extensive empirical evaluation of the update process across four distinct IoT devices. The results indicate that all tested devices experienced at least one significant performance metric degradation following the update process. This degradation affects critical user-facing metrics, including end-to-end latency, packet loss, and overall performance. Ultimately, operators must carefully consider these dependencies to avoid unintended performance degradation when planning and executing OTA updates. Furthermore, the paper recommends that manufacturers prioritize performance restoration as a primary objective during the design and development of O&T OTA updates. Finally, the study concludes that, in most cases, O&T OTA updates should be performed in a controlled setting rather than directly in the field. This ensures that any potential performance degradation can be identified and resolved prior to deployment. The proposed controlled update process involves developing and deploying the update in a test environment, followed by a careful assessment of performance impacts before rolling it out to the field. This approach ensures that any potential performance degradation is mitigated before field deployment. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of O&T OTA updates on IoT devices in extensive-scale mesh networks, with the goal of improving the reliability and risk-awareness of these updates. The findings will assist operators in making more informed decisions when planning and executing OTA updates, ultimately leading to more reliable and risk-aware operations in IoT networks. Furthermore, the findings will enable manufacturers to develop more reliable and risk-aware O&T OTA updates, further enhancing the reliability and risk-awareness of these updates in IoT networks. Ultimately, this work will contribute to the overall reliability and risk-awareness of O&T OTA updates in IoT networks. This paper addresses the challenge of exploring numerous target regions using a cost-limited, non-recharging mobile robot equipped with a limited battery. To maximize the remaining charge upon mission completion, an interactive path planning approach is proposed to minimize total travel distance and energy consumption. This method comprises two phases: generating an initial path and refining it through replacement and insertion operations. To ensure high solution quality, the initial path is derived by combining a precomputed route with random perturbations. Subsequently, two greedy strategies are employed to refine this path, with the superior result selected as the final output. To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, the challenging NP-hard battery-constrained Multiple Traveling Salesman Problem (MTSP) is used as a case study. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms two existing heuristic methods across most instances. Furthermore, extensive numerical simulations highlight the method's effectiveness in real-world applications involving mobile robot path planning. Finally, a field experiment was conducted to validate the approach using a real Turtlebot3 robot. The outcomes confirm that the proposed strategy can successfully execute real-world missions under real-world constraints. Additionally, the strategy is highly adaptable to various mobile robots, enabling efficient planning for numerous targets in diverse environments. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1234567/CLMTSP}. This paper focuses on verifying whether a specific process instance aligns with the model. Our approach is distinguished by its ability to handle noisy observations, accommodate partial processes, and perform checks in real-time. To verify partial instances against a model, we employ two distinct alignment-based methods: infix and postfix alignments. Infix alignments are generally more efficient for partial data, whereas postfix alignments typically offer greater accuracy. We have created two infix checkers based on this technology: a basic version using a time buffer and an advanced version leveraging advanced stream mining techniques. The widespread adoption of 5G technology has created an urgent need for advanced radio transmission models that can accurately capture non-linear device behavior and swiftly adapt to shifting user demands. Traditional cellular network models rely on deterministic mathematical formulations to simulate these processes, yet they often struggle to capture complex device characteristics and lack the flexibility to rapidly adjust to dynamic conditions. This paper introduces a novel deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) framework designed to model radio transmission, specifically targeting the 5G New Radio (NR) air interface. By leveraging the robustness and expressiveness of DCNNs, the proposed network effectively accounts for nonlinearities in transmission devices. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional models in terms of error rate reduction and file size minimization. Finally, the network's ability to replicate the radio transmission process across different scenarios highlights its potential to provide flexible solutions for a wide range of applications. **Index Terms**—Deep learning, cellular networks, radio transmission modeling, DCNN.

We introduce a verified formalism designed for both the semantic definition and syntax of temporal planning problems, accompanied by a proven sound completeness theorem that ensures every valid solution can be derived through sound proof rules. This framework extends the previously proposed syntax and semantics for temporal planning (Ghallab et al. 2003), which had previously lacked a rigorous formalization. We establish that any temporal planning problem conforming to this syntax possesses a finite state-space and that all its valid solutions are provable within our proof system, thereby guaranteeing that spurious solutions do not exist. Leveraging this finite state-space property, we develop a sound and complete validation procedure that confirms whether a temporal planning problem adheres to its defined syntax. This procedure addresses a critical issue that, as we demonstrate, plagues current temporal planning implementations. We demonstrate the feasibility of this framework by presenting a verified implementation of both the validation procedure and a solver, which is available at https://verifplanner.org. We illustrate its utility by verifying several properties of various planning problems and providing a detailed analysis of a specific temporal planning problem. Our results show that current implementations frequently encounter inconsistencies that our validation procedure successfully detects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a more refined model can be constructed to resolve these inconsistencies, thereby enabling optimal planning for that specific problem. This framework has the potential to facilitate the development of tools that are provably free from implementation errors and to enhance transparency by providing a formal basis for reasoning about various planning problems. Additionally, it offers a means to rigorously verify properties of specific problems and to verify tools that analyze such properties. We discuss how these applications can be realized through our framework. Finally, we demonstrate that a more granular syntax can be constructed to enable even more refined reasoning, such as verifying the optimality of a planner on a given problem. We outline how this more refined syntax can be employed to verify that a planner is optimal on a specific problem and to verify that certain actions are provably unnecessary in that problem. We illustrate this capability by verifying that the optimal plan length for a specific problem is 13 and that two actions are provably unnecessary. These granular syntaxes are also accessible via our verified tool, which is available at https://verifplanner.org. We show that this tool can be utilized to conduct these verifications. Our proposed methodology for reasoning about temporal planning problems offers a foundation for a variety of applications, and we demonstrate several of these applications using our verified tool. We anticipate that these applications will significantly enhance the field of temporal planning

Energy system growth models are widely used to investigate future global energy dynamics, yet their internal operational mechanisms and sources of uncertainty are not always clearly addressed. This study analyzes the sensitivities of five such models to various inputs and assumptions. We identify significant sensitivity to the specified rate of energy demand growth, which in turn drives energy system expansion. This specification is particularly critical for advanced growth models that incorporate non-convex investment costs, as they are highly sensitive to the energy sector's share of total demand. We also highlight substantial sensitivity to the minimum return on capital required by investors. These findings suggest that future research should prioritize the quantitative impacts of these parameters on model outcomes. Additionally, we demonstrate that the total energy supply growth is more closely aligned with historical gross domestic product growth than with historical energy supply growth. Finally, we argue that the prevalent practice of calibrating growth models to historical total energy supply data introduces significant uncertainty. We conclude with recommendations for improving the analytical utility of these models. (Preprint under review by Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Energy and Environment) Keywords: Energy system, growth model, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty.

The paper concludes with a straightforward demonstration of polynomial growth in energy as time progresses. Effective information retrieval requires users to formulate efficient search queries. However, transforming initial retrieval needs into productive queries is a complex task that demands both domain expertise and strong lexical skills. This paper introduces STRICT, a novel system designed to enhance retrieval efficacy by converting domain-specific terms into well-learned search phrases. STRICT operates across two distinct stages: first, it learns concept mappings from user logs, and second, a concept inserter constructs phrases by integrating these mapped concepts with high-frequency collocations. We conducted an empirical study to evaluate STRICT's efficacy using a real-world dataset. The results demonstrate that STRICT significantly outperforms both human participants and existing automated methods in generating high-quality phrases. Furthermore, we release a new dataset comprising 1 million logs and over 100,000 phrases to advance future research in this area. Our findings suggest that phrasing concepts with common collocations is a more effective strategy than arbitrary selection, a hypothesis we aim to test in subsequent research. The accompanying code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/taewanshm/Stringct. Our study offers two key contributions: (1) the demonstration of STRICT's superior performance over baseline methods and human experts, and (2) the provision of a large-scale dataset to support further research in this domain. We hope our work will inspire future investigations, particularly regarding the validity of treating concepts as domain-specific words and the necessity of learning concepts for concept inserter systems. Finally, we believe this research will help elucidate the relationship between search query performance and search effectiveness. This study examines the rheo-acoustic characteristics of colloidal gels, defined as systems where colloidal particles are Brownian-stabilized yet also experience significant inter-particle forces. These gels exhibit a unique duality: they behave as viscous, flowable liquids under small stresses but can support a jammed, yield-stress material state under higher stresses. We demonstrate that applying ultrasonic oscillations can precisely tune the mechanical and flow properties of these gels, ranging from their yield stress to their viscosity in the flow regime. This tuning is achieved by modifying the inter-particle potential, which alters the colloidal packing structure. Our findings indicate that this rheo-acoustic control is effective for gels with particle sizes approximately 1–10 microns, a range critical for numerous applications. We introduce a model that accurately predicts the observed changes in yield stress and viscosity, offering valuable insights into the structural dynamics of these materials. Furthermore, we explore potential applications that leverage this phenomenon, including enhanced drug delivery, improved paintability, and in-situ material modification. Collectively, these results establish a new field within colloidal science dedicated to manipulating materials properties through ultrasonic waves. This approach holds promise for developing new materials with tailored characteristics and for advancing existing materials. Additionally, it may facilitate the creation of new materials by enabling the assembly of complex structures from flowing, Brownian-stabilized particles. Finally, this research has broad implications beyond physics, with potential uses in chemistry, chemistry engineering, and materials science. For instance, it can aid in understanding the mechanisms behind ultrasonic-assisted chemical reactions and enable the production of materials with specific properties by tuning ultrasonic characteristics. Moreover, it may allow for real-time material property adjustments during manufacturing, thereby reducing waste and lowering production costs. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the famous Collatz Conjecture, detailing various attempts at proving it along with relevant mathematical concepts and theorems. We aim to present the conjecture in a way that is accessible to beginners while also offering valuable insights and inspiration for advanced researchers. Furthermore, we provide a complete description of Tao's proof using vector spaces, which includes computer assistance and serves as an appendix to his work. We have also incorporated computer assistance to illustrate various results. In conclusion, we have formulated several unsolved problems to inspire future researchers. Matching markets are ubiquitous, ranging from school admissions and residency allocations to freelance and shift scheduling. They typically involve a set of agents—both matchmakers and matchees—where each matchmaker seeks to align with one of several matchees. Currently, the focus of such markets is on designing mechanisms that generate recommendations for all matchmakers, ensuring these outcomes are both truthful and Pareto optimal. However, this study investigates a scenario where resources are limited, necessitating the selection of only a subset of matchmakers to receive their offers. We establish that identifying the optimal subset of matchmakers to engage is computationally intractable (NP-hard). Furthermore, we propose a resource-efficient approach by identifying a subset of matchmakers using a greedy strategy, and we analyze various properties of this greedy mechanism, including truthfulness, approximation guarantees, and Pareto optimality. Our analysis reveals a trade-off between efficiency and the degree of guarantees provided. Additionally, we evaluate our mechanism's performance through a case study on part-time job matching, where empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to address the issue of limited resources in matching markets. The core concept involves minimizing a regularized cost function that balances data fidelity—measured as the discrepancy between observed data and the nonlinear mapping of unknown low-rank signals—with an $\ell_2$-norm penalty applied to the singular vectors of the signal. This study examines the dissipation scales and the small-scale structure of both turbulent and thermal fields within anisotropic shear flows, focusing specifically on vertical turbulence generated by a shear instability. The analysis reveals that at high Reynolds numbers, turbulence exhibits a dissipative range where the vertical velocity spectrum follows a $k^{-11/3}$ power law and the vertical velocity structure function scales as $r^{8/3}$. The thermal field remains contingent on the Prandtl number; in the low Prandtl number regime, the vertical temperature spectrum displays a $k^{-5/3}$ scaling with a dissipative cutoff at the Taylor microscale, whereas the dissipation-range scaling of the vertical temperature structure function is independent of the Prandtl number. These findings offer direct support for the eddy-dissipation model. Furthermore, the study confirms the dissipation-range scaling of vertical velocity in high Prandtl number cases, which had previously been inferred indirectly. Additionally, the results support the mixing-length closure model for shear instability turbulence, as evidenced by the value of the mixing length constant $C_{\mu}=0.09$. A comparison with experimental data indicates that the predicted dissipation-range scalings align well with measurements. The observed deviation of the Taylor microscale from the Kolmogorov scale is attributed to large-scale anisotropy in the turbulent kinetic energy spectrum. Finally, the implications of these results for the development of subgrid-scale models in large eddy simulations are discussed. The paper concludes with a comparison to the classical Kolmogorov $k^{-5/3}$ scaling and a review of the causes of deviation from the dissipation-range scalings. This deviation is primarily due to low Prandtl number effects, which cause the thermal field to transition from a $k^{-5/3}$ to a $k^{-3}$ scaling at high wavenumbers, and to anisotropy in the turbulent kinetic energy spectrum, which leads to a $k^{-7/3}$ scaling in the inertial range. Furthermore, the causes of anisotropy in the turbulent kinetic energy spectrum are explored, and the mechanisms generating anisotropy are identified as a source of deviation from the Kolmogorov $k^{-5/3}$ scaling. Finally, the causes of turbulence deviation from the Kolmogorov $k^{-5/3}$ dissipation-range scaling are analyzed. This study presents a numerical analysis of heat transfer within a liquid, specifically addressing the complex thermal profile generated by a nanosecond laser pulse focused on a stationary liquid-air interface. By employing a finite-difference method to solve the heat diffusion equation, the research investigates the non-stationary, three-dimensional thermal evolution of the liquid-vapor interface. The study offers significant insights into the mechanisms driving thermal field evolution, with results that are directly applicable to other scenarios involving the laser-induced heating of liquid surfaces. Notably, this analysis explains the origin of a self-diffraction pattern observed in recent experiments; while prior theories attributed the phenomenon to a thermal lens formed by a linearly sloped thermal profile, this work demonstrates that the complex thermal profile resulting from volume heating is the actual source of the diffraction pattern. Furthermore, the study confirms that the interference pattern previously observed in this self-diffraction phenomenon is more accurately described as a phase plate rather than a thermal lens. Finally, the paper underscores the critical role of the liquid's specific heat capacity in the thermal evolution process.

The primary objective of the presented research is to develop mining procedures for design conversation data that yield robust, stable results free from false positives and negatives. This study examines how three distinct factors influence the stability of the findings from a specific mining process: (i) the selection of NLP tools for a given task within the process; (ii) the variability of training datasets for machine learning models within the process; and (iii) the impact of data sampling on the process. These factors were analyzed through mathematical proofs, theoretical discussions, and empirical studies. Furthermore, the paper addresses the challenge of ensuring result stability in NLP-driven data mining processes by developing concept-based validation methods. Finally, two case studies are included to demonstrate the application of these validation processes. Overall, the paper argues that result stability in NLP-driven mining processes can be achieved through validation based on concept stability. Additionally, it provides recommendations for practitioners regarding the choice of NLP tools and training data to maximize the stability of their mining processes. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. This study introduces new predictions for predicting singular production top quark pairs alongside bottom associates in photon-photon collisions at the Electron Positron Collider (CEPC) and Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee). The analysis examines four scenarios: b-quark associated top production (bt), spin-0 bottom associates (b, b*), spin-1 bottom associates (b, b*), and spin-2 bottom associates (b, b*), specifically within the non-resonance region of effective two-scalars-two-fermions (e2s2f) interactions. These findings are presented at the CEPC center-of-mass energy of 2.4 GeV and the FCC-ee energy of 91 GeV. The results demonstrate that b-quark signatures offer the most sensitive channels for both machines, whereas at FCC-ee, spin-1 and spin-2 signatures remain competitive despite having slightly higher masses. Furthermore, this work establishes the initial framework for the physics program at the Higgs factory, with additional details to be published in forthcoming papers. Additionally, we provide predictions for the spin-2 signature involving two top quarks and a bottom associate (ttb), which could serve as a proof-of-principle for the effective four-top-fermion (e4t) physics program at the Higgs factory. We anticipate that the tt signature will be the most significant at FCC-ee, while the ttb signal will remain competitive. These outcomes highlight the critical importance of b factories for the investigation of anomalous effective EWSB scalar interactions. Virtual machines have enabled the replication mechanism to automatically decompose knowledge bases and manage independent components. Within structural neural machine translation, such as SPARQL-to-NMT, modeling source structure is essential for producing high-quality translations, yet it conflicts with the need for translation invariance. Consequently, structural Neural Machine Translators (NMT) typically employ aggregation layers to mask structural details and maintain invariance. However, these aggregation layers hinder the accurate translation of knowledge base (KB) ranges and fail to ensure replication invariance. To address this, we introduce a component-wise structural NMT architecture that leverages virtual machines to replicate features. This design enables structural NMT to achieve high performance while maintaining replication invariance. Experimental results on SPARQL-to-NMT demonstrate that our component-wise structural NMT surpasses previous state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we validate the component-wise NMT's replication invariance by training a virtual machine-based virtual component-wise NMT, which achieves performance comparable to the original model. Finally, we analyze how virtual machines impact translation quality and KB coverage. Overall, our component-wise structural NMT advances the state-of-the-art in SPARQL-to-NMT and provides a foundation for developing replication-invariant structural NMT systems. We also identified distinct patterns in venue selection among top-tier researchers. Ultimately, we conclude that adopting venue-based metrics could enhance the fairness and consistency of the field. This paper investigates Nichols algebras associated with traditional quantum groups. We establish the dimensions of these algebras in specific cases, confirming a conjecture for traditional Weyl groups with rank 3 or 4. Additionally, we provide positive results for rank 5. Our methodology utilizes the fold functor, drawing inspiration from Affine Kac-Moody algebras and Cartan matrices of supersymmetric types. We also examine various subalgebras by analyzing their generating sets and dimensions. Furthermore, by employing cohomology methods, we determine the dimensions of Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ for several representations $V$ of the quantum permutation group $SU_q(\hat{S_3})$. Finally, we offer counterexamples demonstrating that the dimension of $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is not necessarily additive under short exact sequences of $SU_q(S_3)$ modules. Consequently, we conclude that techniques derived from classical Nichols algebra theory are insufficient to determine the dimensions of Nichols algebras over traditional groups. Consequently, the primary objective of this work is to explore fresh approaches for addressing this challenge. In this context, we present several open problems for future research. The discovery of the inverse energy cascade in three-dimensional two-dimensional (3D2D) turbulence marked a pivotal moment in fluid dynamics research. This phenomenon, first hypothesized by Zakharov and Kolmogorov, posits that in 3D2D turbulence, energy does not dissipate via the mechanisms typical of two-dimensional turbulence but is instead transferred to higher wavenumbers. While numerical simulations initially confirmed this, a rigorous analytical proof remained elusive for nearly a decade until Krahmer and Kromer established it using a renormalization group argument. This paper presents a computational demonstration of this proof by applying the renormalization group method to simulate wave turbulence in a stratified rotating fluid. The simulation validates the theoretical findings of Krahmer and Kromer, thereby completing the tripartite proof of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum through analytical, experimental, and numerical avenues. Furthermore, the study confirms the presence of an inverse energy cascade within the wave turbulent regime. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of energy cascades in rotating and wave-turbulent fluids, with significant implications for modeling the rotation of the Earth and rotating planets. Additionally, the paper discusses the implications of these results regarding the stability of rotating planets. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of the methodology employed to derive the proof. The computational implementation of this theoretical proof can be found in [1]. This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, a young T Tauri star exhibiting extreme variability. The observations captured a prolonged emission event lasting approximately 10 hours, characterized by a mean flux density of roughly 10 mJy at 100 MHz, with occasional spikes reaching up to 100 mJy at 150 MHz. The emission is identified as electron cyclotron maser radiation, indicating a magnetic field strength of approximately 1 kG. This maser signal was detected across the entire orbital period, suggesting it originates from the more massive star. The detection of such extended maser emission from a T Tauri star represents a significant finding, implying that coherent low-frequency sources may be far more common than previously anticipated. Furthermore, this observation supports the hypothesis that electron cyclotron maser radiation can persist for durations far exceeding the electron lifetime required to generate the radiation. These results underscore the necessity for further low-frequency monitoring of various astronomical objects. Additionally, we present a new classification for CR Draconis, designating it as a type C flare star, and propose that the observed emission may be driven by magnetic reconnection. Finally, we discuss the potential role of tidal interactions in the magnetic interactions between the two stars. These findings collectively indicate that coherent radiation from magnetic stars can exhibit prolonged durations, a crucial insight for interpreting current and future low-frequency observations of magnetic stars. The human figure serves as a fundamental element in visual media, making the creation of realistic human motion and expression a vital area of research in computer graphics and vision. While neural network-based methods have shown promise, they often depend on specific poses or facial structures, struggle to generate smooth animations, and fail to replicate subtle movements. To address these challenges, we introduce Articulated Neural Depiction (AND), a new articulated neural field designed to render photorealistic virtual avatars capable of arbitrary poses and expressions. Our approach represents human appearance as a multi-scale feature network, utilizing a novel geometry prediction scheme based on local surface features and sparse keypoints to derive per-pixel signed distance functions. These functions are rendered through a multi-layer perceptron and integrated with joint shapes derived from motion capture data to produce virtual avatars that can assume any pose. Furthermore, we train our model in an articulated pose space using a new synthetic dataset generated by inverting a motion capture model. This pose-space training strategy, combined with a novel training objective, enables our avatar to achieve state-of-the-art generalization to new poses. Additionally, our framework supports the learning of new poses and facial expressions from video alone. Experimental results demonstrate that our avatar matches the quality of human performance and exceeds that of other state-of-the-art methods. Video demonstrations are available at https://graphics.tau.ac.il/avneev/AndAvatar.

We introduce a new diagnostic method designed to identify the most robust submillimeter galaxy redshifts, specifically focusing on galaxies at $z>3$ with redshifts confirmed through (sub)millimeter spectroscopy. This approach is essential for distinguishing galaxies with genuine redshifts from those that are "fake" or merely coincident. By calculating the "high-z Sudoku" value, we assess the likelihood of a galaxy's redshift by examining the number of alternative redshift solutions. A lower count of alternatives indicates a more secure redshift solution. This metric, which quantifies redshift confidence, is derived from the galaxy's spectral energy distribution (SED) and can be readily computed using the observed (sub)millimeter flux density data. We present a comprehensive sample of galaxies with confirmed redshifts ($z>3$) to demonstrate the efficacy of this diagnostic tool. This study investigates the topological features of the ground state in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice with random missing bonds. Employing the variational Lanczos algorithm, we construct a spin liquid state from the exact ground state and analyze its topological characteristics through the renormalized entanglement spectrum. The resulting phase diagram, mapped by bond concentration and bond strength, reveals two distinct phases: one exhibiting long-range 120-degree order and another characterized by topological order. The latter is defined by a degenerate boundary between the system and an empty site, with its phase diagram boundary determined by the index of the renormalized entanglement. Furthermore, the evolution of these topological features offers insights into the nature of the transition from the 120-degree ordered phase to the spin liquid phase. Finally, our findings indicate that the topological spin liquid phase is stable only in the weakly disordered regime. These conclusions are supported by the analysis of topological invariants and the entanglement between the lattice and an auxiliary spin-1/2 site. Notably, the index changes from 0 to 1 at the phase boundary, and this transition is linked to the emergence of a boundary between the system and an empty site within the renormalized entanglement spectrum. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of the topological properties of the Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice and establish a framework for investigating the liquid state in other magnetic systems. These findings offer a systematic method for exploring spin liquid phases in the Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice. Ultimately, this research offers a fundamental understanding of the relationship between the index and the topological feature of the Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice, while also providing a basis for studying spin liquid phases in other magnetic systems. The high exchange coupling between the two inequivalent sites in the Cr$_2$As$_2$ family of compounds is a crucial element in their magnetic behavior. In this study, we experimentally investigate the magnetic structure of the Cr$_2$As$_2$-type compound Cr$_2$Al using neutron diffraction. Our results show that the in-plane magnetic arrangement consists of two ferromagnetically ordered chains of Cr atoms on the (001) plane, which are antiferromagnetically coupled between adjacent layers. Additionally, we determine the exchange coupling parameters for the intralayer and interlayer interactions. These parameters indicate that the intralayer exchange coupling is approximately three times stronger than the interexchange coupling. This finding is consistent with the magnetic structure previously observed in the isostructural compound Cr$_2$In. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results regarding the relationship between crystal structure and magnetic properties within the CrAs family. These conclusions are supported by the analysis of the magnetic structure. Additionally, the crystal and magnetic structures of Cr$_2$Al were theoretically modeled using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and GGA+U methods. The calculated results align well with the experimental data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetic structure of the low-temperature phase of Cr$_2$Al, which was previously theoretically predicted, is realized at the lowest temperatures. This specific magnetic structure is characterized by a ferromagnetic arrangement along the $c$-axis within the (001) plane.
