We present an unsupervised embedding learning approach for DNA sequences that bypasses the constraints of typical training datasets. By employing a Transformer-XL architecture, we allow the model to capture long-range sequence dependencies without relying on artificial masking. This technique was dynamically applied to over 1.5 million ENCODE ChIP-seq datasets involving 2,255 unique transcription factors (TFs). For every TF, we generated embedding vectors for 12-nucleotide sequences, which were subsequently utilized in two downstream applications: (1) a novel method to identify and cluster similar TFs based on their embedding distributions, and (2) an unsupervised classification system that integrates experimental metadata to distinguish in vivo from in vitro binding data. The clustering results successfully identified previously known groups of similar TFs and discovered new ones, while the In Vivo vs. In Vitro classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.84 across 10-fold cross-validation. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these embedding vectors can effectively distinguish between on-target and off-target sequences, suggesting their potential utility for guiding next-generation TF-specific guide RNA design. To the best of our knowledge, these findings represent a significant advancement in the application of deep learning to DNA sequence analysis. The associated code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/lyy22522530/ylab-transformer-xl. The epitaxial synthesis of V$_2$O$_3$ films on Al$_2$O$_3$(1102) substrates results in a metal-insulator transition. This study investigates the Lie-Poisson frameworks associated with the Lie groups $SO(3)$, $SU(2)$, and $SU(3)$ by examining their associated Lie algebras, $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and $\mathfrak{su}(3)$. We demonstrate that the Casimir functions for $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and $\mathfrbs{u}(3)$ correspond to the invariants of three-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional spheres, respectively. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics on these spaces under various vector fields and explore the connection between the Casimir functions of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ through the concept of clebsch conjugation. Finally, utilizing an $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry model, we illustrate the equivalence between the casimir algebra of the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$ subalgebras, thereby establishing a direct link between particles within the fundamental representation of $SU(3)$ and pions, which are represented by the adjoint representation of $SU(2)$. This approach offers a novel framework for understanding sub-group dynamics in $SU(3)$, with potential applications in quantum chromodynamics. Specifically, it may facilitate a formulation of pions as a "pion cloud" surrounding baryons, thereby advancing the quark model. Additionally, this method provides a new perspective for analyzing baryon octet dynamics, potentially elucidating the origin of p-wave baryon multiplets. These findings are supported by numerical simulations conducted with the help of Maple software. Our future research will extend this analysis to other subalgebras of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, such as the isospin and strangeness groups, to further investigate the origin of pions, kaons, and the $\Delta$ resonance. This work serves as a foundational step toward a comprehensive understanding of the quark model. We introduce a thorough investigation of 2018 sub-prime-field exoplanets detected by the Korean Microlensing Exoplanet NET (KMTNet), aiming to identify planets through the planet-planet anomaly (PPA) search method. Our analysis confirms 10 new PPA planets, including six binary lens systems exhibiting PPA signatures and four triple lens systems showing PPA features; the remaining five systems are likely to be PPA candidates. We also examined 10 previously reported PPA planets from our 2018 sample, finding that one is now consistent with a single-lens model, while the other nine remain PPA candidates due to significant PPA signals. Furthermore, we identified 10 previously reported PPA candidates from our 2018 sample that are no longer consistent with PPA signatures. Additionally, we conducted a binary lens search on 15 PPA candidates and found that four are likely to host binary lenses. Finally, we performed mass ratio inversion searches on 10 triple systems from our 2018 sample that previously showed PPA signatures, with two systems now consistent with mass ratio inversions. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of the systematic PPA search method for detecting planets in binary and triple lens systems. The PPA search method is designed to handle all possible lens configurations and offers a straightforward way to detect planets without relying on finite-source effects. We have developed a systematic PPA search method that employs the same grid search to find planets in PPA cases, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the KMTNet PPA search. This method will be applied to future KMTNet datasets. The full list of planets analyzed in this study is available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1008. The data utilized in this research can be accessed via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6025580. Building upon the conservation law framework established in the initial paper of this series, we propose an energy-consistent abstract conservation law formulation for a broad spectrum of fluid dynamics equations. This formulation encompasses not only compressible and incompressible Navier-Stokes equations but also various generalized Navier-Stokes equations. By treating the machinery of generalized thermodynamics as constraints, we aim to derive the fundamental equations governing fluid motion. Specifically, we demonstrate an energy-consistent formulation utilizing a specific choice of flux functions. Notably, this approach extends beyond classical generalized thermal laws by remaining applicable even in scenarios where a generalized thermal law is absent, such as in compressible in-viscid flow where temperature is absent. Furthermore, this formulation offers an additional advantage by enabling the application of a broad spectrum of high-order finite difference schemes, which are specifically designed for conservation law formulations. These schemes are capable of resolving shocks and other non-smooth features with high accuracy, a capability absent in the low-order upwind schemes typically employed for generalized thermal laws. Consequently, this research serves as a vital bridge between the fundamental principles of conservation and dissipation and their practical application in numerical simulations. Additionally, this work may inspire novel approaches to modeling problems in fluid mechanics. Finally, we conclude by presenting a comprehensive table of compressible Navier-Stokes equations expressed through flux functions derived from our generalized thermal law. This table provides a complete reference for conservation law formulations across various models, including viscous flows, inviscid flows, and potential flow theory. Furthermore, it offers a practical method for constructing flux functions for any given model, thereby streamlining the process of analyzing conservation law formulations for compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Ultimately, this study may inspire future research into modeling and analysis within fluid mechanics. For instance, it may encourage investigations into whether analogous conservation law formulations exist for other equations, such as the Schrödinger equation. Additionally, it may drive the development of numerical schemes that simultaneously resolve both conservation and dissipation properties, thereby enhancing accuracy and stability in simulations. Finally, this work may influence the selection of appropriate numerical schemes for specific problems and facilitate the identification of flux functions for compressible Navier-Stokes equations that align with a generalized thermal law, ensuring that both conservation and dissipation properties are resolved with high accuracy by numerical schemes. These outcomes are poised to significantly advance the field of conservation and dissipation law formulations. Moreover, these findings may inspire further research into whether analogous conservation law formulations exist for other equations, such as the Schrödinger equation. This study evaluates the performance of 21 machine learning algorithms using 11 significance tests across 12 years of data from the Chinese NPL dataset. Initially, the dataset was divided into two subsets by year to serve as training and testing groups. Furthermore, 10 years were excluded from the split because insufficient data existed to create two equal-year subsets. These algorithms span a broad spectrum of supervised learning techniques, including support vector machines, decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, and various neural network types. The analysis also incorporated feature significance tests to identify the most critical variables within the dataset. Ultimately, XGBoost emerged as the highest-performing algorithm, achieving an accuracy of 96.15%, followed closely by LightGBM at 96.04%. Additionally, feature significance results indicated that the "year" and "quarter" fields are the most influential in predicting network failures. The research concludes that decision tree and tree-based methods are the most effective for failure classification on the Chinese NPL dataset, while also offering recommendations for future enhancements to the study. This work serves as a foundation for subsequent research. Additionally, the source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/ML-Assessment-NPL-Data.

Keywords: Data Mining, Machine Learning, Significance Test, Classification, Network Failure Prediction.

This work introduces two families of Dyck paths, $\mathcal{D}_n(q)$ and $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$, which are constructed from symmetric functions and Schur functions. The cardinality of $\mathcal{D}_n(q)$ corresponds to the value of the Gaussian polynomial $\binom{n+1}{\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor + 1}_q$, representing the count of subspaces within a vector space over a finite field. Similarly, the size of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ is given by $\binom n{\lfloor \frac n3 \rfloor}_q$. This latter finding provides a combinatorial interpretation for the colorings of $n$ points arranged in a triangle, thereby extending the classical theory of non-colorable maps on triangles to the realm of combinatorial geometry. These results offer a natural extension of the theory of non-colorable combinatorial maps on triangles, as formulated by Kozlov and Ziegler. Furthermore, the proof relies on concepts from quantum mechanics, including density matrices and the Pauli matrices. This research forms part of the author's doctoral thesis. This paper introduces a convolutional architecture designed to address image overfitting by incorporating an orientation filter bank. We demonstrate that an orientation filter provides a more effective image representation than conventional convolutional filters by capturing both local features and orientation. This approach is particularly advantageous for the first layer layer in small convolutional networks, as it reduces the number of parameters required in subsequent layers. We present the orientation convolutional network (OCN) and evaluate its performance against standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Results indicate that ON performs comparably to traditional CNNs on MNIST but achieves a 3.2% improvement on CIFAR-10. Furthermore, we show that OCN is significantly more sample-efficient on CIFAR-10, reaching the final test accuracy of a standard CIFAR-10 CNN with merely 10% of the training data. Additionally, we observe that OCN exhibits greater robustness to noise on CIFAR-10 relative to a conventional CNN. Finally, we demonstrate that OCN can be extended to other convolutional architectures, such as ResNet, to achieve similar outcomes. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/OracleFilterBanks. Let $G_0$ and $G_1$ be simple Lie groups of rank $d_0$ and $d_1$ respectively, where $d_0 \le d_1$, considered as constant-coefficient differential operators on the line. We define a "linear interval with curvature $K$" as the range $[e^{-|K|\tau}, e^{|\K|\tau}]$. For any $\tau > 0$, we construct a novel relative trace formula featuring novel Fourier expansions that enumerate joint spectral values for operator pairs. When $k=0$, we demonstrate that this formula reduces to the Petersson-Kuznetsov formula. Furthermore, we establish that the Fourier expansions of the linear trace equation correspond to zeroth-order terms in the Feynman expansion of the propagator for a Schrödinger operator, as well as the long-time asymptotics of solutions to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Additionally, we explore a significant connection between this new framework and number theory. Specifically, we derive an explicit constant-term expansion for real Mellin transforms, which relates to the spectral expansion of the constant term in a Petersson inner product of modular forms. This relationship is achieved by equating "curvature" with the weight of modular forms and the degree of cusp forms. We also examine a connection with Hecke operators on Sp(2), linking this interaction to the work of J.-K. Liu on Poincar\'e series and Y. Tsushima on Siegel modular forms. Finally, we provide an overview of several other relationships with contemporary research, including works by R. Beilinson, A. Bejleri, C. Deninger, C. Skinner, and B. Zhang. Through these relationships, we demonstrate that the linear interval with curvature $K$ encompasses both the Archimedean curvature of Lie groups on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the ramification of field extensions of degree $n$. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grants 11771397 and 11971429). Our approach offers a unified perspective on curvature, ramification, and complex structures. Notably, the curvature $K$ arises from the noncommutativity of the Hamiltonians governing time evolution, a feature that may hold broader significance. We anticipate that this framework will inspire further developments in various mathematical disciplines. This manuscript serves as an introduction to our forthcoming publications. We measure the mass of the 175 GeV/top qu particle by analyzing the kinematics of its decay products, which include a B-hadron, a W boson that decays leptonically, and additional jets. The primary systematic uncertainty in our top quark mass determination stems from the parton distribution functions of the proton. This function uncertainty influences the reconstruction of the primary collision vertex and the resulting kinematic properties of the top quark's decay products. Furthermore, it alters the predicted rates of the observed event topology. To quantify this uncertainty, we employ a Monte Carlo simulation that fits the mass of the decay products for a hypothetical particle (the top quark) to experimental data. We compare two scenarios: the first assumes massless parton distribution functions, while the second accounts for their inherent uncertainties. The difference between the mass values derived from these two scenarios represents the systematic uncertainty due to parton distribution function uncertainty. Our analysis reveals that this uncertainty is not constant; it varies depending on the quark flavor of the B-hadron, a dependence that is more pronounced when using Monte Carlo event generators based on next-to-leading order (NLO) perturbative QCD theory rather than those relying on the collinear factorization approximation. This observation is particularly relevant for the ATLAS experiment's recent determination of the most precise top quark mass value to date. We have developed a new method to account for the substantial flavor dependence of parton distribution function uncertainty in extracting physical parameters from collider data. Applying this approach to the recent ATLAS mass measurement, we find that it could lead to a reduction in the associated systematic uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the significance of this effect is particularly pronounced in analyses utilizing the pinched spectral shape technique. This finding is especially pertinent to CMS's upcoming determination of the most accurate top quark mass value ever recorded, which will rely on this method. Our findings suggest that the contribution of parton distribution function uncertainty to the total mass measurement precision could be greater than previously estimated. This insight is especially valuable for the upcoming ATLAS and CMS measurements, which aim to achieve even higher precision. We conclude that the parton distribution function uncertainty could constitute a non-negligible component of the total systematic uncertainty affecting these measurements. Our conclusions are supported by the substantial flavor dependence observed between the bottom quark and the strange quark. This dependence is particularly significant when employing pinched spectral shape techniques. Our findings are consistent with those reported in other studies. A graph $G$ is defined as nearly regular if it exhibits a strictly positive edge-coloring where every color class forms a regular graph. In this work, we investigate vertex subsets $V$ within such graphs $G$ that admit a coloring of all edges incident to vertices in $V$ using a specific subset of the total colors, ensuring that for each color $c$, the subgraph consisting of edges with color $c$ incident to $V$ is isomorphic to the regular color class of $G$ associated with $c$. We establish sufficient conditions under which vertices can be consecutively colored. Furthermore, for nearly regular graphs $G$ with a regular degree of $r$, we derive an upper bound of $r+1$ that applies to the length of any necessary subset of vertices requiring a color. This bound is tight when $r \geq 2$. Additionally, for nearly regular graphs $G$ with a regular degree of $r=1$, we demonstrate that the subset of vertices necessitating a color can be selected with a size no greater than $r^2+r$. We also present a construction of such a graph $G$ where the required vertex subset size equals $r^2+r$. Finally, for regular graphs, we provide an alternative proof of a result by Dvo\v{r}\'{a}k and Volec, which stems from a conjecture by Galvin. Specifically, we show that for any regular graph $G$ of degree $r$ and any vertex $v$, there exists a coloring of the edges incident to $v$ such that for every color $c$, the neighbor of $v$ obtained via color $c$ has a neighbor connected to $v$ through an edge with a different color. We further propose a conjecture regarding the maximum size of the vertex subset $V$ and generalize the findings applicable to nearly regular graphs with a regular degree of $r=1$. Finally, we propose a conjecture concerning nearly regular graphs $G$ with a regular degree of $r \geq 2$, which is supported by the example of the complete graph $K_{r+1}$. This conjecture suggests that for any vertex $v$ in $G$, there exists a coloring of the edges incident to $v$ such that the subset $\{v\}$ satisfies the required color properties. This study establishes strong type inequalities for scaled Bergman spaces on the complex half-plane, thereby extending a finding originally attributed to the unit disk by Bernicot and Carron. Furthermore, we provide tensorel strong inequality inequalities regarding the Hilbert-Schmidt class for operators acting on scaled Bergman spaces. Notably, the exponent determining the strong inequality remains identical to that of the $L\infty-$norm, a characteristic also observed in the unit disk. Additionally, the proof yields a correspondence between scaled Bergman spaces and weighted Bergman spaces defined on the unit disk. Specifically, certain scaled Bergman spaces are identified that correspond to every possible exponent within the family of weighted Bergman spaces of the unit disk, where the exponents of these latter spaces range over the entire set of positive real numbers. This result offers a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between scaled Bergman spaces and weighted Bergman spaces of the unit disk. The methodology employed herein utilizes the Cayley transform, which maps the complex half-plane to the unit disk, to transform the problem into the disk and subsequently utilizes the scaled radial Laplacian to transform it back to the half-plane. This approach represents an extension of the technique previously used to address a similar issue on the disk. The text is structured into four sections. Section 2 provides the necessary background and notation. Section 3 introduces scaled Bergman spaces on the complex half-plane and the scaled radial Laplacian. Section 4 presents the main results of this paper. Finally, Section 5 explores the relationships between scaled Bergman spaces on the complex half-plane and weighted scaled Bergman spaces on the unit disk. This relationship is derived from strong type inequalities for the scaled radial Laplacian with respect to various weights, a finding detailed in the reference [1]. To establish these strong type inequalities, the authors employ the abstract weighted Laplacian framework developed in [2]. We have adopted this theoretical approach in our work. The reference list includes: [1] N. Bernicot and N. Carron, "Poisson kernel and strong inequalities for the Laplacian in the ball," *Revista Matemática Iberoamericana*, 2015; and [2] T. Coulhon, C. K. Li, and J. Wang, "Strong inequalities for the Laplacian on Riemannian manifolds and applications," *Journal of Functional Analysis*, 2009. Keywords: Scaled Bergman spaces, Strong type inequalities, Scaled radial Laplacian,

The escalating global threat of the COVID-19 pandemic has created an urgent need for rapid, accurate, and automated diagnostic methods to contain its spread. While Computed Tomography (CT) imaging offers a reliable means of detecting the virus, this research specifically targets low-dose CT (LDCT) scans to minimize radiation exposure. Although LDCT is less effective than standard-dose CT for diagnosis, its superior accessibility makes it a valuable alternative for screening and early detection. This study introduces a two-stage Time-Distributed Capsule Network (TD-CN) designed for classifying LDCT images into three categories: normal, infected, and having Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD). To enhance feature extraction, the proposed model incorporates additional layers that analyze image patches at various scales and positions. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of a fully convolutional network (FCN) with extra filter extraction layers and a state-of-the-art FCN model known as ResNet101. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies confirm the model's effectiveness and highlight the significance of the proposed enhancements. Finally, the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art models in human-level detection across all three classes. These findings suggest the model is highly effective for screening and early detection, offering potential for integration into automated CT classification systems. This study examines the distribution of active and inactive active satellites in low-Earth orbit across specific altitude and inclination ranges. It introduces a spherical shell-based spatial distribution model, which represents low-Earth orbit as stacked spherical shells corresponding to altitude and inclination. The research validates this model using a catalog of 1,030 active satellites from 2018 and compares the results of a simulation involving 106,000 satellites against both the 2018 data and existing literature. The findings indicate that the size of spherical shells and inter-satellite distances are critical factors in accurately predicting satellite distribution. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model can effectively estimate satellite distributions and support space situational awareness and traffic management. Furthermore, the study offers insights into potential future distribution patterns, aiding in the planning of satellite constellations and the design of ground-based observation systems. Finally, the paper addresses the challenges and opportunities for achieving sustainable low-Earth orbit operations. To my knowledge, this model is the first of its kind to be applied for space traffic management. Additionally, the satellite catalog used is, to the best of my understanding, the first to be employed for any spatial distribution analysis of low-Earth orbit satellites. This work is partially funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 61973055). In this manuscript, I introduce a novel spherical shell-based spatial distribution model for low-Earth orbit satellites. Satellites are represented as point particles within spherical shells defined by altitude and inclination. I demonstrate that shell size and inter-satellite distance are pivotal in characterizing the distribution, with 2018 data revealing that 90% of active satellites occupy only 10% of the Low-Earth Orbit volume. I also apply this model to forecast the distribution trends for 2028 and 2038. The resulting spatial distribution model holds significant potential for supporting space traffic management. To my knowledge, applying such a model for space traffic management is a first. This study addresses the generation of coarse quadrilateral meshes for three-dimensional CAD-based finite element models, focusing on the challenge of creating coarse quadrangular meshes free of mesh singularities. To achieve a whole-count relationship between internal and boundary triangulations, we employ general linear programming. The resulting quadrangular mesh is then refined using the three-way algorithm to produce a high-quality quadrangular mesh. A numerical example and established test cases demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology. The approach is implemented in C++ and made accessible via the open-source platform www.github.com/QuadrilateralMesh. Future research will investigate the creation of quadrangular meshes with high-order continuity. This work forms part of a thesis completed at the University of Duisburg-Essen, Duisburg, Germany. For inquiries, contact me at contact@alirezaafshar.net. Additional details are available at www.alirezaafshar.net. Keywords: Coarse Quadrilateral Mesh Generation, Three-Way Algorithm, Linear Programming, High Order Continuity.

This paper derives analytical formulas for the expected value, variance, and higher-order moments of a sample correlation coefficient, accommodating an arbitrary finite effect size. These formulas are specifically calculated across three distinct data distributions: (i) data generated uniformly within a bounded region of $\mathbb{R}^2$, (ii) data following a $\mathbb{R}^2$ uniform tail distribution characterized by negative or zero correlation in its unbounded section, and (iii) data following a Gaussian uniform tail distribution with similar properties. Additionally, numerical results are provided for data drawn from $\mathbb{R}^2$ Cauchy and $\mathbb{R}^2$ Lorentzian distributions, both featuring a finite domain and a specific correlation between components. Furthermore, the study presents data from a well-mixed ideal diatomic gas, where velocity data follows a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at a fixed temperature; in this scenario, components are uncorrelated, yet finite samples yield non-zero correlation coefficients. Finally, data is presented from an experiment involving a non-mixed diatomic gas mixture, where correlation coefficients exhibit non-ergodic behavior. These findings are formulated as a hypothesis regarding the finite-time validity of the ergodic hypothesis. Overall, the results are expressed in a general framework applicable to any distribution function of finite samples from a bivariate distribution. This leads to a set of general recommendations concerning the selection of data sources and sample sizes for estimating the expected value, variance, and higher moments of the sample correlation coefficient. Such information is particularly valuable for researchers developing new nonparametric or semiparametric statistical methods that utilize the correlation coefficient. Finally, the paper includes computer code written in the Julia programming language to compute these moments for the specified distributions. This code is distributed under a free license and can be easily adapted to calculate moments for any distribution of bivariate data.

**Keywords:** bivariate data, sample correlation coefficient, expected value, variance, higher moments, ergodic hypothesis.

The S-matrix approach to quantum field theory remains a topic of ongoing research. In this study, we apply the S-matrix framework to general relativity and its extensions, specifically examining black hole physics via the principle of unitarity. Our calculations reveal that the scattering amplitudes for black holes deviate from the $1/s$ behavior predicted by the partial wave expansion of the graviton propagator. Consequently, the S-matrix analysis suggests that strings must exist at a mass scale lower than the black hole mass scale. This finding offers a potential resolution to the hierarchy problem between QCD and gravity within the standard model. Additionally, we explore an extension of general relativity incorporating a positive cosmological constant and analyze its corresponding S-matrix. We demonstrate that this S-matrix exhibits unitary s-channel behavior but violates the expected black and white channel conditions. This discrepancy highlights the necessity of incorporating extended objects to ensure the unitarity of the S-matrix. This study addresses the global stabilization of 3D Navier-Stokes equations, which describe a viscous, incompressible Newtonian fluid within a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. The system incorporates finite-dimensional localized feedback controls applied internally to velocity traces on specific boundary subsets $\Gamma_j$ (where $\overline{\Gamma_1} \cap \overline{\Gamma_2} = \emptyset$ and $\bigcup_{j=1}^2 \Gamma_j = \overline{\Gamma}$). These controls function as "velocity sensors" that measure the velocity on each $\Gamma_j$ and adjust the normal velocity on $\Gamma_j$ to drive the Navier-Stokes equations toward zero. The study demonstrates that the closed-loop system stabilizes the Navier-Stokes equations to zero in critical $H^1$ spaces. Furthermore, it establishes local stabilization within $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. This approach represents a stabilization technique based on "velocity feedback" that differs significantly from traditional methods. Specifically, it diverges from "position feedback" strategies, which rely on full-state velocity measurements across the entire boundary $\partial \Omega$ and are applicable to both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. In contrast, the proposed position feedback mechanism relies on partial velocity data and is restricted to Newtonian fluids. Additionally, this work complements recent findings by the authors regarding the stabilization of non-Newtonian Navier-Stokes equations. Those earlier results utilized "velocity sensors" that provided full-state velocity measurements on the entire boundary $\partial \Omega$, thereby enabling broader applicability to both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. The current paper narrows the scope to Newtonian fluids but achieves the same stabilization outcome. The stabilization of non-Newtonian Navier-Stokes equations by the velocity feedback law is detailed in a separate publication. This paper focuses on proving the stabilization of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in $L^q(\Omega)$ for $1 \le q < 6/5$. This functional setting is significant because it encompasses critical $H^1$ spaces. The stabilization is further analyzed in critical Besov spaces, which are closely related to Navier-Stokes dynamics. Recent studies have shown that the popular post-hoc explanation method LIME can significantly alter recommendation scores, thereby compromising the stability of LIME-RS. This paper investigates the compliance of LIME-RS with three key human preferences: compliance to (i) group fairness constraints, (ii) sensitivity to the explanation local weighting function, and (iii) the importance and treatability of fair groups. Our experimental results indicate that while LIME-RS is compliant with local weighting, it fails to ensure compliance with fairness constraints and the sensitivity of its base model. We further demonstrate that the stability of LIME-RS can be improved by at least 20% through regularization techniques. Finally, we introduce a novel regularization approach that leverages the metric properties of a recommendation model's embedding space to generate synthetic samples for local weighting. We find that this proposed method enhances the stability of LIME-RS by over 50%. Furthermore, it improves the compliance of LIME-RS with fairness constraints by 15% and to over 80% with local weighting preferences. These findings underscore the critical role of the local weighting function in LIME-RS and highlight the necessity of carefully considering the properties of the input space. Additionally, we offer practical guidance for selecting an appropriate weighting function to ensure the compliance and stability of LIME-RS. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rggarg/LIME-REX. Finally, we have developed an open-source Python package, LIME-REX, which implements LIME post-hoc explanations for Recommendation post-processing, including a flexible local weighting interface, a local dataset generator, a fair post-processing algorithm, a regularization interface, a stabilizer, a stabilizer interface, a fairness checker, and a fairness constraint checker. In semiconductor quantum wells, near-surface barriers can become depleted, leading to the self-fixation of the electronic Fermi level at the band edge. This phenomenon is particularly significant in Fermi energy ladders and gate-defined quantum dots where only a few subbands are occupied. In this study, we examine this effect in near-surface quantum wells within doped InAs layers. We analyze how quantum confinement and surface confinement energies influence the fixation of the Fermi level, specifically within an InAs quantum well under various surface treatments. Furthermore, we explore methods to lift the Fermi level into the gap, moving away from fixation at the band edge. These findings are essential for both fundamental research and the development of advanced two-dimensional semiconducting heterostructures. Additionally, the results provide critical context for the recent observation of a "magic angle" in the gate capacitance of monolayer InAs quantum wells fabricated via near-surface ion implantation. This magic angle arises from a transition between two distinct regimes: one where the Fermi level is self-fixed at the band edge, and another where it floats within the gap. Our work elucidates the specific roles of quantum confinement and surface effects in driving this transition. Finally, we discuss the implications for implementing spin qubits via ion implantation. Since spin qubits typically require gate-defined potentials within the gap, our results indicate that without appropriate surface treatments, the implantation technique may inadvertently fix the Fermi level at the band edge, hindering qubit operation. We find that geometrically structured regions aligned with the data distribution yield better quality than uniform regions, while topologically contiguous regions matching the input manifold outperform both uniform and non-contiguous designs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quality improvements from regionally guided learning are more pronounced in the later stages of training, suggesting that this approach should be implemented during the fine-tuning phase. Additionally, fine-tuning with regional queries helps the model generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, such as Gaussian noise. Finally, we observe that fine-tuning with regional queries results in a more robust model against adversarial examples. These insights deepen our understanding of the relationship between training methodology and final model performance. Additionally, the use of regional queries enables the training of larger models within the same computational budget, with evidence indicating that these models achieve superior quality. This study investigates the precise computation of optimal transport using the recently developed RAPID Sinkhorn operator, demonstrating that RAPID achieves linear complexity across all initial points, in contrast to the exponential complexity of standard Sinkhorn and the varying linear complexity of RAPID I. RAPID II operates by iteratively applying two distinct operators: $T$ and $S$. For any given initial cost matrix, there exists a unique fixed point where the $T$ and $S$ operators coincide; however, convergence depends on the starting point, with complexity generally increasing based on the initial separation between these two operators. We establish that for a specific class of problems featuring collinear marginal problems, this critical point can be characterized by a "triangular array." In such scenarios, we identify the problem substructure that ensures the final $T$ and $S$ operators become identical immediately, regardless of the initial separation. Leveraging the ability of RAPID II to detect and bypass the "stuck" state upon identifying this substructure, we develop a new algorithm for precise optimal transport computation with linear complexity independent of the initial starting point. This approach offers superior speed compared to both standard Sinkhorn and RAPID II, while delivering solutions of equal precision and validity. Furthermore, we show that this algorithm facilitates the construction of a valid optimal transport plan in linear time, effectively resolving the practical "weakness" of RAPID II solutions, which previously lacked an explicit plan despite providing marginal approximations. Finally, we broaden the scope of this work to address a more general class of problems that encompasses the collinear case, maintaining the same algorithmic characteristics. Extensive numerical experiments confirm that this approach offers consistent performance and reliability across all tested problems. These findings hold significant practical value, as they enable the rapid and precise resolution of optimal transport problems for all real-world applications. Notably, this work represents the first instance where the exponential complexity barrier of standard Sinkhorn and RAPID I has been overcome for all problems, achieving linear complexity without sacrificing precision. This advancement significantly expands the range of solvable problems and enhances the reliability of solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate that RAPID II can be adapted to solve a more general class of problems, including those that are not collinear, by introducing a novel algorithm capable of detecting the triangular array structure and bypassing the stuck state in linear time. This algorithm exhibits the same behavior as RAPID II but operates at linear complexity from the outset. Experimental results indicate that this algorithm is not only faster than RAPID II but also more robust, maintaining consistent performance

AU Microscopii serves as a critical model for understanding the interaction between protoplanetary disks and their central stars. This study examines the far-ultraviolet (FUV) emission of the AU Mic system across three epochs: a quiescent phase and two active phases coinciding with X-ray and optical eruptions. We analyze these observations using a model that incorporates both the far-UV excited C II 1585, 1600 Å doublet and the C IV 1548, 1549 Å resonance lines. Our results indicate that the C II emission is primarily driven by C II rich material located at the disk surface, which is illuminated by the far-UV radiation field. In contrast, the C IV emission originates from a hot coronal plasma at the disk surface, heated to temperatures between 80,000 K and 100,000 K by the far-UV field. This coronal gas is observed at a height of 0.5 to 1 stellar radii. Furthermore, we find that the intensity of the C II 1585, 1600 Å doublet is directly correlated with the intensity of the C IV 1548, 1549 Å resonance line, suggesting that the far-UV field is the primary driver of the observed coronal activity. Finally, we assess the impact of these variable stellar winds on the AU Mic disk and planets. The increased mass loss rates resulting from these eruptions could accelerate the disk's dispersal and influence the atmospheric escape of AU Mic b and c. Additionally, the variable mass loss may contribute to the dynamical instability noted between AU Mic b and c, potentially explaining their observed orbital configurations. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for variable mass loss when interpreting the evolution of young planetary systems. This research is based on data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph. This study introduces a statistical variant of the close-near classification method, which functions as a specialized iteration of the nearest neighbor classification tailored for binary decisions. While a standard KNN classifier typically requires roughly K data points to determine the label of a "near" neighbor, an equal-K approach assumes that all points within distance $k$ contribute equally. In contrast, the close-near rule allocates influence proportionally based on their relative distances to the classifier. This paper investigates the properties of the close-near rule within the binary classification framework and demonstrates its superior performance compared to equal-K rules under certain conditions. Furthermore, we develop bootstrap procedures to estimate misclassification rates for these classifiers. Finally, we validate the theoretical findings through a simulation study and an analysis of real-world data. Our results indicate that close-near rules outperform the standard KNN (using equal-K) classifier when class-conditional densities are well-separated, and they achieve comparable results to KNN classifiers when classes are not well-separated. Additionally, we observe that the KNN classifier utilizing the optimal K value is statistically equivalent to the close-near rule in this context. Finally, we demonstrate that close-near rules maintain robustness against outliers. These conclusions are supported by an R package named `clsnnr`, which implements various versions of the close-near rule alongside KNN classifiers with optimal K selection. The package also provides bootstrap tools for misclassification estimation and includes an example dataset. The R package is accessible at: https://cran.r-project.org/package=clsnnr. Our findings suggest that close-near rules are particularly beneficial for datasets containing outliers. Single-view eternal views offer a comprehensive and panoramic depiction of physical environments, making them highly valuable for human-computer interaction and various computer vision applications. Nevertheless, creating such views remains difficult due to significant challenges, including occlusions, inconsistent focal points, and vanishing point misalignments. While previous approaches have relied on generative models to synthesize new viewpoints from existing images, they often produce unreliable results. To address this, we introduce DiffDreamer, a two-stage framework that generates reliable and high-quality global-consistent images. The first stage, DiffMask, creates a reliable 3D-consistent image by removing occlusions and resolving view-inconsistent regions. The second stage, PanDiff, produces a high-quality, coherent eternal view by simultaneously addressing FOV alignment, resolution, and color consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art on both quantitative and qualitative metrics. This paper introduces a novel concept of feature exchanging within multi-input multi-output (MIMO) frameworks. We demonstrate that an optimal strategy for maximizing the mutual information between the original and exchanged features involves a linear transformation, meaning any non-linear exchange can be optimally represented by an equivalent linear one. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form solution that uniquely identifies a sub-optimal exchange capable of achieving any specific target mutual information value. These theoretical findings hold significant potential for various machine learning applications, including domain adaptation, feature selection, and feature fusion. In our study, we focus on feature fusion, where we propose a new method for learning deep symmetric feature exchanging MIMO frameworks. Unlike current approaches that treat exchanged features as auxiliary constructs dependent on inputs and outputs, we demonstrate that these features serve as essential components for the task. We evaluate this approach on two domains: image denoising and speech enhancement. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both scenarios. **Background**: Life course epidemiology seeks to understand how early-life factors influence the likelihood of developing chronic diseases later in life. This research focuses on patients who experienced myocardial infarction (MI) in midlife, aiming to determine how early-life health-related variables affect both short-term survival post-MI and the long-term risk of future heart failure. **Methods**: We employed Multiple State Evaluation (MSE), a statistical framework designed for multi-dimensional analysis of heterogeneous time-to-event data. The study utilized a retrospective cohort from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) Cardiovascular Health (CVH) sub-study. Participants were divided into two groups based on their MI occurrence relative to the baseline examination: those who had an MI before the baseline visit (MI group) and those who had not (non-MI group). Within each group, individuals were further stratified by whether heart failure developed after the baseline assessment (HF group) or did not (non-HF group). This created a 2×2 state space where each cell represents a unique life course health trajectory. **Results**: The resulting MSE results indicated that lower birth weight, lower birth order, and lower childhood height were associated with a higher probability of transitioning from the non-MI to the MI state within the first year, as well as a higher probability of transitioning from the non-MI to the HF state within the first year for the MI group. Additionally, the number of pregnancies was linked to a reduced probability of transitioning from the non-MI to the MI state within the first year across both groups. **Conclusions**: These findings suggest that the adverse effects of low birth weight, low birth order, low childhood height, and a high number of pregnancies on post-MI survival and long-term heart failure risk may operate through distinct biological mechanisms. The MSE approach offers a novel analytical strategy for investigating how early-life factors influence the probability of multiple, mutually exclusive health trajectories. Furthermore, the MESA CVH study demonstrates the value of a well-designed, population-based prospective study in addressing complex multi-dimensional health questions. The MSE method represents a significant advancement for analyzing diverse time-to-event data, such as MI and heart failure, and holds broad applicability for investigating how early-life factors influence the probability of diverse life course health pathways. This study is the first to apply MSE to a multi-state model. Additional MSE applications are anticipated in future research. The MSE R package is accessible at http://www.stat.duke.edu/~jgill/mse/. This paper introduces a quadrature approach to solve the one-electron continuum Kohn-Sham equation within DFT and the Schrödinger equation. The method begins by dividing the continuum region into subregions, with boundaries defined by the molecular surface and the zero-potential surface. It employs a non-orthogonal basis set where orbitals are represented as a sum of functions localized at the origin and at the frontier of the vacuum region. Parameters for the global sum are determined by numerically solving a reduced-size Hamiltonian matrix element equation, while parameters for the inner sum are optimized numerically. After determining these parameters, the Hamiltonian is applied to each orbital to yield optimized eigenfunctions. Testing on LiH, H$_2$, and I$_2$ indicates that this technique is both efficient and precise. Furthermore, the method demonstrates scalability across multi-site systems, such as the H$_2$ + He dimer, suggesting its potential for large-scale applications in chemistry and physics. This approach offers a viable path toward achieving a truly continuum-free resolution of the Kohn-Sham equation in DFT. Keywords: Density Functional Theory; Continuum Region; Quadrature Method. This study examines the decision problem of determining whether a graph's metric dimension is at most $k$ is NP-hard. Leveraging this finding, we introduce numerous algorithms, many of which are parameterized. Notably, we present a condition-based fixed-parameter algorithm with runtime $O(c^n)$ for any base $c > 1$, a fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by the size of feedback vertex set ($k + n$), and a fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by the union of metric dimension $k$ and vertex cover ($k + n$). Additionally, we develop an exact fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by vertex cover, and an algorithm with runtime $O(k^{k+1})$ for finding the minimum metric vertex cover when it exists. Finally, we establish an exact fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by treewidth, yielding a runtime of $O(k^{tw+k+twn})$. In each scenario, $k$ represents the parameter, $n$ the vertex count, and $tw$ the treewidth. Furthermore, we demonstrate an exact fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by pathwidth, achieving a runtime of $O(k^{tw + k + 2^n})$. Throughout this work, we assume $k$ is a fixed natural number. Additionally, we present an algorithm with runtime $O(k^{k + n})$ to identify a metric dimension achieving value $k + n$ whenever such a dimension exists. Finally, we provide an exact fixed-parameter algorithm parameterized by the size of a minimum edge deletion set required to eliminate all $K_4$-minor graphs, which runs in $O(k^{k + n})$ time. In every case, $k$ denotes the parameter. We conclude that finding the metric dimension is fixed-parameter tractable for $K_4$-minor free graphs. Central to this generalization is the concept of a directed area, which comprises all regions within a directed area possessing a specific property known as subadditivity. Hothouse Earth scenarios, characterized by elevated CO2 levels and temperatures exceeding 2°C, may induce hydrologic feedbacks that intensify the global hydrologic cycle. This study examines the feedbacks between a warmer, higher-CO2 atmosphere and the resulting hydrologic response. We analyze the frequency and intensity of simulated precipitation events in both warm, high-CO2 and cool, low-CO2 atmospheric conditions using the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM5). Our findings indicate that while the hydrologic cycle is amplified by higher CO2 concentrations, the most extreme precipitation events are primarily driven by higher temperatures. We further demonstrate that the distribution of precipitation intensity shifts non-linearly in these warmer environments, leading to a disproportionate increase in the intensity of the strongest storms. This non-linear response is more pronounced in hothouse conditions, where the precipitation intensity distribution exhibits a "fat tail" at higher CO2 concentrations. Additionally, we observe that the magnitude of the most intense precipitation events scales linearly with temperature, regardless of the CO2 concentration. These results suggest that the precipitation intensity distribution responds differently to temperature in warm versus cool environments. Specifically, the precipitation intensity distribution in a hothouse environment, even one achieved through moderate warming, is significantly "fatter" than that of a much colder state reached through high CO2 concentrations. These non-linear responses to temperature could trigger positive feedbacks, potentially making hothouse environments more prone to extreme precipitation events. Consequently, the non-linear precipitation intensity response to temperature in hothouse environments could be a critical feedback mechanism in future climate change. This becomes increasingly relevant as Earth approaches critical temperature thresholds, such as a 2°C rise, which could lead to tipping points and irreversible changes in the climate system. We conclude that non-linear responses to temperature should be considered when evaluating the effects of the hothouse feedback loop. Furthermore, we recommend that climate models be evaluated against the precipitation intensity distribution, particularly regarding their sensitivity to temperature. Finally, we note that the non-linear response of precipitation intensity to temperature is not unique to hothouse environments; it is also observed in much cooler conditions, such as those that occurred during the last glacial period. This suggests that the non-linear response of precipitation intensity to temperature is a fundamental characteristic of the coupled climate system. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the precipitation sensitivity to temperature and the potential for a "precipitation threshold" in climate change. Timed definitions offer an alternative to standard hol_defer and hol_promote, balancing the promptness of defer with the delayed evaluation of promote, with the duration of the delay determined by EBNF syntax. In extended definitions, timing information is shown alongside each clause, while in mini-definitions, it is displayed only for specific clauses. The hol-defer and hol-promote commands function as special cases within the framework of timed definitions. The syntax for timed definitions was introduced in 2012 and has since been refined through various iterations. This paper examines the syntax and semantics of both extended and mini-definitions, analyzes the rationale behind the implementation decisions, and details the various semantic options available for each style. Finally, several examples illustrate the advantages of using timed definitions. All code related to this study is available in the h4ex repository. The suggested syntax for timed definitions has been adopted by the HOL community and is now supported by HOL Light, HOL 4, and EDTB. Furthermore, the EDTB system includes a command to enable or disable timed definitions. EDTB also features an option to choose between the two semantics for extended definitions. The authors thank the HOL community for their feedback, which led to improvements in the syntax. Specifically, clause timing is now indicated using brackets rather than square brackets, and the definition body is referred to as the "clause set" instead of the "specification." The authors also acknowledge the contributions of the HOL community for the terminology used to describe conflicts. Magnetic flux applied to a two-dimensional lattice distorts the band structure, giving rise to the Hofstadler spectrum. We demonstrate that Hofstadler physics can emerge without a magnetic field if time-reversal symmetry is violated through a specific pattern of spin-orbit coupling. This mechanism generates topologically protected Weyl points, the number of which depends on the flux per unit cell. Furthermore, a chiral anomaly manifests as a negative magnetoresistance when a weak third magnetic field is introduced. These findings indicate that Weyl points can be realized within the Hofstadler domain using electric fields alone, offering a promising avenue for experimental verification. Additionally, we show that these Hofstadler Weyl points remain robust in three dimensions, even when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the layers. Finally, we find that a three-dimensional version of the Hofstadler model, based on a simple cubic lattice, supports multiple Weyl points even without an external magnetic field. This represents a novel class of Weyl semimetals, potentially accessible through electrostatic doping in existing semiconductor heterostructures. We have created and experimentally analyzed hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas featuring a silicon base with a top-layer pattern of gold nanodisks. These structures support two distinct optical resonances: a dielectric mode within the silicon base and a plasmonic mode in the gold nanodisks. By adjusting the size of the gold disks, the weakly-damped dielectric resonance can be excited at longer wavelengths, while the strongly-damped plasmonic resonance shifts to shorter wavelengths. The hybrid nanoantennas support a long-lived, lasing-like dielectric resonance at approximately 1.05 eV, accompanied by a short-lived, non-radiative plasmonic resonance near 2.05 eV. This non-radiative resonance facilitates a strong local field within the silicon base, enabling a lower laser threshold compared to antennas with only a plasmonic top layer. Conversely, the dielectric resonance ensures a high far-field radiation efficiency, allowing for strong unidirectional and luminous output. This device functions as a reliable, unidirectional, and efficient "artificial light source," which is essential for numerous fundamental and applied research applications. Additionally, the nanoantenna displays a tunable "photo-electrochemical" response to light, which is a critical feature for photovoltaic and photodetection technologies. This hybrid approach offers an effective solution to the inherent trade-off between high field confinement and far-field efficiency found in purely dielectric or purely plasmonic nanoantennas. Within this framework, coherent force chains form within the grains, enabling the granular medium to exhibit anomalous acoustic shielding that surpasses the scattering mean free path—contrasting sharply with the percolation behavior observed in random systems. This study reports the first experimental verification, utilizing high-speed imaging, of this theoretically predicted anomalous shielding effect, which aligns closely with prior predictions derived from numerical simulations. This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) with individual Mn atoms adsorbed at various high-symmetry sites. The most stable configuration corresponds to the Mn atom occupying the Si-centered position. Spin-polarized calculations reveal that the Mn atom contributes seven unpaired electrons to the system, inducing a ferromagnetic coupling between the Mn spin and the Si sheet. This interaction opens a gap of approximately 120 meV at the Dirac point of the semimetallic silicene, transforming it into a quantum spin Hall insulator. Furthermore, a flat band appears near the Dirac point, suggesting potential applications as single-spin sources in spintronic devices. These findings indicate that Mn-adorned silicene on hBN exhibits promising magnetic characteristics, making it a viable two-dimensional material for room-temperature spintronics. Additionally, the system displays robust magnetism, remaining stable up to temperatures as high as 400 K. Finally, a detailed analysis of the spin texture and exchange interaction is provided, demonstrating that this two-dimensional structure holds significant promise for developing quantum information technologies. Overall, Mn-decorated silicene on hBN emerges as a strong candidate for future spintronic applications. A comprehensive exploration of the system's properties is available in our prior work [1].

We examine the three-dimensional morphology of the platen-like structure known as Sgr A East, the Sgr A East nebula, and the associated Sgr A East supernova remnant. By analyzing the spatial distribution of Sgr A East, we propose a model in which a core-collapse supernova occurred at a distance of approximately 100 parsecs from the Galactic center. This location aligns with a recently identified molecular cloud situated in a gap within a circumnuclear ring of dense gas. Our findings indicate that the supernova's ejecta were directed toward the south-east, creating a more complex and varied remnant structure in that direction. Furthermore, the Sgr A East supernova may have triggered the formation of the Sgr C molecular cloud. We conclude that supernovae serve as a critical source of material for the circumnuclear region, thereby influencing the growth of the central supermassive black hole. These results highlight the significance of three-dimensional observations for comprehending the formation and evolution of supernova remnants. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research. Multi-label text classification involves assigning one or more of numerous possible categories to each document based on its content. In these tasks, datasets often suffer from class imbalance, where some categories contain significantly fewer samples than others. This paper examines three artificial over-sampling techniques to enhance performance in such imbalanced scenarios: (1) repeating existing samples, (2) over-sampling via word insertion, and (3) autoencoding. Experiments were conducted across three English document corpora for multi-category classification. The results indicate that for very large datasets, the basic approach of simply repeating existing samples yields the strongest performance, whereas the word insertion method produces the best outcomes for the coarser corpus. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that over-sampling remains effective even in large-scale settings containing over 100 million training samples. A comprehensive set of results is available at https://github.com/robertost/oversampling-mtclc. The source code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/robertost/oversampling-mtclc. Our findings suggest that over-sampling offers a straightforward and effective means to improve large-scale multi-category text classification. The preservation of total angular momentum is a critical factor when assessing the precision and reliability of the Rapid Multipole Technique (RMT) for simulating heavy-ion collisions. Utilizing the equation of state from the third-order speed-of-sound parametrization, the study demonstrates that the method accurately maintains the angular momentum of an initial Gaussian beam with $l=2$ over extended simulation periods. The results indicate that the width of the beam in internal transverse space has minimal impact on both the accuracy and stability of the simulation. Furthermore, it is established that the spread in $J_y$ results from the superposition of $J_x$ and $J_z$ components, which oscillate with varying frequencies throughout the evolution. The technique is also shown to successfully simulate head-on beam collisions involving two vortex beams with $l=1$. Additionally, the RMT proves capable of accurately modeling the evolution of $k$-vortex beams, characterized by vortex charges of $k, 0, -k$, across a broad spectrum of initial conditions. Finally, the technique enables the study of angular momentum transfer between beams and a plasma with non-trivial transverse structures, including a soliton and a dark soliton. In all scenarios, the RMT is confirmed to be highly effective and precise. These findings suggest that the RMT is well-suited for investigating the topological properties of quantum plasmas within heavy-ion collision experiments. High-energy elastic electron-proton scattering offers a precise avenue for investigating the internal structure of the ultimate proton, provided one can reliably infer properties of these fundamental constituents from measurable observables of the parent proton. This paper examines the transfer of polarization information from the incident spin-polarized electron to the scattered electron at both tree level and one-loop order. We present the formula for the polarization asymmetry in elastic scattering, derived up to order $\alpha^2$, alongside the corresponding spin-dependent cross section. Furthermore, we analyze the longitudinal polarization transfer coefficient, $A_l$, in the rest frame of the ultimate proton, accounting for radiative corrections. Finally, we explore the conditions necessary for $A_l$ to remain non-zero and discuss the implications of these findings. Our results are directly applicable to the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV Electron Accelertor (JLab-EP) experiment, where the spin of the ultimate proton will be probed via the process $e^- + p \to e^- + p$. We have also established the necessary experimental conditions to observe the polarization of the ultimate proton. The complete set of formulas is available online.

This study examines the simultaneous production of two Higgs bosons in conjunction with a vector boson at the LHC. Specifically, we investigate the ggV$\to$HHV and qqV$\to$b\={b}HHV and ggHHZ processes at $\sqrt{s}=$ 15 TeV using ultrahigh-energy ultra-relativistic proton-proton collisions at the ATLAS experiment. We present the cross sections for these processes at tree level within the Standard Model. Our analysis demonstrates that the production of two Higgs bosons alongside the Z boson via the ggHHZ mechanism can exceed the production of two Higgs bosons with a W boson through the ggWWZ channel by approximately a factor of 2.5. Furthermore, the ggHHZ and qqHHZ processes yield total cross sections of 1.11 fb and 0.15 fb, respectively. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of 10% parton distribution function (PDF) uncertainties on the cross sections for these relevant processes. Finally, we discuss the potential for measuring the coupling constant between Higgs bosons and Z bosons by investigating the ggHHZ process at the ATLAS experiment. The recent introduction of quantum logic gates operating on alkaline earth metal ions within a quantum dot has sparked a surge in research into such systems [1-3]. Although these platforms offer exceptional control, fidelity, and scalability, they face significant hurdles in achieving scalable readout. In this work, we present a novel approach to readout that leverages a collective spin-1/2 maser mode, which is dispersively coupled to a transmission line. This setup allows for the detection of maser radiation at a port while the system remains in the maser state. The proposed system is compatible with current experimental techniques, requiring only a minor increase in laser power and a single additional connection to a transmission line. This method establishes a new foundation for the future development of maser-based quantum readout. Furthermore, we show that maser operation can be sustained indefinitely while reading out the masorite state with near-perfect fidelity. This capability addresses a longstanding challenge in maser-based quantum computing: the simultaneous preservation of maser coherence and high-fidelity readout. Our study demonstrates that a single readout event can collapse the maser state to the masorite state without degrading maser coherence. Additionally, we explore a scenario where maser operation is sustained for extended periods, limited only by the time required to complete the readout. Our proposal offers a viable path toward high-fidelity qubit readout using alkaline earth ions in quantum dots, a technology essential for their realization. Our findings also highlight the potential of collective masers in quantum information processing, thereby opening new avenues for their application. Specifically, we illustrate that masers can facilitate the coherent transfer of quantum information between masorites and remote qubits. This capability expands the utility of masers beyond simple readout functions, positioning them as a fundamental component in the development of future quantum technologies. Our results are supported by comprehensive numerical simulations.

This research examines K3 surfaces defined over number fields, $K$, that admit a symplectic action by a finite group, $G$. We derive an upper limit for the average number of points with coordinates in every finite extension $K_s$ of $K$, considering all $G$-invariant surfaces. Furthermore, when $G$ is cyclic, we demonstrate that this bound is sharp. Additionally, we formulate a conjecture asserting that for any finite, non-symplectic group $G$, every $G$-K3 surface exhibits superabundance. This conjecture follows directly from an alternative method for describing the associated Siegel domain. Finally, we present a conjecture providing an effective bound for the degree of the field required to attain the maximal number of $G$-K3 surfaces, a result that is proven in the case where $G$ is cyclic. These two conjectures are supported by a family of examples generated by theta multiplication, involving representations as monomial groups, which are known to achieve the proposed bounds. We also address several open questions and conjectures regarding the arithmetic of K3 surfaces found in the literature. This study revisits the concept of neutral dark energy composed of neutralinos. In this framework, the energy density of neutralinos closely matches that of the universe, implying the latter is significantly influenced by the former. To explain the observed accelerated expansion, the neutral dark energy model must deteriorate over time, meaning the neutralino mass decreases as cosmic acceleration increases. The rate of this decay is governed by the equation of state parameter. The paper outlines this model and calculates the gamma-ray spectrum, finding that it aligns well with the "cosmic gamma-ray background" data. Consequently, neutral dark energy emerges as a viable candidate. Additionally, the research examines the impact of neutral dark energy on the growth of cosmic structures. It is concluded that, similar to other dark energy scenarios, neutral dark energy hinders structure formation, though it does not stop it entirely. The study further demonstrates that the power spectrum of matter remains nearly scale-independent, and the matter density evolves according to the universe's accelerated expansion. Finally, the redshift at which the transition from deceleration to acceleration occurs is determined by the equation of state. For a typical value of the Hubble constant, the transition redshift is approximately 0.7. These findings indicate that the model can be tested against redshift survey data. Overall, the paper presents a comprehensive analysis of neutral dark energy, a previously underexplored possibility. It is suggested that the Hubble tension could potentially be resolved within this framework. Furthermore, the paper explores the viability of using neutralino decay to drive accelerated expansion, noting that such decay would also address the baryon asymmetry problem. In this context, a typical decay time of $10^{17}$ seconds is proposed, with the corresponding gamma-ray spectrum also calculated. Finally, the paper briefly discusses the possibility of dark matter transitioning into dark energy. These results may provide new avenues for future research. Additionally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the calculation of the gamma-ray spectrum. Specifically, it is shown that, unlike in other theories, the gamma-ray spectrum in this model is independent of the background matter distribution. This feature may offer a new approach to investigating the cosmic gamma-ray background. Overall, this work provides a detailed investigation of neutral dark energy, with several conclusions that may offer new perspectives on the field. The paper is highly recommended for researchers in the field. We present a study on the electrophoretic movement of negatively charged ions within a gas mixture of 90% argon and 10% isobutane, utilizing a high-resolution two-dimensional time projection chamber. The resulting data aligns closely with theoretical predictions, demonstrating an accuracy of 3%. This phenomenon enables the discrimination of nuclear and alpha recoil energies in high-resolution gas TP Cs, thereby improving sensitivity to nuclear WIMPs and CNRs. Additionally, we propose a method for estimating 3D ion trajectories by incorporating the temporal dimension into spatial data collection. By employing a charge readout system that captures both the magnitude and timing of induced signals, we can determine the drift time of ions, which correlates directly to their position in the detector's transverse plane. We outline the development of a data analysis framework designed to extract ion trajectories from existing charge readout data, which may facilitate the implementation of electrophoretic ion movement for recoil discrimination in current TP C detectors. Furthermore, we describe a technique for estimating 3D recoil positions from existing trajectory data, offering a means to correct for ion drift distortions. This approach holds promise for enhancing the spatial resolution of existing TP C datasets. Ultimately, incorporating electrophoretic movement to achieve 2D TP C spatial resolution could yield significantly superior nuclear and neutron WIMP searches. Our findings are applicable to existing TP C detectors, including the XENON100 TP C, the 200 L TP C at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, and upcoming large-scale detectors such as XENONnT, ARGO, and the DARWIN 50t TP C. We anticipate that this research will enable 2D TP C detectors to achieve sub-1 keVee resolution. This work was conducted prior to the DARWIN collaboration's transition to collaboration with the SNOLAB TP C collaboration to establish the project as a joint effort. We also acknowledge the entire SNOLAB TP C collaboration for their insightful discussions regarding ion movement. Finally, we thank all members of the former DUNE-SD TP C group for their contributions and for sharing their knowledge on ion movement with us. Commercial driving represents a labor-intensive and physically demanding field, characterized by long hours, frequent shifts, and the need for significant physical exertion. Given the high stakes of unsafe road conditions, the availability of skilled drivers is critical. This study introduces a new framework for evaluating commercial driving outputs to enhance their safety and efficiency. By combining machine learning with computer vision, we develop contextual intelligence to generate intelligent outputs from commercial driving data. We validate our method using driver safety as a case study. Specifically, we assess whether deep learning can improve the safety of existing driver classification models by providing specialist moderation. Our findings indicate that while current deep learning models achieve high accuracy in classifying driving behaviors, they often produce misleading results that could negatively impact driver careers. We propose a framework for moderating machine outputs to mitigate these adverse effects, thereby promoting greater fairness and safety for drivers. This approach may inspire further research into contextual intelligence to improve the efficacy of machine learning applications. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research in commercial driving. This work was conducted within the Intelligent Transportation Systems Laboratory (ITSLab) at the University of Maryland. We demonstrate that, to leading order, this metric corresponds to the Fisher information metric for random fields. We utilize geodesic distances within this structure to calculate the average field evolution driven by theory errors, potential energy, and stochastic noise.
