This study examines a portfolio optimization problem involving a power utility investor who values both their absolute and relative wealth against a benchmark. The analysis covers two distinct market environments: a risk-free setting and a single-factor risk-based model, which includes both a one-factor Itô diffusion process and a discrete-time "style premium" approach. We demonstrate that the optimal investment strategy can be derived through variational inequalities in the risk-free case and by solving a forward-backward stochastic differential equation (FBSDE) in the risk-based case. Additionally, we provide numerical simulations for the relative wealth utility under the stochastic factor model. Our findings indicate that as the elasticity parameter approaches zero, the attitude toward risk becomes more conservative, resulting in a higher allocation to safe assets. Conversely, as relative risk aversion increases, the investor becomes more cautious, further boosting investment in risk-free assets. These results align with established economic principles. Furthermore, we observe that the utility of relative wealth exhibits greater sensitivity to the elasticity parameter than to the level of relative risk aversion. The paper concludes with several remarks and directions for future research. Finally, it is noted that the proposed utility framework extends beyond the Constant Elasticity of Inter-temporal Substitution (CEIS) model commonly associated with power utility. Specifically, while the dual utility function for power utility under the Merton model exhibits power-type properties, the dual function derived in this paper displays characteristics of a piecewise power function. This suggests that the relative wealth utility framework developed herein may hold significant potential for application in behavioral finance. **Keywords:** Portfolio optimization, Power utility, Relative wealth, Risk-free, Risk-based, Style premium, Variational inequality, Forward-backward SDE, Behavioral finance. **MSC2020:** 91G10, 91G80, 49N15, 91G17. **Authors:** Y. We introduce a novel framework for the co-evolution of galaxies and their surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM), investigating how galactic properties influence the IGM. This model integrates a galaxy population synthesis algorithm with a multi-phase, multi-component intergalactic gas algorithm, uniquely incorporating a feedback loop where galactic feedback regulates the IGM. By utilizing a bottom-up assembly approach for galaxies and top-down fragmentation for intergalactic gas, we examine how feedback mechanisms from galaxies of varying sizes and types—such as dwarfs, spirals, and ellipticals—affect the IGM across different redshifts. Our results indicate that the feedback from diminutive galaxies is predominantly non-thermal, driving gas into the IGM at moderate temperatures and generating supersonic turbulence. This process creates intricate filamentary structures that scatter gas throughout the intergalactic space. Consequently, this non-thermal feedback from small galaxies plays a crucial role in populating the IGM with matter at moderate temperatures, thereby suppressing star formation in nearby galaxies. We conclude that these IGM reservoirs, filled with matter at moderate temperatures due to small galaxy feedback, serve as a primary source for galactic accretion. This mechanism is vital for understanding the formation of both massive and low-mass galaxies, particularly in the local universe. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these IGM reservoirs are not homogeneous; they exhibit a multi-phase structure where non-thermal processes induce supersonic turbulence, leading to the formation of cold clouds. This provides a physical basis for the cold gas observed in the halos of galaxies. Finally, we show that this multi-phase structure in the IGM can be detected via absorption line observations, offering a means to probe the impact of galactic feedback on the IGM. Overall, this study underscores the significance of the IGM reservoir surrounding galaxies in galactic evolution and provides a pathway to observe and quantify the effects of galactic feedback on the IGM. These findings have profound implications for understanding the evolution of galaxies and the universe. To facilitate future research, we have made the model's source code publicly available. This study theoretically examines the stability of fermionic quasiparticles within strongly correlated systems using a minimal $\sigma$-$q$ Hubbard model featuring two sites strongly connected by a bridge. Through both analytical derivations and numerical methods, it is demonstrated that the local integration of a bosonic degree of freedom results in the complete destruction of the fermionic quasiparticle. This collapse occurs because time-reversal symmetry breaking induces a finite bosonic field on one site, generating a mass gap for the fermionic quasiparticle. Consequently, the stability of fermionic quasiparticles is contingent upon both the quasiparticle-boson coupling strength and the magnitude of the bosonic self-energy. These findings underscore the critical role of the self-energy in governing quasiparticle stability and offer a potential explanation for the unresolved mystery regarding the disappearance of the Kondo resonance in two-probe Kondo systems. Furthermore, the mechanism behind the suppression of quasiparticle coherence in this context is clarified by the non-local character of the bosonic field. Finally, the implications of these findings for the Kondo effect are briefly explored. Finally, it is worth noting that the findings of this work can be readily applied to other minimal models, such as the $\sigma$-Dirac and $\sigma$-Hubbard models. This paper investigates the divergence behavior of the generalized Thompson groups $A_n$ for $n \geq 1$ and the braided-Thompson groups $B_n$ for $n \geq 2$. It is established that both $A_1$ and $B_2$ exhibit linear divergence, confirming earlier findings by A. Olshanskii and D. Osin. Furthermore, $A_n$ groups for $n \geq 1$ display superlinear divergence, while $B_n$ groups for $n \geq 2$ are shown to have exponential divergence. These results provide significant insights into the large-scale geometric properties of generalized and braided-Thompson groups. The proofs rely on $n$-dimensional cell complexes constructed using $n$-dimensional rectangles and incorporate techniques from model theory. Specifically, ultra-products of groups with linear divergence and a finitely generated subgroup possessing a non-trivial center are demonstrated to possess superlinear divergence. This approach utilizes the well-known embedding of $A_1$ into the ultra-product of $A_n$ to establish the divergence properties of $B_n$ groups. Recent years have seen significant advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to the emergence of the Question Answering (QA) task. However, traditional closed-book LLMs often struggle with factual accuracy, prompting the development of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework. This approach combines an external knowledge retrieval mechanism with an LLM to enhance factual precision. Nevertheless, current RAG methods typically focus on open-domain QA, failing to effectively address the more complex task of Inquiry-Response (IR). IR demands not only factual accuracy but also logical reasoning, information screening, and structured output organization. To meet these challenges, this paper proposes a multi-stage framework that integrates LLMs with knowledge retrieval systems to solve IR problems. Specifically, we integrate a dense retrieval module from Dual Encoder (DPR) into the retrieval stage and a generative LLM into the answer generation stage. Furthermore, we apply self-consistency to the generation process, selecting the most frequent answer from multiple samples to ensure the output is well-organized and easy to understand. Extensive experiments across IR datasets confirm the effectiveness of this approach. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the CoIR and CoSQA datasets and attains competitive performance on the COTIR dataset. This paper presents a detailed analysis of 3,000 crowdsourced Wikipedia summarization tasks conducted on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) over three weeks. We investigate the characteristics of workers capable of producing high-quality outputs and identify the specific factors enabling their success. Our findings indicate that the skill required to perform effectively on Wtourk is rare among general MTurk workers, necessitating extensive screening to identify even a single competent individual. Consequently, we propose four practical strategies for researchers aiming to minimize the time and effort needed to locate at least one qualified worker. These approaches offer valuable guidance for other researchers seeking to recruit qualified personnel for the generic summarization task on MTurk. By adopting these methods, the cost of finding at least one qualified worker can be reduced to under 100 hours and 10,000 crowdsourcing requests. Video retrieval tasks, such as text-to-clip search, present a significant challenge due to the disparity between concise textual tokens and complex video temporal structures. To address this, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection (TS2) network for text clip retrieval. First, we employ a Transformer architecture to generate dynamic temporal structures for each clip. Second, we implement a token shift mechanism that leverages these temporal structures to rearrange text tokens, thereby enhancing the alignment between language and video content. Third, we develop a self-paced selection strategy to filter out redundant tokens and boost model performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both zero-shot and learned rank metrics on the CaptionHQ and MSRVTT-Caps datasets. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that our model generalizes effectively to image captioning and rolling text recognition tasks. Heterogeneous networks, characterized by their low density, are defined by the dominance of strong ties amidst a background of weak ones. To analyze these structures, we introduce a pair of stochastic blockmodels that incorporate both uniform and preferential attachment processes. In these models, nodes within the same community are more likely to establish connections when given a preference to attach to similar neighbors. We derive the corresponding hybrid random graph frameworks for both the degree-preserving and erdos-renyi preferential attachment cases. Furthermore, we investigate the degree distribution, clustering coefficients, and the emergence of low-degree giant components across all variants. Finally, we demonstrate that the preference factor can be interpreted as the difference between the probability of nodes in the same community connecting and the probability of such connections occurring in a homogeneous network. This interpretation holds in the large-degree limit for the erdos-renyi preferential attachment model but is less intuitive for the degree-preserving model. Additionally, we observe that the clustering coefficient in the degree-preserving model is primarily influenced by the degree distribution rather than the preference factor. To our knowledge, no existing literature addresses the characterization of heterogeneous networks that include a preferential connection mechanism. Our proposed hybrid models offer a valuable tool for understanding the network properties resulting from such mechanisms. Specifically, the uniform preferential attachment mechanism serves as a natural extension to degree-preserving preferential attachment models, while the erdos-renyi preferential attachment mechanism provides an alternative perspective to constant and exponential preferential attachment. The latter is particularly relevant for modeling networks with a significant population of low-degree nodes. Our methodology for analyzing heterogeneous networks is also applicable to other scenarios. Notably, we show that the analysis for a degree-preserving preferential connection mechanism is equivalent to treating the scenario as a uniform preferential connection case with homogeneous communities. This finding is significant because it allows us to leverage the more intuitive erdos-renyi preferential attachment mechanism as a means to understand preferential connection behaviors. Furthermore, our findings align with empirical evidence regarding the prevalence of low-degree nodes in real-world networks. For instance, a study by Newman and Barabasi on the human protein interaction network notes that while high-degree nodes are responsible for the network's clustering, the majority of proteins remain low-degree. Similarly, another study by the same authors on social networks indicates that the network's clustering arises from high-degree individuals, whereas most individuals are low-degree. These empirical observations underscore the necessity of analyzing heterogeneous networks with a focus on their low-degree components. Our work addresses this by providing a comprehensive analysis of low-degree properties

Multimedia content, including images and video, is frequently distributed across various media and discussed on social media platforms. These materials often contain sections irrelevant to the narrative, such as backgrounds, and can be distorted or manipulated to mislead viewers. To address this, it is essential to detect and classify the types of disturbances present in media files. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify and segment wireless disturbances within multi-label wireless capture tasks. The proposed approach utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to learn the spatial patterns of these disturbances. By employing a one-hot encoding scheme as the target label for CNN training, the system learns to extract spatial features specific to each disturbance type. This enables the model to not only detect the presence of multiple disturbance instances within media files but also to accurately estimate their locations. Experimental results on a specialized wireless disturbance dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a mean Average Precision of 0.71, surpassing existing techniques by 11.5%. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234567890/Wireless-Disturbance-Segmentation. This study examines the proton's polarized structure function, $d\sigma/dx_{bj}dy dy_p d\phi\propto\sqrt{s}\sin\phi F_{\rm pol}$, within the framework of Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS). We demonstrate that measuring this proton polarization offers a sensitive method for extracting the proton's polarized parton distribution function, $g_{1p}(x_{bj})$. Notably, the DVCS contribution to this observable exhibits a unique characteristic: it vanishes at the limit $y=y_p=0$. This distinctive feature allows for a direct and unambiguous separation of the DVCS signal from the Bethe-Heitler background, which is a critical advancement for future experiments. We further illustrate that the sign of the proton's polarized structure function $g_{1p}(x_{bj})$ is expected to invert at $x_{bj}\approx 0.3$, a finding that aligns with recent analyses of JLab Hall B data. Additionally, we explore the potential to measure the proton's transverse spin polarization, $d\sigma/dx_{bj}dy dy_p d\phi_{l}d\phi_{h}\propto\sin(\phi_{l}-\phi_{h})\Sigma\mathcal{A}_{TT}$, in the helicity frame, where $\mathcal{A}_{TT}$ depends on the transverse generalized form factors $H^{T}(t)$ and $\bar{E}^{T}(t)$. Our analysis indicates that $H^{T}(t)$ is likely negative, whereas $\bar{E}^{T}(t)$ is positive. These results are directly applicable to experiments at the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV, HERA, and the Electron-Ion Collider. We also address the challenges associated with determining the polarization of the final-state proton. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the 3D structure of the proton. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a central focus of the last half-century, driven by the goal of replicating human cognitive capabilities. However, the fundamental premise of this pursuit remains unexamined: the specific human mental functions that are actually relevant to AI development. This paper proposes a new theoretical framework grounded in a reinterpretable set of human cognitive skills. We argue that the traditional AI goal is fundamentally flawed and propose an alternative vision where the primary objective is to investigate and model the specific human cognitive abilities that can be enhanced or multiplied through interaction with AI systems. Consequently, we introduce the concept of Enhanced AI (EAI), which represents a paradigm shift in how we approach the design and deployment of intelligent machines. This foundational change necessitates a reevaluation of current AI practices and a redirection of research and development efforts toward the principles of EAI. To illustrate this framework, we analyze various human-AI interaction scenarios and outline the computational challenges needed to operationalize enhanced intelligence. Ultimately, we believe Enhanced AI offers a vital new perspective that will reshape the future trajectory of the field. A detailed proposal for this work is available at https://enhanced-ai.org. We present a theoretical framework for calculating the thermal modification of the superfluid transition temperature in correlated bosons within an optical lattice, specifically under a periodic Floquet modulation. This modulation effectively lowers the barrier for particle hopping. Our analysis addresses a two-band model representing cold atoms in a lattice, where Floquet modulation induces resonant coupling between these bands. This multi-band scenario generates an effective spin-orbit coupling linking the pseudo-spin (band pseudo-spin) and hyper-spin (spin projection). This setup simulates the experiment by Wu et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213401 (2019)], which observed that Floquet modulation increases the superfluid transition temperature. Our findings indicate that the thermal shift in the transition temperature can be either positive or negative, depending on the spin-orbit coupling strength, chemical potential, and modulation intensity. Furthermore, at a constant modulation intensity, the thermal shift exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the hyperfine interaction strength, a phenomenon we attribute to the emergence of a Mott insulator in one of the bands. Our results provide a valuable theoretical basis for interpreting the thermal behavior of the superfluid transition in spin-orbit-coupled, correlated bosons within an optical lattice. Additionally, this work offers a pathway to investigate the thermodynamics of solid-state systems with spin-orbit coupling using cold-atom systems. Finally, we discuss the potential to probe the topological phase of a Chern insulator in a Floquet-modulated, driven cold-atom system. We investigate a graph family defined by cosets within finite abelian groups. Our analysis focuses on determining the parameters of random $r$-regular graphs belonging to this family, specifically exploring coset structures in the symmetric group. Furthermore, examining the action of the automorphism group of these graphs leads us to identify their connected components, highlighting several notable examples. Finally, examining extreme cases of type 1 graphs in this family reveals two significant instances: the coloring of graphs formed by the union of two cliques, and graph degeneracy. Additionally, we present two notable results: first, that random graphs in this family are asymptotically almost surely disconnected, and second, that for every abelian group $G$, there exist two cliques whose vertex sets form a $2$-degenerate graph. These findings and their associated proofs contribute to the broader field of algebraic combinatorics, with applications in computer science. This work is presented in the language of group theory. Our approach involves analyzing the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix for graphs in this family, deriving formulas for these eigenvalues based on character theory, and examining the group actions inherent in the problem. Consequently, we believe this paper offers a valuable introduction to algebraic combinatorics for students of group theory. We hope this research encourages others to explore this fascinating area. A primary challenge in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate kernels that reflect the underlying characteristics of the data. While the statistical properties of data are typically unknown a priori, this paper proposes a method for deriving GP kernels based on fundamental mathematical expressions. We demonstrate that common kernels, such as the white noise kernel, can be understood as solutions to one-dimensional boundary value problems. This perspective is extended to multi-dimensional anisotropic kernels, offering a framework for generalization. These derived kernels are particularly well-suited for regression tasks involving functions with limited smoothness. Numerical simulations indicate that these multi-dimensional kernels are computationally efficient for large-scale applications and offer superior fitting accuracy for white noise regression compared to the exponentially decaying kernel. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of their information capacity regarding function derivatives and propose an information-theoretic approach for parameter selection when the GP model is placed over a finite domain. Finally, we apply these kernels to a real-world dataset, demonstrating their effectiveness in processing noisy data with an irregular grid. Overall, this work establishes a pathway for creating GP kernels grounded in mathematical expressions, providing a framework for future research into GP applications. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbharath/gp_kernels_from_mathematical_expressions. Additional details regarding this research can be found at https://ashwinbharath.github.io/limited_smoothness_gp/. The first author's website is located at https://ashwinbharath.github.io/. The corresponding author is https://www.sathyabhama.gov.in/DrSVenkataramana/index.php. The paper's title is Limited Smoothness Gaussian Processes from Boundary Value Problems. The authors are Ashwin Bharath from the University of Oxford, S. V. Venkataramana from Anna University, and Satheeshkumar Suresh from the University of Oxford. The abstract explores the link between GP kernels and ordinary differential equations, showing that solutions to specific initial and boundary value problems yield kernels applicable to noisy regression with limited data and low smoothness. These kernels offer interpretability through their connection to boundary value problems and possess an implicit length scale for parameter selection. Additionally, the authors examine the information content within the resulting GP models. The computational efficiency of these proposed kernels was evaluated using various datasets, including the Boston housing dataset, showing performance comparable to or better than existing kernels like RBF, Matern, and White Noise. A muon collider is a proposed facility that could investigate physics beyond the Standard Model up to the tens of TeV scale. However, constructing such a collider presents significant challenges, particularly regarding beam-induced noise. This noise manifests in three primary forms: beam loss activation, bubble formation within the accelerator cavity, and spallation on the collider's hardware. These effects are exacerbated by the high intensity required by muon beams, which decay rapidly. Consequently, substantial research and development are necessary to implement effective mitigation strategies, thereby establishing the feasibility of a muon collider. This review examines existing approaches to controlling beam-induced emittance growth and other major sources of beam loss activation. Additionally, it addresses the challenge of beam loss mitigation in accelerators, where the short muon lifetime necessitates lower loss thresholds compared to other particle accelerators. The review also explores methods for reducing cavity bubble formation and its impacts, as well as minimizing spallation-induced emittance growth. Finally, the report identifies potential areas for future research. The analysis draws upon various collider designs, including the linear and circular configurations proposed in the Muon Collider Design Study. While the discussion is not exhaustive, it aims to highlight key issues and opportunities that will advance the field of muon collider design. A companion paper, to be published alongside this one, will compile the associated references. These efforts underscore the critical need for mitigation techniques to ensure the success of a future muon collider. Furthermore, the strategies discussed may prove applicable to other particle accelerators, such as the muon collider component of the Future Circular Collider. The review is structured into the following sections: Section 2 covers beam loss mitigation, with a focus on the algorithms and techniques that form the core of this work; Section 3 addresses beam loss mitigation in the accelerator, emphasizing the unique constraints imposed by the muon's short lifetime; Section 4 discusses beam loss mitigation strategies specifically for the collider; Section 5 presents a summary and conclusions; and Section 6 offers an overview of future research directions. References [1]-[100] support this review. The remaining sections provide an overview of beam loss characteristics and their consequences. The discussion begins with an introduction to beam loss phenomena, their origins, and the methods used to mitigate them. It is important to note that while emittance growth is a significant concern, other aspects of beam loss mitigation are equally crucial. We introduce Spartan, a framework that integrates sparsity regularization into optimal transport (OT) to create models with group sparsity. OT is a well-established technique for quantifying distributional differences, which can be utilized in a minimax game to separate distinct distributions via their difference in average predicted outputs. Spartan extends this approach by applying group-wise sparsity regularization to the transporter, thereby restricting the transporter to zero-based outputs for a selection of groups. This constraint effectively reduces the number of source tokens the transporter can assign to any specific target group. Empirical results demonstrate that Spartan surpasses current state-of-the-art sparse models, such as SparseAutoencoder and GroupLasso, in the sparse classification task of Digits2ZeroC. Furthermore, Spartan successfully generates sparsity in Large Language Models without compromising their generative capabilities. The Pauli principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, dictating that fermions cannot occupy the same state, a constraint that generates unique many-body behaviors. In contrast, fermionization—the emergence of Pauli-like obstructions in systems composed of bosons or superpositions of both—is a less common phenomenon. This work demonstrates within the framework of quantum hydrodynamics that weakly interacting Bose fluids naturally give rise to such obstructions. These effects become prominent when a large number of fluid particles coordinate to maintain weak interactions. Many-body phenomena driven by this emergence include Pauli repulsion, correlated oscillations, and the formation of standing waves. Notably, standing waves of significant amplitude can arise from the constructive interference of external driving forces. Our findings offer fundamental insights into weakly interacting Bose gases and suggest new avenues for observing emergent Pauli obstructions in weakly coupled systems of light particles. Specifically, we propose that standing waves in superfluid $^4$He can be interpreted through Pauli obstructions, thereby enabling the observation of these effects in $^4$He and opening the door to realizing them in other Bose fluids. Finally, our methodology establishes a foundation for engineering systems where Pauli obstructions in bosonic fluids play a critical functional role. As a preliminary example, we illustrate how these obstructions can regulate the structural integrity of Bose fluid jets. This mechanism holds potential for developing novel Bose-fluidic devices that leverage Pauli obstructions to control the structural stability of the fluid. Additionally, this approach represents a promising pathway for weakly interacting Bose fluids to function as energy barriers. These insights are essential for advancing the field of Bose-fluidics and may find applications in areas such as shock wave mitigation and microfluidic flow control. Furthermore, the proposed methodology can inform the design of new Bose-fluidic technologies. For instance, it may guide the development of microfluidic systems that utilize standing waves to manipulate fluid flow, thereby enabling the creation of advanced Bose-fluidic devices. Finally, our research provides a framework for investigating the fundamental properties of weakly interacting Bose fluids, with the goal of uncovering new phenomena driven by emergent Pauli obstructions. This could lead to a deeper understanding of weakly interacting Bose fluids and facilitate the discovery of further emergent effects. Finally, the work establishes a foundation for exploring the connection between emergent Pauli obstructions and Bose-Einstein condensation in weakly interacting Bose fluids. Software testing is frequently perceived as a time-intensive endeavor, often leading developers to resist or resist adopting the practice within their teams. This study investigates the perceived severity of test-related odors among software professionals. Through an online survey of 110 participants, we examined their attitudes toward these odors, their perceptions of the risks associated with ignoring them, and their views on how such odors impact software quality. The collected data was analyzed using both statistical methods and qualitative approaches to derive these insights. The survey results provide a comprehensive understanding of how a "test odor-free" environment is valued by the industry, revealing that the majority of respondents consider these odors serious. These findings can inform strategies to promote testing practices by highlighting the potential consequences of test odors. Furthermore, the insights into how industry practitioners perceive these odors may assist testing professionals in communicating more effectively with their teams about the significance of test odors. Finally, this research enhances our understanding of industry attitudes toward testing, thereby aiding in the development of more effective methods to encourage its adoption. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first of its kind. We anticipate that the findings will significantly advance our comprehension of how developers perceive testing. Additionally, we aim to facilitate a broader discussion within the industry regarding the seriousness of test odors, a topic that has not previously been explored empirically. Consequently, this research addresses a critical gap in current literature. Finally, we hope these results will assist software professionals in better communicating with their teams about the importance of test odors. We develop a novel sweeping procedure tailored for nonconvex sets of integro-differential functions. This approach facilitates the local minimization of such sets and enables the construction of a nonconvex analogue to the convex reconstruction technique. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our procedure resolves specific problems stemming from mathematical physics, including the minimization of the Dirichlet integral, the Sobolev integral, and the Caccioppoli perimeter. Additionally, we find that the procedure can address certain problems in image processing, such as edge detection, denoising, and image restoration. Numerical examples are provided to validate these applications. Notably, the algorithm is designed to be adaptable for both numerical and practical implementation. Implemented in MAPLE, it is accessible via a website for user access. The methodology is further extended in other research by the same authors. Specifically, reference [10] presents an analysis of the sweeping process on nonconvex sets of integrand functions and its application to the Minkowski sum of two sets of integro-differential nonconvex functions. Reference [11] investigates the asymptotic behavior of the proposed sweeping procedure for sets of integro-differential nonconvex functions that contain sets of affine functionals, with applications to the motion of a set of points under a set of hyperplanes. These related studies will be elaborated upon in future work. The theory of set-valued mappings and variational analysis serves as a foundational element for the sweeping procedure. We introduce {\tt KKMCee}, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron annihilation, capable of simulating the production of lepton and quark pairs alongside various photons, gluons, and electroweak bosons. Built upon the lepton collider-focused {\tt KKMC} framework, the {\tt EE} extension incorporates additional physics models, most notably those for Higgs boson production and decay. This capability is essential for precision measurements at colliders such as the International Linear Collider and the Circular Electron Positron Collider. The {\tt EE} module utilizes electroweak one-loop corrections and effective field theory-based contact interactions to calculate the differential cross section for Higgs production across a broad mass range. Furthermore, it covers a wide array of backgrounds, including multi-photon and multi-jet processes arising from EW boson or QCD backgrounds, as well as EW boson pair production. Finally, a set of decay chains enables the simulation of complete processes for various final states. We provide a user-friendly interface for the {\tt EE} extension and outline its primary capabilities and applications. Heart rate variability (HRV) serves as a critical indicator for diagnosing various conditions, including cardiac disease, diabetes, and stress. Consequently, accurately detecting vital signs via HRV analysis has become a significant area of research. This study introduces an inter-beat interval (IBI) assessment technique grounded in the Tiramisu framework, which leverages the parallelization capabilities of Tensor Processing Units (TPU). Additionally, because RNN models can be trained and deployed on cloud TPUs, this approach offers high computational efficiency and accessibility. Given its robust performance, the proposed method is well-suited for real-time, large-scale deployment. This paper introduces a new stochastic algorithm for Singular Value Factorization (SVF) of tensors. Designed to operate with an unrestricted count of passes, the method calculates singular values and factors using a predetermined set of indices. Each pass processes a specific index set, generating a singular value estimate from a weighted average of selected entries. The initial factor estimates are derived directly from these first-order singular value approximations. The algorithm supports two modes: one with a fixed number of passes and another unrestricted mode that terminates when all entries are utilized. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness in generating accurate singular value estimates, with the unrestricted pass variant proving particularly advantageous. The procedure is applicable to both symmetric and non-symmetric tensors. Additionally, the approach is robust against noise, though its performance in noisy environments requires further investigation. The proposed method is recommended for applications involving singular value estimation, dimensionality reduction, and data compression. A Python library implementing the method is available at https://github.com/abdullahkaya123/SingularValueFactorization. We investigate methods for modeling the temporal evolution of graphs, a critical task with extensive applications. Specifically, we introduce a framework for dimensionality reduction that captures both static and dynamic properties of a single graph and its successive states. We provide theoretical guarantees regarding the preservation of essential graph characteristics during the dimensionality reduction process and demonstrate how to achieve embedding distortion close to the optimal value efficiently. Our numerical experiments confirm that these theoretical findings are valid in practice. Furthermore, we highlight the significant advantages of our approach over competing methods by leveraging its capacity to exploit both distortion functions and the temporal ordering of graph changes. Finally, we illustrate how such embeddings can be utilized to recover sparse and low-rank structures within a sequence of evolving graphs. As an application, we apply our proposed algorithm to a real-world social network, revealing that it successfully identifies the core community and its members. Additionally, we show that the method can detect anomalous users who join the network at irregular intervals. To our knowledge, no existing algorithm is capable of simultaneously accomplishing these two objectives. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ehsan-rahimi/Temporal-Embedding. This work is based on our PhD thesis. Any inquiries are welcome. Thank you.

Building upon the research of Lin-Gu-Xiong and Xiong, which established the existence of at least one and potentially multiple smooth solutions, Xiong demonstrated that for dimensions $n \geq 4$, multiple solutions can exhibit a non-trivial blow-up pattern. Specifically, at any blow-up point $p$, the yamabe constant of the standard sphere serves as an upper limit. In this study, by adapting Xiong's variational approach, we demonstrate that for any target yamabe constant strictly less than that of the standard sphere, there exists a solution with the non-trivial blow-up property. This finding confirms a conjecture by Xiong. Furthermore, when considering the casewise conformal flat scenario, our result resolves Li's conjecture for dimensions $n \leq 6$. Additionally, we present a variational proof of Xiong's theorem for dimensions $4 \leq n \leq 6$. Finally, in the context of conformal flatness, we establish a sufficient condition for the existence of multiblow-up solutions. We conclude this work by presenting a sufficient condition under which all multiblow-up solutions possess at least one simple blow-up point. However, the possibility of preventing multiple blow-up points simultaneously remains an open question. Finally, the conclusion briefly addresses the case where the target yamabe constant equals that of the standard sphere. In this scenario, no C2-continuous solution exists; instead, we identify a weak solution that conforms to the multiblow-up property. This solution is derived using a concentration compactness framework, which provides a positive resolution to Ghimenti's question. The weak solution is obtained by modifying the concentration compactness argument. Specifically, we demonstrate that the relevant energy functional is weakly lower semi-continuous, thereby circumventing the need for a direct minimization argument. Instead, we construct a specific Palais-Smale sequence with a well-defined concentration compactness structure. By applying the weak lower semi-continuous property, we establish that this sequence converges to a multiblow-up solution. This approach also clarifies why Xiong was unable to prove the existence of a multiblow-up solution via a direct variational method. The success of Deep Learning is largely attributed to its capacity to automatically derive optimal feature representations from data. However, this representation learning process is inherently dependent on the quality of supplementary labels. In many scenarios, these optimal representations are not required; instead, sufficient representation learning can be achieved through standard labels alongside constraints such as clustering information, nearest neighbor relationships, or distance metrics. Drawing inspiration from information theory, we introduce a novel unsupervised deep feature learning algorithm termed FDRNN. This approach integrates a composite loss function consisting of a clustering term and a quantized information bottleneck constraint, effectively balancing cluster discovery with the preservation of information relative to the fuzzy 0-1 encoding of nearest neighbors. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this quantized information bottleneck constraint and the Sinkhorn distance between latent features and empirical cluster labels. By analyzing this relationship, we provide a new perspective on feature learning that unifies popular methods like Deep Clustering and Deep Embedded Metric Learning under a single framework. Experimental results on single and multi-label clustering tasks demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework. Additionally, on multi-label image recognition tasks, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing methods. This study employs a computational model to assess how mutual information sharing between the NHS COVID Trace app and regional tracing efforts, such as those in Scotland's, impacts the efficiency of both initiatives for both interventions in curbing COVID-19 transmission. We utilize an individual-based model grounded in network theory to simulate the flow of infections within a community. The model incorporates the configuration and dynamics of the COVID Trace app across England and one of its constituent nations (either Scotland or Wales), utilizing the latest available data on app adoption rates. Our findings indicate that when national and regional apps operate in isolation, the integration of a regional app significantly enhances its ability to identify and isolate cases. However, this advantage diminishes or vanishes when the regional and national systems operate in parallel and are not integrated. Consequently, for a national tracing intervention to succeed alongside a regional system, robust integration is essential. This could be achieved through the early unification of national and regional tracing efforts or by incorporating regional data into future tracing strategies. We conclude that achieving this integration requires a concerted effort from the UK government to ensure that the UK COVID Trace app, once implemented, is fully integrated with any regional system that adopts it independently. Additionally, we have made our model code accessible via GitHub. This study presents the results of applying the RAVE-Gaia-Data Release 2 (Gaia DR2) six-dimensional velocity space analysis to the open cluster Melotte 72. We identified 11 cluster members, with two previously known members and five new ones. The remaining four objects exhibit velocity differences from the cluster mean of less than 1 km/s in each dimension. We provide the members' coordinates, proper motions, and heliocentric radial velocities. Additionally, we estimate the cluster's age at $1.0 \pm 0.1$ Gyr and its galactic orbital parameters. We calculate the dynamical mass within the cluster's tidal radius to be $(1.0 \pm 0.1) \times 10^4 M_{\odot}$ and the mass-to-light ratio as $(1.0 \pm 0.1) M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we determine the cluster's galactic distance to be $1.0 \pm 0.1$ kpc and its galactic coordinates to be $(l, b) = (170.0 \pm 0.1, 17.0 \pm 0.1)$. We establish bounds on the average Betti numbers for Gaussian algebraic varieties that are either union or intersection of linear spaces in the sparse regime, specifically where the support sets are pairwise nearly disjoint. These varieties exhibit low average Betti numbers in this context. Our approach integrates combinatorial techniques, drawing on the Eulerian integral formula and sheaf-theoretic persistence modules, with probabilistic arguments. Furthermore, our established link between sheaf-theoretic persistence modules and Betti numbers extends to broader scenarios beyond the scope of this study. Finally, we demonstrate that these findings apply to random Gaussian polynomials defining sparse sparsity varieties, yielding low average Betti numbers as $\mathbb{Z}$-modules. This supports the hypothesis that such low Betti numbers also hold true in the real domain. The latter result stems from an analysis of the Betti numbers of random sparsity varieties using commutative algebra and combinatorial methods. Our main innovation lies in extending sparsity ideals, originally developed for the Boolean case, to arbitrary sparsity supports. Additionally, we derive new combinatorial identities that relate Betti numbers to hypergeometric functions. This work represents the first instance of applying the sparse domain method to intersection problems. Through this research, we identified several open questions in combinatorics, algebra, and probability theory that arise. Notably, our results regarding Gaussian sparsity varieties suggest a pathway for investigating the complex landscape of the Boolean $k$-XOR problem. Furthermore, the techniques employed here may hold significance for data analysis, given their capacity to characterize the topological features of random Gaussian data residing on sparsity varieties. Acquiring a suitable perspective is critical for many vision-driven robotics applications. When an image is inadequate, the robot must reorient itself to gather valid data. While current research predominantly addresses eye-to-world vision and task planning for free-flying robots, this paper concentrates on eye-in-hand vision within a constrained robotic arm system. We introduce a novel method for teaching robots how to identify and learn poses that yield desirable vision setups. This approach utilizes a single example image featuring the target object, eliminating the need for physical access to the teaching device or the definition of specific pose requirements. The method is naturally parallelized, allowing for rapid training of deep neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that the trained model can effectively adjust pose parameters to capture desirable images. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness in handling various desirable inputs and can generate images that satisfy user-defined criteria. Although trained in a specific view, the model demonstrates generalization across different views. Finally, we outline an implementation using a parameter generator based on an encoder-decoder architecture and validate the approach with real-world experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer123/teaching-eye-in-hand-camera-adjustment. This work represents an initial step toward teaching constrained robots to acquire images for task execution. A subsequent paper will explore techniques for learning task requirements from a single example image to guide the robot. Both studies share the underlying concept of utilizing a single example to establish a vision setup. Our approach differs from few-shot learning, which aims to identify unknown entities with limited examples; instead, we seek to discover poses that reveal the identity of known entities. We also distinguish ourselves from inverse graphics research, which typically involves learning complex generative models from data; we train a model on a single image. Additionally, our work diverges from interactive systems that determine optimal poses through human input, as we train the pose generator using just one image. Finally, unlike methods that plan poses based on human-specified criteria, we present a user-centric approach where the user defines criteria based on a single example image. The model then adjusts the robot's pose to capture images that best align with the user's preferences. Overall, our work advances the field of learning from demonstration by enabling robots to infer useful information from a single example. Furthermore, learning from a single example surpasss few-shot learning, as it removes the necessity for multiple examples and facilitates real-world deployment. This paper explores the treewidth of terrain graphs, defined as those formed by the union of a planar graph and a line. This structure is significant because it guarantees a triangulation that includes a facial cycle encompassing all vertices, a property that has driven various graph drawing techniques. We introduce a new class of vertex-dividers, which are vertex-star forests with a specific property: they can be embedded such that the divisioner and the diver share the same side of the plane. We demonstrate that for every terrain graph, there exists a vertex-divider that partitions the graph into subgraphs with a treewidth no greater than two plus one-third of the divisor's degree. This result yields a randomized algorithm capable of producing a triangulation of any terrain graph with a treewidth of at most five. Furthermore, we examine how to minimize the space required for these vertex-dividers. Our findings indicate that for any terrain graph, a triangle-free, minor-minimal vertex-divider with a treewidth of at most one can partition the graph into subgraphs with a treewidth of at most three. We also establish several upper and lower bounds regarding the attainable space efficiency of such dividers. Notably, we establish both an upper bound and a matching lower bound for the divisors generated by our algorithm. Additionally, we present a randomized algorithm to construct a vertex-divider for any terrain graph that partitions it into subgraphs with a treewidth of at most three. Our analysis suggests that the algorithm's performance is near-optimal, as this optimality aligns with the minor structure of the terrain graphs. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for graph drawing. We present a probabilistic Bayesian grouping framework designed to address the challenges of identifying communities within heterogeneous data, inferred networks, and systems containing observed networks of diverse types. The model's flexibility allows for directed graph analysis, the inclusion of node attributes, and weighting of observed networks based on reliability. By leveraging reference networks, it can assign weights to inferred nodes through data integration. Community detection is conducted without prior knowledge of how many communities exist or which nodes belong to them. The framework utilizes a Bayesian stochastic block model to define network types and probabilities, while community assignment is governed by a hierarchical grouping process. This approach calculates partition probabilities to derive inferred network weights and integrate multiple reference networks. Furthermore, the model supports community detection across networks of varying sizes and types, including cases where some nodes lack network information. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness on a large-scale, high-resolution directed graph derived from an integrated inferencesome that combines data from 14 different studies, alongside a smaller, multi-tissue dataset featuring mixed undirected and directed networks. Finally, we discuss applications in a type-specific context involving a large, high-resolution undirected graph built from an integrated YeastEP dataset comprising 11 studies. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a hybrid approach integrating data-driven and physics-based modeling, where an artificial neural network is trained using both measurement data and the equations governing the system. The resulting PINN serves as a viable alternative to traditional data-free physics-based models. However, when measurement data is available, PINNs rely on this data for both initial and boundary conditions, as well as for calibration. This study investigates the extent to which measurement data can be substituted with reliable estimates to minimize the impact of potential data errors. We propose a technique that evaluates the reliability of data versus physics-based models through an assessment of accumulated prediction errors. This method enables the quantification of a model's reliability and can be applied to any data-driven model. We validate this approach using a simple linear heat conduction problem. Finally, we outline how this methodology can be leveraged to design a novel, more robust PINN that is less dependent on data. This enhanced PINN is expected to be more robust and capable of providing more accurate solutions than conventional data-free physics-based models. This paper serves as a proof of concept for this proposed design. (This work is based on the first author's PhD thesis [1-3].) Atmospheric pollution serves as a critical driver of numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory conditions, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Consequently, researchers are increasingly focused on minimizing exposure by addressing at-home sources like cooking emissions and cigarette smoke. However, such exposure reduction often results in a phenomenon known as the "biological contamination effect," where individuals seek shelter within their homes. This paper presents an analysis of current atmospheric contamination models used in epidemiological studies, with a specific emphasis on geostatistics and artificial intelligence applications. Furthermore, the concept of indoor contamination is illustrated through a case study examining the biological contamination effect related to atmospheric air pollution. The study utilizes a statistical atmospheric model incorporating an indoor-outdoor exchange coefficient, calibrated via a mobile measurement campaign conducted in Turin, Italy. Finally, the paper explores the potential for future exposure assessment improvements by integrating mobile monitoring with satellite data. To achieve this, machine learning and deep learning techniques are proposed to enhance both the resolution and accuracy of atmospheric contamination modeling. A specific instance of this approach is demonstrated using data from the Sentinel-5P satellite. Finally, the potential impact of atmospheric exposure reduction on public health is examined through the lens of indoor air pollution contamination. Keywords: Atmospheric exposure, indoor air pollution, atmospheric contamination, exposure assessment, geostatistics, artificial intelligence, deep learning, mobile monitoring, Sentinel-5P.

We introduce a technique for detecting the Majorana peak, which leverages Ohmic dissipation. This dissipation is driven by thermal fluctuations in a high-impedance environment, causing tunneling electrons to experience an effective Ohmic bath. A critical component of this approach is the utilization of resistive electrodes; their finite two-terminal resistance generates the necessary high impedance. This method is applicable to systems hosting a single Majorana mode, including those with a second mode that is localized far away. Furthermore, this dissipation introduces an energy scale, $k_{B}T\sqrt{GL_{C}}$, where $G$ represents the conductance and $L_{C}$ is the critical temperature's characteristic length. When $GL_{C}\gg 1$, the resulting broadening of the Majorana peak is negligible. However, if $GL_{C}\ll 1$, the broadening is substantial, thereby distinguishing the Majorana peak from other peaks. This mechanism is relevant to various experimental setups, such as those involving a tunnel junction connected to a quantum dot, a superconductor, and a normal metal. Additionally, the dissipation-induced peak can be analyzed to determine the intrinsic lifetime of Majorana modes. Finally, we examine the relationship between this dissipation and the Landauer-Zener backscattering mechanism. Our approach is particularly pertinent to recent experiments involving a tunnel junction linked to a quantum dot, a superconductor, a Kerr resonator, and a microwave transmission line. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prominent low-energy peak reported in Ref. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 130501 (2021)] is caused by Ohmic dissipation. However, the implications of these varying set sizes remain unclear. This study addresses two key questions: first, how the structure of the action space influences the sample complexity of linear bandit algorithms; and second, how it affects the confidence intervals generated by these algorithms. To address the first question, we introduce a novel algorithm, \textit{CVOL}, which operates without prior knowledge of the number of actions. We establish a confidence-bound regret guarantee for \textit{CVOL} under conditions of varying action set sizes and demonstrate that our regret bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Turning to inference, we show that standard confidence intervals produced by \textit{CVOL} are suboptimal when the number of actions is small. To resolve this, we introduce a \textit{linear inference algorithm (LIA)} that leverages the geometric properties of the action space to construct statistically sound confidence intervals with a provably optimal convergence rate. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data confirm that \textit{LIA} achieves statistically significant improvements in confidence intervals compared to \textit{CVOL}. Additionally, it paves the way for future developments in decision support systems, particularly in critical domains such as healthcare and finance. Graph Neural Architectures (GNA) represent a distinct category of neural networks designed to learn on graphs by propagating messages between nodes and utilizing structural information. Their architecture allows for data contamination, where modifying inter-node connections can significantly impair model generalization. This study investigates the most effective strategies for such attacks, evaluating the influence of various factors including model size, specific graph topology, and the nature of the training data on the efficacy of these attacks. Our experimental results across diverse graphs and datasets indicate that: i) the model's size is a critical determinant of attack success, with larger models proving more vulnerable; ii) the specific graph topology employed during training exerts a substantial impact on susceptibility, particularly when training on heterogeneous graphs; and iii) even when the graph topology varies only during the evaluation phase, the attack can still inflict severe damage to model generalization. These insights offer a comprehensive perspective on the design choices essential for developing robust GNA-based models. Furthermore, we provide an open-source toolkit to facilitate future research in this domain, available at https://github.com/DeepGraphSecurity/GNA-Data-Contamination. Our findings underscore the necessity for a holistic design approach when constructing GNA models to ensure resilience against data contamination. This paper investigates the properties of minimal finite vertex sets $V^\star\subseteq V$ within infinite hypergraphs $\mathcal{G}=(V,E)$, where each set $V^\star$ induces a subhypergraph that is strictly super-edges, strictly 2 super-edges, or strongly super-edges. We present various characterization theorems and examine the characteristics of all finite minimal sets $V^\star$. Furthermore, we explore the existence of collection properties for these minimal vertex sets, demonstrating that the associated set-theoretic axioms—such as the Axiom of Choice—are necessary for certain statements. We also analyze the concept of selective vertices and their significance in determining collection properties. Finally, we offer applications of our findings to combinatorial optimization problems. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain discrete optimization problems, which involve selecting facilities, networks, or networks of networks, reduce to identifying the strictly super-edges, strictly 2 super-edges, or strongly super-edges induced by minimal vertex sets. We highlight that our approach offers a novel, exact, and efficient method for resolving these optimization challenges. Additionally, we discuss applications in the context of the Hahn-Banach theorem and prove the existence of a linear function possessing a specific characteristic. In this instance, we establish that the Axiom of Choice is required to guarantee the existence of a finite set $V^\star$ possessing a particular property. This specific problem is significantly more complex than the combinatorial optimization problems mentioned earlier. We conclude by outlining several open questions and directions for future research. Notably, we demonstrate that no super-edges, 2 super-edges, or strongly super-edges can be induced by minimal vertex sets. This indicates that certain combinatorial optimization problems, such as those related to network monitoring and network interdiction, require an exact and efficient algorithmic solution rather than a theoretical existence proof. We suggest that such an algorithm could be developed using the same approach employed for characterizing strictly super-edges, strictly 2 super-edges, and strongly super-edges. Ontologies serve as structured frameworks for knowledge, facilitating the organization and sharing of information. While general-purpose ontology editing tools support both individual and collaborative knowledge management, they often struggle to scale when managing vast collections of concepts and relations, as visualizing such volume quickly becomes overwhelming. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization system designed to handle large ontology projects with over 10,000 entities. It employs innovative layout algorithms to automatically arrange concepts and their relationships, delivering clear visual insights into the ontology's structure. Furthermore, the system provides interactive features for users to explore, navigate, and modify the ontology, including the ability to freeze specific entities during layout computation and to dynamically manage entity visibility. The paper details the automatic visualization technology, describes the user interface, and presents a case study that highlights OntoPlot's user-friendly design and robust, scalable visualization capabilities. We present a method to improve semi-supervised end-to-end speech transcription by training an end-to-end model across two speech databases featuring different noise conditions. To address a common issue in such systems, where excessive noise reduces the benefit of semi-supervised learning, we employ CycleGAN to learn a mapping from noisy speech to clean speech, subsequently training the end-to-end speech-to-text model using the generated synthetic data. Additionally, we explore various ways to incorporate a penalty term into the end-to-end loss function that enforces consistency between the original and synthesized noisy data. Experimental results demonstrate that our penalties enhance speech text recognition by 2-4 WER points compared to the case without them. Furthermore, these semi-supervised models with penalties yield a 2-4 WER point improvement over a baseline end-to-end model trained solely on clean speech. Finally, our penalties yield a 3 WER point improvement when applied to an enhanced end-to-end speech-to-text model that integrates acoustic and language priors. This approach achieves a 4 WER point improvement over the semi-supervised model without penalties and a 6 WER point improvement compared to the baseline end-to-end model trained exclusively on clean speech. This paper introduces a novel framework for deducing and utilizing new rules to enable self-governing robot navigation. Unlike traditional navigation, which depends on pre-defined environments and behaviors, our approach allows a robot to independently deduce and employ new rules for navigation. The study is supported by two case studies: one examining a robot's deduction of a new traffic rule to navigate a newly designed city, and another detailing how a robot generates and uses new traffic rules to navigate unfamiliar cities. The framework comprises two core components: an action theory deduction component and a plausibility inference component. The former deduces new rules based on current beliefs and goals, while the latter assesses the possibility of a rule being valid by integrating observations, sensorimotor capabilities, and the robustness of the original rule. Our evaluation demonstrates that this framework successfully deduces new traffic rules in both scenarios and effectively combines them with existing beliefs to guide the robot through both familiar and unfamiliar urban environments. Furthermore, we highlight that the proposed plausibility inference surpasses standard probabilistic inference by effectively incorporating domain-specific knowledge, such as sensorimotor data and theoretical knowledge. Finally, the paper outlines several potential extensions, including the deduction of multiple new rules, the inference of new rules across diverse domains, and the possibility of collaborative rule deduction by multiple robots. Keywords: active deduction, reasoning, learning, robot navigation.

Thermally induced particle migration in polar molecules under temperature gradients is a complex phenomenon. This study examines the contribution of internal flexibility in polar molecules to this effect, specifically looking at PCl$_3$ and SiCl$_4$. Our findings indicate that internal flexibility significantly influences both the sign and magnitude of the Soret coefficient. Specifically, the sign of the Soret coefficient can invert when transitioning from a rigid to a flexible molecule, and its magnitude can increase by up to two orders of magnitude. These results are corroborated by experimental data. We attribute these observations to the role of internal flexibility in altering the effective mass of polar molecules and facilitating charge separation, both of which impact thermophoretic motion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating an additional internal degree of freedom into the test particle model for thermophoresis allows for a precise prediction of the Soret coefficient across various concentration ranges. Finally, we propose that molecules exhibiting a reversible sign change in the Soret coefficient possess a substantial dipole moment and a low rotational barrier. These insights could guide the design of molecules with optimized thermophoretic properties for applications in microfluidic separation and separation by density. Recent studies in pedestrian re-identification (re-id) show that unsupervised domain adaptation is essential for enhancing cross-dataset performance. However, because most existing adaptations rely on learning exclusive discriminative features for mapping domains, they often result in excessive false positives. To address this, we introduce Box Reordering, a straightforward approach for unsupervised adaptation that significantly reduces false positives. Our core insight is that while attributes like clothing and posture vary within a single image, the spatial relationships between detected pedestrians and their bounding boxes remain constant across datasets. Consequently, these box coordinates serve as a robust attribute for pedestrian identification, allowing us to adaptically reorder boxes across datasets without needing to learn complex mappings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art re-id techniques on the Market1501 and CAMEL datasets. Human throwing is a complex skill requiring precise coordination across multiple joints and the efficient use of energy. Prior research indicates that errors in the swing phase, specifically the point of release, often result in significant reductions in distance. However, it remains uncertain whether these premature release errors also diminish accuracy. To address this, we introduced a precise modification to the Microsoft Kinect sensor, creating a novel input device called FauxThrow. This device enables individuals without throwing expertise to intentionally simulate proficient throwers by delaying the release point. Our study involved ten participants who performed both intentional and unintentional modifications of their throwing technique. The results demonstrated that FauxThrow significantly outperformed the baseline by increasing average distance by over 100% while maintaining comparable accuracy levels. Furthermore, our analysis of the throwing motion revealed that the primary distinction between the two conditions lies in the utilization of body energy. These findings offer critical insights into the coordinated actions required for effective throwing and introduce FauxThrow as a new, intuitive input mechanism that taps into users' latent physical capabilities. The source code for FauxThrow is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2017/FauxThrow. This paper outlines the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a web-based repository hosting an extensive collection of molecular binding energy data derived from quantum chemical calculations. Designed to serve the broader astrochemical community, BEAP offers a straightforward, single-interface method for accessing this information. The platform is built upon the Bead code, which generates binding energy distributions for small molecules across a wide array of grain surface sites. These calculated values are derived using various potential energy surfaces (PES), thereby accounting for variations among different theoretical models. Users can query BEAP to obtain material for numerous popular astrochemical kinetic and kinetic/thermalization (KT&T) models, including SAHA/MA, Leiden, UMIST, and NASA. Additionally, the platform supports specific applications such as astrochemical modeling, thermal desorption simulations, and experimental design. By offering access to a diverse range of binding energy distributions, BEAP facilitates a critical assessment of the reliability of astrochemical models that rely on molecular binding energy data. This includes enabling users to evaluate the impact of different PES and theoretical approximations on simulated outcomes. This capability is particularly valuable for modeling the formation of complex organic molecules (COMs) in star-forming regions, where molecules often exhibit a broad spectrum of binding energies. Consequently, BEAP provides a comprehensive approach to addressing the significant uncertainty regarding COM binding energies, a factor that has previously hindered progress in astrochemistry. This work details the BEAP platform and its underlying code, BEAD, and demonstrates its utility for assessing binding energy distributions. The platform is accessible online at http://www.chemistry.msu.be/BEAP. This study investigates a multiplicative stochastic model featuring a sample-related lower boundary, originally formulated by the author in 2009 for analyzing the annual growth of the global human population. Although the human population is inherently a multiplicative process, that earlier framework proved insufficient for recent decades due to its inability to account for the post-1960 slowdown in annual birth rates. To address this, the current paper introduces a more refined model where the lower bound reflects this recent deceleration. The validity of both the prior and new models is assessed by comparing model predictions with observed population data. Additionally, the work examines a specific property of the lower boundary that was previously overlooked in the 2009 analysis. These findings suggest that multiplicative models possessing sample-related lower limits are particularly effective for analyzing processes within a specific timeframe, where the dataset is large enough to capture initial slowdowns in growth rates. This approach is applicable to various fields, including economics, ecology, and evolutionary biology. To demonstrate the model's broader utility, two further examples are provided: one tracking the historical rise in global life expectancy and another describing the exponential increase in computer processing power over time. In each case, the model's lower bound accurately reflects the respective slowdowns in population growth, life expectancy increases, and computational capacity. Finally, the paper concludes with suggestions for future extensions of these models. This article serves as a sequel to the author's 2009 study, which is available as a PDF at http://www.barrymccaffrey.net/Population_Growth_2009.pdf. The current work can be accessed at http://www.barrym Caffrey.net/Bounds_on_Multiplicative_Processes_2020.pdf. The author thanks Dr. John Beatty for his valuable comments and suggestions. Additionally, the author acknowledges that the title should have been chosen more carefully, as it may inadvertently imply that all multiplicative stochastic models possess a sample-related lower bound at their initial stage, a claim that is not universally true. However, such models typically begin with an additive bound, which is appropriate for the early stages of a multiplicative process, particularly when the number of terms is small. In this context, "multiplicative" refers to a sequence of events occurring sequentially over time, where the outcome of each subsequent event depends on the product of all previous outcomes. For instance, in the human population example, the total count at the end of year $n$ is the product of the initial population and the annual growth rates

A primary hurdle in the emerging field of quantum advantage testing for shallow layers is efficiently comparing the "shadow" characteristics of unknown states or unitaries. We introduce a novel random projection technique that facilitates such comparisons, leveraging the "classical shadow" framework to estimate various metrics between layer parameters using minimal measurement data. By employing random Clifford circuits up to depth three, we enable the computation of shadow inner products, distances, and ratios. Furthermore, this projection method can identify non-invariant structures within a layer that remain invisible to standard invariants like Fierz norms or operator norms. Finally, we present a new metric for quantifying entanglement in bipartite states via these projections and report on experiments validating this metric against the H2-2Bench benchmark. Our findings demonstrate that shallow layers can be effectively differentiated, with a notable focus on bipartite entanglement estimation. These results offer valuable insights for the development of quantum advantage protocols in this domain. Additionally, all code required to generate our results is publicly accessible. Categorizing text is a fundamental task with broad applications, yet it remains vulnerable to adversarial attacks. To enhance resilience, we introduce Sibyl, a framework that leverages Sibyllic sampling to create a resilient classifier. This approach samples training instances based on their predicted probabilities from a base model, aiming to concentrate on difficult examples. We demonstrate that Sibyl sampling effectively identifies and prioritizes the most informative data for the resilient classifier. Furthermore, Sibyl sampling biases the resampler toward diverse instances, thereby reducing overfitting. By combining these methods, Sibyl significantly outperforms the base classifier on both trained and unseen attack distributions. Additionally, we show that Sibyl resiliently classifies out-of-distribution text, offering a promising direction for text classification in safety-critical domains. Meta-learning, or learning-to-learn, seeks to train models on a diverse set of tasks so they can quickly adapt to novel, unseen tasks. Although this field has seen significant advancements, it has largely overlooked a fundamental capability of humans: the ability to generalize across representations. This paper introduces an approach to demonstrating meta-learning with non-parametric linear models, where the underlying function is stored in task-specific parameters rather than shared weights. We apply this method to linearly depict human preferences in domain adaptation scenarios, utilizing data from online experiments involving participants selecting between movies. Our results indicate that these linear models, learned via meta-learning, achieve performance comparable to parametric models while requiring orders of magnitude fewer samples. Furthermore, we show that our models can depict unseen movies with greater consistency among human participants, suggesting they capture more robust representations of utility. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach can learn multiple distinct representations within a single model that are tailored to specific tasks. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance of meta-learning achieved with non-parametric models. We have made our implementation and data available at https://github.com/alexmaher/online_data/. The source code for replicating all experiments can be found at https://github.com/alexmaher/linear_meta_learning.
